9. Interview Questions
What is callbackFlow and when would you use it?
Basic⌄
callbackFlow is a Flow builder that creates a Channel internally, allowing you to bridge callback-based APIs (GPS, Bluetooth, WebSocket, Firebase) to the Kotlin Flow world. Callbacks call trySend(value) (non-suspending) to put values in the channel, and awaitClose { } handles cleanup when the flow is cancelled.
What is the purpose of awaitClose in callbackFlow?
Basic⌄
awaitClose { } does two things: (1) it keeps the callbackFlow alive — without it, the flow would complete immediately after the block, before any callbacks fire; (2) its lambda runs when the flow collector cancels, providing the cleanup hook to unregister the callback. Missing awaitClose causes both premature completion and listener leaks.
What does flowOn do and where does it apply?
Basic⌄
flowOn(dispatcher) changes the dispatcher for all operators upstream (above it in the chain). It does NOT affect the collector — the collector always runs on the coroutine that called collect(). It creates a coroutine boundary between the upstream and downstream sections, allowing them to run on different threads concurrently.
What are the 4 channel capacity types and when would you use each?
Intermediate⌄
Rendezvous (0): strict handshake — sender and receiver must be ready simultaneously. Good for controlled producer-consumer pairs. Buffered: N items queued; sender suspends when full. Good for bursty producers that outpace consumers temporarily. Conflated: 1-element buffer, overwrites; sender never suspends. Good for state updates where only the latest matters (sensor data, UI state). Unlimited: unbounded queue; sender never suspends. Use carefully — can OOM with fast producers.
Why can't you call emit() from a different coroutine inside flow { }?
Intermediate⌄
flow { } is a sequential cold flow builder — it enforces that emissions come from a single coroutine, preserving sequential guarantees. Calling emit() from a launched coroutine inside flow{} would violate this contract, potentially causing concurrent emission which is not safe for all collectors. The runtime throws "Flow invariant violated" to catch this. Use channelFlow { } for concurrent emissions.
What is the difference between buffer() and conflate() for backpressure?
Intermediate⌄
buffer(n) allows the producer to run ahead of the consumer by up to n items — both run concurrently with a queue between them. No items are lost; sender suspends when buffer is full. conflate() is a special case: the producer and consumer run concurrently, but intermediate values are dropped — the consumer only ever processes the most recent value. Use buffer() when you need all items (events, orders); use conflate() when only the latest matters (GPS updates, price ticks).
How do you bridge a Bluetooth LE scan callback to a Flow in Android?
Intermediate⌄
fun bleScanFlow(scanner: BluetoothLeScanner): Flow<ScanResult> = callbackFlow { val callback = object : ScanCallback() { override fun onScanResult(callbackType: Int, result: ScanResult) { trySend(result) } override fun onScanFailed(errorCode: Int) { close(BleScanException(errorCode)) } }; scanner.startScan(callback); awaitClose { scanner.stopScan(callback) } }. Key points: use trySend() (not send()), call close() on error, and always stopScan in awaitClose.
A GPS flow emitting 10 updates/second is connected to a route calculation that takes 500ms. What happens and how do you handle it?
Senior⌄
Without backpressure handling: the callbackFlow's internal channel buffers updates (default 64); once full, trySend() starts dropping updates silently. The route calculation falls further and further behind, processing stale GPS data. Fix: callbackFlow { ... }.conflate() — the producer runs at full speed but only the latest GPS update is processed by the route calculator. Since route calculation needs the current position, dropping intermediate positions is correct. Add .flowOn(Dispatchers.Default) to move the heavy calculation off Main.
Explain how flowOn creates a coroutine boundary and what happens to backpressure at that boundary.
Senior⌄
flowOn creates a Channel between the upstream (new coroutine on the specified dispatcher) and the downstream (existing collector coroutine). This channel acts as a buffer between the two. By default, the channel is buffered (64 items). If the upstream produces faster than the downstream consumes, the buffer fills and the upstream suspends. This is similar to calling .buffer(64).flowOn(dispatcher) explicitly. You can control the buffer size using buffer(n) placed before flowOn.
When would you use a raw Channel instead of Flow?
Senior⌄
Raw Channel is appropriate when: (1) you need bidirectional communication between exactly two coroutines (producer-consumer pair, not broadcast); (2) you need to close the channel explicitly from the producer side with a result or error; (3) you're implementing a work queue where multiple producers send to one consumer (fan-in pattern). In most Android code, Flow provides a better abstraction with operators, lifecycle support, and backpressure. Use Channels for internal coroutine-to-coroutine communication; expose Flow for the outside world.

6D — Sharing: stateIn & shareIn

stateIn() converts cold Flow to StateFlow. shareIn() to SharedFlow. SharingStarted strategies: Eagerly, Lazily, WhileSubscribed(5000). When to use each.

ID: 6D ⭐ Tier 1
🔍
1. Overview

The problem they solve

Repository functions typically return cold Flow<T>. If two collectors subscribe, the upstream (network/DB) runs twice. If a collector comes and goes, the network call restarts. stateIn and shareIn convert cold flows to hot flows, sharing one upstream execution among all collectors.

stateIn vs shareIn

  • stateIn() — converts to StateFlow; requires initial value; always has a current value; deduplicates; use for ViewModel UI state
  • shareIn() — converts to SharedFlow; configurable replay; no required initial value; use for shared event streams

SharingStarted strategies

  • Eagerly — starts immediately when scope starts; never stops
  • Lazily — starts when first subscriber appears; never stops after that
  • WhileSubscribed(stopTimeoutMillis) — starts on first subscriber; stops after the last subscriber leaves (with optional delay)
Senior Mental Model
WhileSubscribed(5000) is the production-grade default. The 5-second timeout means a configuration change (Activity rotation) won't cancel the upstream — the ViewModel survives rotation, and the new Activity subscribes within milliseconds. But navigating away and the upstream cancels after 5 seconds, saving battery and network resources.
⚙
2. stateIn()

Signature

fun <T> Flow<T>.stateIn(
    scope: CoroutineScope,       // where the shared coroutine lives
    started: SharingStarted,    // when to start/stop upstream
    initialValue: T              // value before first emission
): StateFlow<T>

Standard ViewModel pattern

class AccountViewModel(repo: AccountRepository) : ViewModel() {

    // Cold Flow from Room (re-queries on every collect without stateIn)
    val accountState: StateFlow<AccountUiState> =
        repo.getAccountFlow()    // cold Flow<Account> from Room
            .map { AccountUiState.Success(it) }
            .catch { emit(AccountUiState.Error(it)) }
            .stateIn(
                scope = viewModelScope,
                started = SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000),
                initialValue = AccountUiState.Loading
            )
    // Now: single shared Room subscription
    // Stops 5s after last subscriber (background navigation)
    // Multiple Compose collectors share one upstream query
}

stateIn with operators

// Complex transformation → stateIn at the end
val filteredProducts: StateFlow<List<Product>> =
    combine(repo.allProducts(), searchQuery, activeFilters) { products, q, f ->
        products.filter { it.matches(q, f) }
    }
    .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), emptyList())
📊
3. shareIn()

Signature

fun <T> Flow<T>.shareIn(
    scope: CoroutineScope,
    started: SharingStarted,
    replay: Int = 0       // how many values to replay to new subscribers
): SharedFlow<T>

Shared event stream

// Share one WebSocket connection among multiple ViewModels
class PriceRepository(private val socket: PriceSocket) {

    // SharedFlow: one socket, multiple subscribers
    val priceUpdates: SharedFlow<PriceUpdate> =
        socket.priceFlow()  // cold callbackFlow
            .shareIn(
                scope = repositoryScope,
                started = SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000),
                replay = 1    // new subscribers get latest price immediately
            )
}

// ProductViewModel and CartViewModel can both subscribe
// without opening separate WebSocket connections
🕑
4. SharingStarted Strategies
StrategyStarts whenStops whenUse case
EagerlyScope startsScope is cancelledMust-have data, app-level streams
LazilyFirst subscriberScope is cancelled (never pauses)Data needed once initialized, keep-alive
WhileSubscribed(0)First subscriberLast subscriber leaves (immediately)Pure resource efficiency
WhileSubscribed(5000)First subscriber5s after last subscriber leavesViewModel with config-change tolerance

WhileSubscribed(5000) — the standard

// Why 5000ms is the magic number:
// - Activity rotation: Activity A destroyed → B created in ~200ms
// - Process death threshold: system kills after several seconds
// - 5000ms safely bridges config changes without killing upstream
// - BUT: navigating away cleans up after 5s (saves battery)

// For critical financial data — may want shorter timeout:
.stateIn(scope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(1_000), Loading)

// For app-global auth state — use Eagerly:
.stateIn(appScope, SharingStarted.Eagerly, AuthState.Unknown)
🏭
5. Production Example

Banking: shared account data across multiple ViewModels

// Repository exposes cold Flow from Room
class AccountRepository(
    private val dao: AccountDao,
    private val api: AccountApi,
    private val scope: CoroutineScope  // inject app-level scope
) {
    // Shared: one DB subscription, multiple ViewModels
    val accountFlow: StateFlow<Account?> =
        dao.observeAccount()  // Room Flow — cold
            .stateIn(scope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), null)
}

// ViewModel transforms the shared flow for its screen
class DashboardViewModel(repo: AccountRepository) : ViewModel() {

    val dashState: StateFlow<DashboardState> =
        repo.accountFlow
            .filterNotNull()
            .map { account ->
                DashboardState(
                    balance = account.formatBalance(),
                    accountName = account.name
                )
            }
            .stateIn(
                viewModelScope,
                SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000),
                DashboardState.Loading
            )
}

// TransferViewModel also uses the same repo.accountFlow
// → No duplicate DB queries, both observe same Room cursor
class TransferViewModel(repo: AccountRepository) : ViewModel() {
    val senderAccount = repo.accountFlow
        .filterNotNull()
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), null)
}
⚠
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1 — Using Eagerly in ViewModel
SharingStarted.Eagerly in a ViewModel starts the upstream immediately and keeps it running forever in viewModelScope. If the ViewModel is created but the screen is never shown, the network/DB query still runs. Use WhileSubscribed(5000) instead — starts when the UI collects and stops when it leaves.
Pitfall 2 — stateIn without initial value in cold start
The initialValue in stateIn is what collectors get before the first upstream emission. If you pass a blank/empty value and the UI renders it, the user sees an empty flash before real data loads. Design your state to include a Loading sentinel: stateIn(scope, WhileSubscribed(5000), UiState.Loading).
Best Practice — stateIn in ViewModel, shareIn in Repository
Use stateIn in ViewModels (to expose UI state as StateFlow). Use shareIn in Repositories (to share one upstream data source — WebSocket, GPS — among multiple subscribers without creating duplicate connections).
Best Practice — WhileSubscribed timeout for config changes
The 5000ms timeout in WhileSubscribed(5000) is the standard for ViewModels. It bridges Android configuration changes (rotation, language change) which typically complete in under 1 second. For app-global state (auth, user session), use Eagerly on the application scope.
🎯
7. Interview Framework

30-second answer

"stateIn() converts a cold Flow to a StateFlow by starting a shared coroutine that collects the upstream and broadcasts to all subscribers. shareIn() converts to SharedFlow with configurable replay. The SharingStarted strategy WhileSubscribed(5000) is the standard — it starts on first subscriber and stops 5 seconds after the last subscriber leaves, bridging device rotations while saving resources when the screen is gone."

2-minute answer

"The problem stateIn and shareIn solve is the cold Flow duplication issue. Without them, if a ViewModel exposes a Flow from a Room DAO and three Compose components collect it, you get three separate database subscriptions. stateIn creates one shared collection coroutine that all subscribers observe — one DB connection regardless of subscriber count.

WhileSubscribed(5000) is carefully designed for Android's lifecycle. Device rotation destroys and recreates the Activity in under a second, so 5 seconds safely bridges the gap without stopping the upstream. But if the user navigates back, the 5-second timeout fires and the upstream stops, freeing the DB connection and stopping network polling.

Eagerly is for app-global state (authentication, user session) — you want it ready before any screen opens. In ViewModels, always use WhileSubscribed — never Eagerly (which would run the upstream even if the UI never subscribes)."

Must-mention points

1
stateIn → StateFlow; shareIn → SharedFlow; both share one upstream
2
WhileSubscribed(5000) — standard for ViewModels; bridges rotation
3
Eagerly = app-scope for auth/session; never in ViewModel
4
initialValue in stateIn — what collectors get before first emission
5
stateIn in ViewModel, shareIn in Repository for shared connections

Follow-up Q&A

Q: "What is the difference between stateIn and creating a MutableStateFlow manually?"

A: With a manual MutableStateFlow, you write the boilerplate: init { viewModelScope.launch { repo.flow().collect { _state.value = it } } } — a coroutine that forever collects and pushes values. stateIn does exactly this but as a one-liner, also handling the SharingStarted lifecycle policy. It's more readable and less error-prone.

Q: "When would you use shareIn with replay=1?"

A: When new subscribers should immediately get the latest value but you don't want the StateFlow semantics (initial value requirement, deduplication). Example: a shared WebSocket price feed where new subscribers should see the current price immediately, but you don't have a meaningful initial price before the first server message.

Senior insight

Senior Insight
In a banking app, put shareIn(appScope, WhileSubscribed(5000)) on the account balance Room flow in the Repository. DashboardViewModel, TransactionViewModel, and any widget that shows balance all subscribe to the same shared flow — one Room cursor open, one DB connection, consistent data. Without sharing, each ViewModel would open its own Room subscription, causing unnecessary DB load and potentially showing briefly inconsistent balances.
📋

stateIn pattern

flow.map { toUiState(it) }
  .catch { emit(Error(it)) }
  .stateIn(
    scope = viewModelScope,
    started = WhileSubscribed(5_000),
    initialValue = Loading
  )

shareIn pattern

coldFlow.shareIn(
  scope = repositoryScope,
  started = WhileSubscribed(5_000),
  replay = 1  // 0 for events, 1+ for state

SharingStarted guide

Eagerly          → app-global (auth)
Lazily           → keep-alive after start
WhileSubscribed  → ViewModel (default)
  (5000)         → safe for rotation

stateIn vs MutableStateFlow

// Manual (verbose)
init {
  launch { repo.flow().collect { _s.value=it }}
}

// stateIn (clean)
val s = repo.flow().stateIn(
  scope, WhileSubscribed(5000), Loading)

9. Interview Questions
What does stateIn() do?
Basic⌄
stateIn() converts a cold Flow into a hot StateFlow. It starts a shared coroutine in the given scope that collects the upstream Flow and broadcasts the latest value to all subscribers. The initialValue is returned to new subscribers before the first upstream emission. Multiple collectors share one upstream execution.
What is WhileSubscribed(5000) and why is 5000ms the standard value?
Basic⌄
WhileSubscribed(5000) starts the upstream when the first subscriber joins and stops it 5 seconds after the last subscriber leaves. The 5-second value is chosen to survive Android configuration changes (screen rotation destroys and recreates Activity in ~100–500ms). The upstream doesn't stop during rotation. When the user navigates away permanently, it stops after 5 seconds, freeing resources.
What is the difference between stateIn and shareIn?
Basic⌄
stateIn produces a StateFlow: requires an initial value, always has a current value, uses equals() deduplication, suitable for UI state. shareIn produces a SharedFlow: no initial value required, configurable replay (0 for events, 1+ for state), no deduplication. Use stateIn in ViewModels for UI state; use shareIn in Repositories for shared connections (WebSocket, GPS).
Why is SharingStarted.Eagerly dangerous in a ViewModel?
Intermediate⌄
Eagerly starts the upstream immediately when the scope starts (ViewModel init) and never stops until the scope is cancelled. This means network/DB calls start even if no collector ever subscribes — wasteful. It also means the upstream runs even when the app is in the background. Use WhileSubscribed to only run while the UI is active.
A ViewModel has a cold Room Flow. Three Compose composables all collect it. How many DB queries happen and how do you fix it?
Intermediate⌄
Three DB queries — each collector starts an independent Room subscription (cold Flow). Fix: convert to a hot flow with stateIn(viewModelScope, WhileSubscribed(5000), initialValue) in the ViewModel. Now there's one shared Room subscription, and all three Compose composables observe the same StateFlow. Result: one DB query regardless of subscriber count.
How is stateIn different from manually collecting a Flow into a MutableStateFlow?
Intermediate⌄
Functionally equivalent, but stateIn is a one-liner that handles: (1) the coroutine launching; (2) the SharingStarted lifecycle policy (WhileSubscribed stops the upstream when no subscribers — impossible to express concisely with manual approach); (3) cancellation and restart logic. Manual approach requires boilerplate in init {} and careful handling of stopping/restarting.
When would you use shareIn in a Repository instead of stateIn?
Intermediate⌄
Use shareIn in a Repository when you want to share an expensive upstream (WebSocket connection, Bluetooth GATT, GPS listener) among multiple ViewModels. shareIn with replay=1 means any new subscriber immediately gets the latest value without opening a new connection. Use stateIn in ViewModel for the UI-facing StateFlow (requires initial value, deduplication).
What happens to a stateIn(WhileSubscribed(5000)) flow when the user rotates the device?
Senior⌄
The Activity is destroyed (Compose unsubscribes) and recreated (Compose resubscribes), typically within 200–500ms. The 5000ms timeout means the upstream does NOT stop — it keeps running throughout. When the new Activity subscribes, it immediately gets the latest StateFlow value and the ongoing upstream. No data is lost, no network call is restarted. Without the 5000ms timeout (WhileSubscribed(0)), the upstream would stop on destroy and restart on the new Activity, causing a brief loading flash.
Design a Repository that shares a WebSocket price feed among multiple ViewModels with appropriate lifecycle management.
Senior⌄
class PriceRepository(socket: PriceSocket, scope: CoroutineScope) { val prices: SharedFlow<Map<String,Price>> = socket.priceFlow().scan(emptyMap()) { acc, update -> acc + (update.symbol to update) }.shareIn(scope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), replay=1) }. The scan accumulates the latest price per symbol. shareIn(WhileSubscribed(5000)) means the WebSocket connects when the first ViewModel subscribes and disconnects 5s after all ViewModels unsubscribe (navigation away). replay=1 ensures new ViewModels instantly get the latest price map without waiting for the next WebSocket message.
What is the difference between SharingStarted.Lazily and WhileSubscribed(Long.MAX_VALUE)?
Senior⌄
Functionally nearly identical in practice — both start on first subscriber and stop only when the scope is cancelled. The subtle difference: Lazily is a first-class API with clear semantics. WhileSubscribed(Long.MAX_VALUE) technically stops after MAX_VALUE milliseconds (after ~292 million years, so effectively never). In practice, use Lazily when you want "start on first subscriber, keep forever" semantics. Use Eagerly when you want to pre-warm before any subscriber. Use WhileSubscribed(5000) for the standard ViewModel use case.

7A — Compose Fundamentals

@Composable, declarative vs imperative UI, the Composition, recomposition mechanics, slot table, State<T>, remember, and the composable lifecycle.

ID: 7A ⭐ Tier 1 🔥 Highest Priority
🔍
1. Overview

Declarative vs Imperative UI

Imperative (View system): You mutate existing UI objects — find the TextView, call setText(). The view lives in memory, you issue commands to change it. You control HOW the view changes.

Declarative (Compose): You describe what the UI should look like for the current state. When state changes, Compose re-runs your function and figures out what changed. You control WHAT the UI should show, Compose handles HOW to update it.

Key concepts

  • @Composable — annotates a function that describes UI; can call other composables and read state
  • Composition — the in-memory tree of composable calls; the result of running all your @Composable functions
  • Recomposition — Compose re-runs composables when their inputs (state) change
  • Slot table — the data structure Compose uses to store composition state (remember values, positions)
  • State<T> — a value holder that triggers recomposition when its value changes
Senior Mental Model
In Compose, a function is not called once. It is called on every recomposition. Code inside a composable runs for every state change that affects it. This is fundamentally different from the View system. Everything that should NOT re-run on every frame must be wrapped in remember { } or moved outside the composable.
⚙
2. How Compose Works

The Composition tree

// This produces a tree in the Composition:
@Composable
fun ProductScreen(product: Product) {
    Column {            // node in tree
        ProductImage(product.imageUrl)    // child node
        ProductTitle(product.name)        // child node
        PriceTag(product.price)           // child node
    }
}
// Compose tracks each node's position using the slot table
// Position = call site in source code (not runtime object)

The Slot Table — how Compose tracks state

The slot table is a flat array of slots. Every composable call occupies a group of slots that store: the node identity, remember values, and position. When recomposition runs, Compose walks the slot table comparing old and new state at each position.

// The POSITION in the call tree is the identity
// Two calls at the same position are the SAME composable
for (item in items) {
    ItemCard(item)  // each has a position based on loop index
}
// If you insert an item at the beginning, ALL positions shift
// → Compose sees all cards as "changed"
// Fix: use key() to give stable identity
for (item in items) {
    key(item.id) { ItemCard(item) }  // stable identity by item.id
}

Composition lifecycle

PhaseDescription
Enter CompositionComposable called for the first time; remember initializers run; effects (LaunchedEffect) are launched
RecomposeState changed; composable re-runs with new inputs; unchanged composables skipped
Leave CompositionComposable removed from tree; remember values cleared; DisposableEffect cleanup runs
🔁
3. Recomposition

What triggers recomposition

Recomposition is triggered when a State<T> value that was read during a previous composition changes. Compose tracks every State read during composition — this is the "snapshot system."

@Composable
fun Counter() {
    var count by remember { mutableStateOf(0) }

    // Compose reads "count" here — this composable is subscribed
    Text(text = "Count: $count")     // re-runs when count changes
    Button(onClick = { count++ }) {   // lambda captures count
        Text("Increment")
    }
}
// When count++ fires: State changes → Compose schedules recomposition
// Only Counter() re-runs (not the whole screen)

Smart recomposition — skipping

@Composable
fun Parent() {
    var count by remember { mutableStateOf(0) }
    Column {
        CounterDisplay(count)    // ← reads count: WILL recompose
        StaticContent()         // ← reads nothing from count
    }
}

@Composable
fun StaticContent() {
    Text("I never change")
    // Compose: if inputs same as before → SKIP this composable
}
// StaticContent is NOT recomposed when count changes
// Compose checks all params — if equal, skips execution
📌
4. State<T> & remember

State<T> — the recomposition trigger

// Three equivalent ways to declare state:

// 1. State + by delegate (most common)
var isExpanded by remember { mutableStateOf(false) }
isExpanded = true   // direct assignment via delegate

// 2. Explicit State object
val expandedState: MutableState<Boolean> = remember { mutableStateOf(false) }
expandedState.value = true

// 3. Destructure (read only + setter separate)
val (expanded, setExpanded) = remember { mutableStateOf(false) }

remember — survival across recompositions

// remember: survives recomposition, does NOT survive Activity recreation
val items = remember { mutableListOf<String>() }
// Created once, stored in slot table, same object on every recomposition

// remember(key): re-creates when key changes
val formatter = remember(locale) {
    NumberFormat.getInstance(locale)  // re-create only if locale changes
}

// WITHOUT remember: object created on EVERY recomposition
val expensiveObj = ExpensiveObject()  // ❌ new instance per recomposition!
val expensiveObj = remember { ExpensiveObject() }  // ✅ created once
Key Rule
Any object creation that should NOT happen on every recomposition must be inside remember { }. This includes: list allocations, format objects, painters, gesture detectors, and any complex objects.
🏭
5. Production Example

E-commerce: product card with composition lifecycle

@Composable
fun ProductCard(
    product: Product,
    onAddToCart: () -> Unit   // event callback — hoisted
) {
    // Local UI state — survives recompositions but not process death
    var isExpanded by remember { mutableStateOf(false) }

    // Expensive object — created once, reused on recompositions
    val currencyFormat = remember(product.currency) {
        NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance(Locale.forLanguageTag(product.currency))
    }

    Card(onClick = { isExpanded = !isExpanded }) {
        Column {
            ProductImage(url = product.imageUrl)

            // This composable only recomposes if product.name changes
            Text(text = product.name, style = MaterialTheme.typography.titleMedium)
            Text(text = currencyFormat.format(product.price))

            // AnimatedVisibility: enters/leaves composition
            AnimatedVisibility(visible = isExpanded) {
                Text(text = product.description)
            }

            Button(onClick = onAddToCart) {
                Text("Add to Cart")
            }
        }
    }
}

// Screen-level: state hoisted to ViewModel
@Composable
fun ProductScreen(viewModel: ProductViewModel = hiltViewModel()) {
    val state by viewModel.uiState.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()

    when (val s = state) {
        is Loading -> LoadingSpinner()
        is Success -> ProductCard(s.product, onAddToCart = viewModel::addToCart)
        is Error -> ErrorMessage(s.message)
    }
}
⚠
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1 — Side effects in composable body
Composables can run multiple times. Writing to a database, logging analytics, or network calls in the composable body (not in a LaunchedEffect) will happen on every recomposition — potentially thousands of times. Side effects must always be in LaunchedEffect, DisposableEffect, or SideEffect.
Pitfall 2 — Creating objects without remember
Creating a new list, Painter, Animator, or any object directly in a composable body allocates a new object on every recomposition. Wrap with remember { } to create once and store in the slot table.
Pitfall 3 — Reading State outside of composable context
If you read a State<T> inside a lambda (like an onClick handler) without reading it in the composable body, the composable doesn't subscribe — it won't recompose when the state changes. Ensure state reads happen directly in the composable body.
Best Practice — Keep composables stateless
Composables should ideally be pure functions: same inputs → same output. Push state up to the ViewModel or calling composable. Stateless composables are easier to test, preview, and reuse.
🎯
7. Interview Framework

30-second answer

"Compose is a declarative UI framework. @Composable functions describe what the UI should look like for given state. When state changes, Compose re-runs affected composables — this is called recomposition. The slot table stores composition state including remember values. Compose skips composables whose inputs haven't changed — smart recomposition."

2-minute answer

"The fundamental shift is from imperative (mutate views) to declarative (describe what you want). In the View system, you call setText() on a TextView. In Compose, you call Text('currentValue') — when the value changes, the composable reruns automatically.

The Composition is the in-memory tree of composable calls. The slot table is the data structure backing it — a flat array where each composable call's position is its identity. This is why key() matters in lists — without stable keys, inserting an item shifts all positions, making Compose think every item changed.

State<T> is the trigger for recomposition. When you read a State value inside a composable, Compose subscribes that composable to the state. When the state changes, only the composables that read it are recomposed — not the whole tree. Everything that should survive recompositions but not re-execute must be in remember { }."

Must-mention points

1
Declarative: describe WHAT; Compose figures out HOW to update
2
Recomposition: triggered by State reads; only affected composables re-run
3
Slot table: position-based identity; why key() matters in lists
4
remember { }: survives recomposition; stores in slot table
5
No side effects in composable body: use LaunchedEffect/DisposableEffect

Follow-up Q&A

Q: "How does Compose know which composables to recompose?"

A: Compose uses a snapshot system. Every State read inside a composable registers the composable as an observer. When the state mutates, all registered observers are scheduled for recomposition. Compose then re-runs those composables and compares their output with the previous run — unchanged subtrees are skipped.

Q: "What is the slot table?"

A: The slot table is the data structure that stores the composition. It's a flat array of slots where each composable call occupies a group of slots containing: the composable's runtime state, remember values, position in the call hierarchy. The position in the source code (call site) is used as the composable's identity — not a runtime object reference like the View system uses.

Senior insight

Senior Insight
Understanding the slot table explains the Compose "if" gotcha: if (condition) { TextA() } else { TextB() } — depending on whether condition is true, a different composable occupies the same slot position. If condition flips, Compose sees a composable "leaving" and "entering" at that position — re-initializing all remember values. This is why conditional composables lose their state when the condition changes, and why you sometimes need key() around them.
📋
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Declarative UI

Imperative: find view → mutate it
Declarative: describe what to show
            → Compose handles update

Text(state.value)  // re-runs when value changes

State declaration

var x by remember { mutableStateOf(0) }
// by = delegate: read/write directly
// without by: state.value required

Composition lifecycle

1. Enter: first call, remember init
2. Recompose: state changed, re-run
3. Leave: removed, cleanup effects

remember rules

remember { }        // survives recompose
remember(key) { }   // re-init if key changes
rememberSaveable{}  // survives process death
❓
9. Interview Questions
What is the difference between declarative and imperative UI?
Basic⌄
Imperative UI: you manage view objects explicitly — find a TextView, call setText(), handle null checks, manage lifecycle. You describe HOW to change the UI. Declarative UI (Compose): you describe WHAT the UI should look like for a given state. When state changes, the framework re-runs your description and applies the diff. You don't touch existing views — you re-describe the desired output.
What triggers recomposition in Compose?
Basic⌄
Recomposition is triggered when a State<T> value that was read during the last composition changes. Compose tracks every State read inside a composable function — when any of those states change, the composable is scheduled for recomposition. Only composables that read the changed state are recomposed — not the entire UI tree.
What is remember and why do you need it?
Basic⌄
remember { } stores a value in the slot table so it persists across recompositions. Without it, the code inside runs on every recomposition — creating new objects, resetting state. Use remember for: mutableStateOf holders, expensive objects (formatters, painters), list instances. remember does NOT survive Activity recreation — use rememberSaveable for that.
What is the Composition and what is the slot table?
Intermediate⌄
The Composition is the in-memory representation of the UI — a tree built from composable function calls. The slot table is the data structure that backs it: a flat array where each composable call occupies slots storing its runtime state and remember values. The composable's identity in the slot table is its position in the call hierarchy (call site), not a runtime object reference.
How does Compose "skip" composables during recomposition?
Intermediate⌄
If all parameters of a composable are equal to their previous values (using equals()), Compose skips executing that composable entirely — its output is assumed unchanged. This is "smart recomposition." For a composable to be skippable, all its parameters must be stable types (primitives, String, data classes, @Stable annotated classes). Unstable types (like plain List<>) prevent skipping.
A composable creates a new List inside its body on every recomposition. Is this a problem and how do you fix it?
Intermediate⌄
Yes. Without remember, a new list is allocated on every recomposition — causing unnecessary GC pressure and potentially triggering further recompositions if the list is passed as a parameter (since new list instance != old list instance in equals()). Fix: val items = remember(key) { buildList { ... } }. If the list is derived from state, use remember(sourceData) { processData(sourceData) } — only recomputes when sourceData changes.
Why might a composable lose its state when a condition around it flips?
Intermediate⌄
Compose identifies composables by their position in the call tree (slot table). if (condition) ComponentA() else ComponentB() — both A and B occupy the same position. When condition flips, Compose sees the previous composable leaving and a new one entering at that position. The new composable's remember values start fresh — state is lost. Fix: use key(condition) { ComponentA() } or restructure so both branches are independent positions.
A developer calls an analytics tracking function directly in the composable body. What is wrong?
Senior⌄
Composables can recompose many times — every state change triggers re-execution. Calling analytics directly in the body would log the event on every recomposition, potentially hundreds of times. Additionally, composables may be run during previews, tests, or Compose internal optimizations (recomposition can be speculative). Side effects must be in LaunchedEffect or SideEffect: LaunchedEffect(Unit) { analytics.track("ScreenView") } — runs once when the composable enters composition.
Explain how the snapshot system works in Compose and how it enables fine-grained recomposition.
Senior⌄
Compose's snapshot system is a transactional state system. Every State value has a list of observers (composable scopes). During composition, reading a State registers the current composition scope as an observer. When you write to a State, it creates a new snapshot. The write is committed atomically — all observers are notified and scheduled for recomposition. This is how two different composables can read the same State and only both recompose when that specific state changes, while other composables that don't read it are untouched. The snapshot system also enables multi-thread safety for State mutations.
How does key() affect composable identity and recomposition in a LazyColumn?
Senior⌄
Without key: each item's identity is its index. Insert an item at position 0 → all items shift → Compose thinks every item changed → full recomposition of all items, all remember values reset. With key = { item.id }: each item's identity is its unique ID. Insert at 0 → only the new item is created, existing items keep their position (by key) → Compose skips recomposing unchanged items. This is critical for lists with animations — without keys, items appear to "jump" because all are treated as new.

7B — State Management

remember vs rememberSaveable, mutableStateOf, derivedStateOf. State hoisting, UDF (Unidirectional Data Flow). ViewModel as state holder. collectAsStateWithLifecycle. When to use local vs hoisted state.

ID: 7B ⭐ Tier 1
🔍
1. Overview

State types in Compose

  • remember { mutableStateOf(x) } — in-composition state; survives recomposition; lost on rotation/process death
  • rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf(x) } — persists through config changes and process death (via Bundle/SavedState)
  • ViewModel StateFlow → collectAsStateWithLifecycle() — screen-level business state; survives rotation
  • derivedStateOf { } — derived computation from other state; avoids over-recomposition

Unidirectional Data Flow (UDF)

State flows DOWN — from ViewModel → composable → child composable (as parameters). Events flow UP — from child composable → parent → ViewModel (as lambda callbacks). The ViewModel is the single source of truth.

Senior Mental Model
State hoisting = moving state up to the lowest common ancestor that needs it. The rule: hoist state to the highest level that needs to read or write it. Local toggle state (isExpanded) stays in the composable. Business data (user profile) belongs in ViewModel. Navigation state belongs in NavController / ViewModel.
⚙
2. remember vs rememberSaveable
// remember: composition lifetime only
var isExpanded by remember { mutableStateOf(false) }
// Survives: recomposition ✅
// Survives: configuration change (rotation) ❌ — resets to false
// Survives: process death ❌ — resets to false

// rememberSaveable: survives config changes + process death
var searchQuery by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf("") }
// Survives: recomposition ✅
// Survives: configuration change (rotation) ✅ — saved to Bundle
// Survives: process death ✅ — saved to SavedStateHandle

// Custom saver for non-primitive types
val scrollState = rememberSaveable(saver = ScrollState.Saver) {
    ScrollState(0)
}

// mapSaver for data classes
val userSaver = mapSaver(
    save = { mapOf("id" to it.id, "name" to it.name) },
    restore = { User(it["id"] as String, it["name"] as String) }
)
rememberrememberSaveableViewModel
Recomposition✅✅✅
Config change (rotation)❌✅✅
Process death❌✅ (Bundle limit)✅ (SavedStateHandle)
Complex data✅⚠️ Custom Saver needed✅ Unlimited
⚖
3. State Hoisting & UDF

Stateful vs Stateless composables

// ❌ Stateful — hard to test, can't be reused with different state
@Composable
fun SearchBar() {
    var query by remember { mutableStateOf("") }
    TextField(value = query, onValueChange = { query = it })
}

// ✅ Stateless — testable, reusable, follows UDF
@Composable
fun SearchBar(
    query: String,                   // state flows DOWN
    onQueryChange: (String) -> Unit   // event flows UP
) {
    TextField(value = query, onValueChange = onQueryChange)
}

// Caller holds the state:
@Composable
fun SearchScreen(viewModel: SearchViewModel = hiltViewModel()) {
    val query by viewModel.query.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    SearchBar(
        query = query,
        onQueryChange = viewModel::onQueryChange
    )
}

collectAsStateWithLifecycle vs collectAsState

// collectAsState: collects even when app is in background
val state by viewModel.state.collectAsState()  // ❌ runs in background

// collectAsStateWithLifecycle: stops collection in background
// Uses repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) semantics
val state by viewModel.state.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()  // ✅
📌
4. derivedStateOf

derivedStateOf { } creates a State that is derived from other State values. It only recomputes when the dependencies change — and only triggers recomposition when the derived result changes.

// WITHOUT derivedStateOf — recomputes filter on every recompose
@Composable
fun ProductList(products: List<Product>, minPrice: Float) {
    // This filters on EVERY recomposition — expensive
    val filtered = products.filter { it.price >= minPrice }
    LazyColumn { items(filtered) { ProductCard(it) } }
}

// WITH derivedStateOf — only recomputes when products or minPrice changes
@Composable
fun ProductList(products: List<Product>, minPrice: Float) {
    // derivedStateOf: runs only when dependencies change
    val filtered by remember(products, minPrice) {
        derivedStateOf { products.filter { it.price >= minPrice } }
    }
    LazyColumn { items(filtered) { ProductCard(it) } }
}

// Classic use case: scroll position → show/hide FAB
val showFab by remember {
    derivedStateOf { scrollState.value > 100 }
}
// scrollState changes hundreds of times per scroll
// But showFab only changes when crossing the threshold
// → FAB composable only recomposes on threshold crossing
derivedStateOf vs remember(key)
Use derivedStateOf when the derivation is expensive and the source state changes frequently but the derived result changes rarely. Use remember(key) { compute(key) } when the computation should run exactly when key changes (simpler, less overhead for cheap operations).
🏭
5. Production Example

Banking: checkout form with state management

// ViewModel: single source of truth
class CheckoutViewModel : ViewModel() {
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow(CheckoutFormState())
    val state = _state.asStateFlow()

    fun onCardNumberChange(number: String) {
        _state.update { it.copy(cardNumber = number, cardError = validateCard(number)) }
    }
    fun onSubmit() { /* validate + submit */ }
}

// Screen composable: stateless, events go up
@Composable
fun CheckoutScreen(viewModel: CheckoutViewModel = hiltViewModel()) {
    val state by viewModel.state.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()  // ✅

    // derivedStateOf: submit enabled only when form is valid
    val isSubmitEnabled by remember(state) {
        derivedStateOf {
            state.cardError == null &&
            state.cardNumber.length == 16 &&
            state.expiryDate.isNotBlank()
        }
    }

    CheckoutForm(
        state = state,
        isSubmitEnabled = isSubmitEnabled,
        onCardNumberChange = viewModel::onCardNumberChange,
        onSubmit = viewModel::onSubmit
    )
}

// Form composable: fully stateless, testable in isolation
@Composable
fun CheckoutForm(
    state: CheckoutFormState,
    isSubmitEnabled: Boolean,
    onCardNumberChange: (String) -> Unit,
    onSubmit: () -> Unit
) {
    // Local UI state: only this composable needs it
    var showCvvHelp by remember { mutableStateOf(false) }

    Column {
        OutlinedTextField(
            value = state.cardNumber,
            onValueChange = onCardNumberChange,
            isError = state.cardError != null
        )
        Button(onClick = onSubmit, enabled = isSubmitEnabled) {
            Text("Pay")
        }
    }
}
⚠
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1 — Using remember for state that must survive rotation
Search query, scroll position, form input — these must survive rotation. remember loses them. Use rememberSaveable for small values or ViewModel + SavedStateHandle for complex data. A classic bug: user fills a form, rotates device, all fields reset.
Pitfall 2 — collectAsState instead of collectAsStateWithLifecycle
collectAsState() continues collecting when the app goes to background — processing updates the user can't see, potentially doing network calls or DB queries. Always use collectAsStateWithLifecycle() in production.
Pitfall 3 — Hoisting too high
Moving state to a parent/ancestor that doesn't need it creates unnecessary recompositions in the ancestor. Hoist state to the LOWEST common ancestor that needs it — not all the way to the ViewModel unless the state is business-critical.
Best Practice — derivedStateOf for expensive filtered lists
For any list filtering or sorting that runs during recomposition, wrap in derivedStateOf. Source state can change frequently (scroll, typing); the derived list should only recompute when actual filter parameters change.
🎯
7. Interview Framework

30-second answer

"In Compose, state flows down as parameters and events flow up as lambda callbacks — UDF. remember stores state in the slot table across recompositions. rememberSaveable persists through configuration changes. For screen-level business data, the ViewModel holds StateFlow and the UI collects it with collectAsStateWithLifecycle. derivedStateOf creates derived state that only recomputes when its dependencies change."

2-minute answer

"State hoisting is the core pattern — separate 'what state' from 'who owns it'. Stateless composables take state as parameters and report events via lambdas. They're testable, reusable, and previewable. Stateful composables own their own state with remember — but that state is local and ephemeral.

The rule: use remember for pure UI state (isExpanded, hasFocus) that doesn't need to survive navigation. Use rememberSaveable for state that must survive rotation (search query, scroll offset). Use ViewModel for business data that drives screens.

derivedStateOf is underused but important: in a banking transaction list, scroll position changes hundreds of times per scroll gesture. Without derivedStateOf, filtering the list on every scroll recompose is expensive. With derivedStateOf, Compose only recomputes the filtered list when the filter criteria actually changes."

Must-mention points

1
UDF: state down, events up — ViewModel is single source of truth
2
remember vs rememberSaveable — rotation kills remember; saves rememberSaveable
3
collectAsStateWithLifecycle — not collectAsState; stops in background
4
derivedStateOf — for expensive derived computations from rapidly-changing state
5
Hoist to lowest common ancestor — not always to ViewModel

Follow-up Q&A

Q: "How do you decide between remember and rememberSaveable?"

A: Ask: "Would it be confusing to the user if this resets on screen rotation?" If yes (search query, scroll position, form fields, selected tab) — use rememberSaveable. If no (tooltip visibility, animation state, hover state) — use remember. Also: rememberSaveable only works for Bundle-serializable types; for complex data, use ViewModel + SavedStateHandle.

Q: "What is the difference between derivedStateOf and remember(key)?"

A: remember(key) { compute() } recomputes when key changes and always triggers recomposition. derivedStateOf { compute() } also recomputes when dependencies change, but it ONLY triggers recomposition if the computed result is different. For the FAB show/hide example: scroll position changes 60 times/second but the boolean threshold crosses once — derivedStateOf prevents 59 unnecessary FAB recompositions.

Senior insight

Senior Insight
In an automotive app dashboard with live sensor readings updating 60fps, every piece of UI that derives a value from sensor state should use derivedStateOf. Speed gauge, warning lights, fuel level — each is derived from raw sensor data. Without derivedStateOf, a 60fps sensor update rate would cause 60fps recomposition of every derived composable. With derivedStateOf, each composable only recomposes when its threshold changes.
📋
8. Quick Revision Sheet

State survival

remember         → recomposition only
rememberSaveable → + rotation + death
ViewModel        → + rotation, complex data

State hoisting

// Stateless (preferred):
fun SearchBar(
  query: String,           // ← down
  onQueryChange: (String)->Unit // ↑ up
)

collectAsState

collectAsState()               // ❌ background
collectAsStateWithLifecycle()  // ✅ STARTED only

derivedStateOf

val showFab by remember {
  derivedStateOf { 
    scrollState.value > 100
  }
}
// recomposes only on threshold cross
❓
9. Interview Questions
What is the difference between remember and rememberSaveable?
Basic⌄
remember stores values in the composition's slot table — survives recomposition but is lost on configuration changes (rotation, language change) and process death. rememberSaveable additionally saves the value to the Bundle/SavedState system, surviving both configuration changes and process death. For primitive types it works automatically; for complex types you need a custom Saver.
What is state hoisting and why is it important?
Basic⌄
State hoisting is moving state from a composable to its caller, making the composable stateless. Instead of the composable owning state internally, it receives the current value as a parameter and reports changes via a lambda callback. Benefits: the composable becomes testable (control state in tests), reusable (caller decides initial state), previewable (pass any state in preview), and follows UDF (single source of truth).
What is Unidirectional Data Flow in Compose?
Basic⌄
State flows down the composable tree as parameters, events flow up as lambda callbacks. The ViewModel holds and owns the state (single source of truth). It exposes state as StateFlow. The UI consumes state via collectAsStateWithLifecycle() and sends events (user clicks) back to the ViewModel via callbacks. The ViewModel mutates state in response to events, triggering a new UI render.
What is derivedStateOf and when should you use it?
Intermediate⌄
derivedStateOf { } creates a State that is computed from other State values. It only recomputes when its dependencies change, and only triggers recomposition when the computed result is different. Use it when source state changes frequently but derived result changes rarely: scroll position (60fps) → show FAB (boolean, changes rarely); item list → filtered list (filtered count changes occasionally).
Why use collectAsStateWithLifecycle instead of collectAsState?
Intermediate⌄
collectAsState() keeps collecting the Flow even when the app is in the background (Activity paused/stopped). collectAsStateWithLifecycle() uses repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) semantics — collection pauses when the app goes to background and resumes when it comes to foreground. This prevents unnecessary processing when the UI is invisible, saving battery and avoiding potential issues with background-only updates.
A form composable has 5 fields. Which state should use remember, rememberSaveable, and ViewModel?
Intermediate⌄
The field values (text, selections) that the user typed: rememberSaveable or ViewModel + SavedStateHandle — user would be frustrated if their input reset on rotation. UI-only state like "is this field focused" or "show password": remember — acceptable to reset on rotation. If the form involves business logic (validation, submission state, server errors): ViewModel StateFlow with collectAsStateWithLifecycle(). Rule: data the user entered → survives rotation; pure UI decoration → doesn't need to.
What is the difference between derivedStateOf and remember(key)?
Intermediate⌄
remember(key) { compute() }: re-runs compute() when key changes, always triggers recomposition. derivedStateOf { compute() }: re-runs when State dependencies read inside the lambda change. Crucially, it only triggers recomposition if the result changes — an additional optimization. Use derivedStateOf when the computation's input (State) changes more often than the output (e.g., filtering a 1000-item list when only 1 item changes but the filtered result doesn't change).
Design the state management for a banking transfer screen with: amount input, recipient selection, real-time validation, and submit-in-progress state.
Senior⌄
ViewModel owns all: data class TransferState(val amount: String = "", val amountError: String? = null, val recipient: Contact? = null, val isSubmitting: Boolean = false) as MutableStateFlow. ViewModel handles events: onAmountChange (validates), onRecipientSelect, onSubmit (sets isSubmitting). Submit button enabled via derivedStateOf { state.amountError == null && state.recipient != null && !state.isSubmitting }. Amount + recipient persist across rotation via SavedStateHandle in ViewModel. No rememberSaveable needed — ViewModel handles it. UI is fully stateless composable.
When should you hoist state to the ViewModel vs keep it in rememberSaveable?
Senior⌄
Use ViewModel when: (1) state is shared across multiple composables; (2) state requires business logic (validation, computation); (3) state needs to survive process death with unlimited size (SavedStateHandle for complex objects); (4) state comes from or must be synced to a data layer. Use rememberSaveable when: (1) state is purely local UI state in one composable; (2) it's a primitive or Bundle-serializable value; (3) no business logic needed; (4) examples: expanded/collapsed, scroll offset for a sub-list. rememberSaveable keeps components self-contained; ViewModel provides testability and data layer access.
A ScrollState-based parallax header is causing 60fps recompositions. How do you fix it using derivedStateOf?
Senior⌄
Instead of reading scrollState.value directly in composables that don't need continuous updates: val isHeaderCollapsed by remember { derivedStateOf { scrollState.value > COLLAPSE_THRESHOLD } } and val headerAlpha by remember { derivedStateOf { (1f - scrollState.value / FADE_RANGE).coerceIn(0f, 1f) } }. The scrollState changes 60fps but isHeaderCollapsed changes once (boolean threshold). The alpha changes continuously — for this, accept the 60fps recomposition on the alpha composable specifically, or use the Modifier.graphicsLayer approach which doesn't trigger recomposition at all.

7C — Side Effects

LaunchedEffect, DisposableEffect, SideEffect, rememberCoroutineScope, produceState, derivedStateOf, snapshotFlow — every side-effect API with its precise use case.

ID: 7C ⭐ Tier 1
🔍
1. Overview

What is a side effect in Compose?

A side effect is any operation that affects state or the outside world and is not directly part of describing the UI. Examples: launching a coroutine, registering a listener, calling analytics, updating external state. Because composables can re-run at any time, side effects must be carefully managed through dedicated APIs.

Side effect APIs summary

APISuspend?Re-runs whenCleanup?Use for
LaunchedEffect(key)YesKey changesCancels coroutineCoroutines tied to composition
DisposableEffect(key)NoKey changesonDispose { }Non-suspend setup + teardown
SideEffectNoEvery recompositionNoSync Compose state to non-Compose code
rememberCoroutineScopeYes (manual)Manual launchCancels on leaveEvent-triggered coroutines (button click)
produceStateYesKey changesawaitDispose { }Convert non-Compose state to State<T>
snapshotFlowYes (in LaunchedEffect)State changesN/AConvert Compose State to Flow
⚙
2. LaunchedEffect

LaunchedEffect(key) launches a coroutine when the composable enters composition. If the key changes, the current coroutine is cancelled and a new one is launched. When the composable leaves composition, the coroutine is cancelled.

// LaunchedEffect(Unit): run once when composable enters composition
@Composable
fun ProductScreen(productId: String, viewModel: ProductViewModel) {
    // Load when screen appears
    LaunchedEffect(Unit) {
        viewModel.loadProduct(productId)
    }

    // LaunchedEffect(productId): re-runs when productId changes
    LaunchedEffect(productId) {
        viewModel.loadProduct(productId)  // new productId → cancel old → start new
    }
}

// Snackbar: show when SnackbarEvent fires
@Composable
fun CheckoutScreen(viewModel: CheckoutViewModel) {
    val snackbarHostState = remember { SnackbarHostState() }

    LaunchedEffect(Unit) {
        viewModel.events.collect { event ->
            when (event) {
                is UiEvent.ShowSnackbar ->
                    snackbarHostState.showSnackbar(event.message)
                is UiEvent.Navigate ->
                    navController.navigate(event.route)
            }
        }
    }

    Scaffold(snackbarHost = { SnackbarHost(snackbarHostState) }) { /* ... */ }
}

// LaunchedEffect with multiple keys: re-runs when ANY key changes
LaunchedEffect(userId, filterType) {
    repo.loadFiltered(userId, filterType)
}
⚖
3. DisposableEffect

DisposableEffect(key) is for setup/teardown of non-suspending resources. It runs the block on composition and its onDispose { } block on disposal or key change.

// DisposableEffect: lifecycle observer registration
@Composable
fun LifecycleObserver(onResume: () -> Unit, onPause: () -> Unit) {
    val lifecycleOwner = LocalLifecycleOwner.current

    DisposableEffect(lifecycleOwner) {
        val observer = LifecycleEventObserver { _, event ->
            when (event) {
                Lifecycle.Event.ON_RESUME -> onResume()
                Lifecycle.Event.ON_PAUSE -> onPause()
                else -> {}
            }
        }
        lifecycleOwner.lifecycle.addObserver(observer)

        onDispose {
            lifecycleOwner.lifecycle.removeObserver(observer)  // ✅ cleanup
        }
    }
}

// DisposableEffect for MediaPlayer lifecycle
@Composable
fun VideoPlayer(url: String) {
    val context = LocalContext.current

    DisposableEffect(url) {        // re-creates on URL change
        val player = MediaPlayer()
        player.setDataSource(url)
        player.prepare()
        player.start()

        onDispose {
            player.stop()
            player.release()     // ✅ no resource leak
        }
    }
}
📌
4. SideEffect & rememberCoroutineScope

SideEffect — every recomposition

// SideEffect: runs after every successful recomposition
// Use to sync Compose state to non-Compose systems
@Composable
fun AnalyticsScreen(screenName: String) {
    val analyticsTracker = LocalAnalyticsTracker.current

    SideEffect {
        // Runs after every recomposition — sync state to external system
        analyticsTracker.setScreen(screenName)
    }
}

// ❌ WRONG: do NOT use SideEffect for one-time operations
SideEffect { analytics.logScreenView() }  // logs on EVERY recomposition!
// ✅ Use LaunchedEffect(Unit) for one-time operations

rememberCoroutineScope — for event-triggered coroutines

// rememberCoroutineScope: a scope tied to composition lifetime
// Used when you need to launch a coroutine from a non-composable callback
@Composable
fun PayButton(onPay: suspend () -> Unit) {
    val scope = rememberCoroutineScope()
    var isLoading by remember { mutableStateOf(false) }

    Button(
        onClick = {                    // onClick is NOT a suspend function
            scope.launch {           // use scope to launch coroutine
                isLoading = true
                onPay()
                isLoading = false
            }
        },
        enabled = !isLoading
    ) {
        if (isLoading) CircularProgressIndicator()
        else Text("Pay")
    }
}
// When composable leaves, scope is cancelled → in-flight coroutines cancelled
📊
5. produceState & snapshotFlow

produceState — convert non-Compose state to State<T>

// produceState: bridge non-Compose async sources to State<T>
@Composable
fun NetworkImage(url: String): State<ImageResult> = produceState(
    initialValue = ImageResult.Loading,
    key1 = url
) {
    value = imageLoader.load(url)   // suspend call
    // awaitDispose: cleanup if composable leaves before image loads
    awaitDispose { imageLoader.cancel(url) }
}

// Usage
@Composable
fun ProductImage(url: String) {
    val imageState by NetworkImage(url)
    when (imageState) {
        is ImageResult.Loading -> Shimmer()
        is ImageResult.Success -> Image(imageState.bitmap)
        is ImageResult.Error -> ErrorIcon()
    }
}

snapshotFlow — convert Compose State to Flow

// snapshotFlow: read Compose State inside a Flow context
// Emits when the read State values change
@Composable
fun AutoSaveForm(text: String, onSave: (String) -> Unit) {
    LaunchedEffect(Unit) {
        snapshotFlow { text }      // reads Compose state → becomes Flow
            .debounce(2000)         // wait 2s after user stops typing
            .distinctUntilChanged() // only if text actually changed
            .collect { onSave(it) }  // auto-save
    }
}

// snapshotFlow for analytics: track what user reads in a list
LaunchedEffect(Unit) {
    snapshotFlow { listState.firstVisibleItemIndex }
        .distinctUntilChanged()
        .collect { index -> analytics.trackItemImpression(items[index]) }
}
⚠
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1 — LaunchedEffect(Unit) for key-sensitive operations
Using LaunchedEffect(Unit) means the effect never re-runs when parameters change. If you load data by ID and the ID can change (navigation backstack, deep links), use LaunchedEffect(id). Forgetting to pass the correct key is a common source of stale data bugs.
Pitfall 2 — SideEffect for one-time operations
SideEffect runs on EVERY successful recomposition. Using it to log a screen view would fire the analytics event on every UI update, not just once. Use LaunchedEffect(Unit) for one-time effects.
Pitfall 3 — rememberCoroutineScope for one-time initialization
rememberCoroutineScope is for user-triggered events (button clicks). For automatic initialization on screen enter, use LaunchedEffect. Using rememberCoroutineScope + launching in the body (not a callback) will launch on every recomposition — same as calling the code directly.
Best Practice — DisposableEffect for any listener registration
Any time you register a listener, callback, or observer in a composable, always use DisposableEffect with onDispose cleanup. This prevents listener leaks when the composable leaves the composition.
🎯
7. Interview Framework

30-second answer

"Compose provides specific APIs for side effects. LaunchedEffect launches a coroutine tied to composition — re-runs when key changes, cancelled on leave. DisposableEffect is for non-suspend setup/teardown with onDispose cleanup. SideEffect runs after every recomposition for syncing external state. rememberCoroutineScope gives a scope for event-triggered coroutines. produceState converts async sources to State, snapshotFlow converts Compose State to Flow."

2-minute answer

"The key decision is: does the effect run once, on key change, on every recomposition, or on a user event? LaunchedEffect(key) handles the first two cases — it starts a coroutine when composition enters or key changes, and cancels it when leaving. The key is the dependency: LaunchedEffect(Unit) = run once; LaunchedEffect(userId) = re-run when user changes.

DisposableEffect handles non-coroutine resources: lifecycle observers, BroadcastReceivers, Bluetooth listeners. The onDispose block guarantees cleanup regardless of why the composable leaves.

SideEffect is specifically for syncing Compose state to non-Compose systems — like updating a legacy View system or a custom analytics SDK's current screen. It fires after every successful recomposition, ensuring external state stays in sync.

rememberCoroutineScope is used in click handlers and other non-composable callbacks where you need to launch a coroutine but aren't inside a suspend context."

Must-mention points

1
LaunchedEffect(key) — coroutine; re-runs on key change; cancel on leave
2
DisposableEffect + onDispose — non-suspend; cleanup guaranteed
3
SideEffect = every recomposition — not for one-time effects
4
rememberCoroutineScope = event-triggered — button clicks, not auto-init
5
snapshotFlow — converts Compose State to Flow; enables Flow operators on UI state

Follow-up Q&A

Q: "When would you use produceState vs LaunchedEffect + mutableStateOf?"

A: They're similar — produceState is cleaner syntactic sugar. produceState is preferred when the result is the entire return value of a composable (a reusable component that wraps an async source). LaunchedEffect + mutableStateOf is more flexible when you need multiple state updates inside the effect or more complex logic.

Q: "What is the key in LaunchedEffect — can it be anything?"

A: The key can be any value. Compose uses equals() to compare old and new key on recomposition. If they differ, the current coroutine is cancelled and a new one starts. Common keys: Unit (run once), a specific ID, a boolean state, a composable parameter. Multiple keys: LaunchedEffect(key1, key2) — re-runs if either changes.

Senior insight

Senior Insight
In a banking app, use snapshotFlow to convert the active account ID state to a Flow, then combine with server-sent events: LaunchedEffect(Unit) { snapshotFlow { activeAccountId }.flatMapLatest { id -> serverEvents.filterByAccount(id) }.collect { event -> handleLiveUpdate(event) } }. This gives you the full power of Flow operators on Compose state, including debounce, filtering, and flatMapLatest for account switching.
📋
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Which API when?

One-time init      → LaunchedEffect(Unit)
Key-sensitive       → LaunchedEffect(key)
Listener reg/unreg → DisposableEffect(key)
Every recompose    → SideEffect
Button click       → rememberCoroutineScope

LaunchedEffect

LaunchedEffect(Unit)   // once
LaunchedEffect(key)    // on key change
// cancelled when composable leaves
// key: anything with equals()

DisposableEffect

DisposableEffect(key) {
  val cb = register(listener)
  onDispose {
    unregister(cb)  // always called
  }
}

snapshotFlow

// Compose State → Flow
LaunchedEffect(Unit) {
  snapshotFlow { scrollState.value }
    .debounce(300)
    .collect { onScroll(it) }
}
❓
9. Interview Questions
What is LaunchedEffect and how does the key work?
Basic⌄
LaunchedEffect(key) launches a coroutine that is tied to the composition. When the composable enters composition, the coroutine starts. If the key changes on recomposition, the current coroutine is cancelled and a new one starts. When the composable leaves composition, the coroutine is cancelled. The key can be any value — Compose uses equals() to detect changes.
What is DisposableEffect and when must you use onDispose?
Basic⌄
DisposableEffect(key) runs a non-suspending setup block when the composable enters composition or when the key changes. The block must end with onDispose { } which runs when: the composable leaves composition, or the key changes (before re-running the setup block). onDispose is mandatory — it provides the cleanup for listeners, observers, resources registered in the setup block.
When should you use SideEffect vs LaunchedEffect?
Basic⌄
SideEffect runs after EVERY successful recomposition — use for continuously syncing Compose state to external non-Compose systems (e.g., updating an analytics SDK's current screen, updating a legacy View's property). LaunchedEffect(Unit) runs once when the composable enters composition — use for one-time initialization, loading data, starting observation. Never use SideEffect for one-time operations.
When would you use rememberCoroutineScope instead of LaunchedEffect?
Intermediate⌄
rememberCoroutineScope when you need to launch a coroutine in response to a user event (button click, gesture) — from a non-composable callback context where you can't call suspend functions directly. LaunchedEffect when the coroutine should start automatically based on composition entry or a state change. Rule: event-triggered → rememberCoroutineScope; automatic/reactive → LaunchedEffect.
A composable uses LaunchedEffect(Unit) to load data for a product. The user navigates to a different product. What happens and how do you fix it?
Intermediate⌄
With LaunchedEffect(Unit), the effect runs only once when the composable enters composition. If the same composable recomposes with a different productId, the effect does NOT re-run — the old data stays. Fix: LaunchedEffect(productId). Now when productId changes (e.g., navigation to a different product), the old coroutine is cancelled and a new one starts loading the new product.
How do you register and unregister a lifecycle observer safely in Compose?
Intermediate⌄
Use DisposableEffect(lifecycleOwner): in the block, create and add the observer; in onDispose, remove it. Use LocalLifecycleOwner.current to get the current lifecycle owner and pass it as the key — if the owner changes (e.g., nested Navigation), the effect re-runs. Without DisposableEffect (e.g., registering directly in the body), the observer would be added on every recomposition and never removed — a leak.
What is snapshotFlow and what can you do with it that you can't do with just collecting a StateFlow?
Intermediate⌄
snapshotFlow { } converts any Compose State read inside its lambda into a Flow. Unlike a StateFlow (which has a value), snapshotFlow can read any combination of State values: snapshotFlow { state1 + state2 } — emits when either state1 or state2 changes. You can then apply all Flow operators: debounce, distinctUntilChanged, flatMapLatest. This enables complex reactive patterns on local Compose state that wouldn't be possible with just StateFlow.
Design an auto-save feature for a notes app that saves to the database after the user stops typing for 2 seconds.
Senior⌄
@Composable fun NoteEditor(noteId: String, viewModel: NoteViewModel) { val content by viewModel.content.collectAsStateWithLifecycle(); LaunchedEffect(Unit) { snapshotFlow { content }.debounce(2000).distinctUntilChanged().drop(1) // skip initial load .collect { text -> viewModel.saveNote(noteId, text) } }; TextField(value = content, onValueChange = viewModel::onContentChange) }. snapshotFlow converts the content state to Flow. debounce(2000) waits 2s after last keystroke. distinctUntilChanged prevents saving if content didn't change. drop(1) skips the initial emission when the composable enters (don't save before user types).
What is produceState and how is it different from LaunchedEffect + mutableStateOf?
Senior⌄
produceState(initialValue, key) { value = compute() } is syntactic sugar for LaunchedEffect + mutableStateOf — internally it does exactly that. The difference is idiomatic: produceState returns a State<T> directly, making it ideal for composable functions that compute and return a State (not just a void composable). It also provides awaitDispose { } for cleanup. Use produceState when building a composable abstraction over an async data source; use LaunchedEffect when the coroutine is a side effect of an existing composable, not its primary purpose.
A developer registers a BroadcastReceiver in a composable body (not in DisposableEffect). What bugs will occur?
Senior⌄
Three bugs: (1) The receiver is registered on EVERY recomposition — if the screen recomposes 10 times, 10 receivers are registered. Each will respond to broadcasts, causing the handler to fire 10x. (2) No unregistration ever happens — when the composable leaves composition, no cleanup runs. The receiver continues receiving broadcasts forever, holding a reference to the composable's context. (3) Memory leak — the receiver holds a context reference; if the context is Activity-scoped, the Activity leaks. Fix: DisposableEffect with onDispose { context.unregisterReceiver(receiver) }.
