7D — Compose Performance

Smart recomposition, stability system, @Stable/@Immutable, unstable List<>, LazyColumn keys, remember for expensive computations, derivedStateOf, lambda stability, Compose compiler metrics.

ID: 7D ⭐ Tier 1
🔍
1. Overview

What triggers recomposition — and what should NOT

Recomposition is triggered by State changes. The performance question is: how much of the tree recomposes? Compose can skip composables where all parameters are equal — this is called smart recomposition. For a composable to be skippable, all its parameters must be stable.

The stability contract

  • Stable type: if a == b then a will never produce a different result for the same inputs — Compose can safely skip it
  • Immutable type: stronger — value never changes after creation (primitives, String, @Immutable data class)
  • Unstable type: Compose cannot trust equals() — cannot skip (List<>, MutableList, regular classes without @Stable)
Senior Mental Model
Every composable parameter that is an unstable type prevents the composable from being skippable — it MUST re-run on every parent recomposition, even if the actual value didn't change. In a 500-item list, this means 500 items recompose when the parent recomposes. Understanding stability is the key to Compose performance at scale.
⚙
2. Stability System

@Stable annotation

// @Stable: promises that equals() is reliable AND observable
// (Compose will be notified when observable properties change)
@Stable
class UserState {
    var name by mutableStateOf("")  // observable via State
    var email by mutableStateOf("")
}
// Compose can skip composables with UserState params if the reference
// is the same — it trusts the State fields to trigger recomposition

@Immutable annotation

// @Immutable: all public properties never change after construction
// Strongest stability guarantee
@Immutable
data class ProductUiModel(
    val id: String,
    val name: String,
    val price: Double
)
// data class is @Immutable IF all fields are val and stable types
// Compose compiler may infer this automatically in some cases

What the compiler infers automatically

TypeStabilityWhy
Int, String, Boolean, FloatStable (immutable)Primitives never change
data class with stable fieldsStableCompiler infers if all fields are val + stable
List<T>, MutableList<T>UnstableMutable interface, equals() unreliable
HashMap, ArrayListUnstableMutable collections
ViewModelStableNever changes reference in the composable
Regular class (non-data)UnstableNo reliable equals() override
⚠
3. Unstable Types — The List Problem

Why List<T> is unstable

// List<T> is an interface — Compose sees it as potentially mutable
// Even if you pass a listOf(), Compose can't trust equals()

// ❌ UNSTABLE: composable cannot be skipped
@Composable
fun ProductList(products: List<Product>) { /* ... */ }
// Parent recomposes → ProductList ALWAYS recomposes, even if list unchanged

// ✅ Fix 1: @Immutable wrapper
@Immutable
data class ProductList(val items: List<Product>)

@Composable
fun ProductListScreen(products: ProductList) { /* stable ✅ */ }

// ✅ Fix 2: kotlinx.collections.immutable
implementation("org.jetbrains.kotlinx:kotlinx-collections-immutable:0.3.7")

@Composable
fun ProductListScreen(products: ImmutableList<Product>) { /* stable ✅ */ }

Lambda stability

// Lambdas that capture unstable values are themselves unstable
@Composable
fun Parent() {
    val list: List<String> = remember { listOf("a", "b") }

    // ❌ Lambda captures unstable list — unstable lambda
    Child(onClick = { process(list) })
}

// ✅ Fix: stabilize the list, or move lambda out of recomposition scope
val stableList: ImmutableList<String> = remember { persistentListOf("a", "b") }
Child(onClick = { process(stableList) })  // ✅ stable
📌
4. LazyColumn Keys & remember

LazyColumn keys — stable item identity

// ❌ Without key: index is the identity
// Insert an item → all positions shift → all items recompose
LazyColumn {
    items(products) { product ->
        ProductCard(product)  // identity = index in list
    }
}

// ✅ With key: item.id is the identity
// Insert an item → only new item created, others keep their composition
LazyColumn {
    items(products, key = { it.id }) { product ->  // stable String ID
        ProductCard(product)
    }
}
// Keys enable: correct animations, proper remember state per item,
// efficient reuse of composition for unchanged items

remember for expensive computations in composables

// ❌ Expensive computation runs every recomposition
@Composable
fun ChartComposable(data: List<DataPoint>) {
    val chartPath = buildBezierPath(data)  // ❌ O(n) on every recompose
    Canvas { drawPath(chartPath) }
}

// ✅ Memoize with remember(key)
@Composable
fun ChartComposable(data: List<DataPoint>) {
    val chartPath = remember(data) {    // ✅ only recomputes when data changes
        buildBezierPath(data)
    }
    Canvas { drawPath(chartPath) }
}

Modifier.graphicsLayer — avoid recomposition for visual changes

// ❌ alpha in modifier triggers recomposition to update UI
Box(Modifier.alpha(animatedAlpha))  // recomposes on alpha change

// ✅ graphicsLayer: runs in draw phase, no recomposition
Box(
    Modifier.graphicsLayer(alpha = animatedAlpha)
) // No recomposition — handled by render layer
🏭
5. Production Example

E-commerce: performant product list

// ✅ Stable state wrapper for list
@Immutable
data class ProductScreenState(
    val products: ImmutableList<ProductUiModel> = persistentListOf(),
    val isLoading: Boolean = false
)

@Immutable
data class ProductUiModel(
    val id: String,
    val name: String,
    val price: String,       // Pre-formatted string — stable
    val imageUrl: String
)

@Composable
fun ProductListScreen(
    state: ProductScreenState,    // @Immutable → stable
    onAddToCart: (String) -> Unit  // lambdas on stable types → stable
) {
    LazyColumn {
        items(
            items = state.products,
            key = { it.id }  // stable String key
        ) { product ->
            // ProductCard: all params are @Immutable types → skippable
            ProductCard(
                product = product,
                onAddToCart = { onAddToCart(product.id) }
            )
        }
    }
}

// ✅ Skippable ProductCard — all params stable
@Composable
fun ProductCard(
    product: ProductUiModel,       // @Immutable → stable
    onAddToCart: () -> Unit        // no capture → stable
) {
    // derivedStateOf for expensive display computation
    val displayPrice by remember(product.price) {
        derivedStateOf { formatWithCurrency(product.price) }
    }
    /* ... */
}
⚠
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1 — Passing List<T> to composables
List<T> is unstable — any composable that takes it as a parameter cannot be skipped. In a list screen, this means every item recomposes whenever the parent updates. Use ImmutableList<T> (kotlinx.collections.immutable) or wrap in an @Immutable data class.
Pitfall 2 — Lambdas capturing non-stable values
A lambda that captures a List<T> or any unstable value is itself unstable. This prevents the composable receiving it from skipping. Fix: ensure captured values are stable, or use remember { { ... } } to stabilize the lambda reference.
Pitfall 3 — LazyColumn without keys
Without stable keys in LazyColumn, inserting or removing items causes all items to recompose and loses per-item state (expanded state, animations). Always provide key = { item.id }.
Best Practice — Compose compiler metrics
Enable compiler reports: freeCompilerArgs += ["-P", "plugin:androidx.compose.compiler.plugins.kotlin:reportsDestination=build/compose_reports"]. The output shows skippable vs restartable composables and identifies unstable parameters. Use this to find performance bottlenecks.
🎯
7. Interview Framework

30-second answer

"Compose performance is about minimizing unnecessary recomposition. A composable is skippable only if all its parameters are stable — equals() is reliable and Compose trusts the value hasn't changed. The biggest issue is List<T>, which is unstable. Fix it with ImmutableList from kotlinx.collections.immutable or an @Immutable wrapper. LazyColumn keys give items stable identity. derivedStateOf prevents over-recomposition from high-frequency state changes."

2-minute answer

"The stability system is the performance foundation. A stable type means Compose can trust equals() — if a == b, the composable doesn't need to re-run. Primitives and Strings are stable. data classes with stable fields are stable. But List<T> is an interface — Compose cannot guarantee it's immutable, so it's marked unstable. This means a composable with a List parameter is non-skippable: it recomposes every time its parent recomposes, even if the list didn't change.

The fix is ImmutableList from kotlinx.collections.immutable, or wrapping in @Immutable data class. The @Immutable annotation is a promise — you're telling Compose 'trust this class, its contents won't change after construction.'

For LazyColumn: keys give items stable identity. Without keys, inserting at position 0 shifts everything, causing all 500 items to recompose. With keys, Compose moves items and only creates the new one.

Use the Compose compiler metrics to discover unstable parameters and non-skippable composables — it generates reports showing exactly which composables have issues."

Must-mention points

1
Stable = trustworthy equals() → composable can be skipped on recompose
2
List<T> is unstable — use ImmutableList or @Immutable wrapper
3
LazyColumn keys — stable identity prevents full-list recompose
4
derivedStateOf — avoid over-recomposition from high-freq state (scroll, sensors)
5
Compiler metrics — diagnose unstable params in production

Follow-up Q&A

Q: "What is the difference between @Stable and @Immutable?"

A: @Immutable: stronger contract — all public properties never change after construction. The compiler treats all fields as constants for stability purposes. @Stable: weaker — equals() is reliable AND changes to public properties are observable (via State/observable property). Use @Immutable for pure value objects (UI models). Use @Stable for observable state holders (StateHolder classes with mutableStateOf fields).

Q: "How do you enable Compose compiler reports?"

A: In your app's build.gradle: kotlinOptions { freeCompilerArgs += ["-P", "plugin:androidx.compose.compiler.plugins.kotlin:reportsDestination=${project.buildDir}/compose_reports"] }. Run a build and inspect the `*-composables.txt` file — it shows each composable as skippable/restartable and lists stable/unstable parameters.

Senior insight

Senior Insight
In a banking transaction list with real-time updates, use @Immutable data class TransactionUiModel with pre-computed display strings (formatted amount, date string) rather than passing BigDecimal and Instant. This ensures all fields are stable primitives/strings, the composable is fully skippable, and formatting happens once in the ViewModel — not on every recomposition.
📋

9. Interview Questions
What does it mean for a composable to be "skippable"?
Basic⌄
A skippable composable can be skipped during recomposition if all its parameters are equal to their previous values. Compose checks each parameter using equals(). If all are equal, it assumes the output would be the same and skips executing the function — saving CPU time. For a composable to be skippable, all parameters must be stable types.
Why is List<T> unstable in Compose?
Basic⌄
List<T> is a Kotlin interface. Compose cannot verify that the implementation won't change after the composable receives it — a mutable list could change without notifying Compose. Since Compose can't trust that equals() reliably indicates whether the content changed, it marks List as unstable. Any composable receiving a List parameter is non-skippable and will recompose whenever its parent recomposes.
What is the difference between @Stable and @Immutable?
Basic⌄
@Immutable: all public properties never change after construction — strongest guarantee. Every field is treated as a compile-time constant for stability. Use for value objects (UI models). @Stable: weaker — equals() is reliable AND any changes to public properties are observable (the Compose runtime will be notified). Use for mutable state holders that use mutableStateOf internally. In practice, most UI model classes should use @Immutable.
Why should you always provide keys in LazyColumn?
Intermediate⌄
Without keys, each item's identity is its index. Inserting an item at position 0 shifts all other items' indices — Compose thinks every item changed and recomposes all of them. Remember state per item is also lost. With key = { item.id }, each item has a stable identity. Compose can correctly identify which items moved, which are new, and which are unchanged — only recomposing what actually changed and preserving per-item state.
How do you fix the performance issue caused by passing List<T> to a composable?
Intermediate⌄
Two approaches: (1) Use ImmutableList<T> from the kotlinx.collections.immutable library — it's a stable type by design. Convert in ViewModel: _state.update { it.copy(products = newList.toImmutableList()) }. (2) Wrap in an @Immutable data class: @Immutable data class ProductListState(val items: List<T>) — the annotation makes the wrapper stable, and the inner List is treated as immutable by contract.
When should you use Modifier.graphicsLayer vs setting a modifier property directly?
Intermediate⌄
Modifier.alpha(value) updates a modifier that Compose reads during composition — if the alpha changes, a recomposition is needed to apply the new modifier. Modifier.graphicsLayer { alpha = value } applies the change in the draw phase — no recomposition required. For animated values that change every frame (alpha, scale, translation), graphicsLayer skips the composition phase entirely, giving better performance. For static properties that only change occasionally, direct modifiers are fine.
A product list screen shows 200 items. Typing in a search box causes all 200 items to flicker/recompose. What is the root cause and fix?
Intermediate⌄
Root cause: either (1) ProductCard takes a List parameter (unstable, non-skippable), or (2) the state update changes the list reference even if content is the same, or (3) the search query state is being read by the parent that contains the LazyColumn, causing the LazyColumn's parent to recompose, and without stable/skippable ProductCard, all 200 items recompose. Fix: ensure ProductCard takes @Immutable ProductUiModel (not List). Hoist the search query state to a ViewModel so it doesn't live in the same composable as the list. Add stable keys to LazyColumn.
How do you use Compose compiler metrics to diagnose performance issues?
Senior⌄
Add to app build.gradle: kotlinOptions { freeCompilerArgs += ["-P", "plugin:androidx.compose.compiler.plugins.kotlin:reportsDestination=${buildDir}/compose_reports", "-P", "plugin:androidx.compose.compiler.plugins.kotlin:metricsDestination=${buildDir}/compose_metrics"] }. Run an assembleDebug/Release. Open build/compose_reports/*-composables.txt. Each composable is marked: skippable/non-skippable, restartable/non-restartable. Non-skippable composables list their unstable parameters. The metrics JSON provides counts. Focus on non-skippable composables in hot paths (list items).
Explain why a lambda that captures a non-stable type is itself unstable and how to fix it.
Senior⌄
Compose compiler analyzes lambda capture sites. If a lambda captures an unstable value (e.g., List<T>), the compiler cannot guarantee the lambda's output is stable — calling it with the same "arguments" might produce different results because the captured state may have changed. The lambda is therefore marked unstable, preventing composables that receive it from skipping. Fix: (1) ensure the captured value is stable (ImmutableList, @Immutable class); (2) use remember { { } } to create a stable lambda reference; (3) in Compose 1.5+, lambdas with stable captures are automatically stabilized by the compiler.
An automotive dashboard has a speedometer recomposing at 60fps. The needle is animated but the rest of the dashboard should not recompose. How do you architect this?
Senior⌄
Isolate the high-frequency state. The speed value from sensors updates at 60fps — keep it in a separate StateFlow or animatable. The Speedometer composable reads this directly. Use Modifier.graphicsLayer { rotationZ = needleAngle } for the needle rotation — this runs in the draw phase without recomposition. For the rest of the dashboard (current music, temperature, warnings), use derivedStateOf for threshold-crossing booleans. Structure: DashboardScreen (reads all states) → SpeedGauge (reads only speed via derivedStateOf thresholds) + StaticDashboardPanels (@Stable, skippable). The needle rotation via graphicsLayer avoids even SpeedGauge recomposition at 60fps.

7E — Compose UI

Tier 1 Row · Column · Box · LazyColumn · LazyRow · Scaffold · Material 3 · Modifiers · Custom Layouts

1 · Overview

Jetpack Compose's UI toolkit provides a set of composable layout functions that replace XML views entirely. Layouts are described in Kotlin as composable function calls, and the Compose runtime handles measuring, placing, and drawing efficiently.

Core principle: Every composable is a function that emits UI nodes into the composition tree. Layout composables (Row, Column, Box) control how child nodes are measured and positioned. Modifier adds decoration and behaviour without subclassing.

2 · How It Works

Layout Primitives

ComposableAxisXML equivalentKey params
RowHorizontalLinearLayout horizontalhorizontalArrangement, verticalAlignment
ColumnVerticalLinearLayout verticalverticalArrangement, horizontalAlignment
BoxStack (Z-axis)FrameLayoutcontentAlignment
LazyColumnVertical, lazyRecyclerView (vertical)items{}, itemsIndexed{}, key
LazyRowHorizontal, lazyRecyclerView (horizontal)items{}, contentPadding
ConstraintLayoutConstraint-basedConstraintLayoutcreateRefs(), constrain{}

Modifiers

Modifiers are applied left-to-right, each wrapping the next. Order matters — padding before background fills the padded area; background before padding fills outside the padding.

// Order matters: size → background → padding → clickable
Box(
    Modifier
        .fillMaxWidth()
        .height(56.dp)
        .background(MaterialTheme.colorScheme.primary)
        .padding(horizontal = 16.dp)
        .clickable { onTap() }
)

Scaffold — Material 3

@Composable
fun BankingScreen(
    viewModel: BankingViewModel,
    onNavigate: (Route) -> Unit
) {
    Scaffold(
        topBar = {
            TopAppBar(
                title = { Text("Accounts") },
                navigationIcon = { IconButton(onClick = { onNavigate(Route.Back) }) {
                    Icon(Icons.Default.ArrowBack, "Back")
                }}
            )
        },
        floatingActionButton = {
            FloatingActionButton(onClick = { onNavigate(Route.NewTransfer) }) {
                Icon(Icons.Default.Add, "New transfer")
            }
        }
    ) { paddingValues ->
        // paddingValues accounts for TopAppBar + FAB insets
        AccountsList(
            modifier = Modifier.padding(paddingValues),
            viewModel = viewModel
        )
    }
}

LazyColumn with Keys

@Composable
fun TransactionList(transactions: List<Transaction>) {
    LazyColumn(
        contentPadding = PaddingValues(16.dp),
        verticalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(8.dp)
    ) {
        items(
            items = transactions,
            key = { it.id }   // ✅ stable key — preserves scroll pos, avoids full recompose
        ) { tx ->
            TransactionItem(transaction = tx)
        }
    }
}

Custom Layout

// Custom layout: vertical list where each item has a dot timeline connector
@Composable
fun TimelineLayout(content: @Composable () -> Unit) {
    Layout(content = content) { measurables, constraints ->
        val placeables = measurables.map { it.measure(constraints) }
        val height = placeables.sumOf { it.height }
        layout(width = constraints.maxWidth, height = height) {
            var y = 0
            placeables.forEach { placeable ->
                placeable.placeRelative(x = 0, y = y)
                y += placeable.height
            }
        }
    }
}

Material 3 Theming

@Composable
fun BankingTheme(
    darkTheme: Boolean = isSystemInDarkTheme(),
    content: @Composable () -> Unit
) {
    val colorScheme = if (darkTheme) darkColorScheme(
        primary = Color(0xFF1565C0),
        secondary = Color(0xFF0288D1)
    ) else lightColorScheme(
        primary = Color(0xFF1E88E5),
        secondary = Color(0xFF0288D1)
    )
    MaterialTheme(colorScheme = colorScheme, typography = BankingTypography) {
        content()
    }
}

3 · When to Use

ComponentUse whenAvoid when
ColumnVertical list of small, known-count itemsLong lists — use LazyColumn
LazyColumnAny scrollable list; unknown/large item countVery few items — Column is simpler
BoxOverlapping elements (badge on icon, overlay)Linear arrangements — Column/Row is cleaner
ConstraintLayout in ComposeComplex layouts that would be deeply nested otherwise; responsive adaptive layoutsSimple linear arrangements
ScaffoldAny screen with TopAppBar, BottomBar, FAB, SnackbarStandalone overlay composables (dialogs)
Custom LayoutUnique placement logic not achievable with built-insAnything achievable with Box/Row/Column

4 · Production Example — E-Commerce Product Screen

@Composable
fun ProductDetailScreen(
    product: Product,
    onAddToCart: () -> Unit,
    onBack: () -> Unit
) {
    Scaffold(
        topBar = {
            TopAppBar(
                title = { Text(product.name, maxLines = 1, overflow = TextOverflow.Ellipsis) },
                navigationIcon = {
                    IconButton(onClick = onBack) {
                        Icon(Icons.AutoMirrored.Default.ArrowBack, "Back")
                    }
                }
            )
        },
        bottomBar = {
            AddToCartBar(price = product.price, onAddToCart = onAddToCart)
        }
    ) { padding ->
        LazyColumn(
            modifier = Modifier.padding(padding),
            contentPadding = PaddingValues(bottom = 16.dp)
        ) {
            item(key = "hero") {
                AsyncImage(
                    model = product.imageUrl,
                    contentDescription = product.name,
                    modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth().height(280.dp),
                    contentScale = ContentScale.Crop
                )
            }
            item(key = "details") {
                Column(Modifier.padding(16.dp)) {
                    Text(product.name, style = MaterialTheme.typography.headlineSmall)
                    Text(product.description, style = MaterialTheme.typography.bodyMedium,
                        color = MaterialTheme.colorScheme.onSurfaceVariant)
                }
            }
            items(product.reviews, key = { it.id }) { review ->
                ReviewItem(review = review)
            }
        }
    }
}

@Composable
private fun AddToCartBar(price: Double, onAddToCart: () -> Unit) {
    Surface(shadowElevation = 8.dp) {
        Row(
            modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth().padding(16.dp),
            horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.SpaceBetween,
            verticalAlignment = Alignment.CenterVertically
        ) {
            Text("$$price", style = MaterialTheme.typography.headlineSmall)
            Button(onClick = onAddToCart) { Text("Add to Cart") }
        }
    }
}

5 · Alternatives and Trade-offs

ApproachProsConsWhen
Compose LazyColumnNo adapter boilerplate, type-safe, easy animationsCan't mix with RecyclerView in same container easilyNew screens; preferred
RecyclerView (XML)Mature, well-tested, supports all adaptersBoilerplate (Adapter, ViewHolder, DiffUtil)Legacy codebase; incremental migration
Column (non-lazy)Simpler API, easy to animateAll items composed at once — OOM for large lists<20 items only
ConstraintLayout ComposeSingle pass measurement, flat hierarchyVerbose API vs Column/Row for simple casesComplex adaptive layouts

6 · Pitfalls and Best Practices

  • LazyColumn without keys: Without key, Compose cannot identify item identity — scroll state lost, animations wrong, unnecessary recompositions.
  • Modifier order: .padding(16.dp).background(Color.Red) vs .background(Color.Red).padding(16.dp) produce different results. Background before padding = background under the padding area.
  • Missing padding(paddingValues) in Scaffold: Content overlaps TopAppBar / BottomBar if you don't apply the Scaffold's paddingValues to your content.
  • Column for long lists: Column measures all children eagerly — use LazyColumn for any list that might grow.
  • Modifier.clickable without ripple: Use Modifier.clickable { } (has built-in ripple) not custom pointerInput unless you need fine-grained gesture control.
  • Hard-coded dp in custom layouts: Use LocalDensity to convert px ↔ dp in custom layouts, not hard-coded pixel values.
Best practices: Always pass paddingValues in Scaffold. Always provide key in LazyColumn. Use Arrangement.spacedBy() for consistent gaps. Use fillMaxWidth() on top-level layout composables. Apply Modifier parameters in a consistent order: size → background → padding → border → click.

7 · Interview Answer Framework

30-Second Answer

"Compose UI is built around three layout primitives — Row (horizontal), Column (vertical), Box (stack) — plus lazy variants LazyColumn and LazyRow for scrollable lists. Scaffold provides the Material 3 chrome (TopAppBar, BottomBar, FAB, Snackbar). Modifiers decorate and add behaviour without subclassing, and their order matters. LazyColumn should always have a stable key per item for correct diffing and scroll preservation. Custom layouts use the Layout composable for full measurement control."

2-Minute Structured Answer

Layouts: Row/Column/Box for simple arrangements; LazyColumn/LazyRow for scrollable lists (analogous to RecyclerView but no Adapter boilerplate). Scaffold is the standard screen wrapper — always pass its paddingValues to the content to avoid overlap with TopAppBar/BottomBar.

Modifiers: Applied left-to-right; each wraps the previous. Order matters — size, then background, then padding, then click is the standard pattern. clickable has a built-in ripple; use it instead of custom gesture handlers unless necessary.

LazyColumn performance: Always provide stable keys — without them, Compose cannot tell which item moved vs was replaced, causing wrong animations and losing scroll state. Use contentPadding and Arrangement.spacedBy() for spacing.

Material 3: MaterialTheme provides colorScheme, typography, shapes. Use MaterialTheme.colorScheme.primary etc. rather than hard-coded colours — themes correctly in dark mode automatically.

Must-Mention Points

  1. Row/Column/Box are the three layout primitives; Lazy variants for scrollable lists.
  2. Modifier order matters (especially padding vs background).
  3. Scaffold for Material 3 screen chrome — always use paddingValues.
  4. LazyColumn keys — critical for correctness and performance.
  5. Custom Layout composable for non-standard placement.
  6. Material 3 theming via MaterialTheme (colorScheme, typography, shapes).

Likely Follow-up Questions

QuestionShort Answer
Why does Modifier order matter?Each Modifier wraps the node; earlier modifiers apply to the outer boundary. padding(16dp).background(Red) draws red only in the inner area. background(Red).padding(16dp) draws red over the full bounds including padding area.
When do you use ConstraintLayout in Compose?When a layout has many sibling constraints that would require deep Row/Column nesting otherwise. ConstraintLayout enables flat single-pass measurement which is more efficient for complex adaptive screens.
How do you add spacing between LazyColumn items?Use verticalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(8.dp) in LazyColumn, or contentPadding for outer padding. Don't add padding to individual items as it creates asymmetric spacing.

Senior-Level Insight

"The key architectural insight with Compose layouts is that there are no XML inflation or view recycling concerns — LazyColumn handles recycling automatically, and the Compose compiler tracks which items need recomposition via stable keys. The main performance lever is stability: if your list item data class is @Stable or @Immutable and you provide a key, Compose will skip recomposing unchanged items entirely. This is more powerful than DiffUtil in RecyclerView because the skip decision happens per-composable rather than per-list-item."

9 · Interview Questions (Self-Check)

Basic Name the three core Compose layout primitives and their XML equivalents.
Row (LinearLayout horizontal), Column (LinearLayout vertical), Box (FrameLayout). LazyColumn and LazyRow are the lazy/scrollable equivalents of RecyclerView.
Basic Why does Modifier order matter in Compose?
Each Modifier wraps the previous one. Modifiers closer to the composable affect the inner content; modifiers further out affect the outer boundary. Example: Modifier.padding(16dp).background(Red) applies background only to the inner content area. Modifier.background(Red).padding(16dp) applies background to the full area including the padding.
Basic What is Scaffold and why must you use its paddingValues?
Scaffold is the Material 3 screen scaffold that provides slots for TopAppBar, BottomNavigationBar, FAB, Snackbar, and DrawerLayout. The paddingValues it passes to the content lambda represent the insets consumed by these components (TopAppBar height, BottomBar height). If you don't apply paddingValues to your content, it will be drawn behind the TopAppBar and BottomBar.
Intermediate Why should LazyColumn items always have a key? What happens without it?
Without a key, Compose uses positional identity (index 0, 1, 2...). When items are inserted/removed/reordered, Compose recomposes all subsequent items because their positions changed. With a stable key (item ID), Compose can identify which items moved vs changed, skip recomposing unchanged items, apply correct animations, and preserve scroll state across recompositions. Key must be unique and stable (no random/UUID generated each time).
Intermediate How do you add equal spacing between LazyColumn items?
Use verticalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(8.dp) in the LazyColumn parameters. Don't add padding to individual item composables — that creates asymmetric spacing (double gap between items, single gap at edges). For outer padding (top/bottom of the whole list), use contentPadding = PaddingValues(vertical = 16.dp).
Intermediate When would you use ConstraintLayout in Compose?
When a layout requires complex sibling constraints that would otherwise need deeply nested Row/Column combinations. ConstraintLayout computes its layout in a single pass regardless of constraint complexity, whereas deeply nested Row/Column can cause multiple measurement passes (though Compose's intrinsic measurement largely mitigates this). Use it for: flexible responsive layouts, baseline alignment between sibling elements, and adaptive layouts that change significantly at different screen sizes.
Intermediate How do you create a custom layout in Compose?
Use the Layout composable: provide a content lambda (child composables) and a measurePolicy lambda. The measurePolicy receives measurables (children to measure) and constraints (available space). Call measurable.measure(constraints) to get a Placeable. Call layout(width, height) { } to set the layout size and position children using placeable.placeRelative(x, y).
Senior/Scenario [Scenario] A LazyColumn with 1,000 items is janky on scroll. How do you diagnose and optimize it?
Diagnosis: Use Android Studio Layout Inspector in Compose mode to see recomposition counts. Check Compose compiler metrics for unstable composables. Use systrace/Perfetto to find dropped frames.

Fixes:
1. Add stable keys to items — prevents wrong recompositions
2. Make item data class @Stable or @Immutable — allows Compose to skip recomposition
3. Use remember{} for expensive computations inside item composable
4. Avoid lambdas that capture state inside item composable (use callbacks passed as parameters)
5. Use contentType = { it.type } in items{} if you have heterogeneous item types — improves view recycling
6. Avoid Modifier.graphicsLayer inside items unless needed for animation
7. Check for nested LazyColumns (not allowed — causes measurement exceptions)
Senior/Scenario [Coding] Implement a horizontally scrollable chip row that wraps to next line if chips don't fit (flow layout). 
// FlowRow is available in Compose Foundation (experimental in 1.4, stable in 1.5+)
@Composable
fun FilterChipRow(
    filters: List<String>,
    selected: Set<String>,
    onToggle: (String) -> Unit
) {
    FlowRow(
        horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(8.dp),
        verticalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(8.dp),
        modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth().padding(horizontal = 16.dp)
    ) {
        filters.forEach { filter ->
            FilterChip(
                selected = filter in selected,
                onClick = { onToggle(filter) },
                label = { Text(filter) }
            )
        }
    }
}
// FlowRow automatically wraps chips to next line when horizontal space is exhausted
Senior/Scenario [Debug] Content in a Scaffold is hidden behind the TopAppBar. What's wrong?
The paddingValues provided by Scaffold's content lambda is not being applied to the content. Scaffold calculates insets from TopAppBar, BottomBar, and FAB and passes them as PaddingValues to the content slot. If you don't apply them (via Modifier.padding(paddingValues)), your content starts at y=0, which is behind the TopAppBar.
Fix:
Scaffold(topBar = { TopAppBar(...) }) { paddingValues ->
    LazyColumn(modifier = Modifier.padding(paddingValues)) { // ✅
        ...
    }
}
Also verify you're not applying contentPadding to the LazyColumn that conflicts with paddingValues.

7F — Compose Navigation

Tier 1 NavController · NavHost · Arguments · Nested Navigation · Deep Links · Back Stack

1 · Overview

Navigation Compose is the Jetpack Navigation library adapted for Compose. It manages a back stack of Composable destinations, enabling type-safe navigation, argument passing, deep links, and nested navigation graphs — all without Activity or Fragment boilerplate.

Core components:
  • NavController — manages navigation state and back stack
  • NavHost — the Composable that renders the current destination
  • NavGraph — the set of destinations and connections, defined in code

2 · How It Works

Basic Setup

MainActivity (single Activity) └── NavHost ├── composable("home") → HomeScreen() ├── composable("product/{id}") → ProductDetailScreen() ├── composable("cart") → CartScreen() └── navigation("auth") → nested AuthGraph ├── composable("login") → LoginScreen() └── composable("register") → RegisterScreen()
@Composable
fun AppNavHost(navController: NavHostController = rememberNavController()) {
    NavHost(
        navController = navController,
        startDestination = "home"
    ) {
        composable("home") {
            HomeScreen(onNavigateToProduct = { id ->
                navController.navigate("product/$id")
            })
        }
        composable(
            route = "product/{productId}",
            arguments = listOf(navArgument("productId") { type = NavType.StringType })
        ) { backStackEntry ->
            val productId = backStackEntry.arguments?.getString("productId")
            ProductDetailScreen(productId = productId!!)
        }
    }
}

Type-Safe Navigation (Navigation 2.8+ with Kotlin Serialization)

// Define routes as sealed class or @Serializable objects (Navigation 2.8+)
@Serializable object HomeRoute
@Serializable data class ProductRoute(val productId: String)
@Serializable object CartRoute

NavHost(navController, startDestination = HomeRoute) {
    composable<HomeRoute> { HomeScreen(...) }
    composable<ProductRoute> { backStackEntry ->
        val route: ProductRoute = backStackEntry.toRoute()
        ProductDetailScreen(productId = route.productId)
    }
}

// Navigate with type safety
navController.navigate(ProductRoute(productId = "abc123"))

Back Stack Management

// Navigate and clear login from back stack (logout flow)
navController.navigate(HomeRoute) {
    popUpTo(LoginRoute::class) { inclusive = true }  // remove Login from stack
}

// launchSingleTop — don't stack duplicates
navController.navigate(HomeRoute) {
    popUpTo(HomeRoute::class) { inclusive = true }
    launchSingleTop = true
}

// Navigate up (Back)
navController.navigateUp()    // preferred over popBackStack()

Nested Navigation Graphs

NavHost(navController, startDestination = "main") {
    // Nested auth graph — separate back stack scope
    navigation(startDestination = "login", route = "auth") {
        composable("login") { LoginScreen(...) }
        composable("register") { RegisterScreen(...) }
    }
    navigation(startDestination = "home", route = "main") {
        composable("home") { HomeScreen(...) }
        composable("cart") { CartScreen(...) }
    }
}

// Scoped ViewModel to nested graph — shared between screens in that graph
val authViewModel: AuthViewModel = viewModel(
    viewModelStoreOwner = remember(navController) {
        navController.getBackStackEntry("auth")
    }
)

Deep Links

composable(
    route = "order/{orderId}",
    deepLinks = listOf(navDeepLink {
        uriPattern = "https://mybank.com/orders/{orderId}"
    })
) { backStackEntry ->
    val orderId = backStackEntry.arguments?.getString("orderId")
    OrderDetailScreen(orderId!!)
}

3 · When to Use

ScenarioApproach
Single-activity Compose appNavHost at the top of the composition tree, all screens as composable destinations
Scoped ViewModel for a flow (e.g. checkout)Nested navigation graph — scope ViewModel to the graph's back stack entry
Bottom navigation tabsEach tab is a nested graph; NavController navigates between them with launchSingleTop=true, saveState=true, restoreState=true
Deep link from notificationnavDeepLink{} in composable, handled automatically by Navigation
Pass complex objectsPass only ID, load in ViewModel — don't serialize full objects into nav args (size limit, no type safety for complex objects pre-2.8)

4 · Production Example — Banking App with Tabs + Auth Flow

// Sealed route hierarchy
@Serializable sealed class Route {
    @Serializable object Login : Route()
    @Serializable object Home : Route()
    @Serializable data class TransactionDetail(val txId: String) : Route()
    @Serializable object Transfer : Route()
}

@Composable
fun AppNavHost() {
    val navController = rememberNavController()
    val authState by authViewModel.authState.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()

    // Navigate to login when auth state changes to logged out
    LaunchedEffect(authState) {
        if (authState is AuthState.LoggedOut) {
            navController.navigate(Route.Login) {
                popUpTo(0) { inclusive = true }   // clear entire back stack
            }
        }
    }

    NavHost(
        navController = navController,
        startDestination = if (authState is AuthState.LoggedIn) Route.Home else Route.Login
    ) {
        composable<Route.Login> {
            LoginScreen(onLoginSuccess = {
                navController.navigate(Route.Home) {
                    popUpTo(Route.Login::class) { inclusive = true }
                }
            })
        }
        composable<Route.Home> {
            HomeScreen(onTransactionClick = { txId ->
                navController.navigate(Route.TransactionDetail(txId))
            })
        }
        composable<Route.TransactionDetail> { entry ->
            val route: Route.TransactionDetail = entry.toRoute()
            TransactionDetailScreen(txId = route.txId, onBack = navController::navigateUp)
        }
    }
}

Bottom Navigation with State Preservation

@Composable
fun MainScreen() {
    val navController = rememberNavController()
    Scaffold(
        bottomBar = {
            NavigationBar {
                val currentDest by navController.currentBackStackEntryAsState()
                tabs.forEach { tab ->
                    NavigationBarItem(
                        selected = currentDest?.destination?.hierarchy?.any { it.route == tab.route } == true,
                        onClick = {
                            navController.navigate(tab.route) {
                                popUpTo(navController.graph.findStartDestination().id) { saveState = true }
                                launchSingleTop = true
                                restoreState = true   // restore tab state on re-select
                            }
                        },
                        icon = { Icon(tab.icon, tab.label) },
                        label = { Text(tab.label) }
                    )
                }
            }
        }
    ) { padding ->
        NavHost(navController, "home", Modifier.padding(padding)) {
            navigation(startDestination = "accounts", route = "home") { /* ... */ }
            navigation(startDestination = "transactions", route = "history") { /* ... */ }
            navigation(startDestination = "profile", route = "settings") { /* ... */ }
        }
    }
}

5 · Alternatives and Trade-offs

ApproachProsConsWhen
Navigation Compose (string routes)Widely used, simple stringsNot type-safe; typos cause runtime crashesPre-2.8 apps
Navigation Compose (typed routes, 2.8+)Type-safe, @Serializable, compile-time errorsRequires Navigation 2.8+ + KSPAll new projects
Fragment + Navigation ComponentMature, Safe Args, well-testedFragment lifecycle complexityExisting XML apps
Custom navigation (state-based)Full control, no library dependencyRe-implementing back stack, deep links, etc.Very simple apps only; not recommended
Voyager / DecomposeThird-party alternatives with different trade-offsLess ecosystem support, more riskSpecific needs not met by official library

6 · Pitfalls and Best Practices

  • NavController not at composition top: Create NavController with rememberNavController() at the top of the composition tree and pass it down. Don't create it inside individual screens.
  • Passing complex objects as nav args: Nav args are strings (Bundle-backed). Serialize only IDs; load full data in the destination ViewModel. Navigation 2.8 typed routes support basic types only via kotlinx.serialization.
  • Missing saveState/restoreState in tab navigation: Without saveState = true / restoreState = true, switching tabs recreates the entire tab screen. This loses scroll position and state.
  • Navigating in LaunchedEffect without correct keys: Always use a stable key (e.g., event or state value) in LaunchedEffect to avoid re-triggering navigation on recomposition.
  • Back stack growth from bottom nav: Without popUpTo(startDestination), repeatedly tapping tab icons stacks destinations. Always use the bottom nav pattern with popUpTo + launchSingleTop.
  • ViewModel scope in nested graphs: Use navController.getBackStackEntry("graphRoute") as the ViewModelStoreOwner to scope a ViewModel to a graph, not to individual destinations.

7 · Interview Answer Framework

30-Second Answer

"Navigation Compose uses NavController to manage a back stack of composable destinations declared in a NavHost. Each destination is a composable{} block with a route string or @Serializable type-safe route. Arguments are typed with navArgument, deep links with navDeepLink. Nested navigation graphs scope back stacks and ViewModels. For bottom tabs, popUpTo + launchSingleTop + saveState/restoreState are the canonical pattern to avoid back stack growth and preserve tab state."

2-Minute Structured Answer

Core components: NavController (back stack state), NavHost (renders current destination), NavGraph (set of destinations defined in code).

Arguments: Typed via navArgument() — NavType.StringType, IntType, BoolType. Navigation 2.8+ supports @Serializable data class routes for full type safety with toRoute().

Back stack: popUpTo() removes destinations; inclusive=true removes the target itself. For logout: popUpTo(0) { inclusive=true } clears the entire graph. For tab nav: popUpTo(startDestination) { saveState=true } + launchSingleTop=true + restoreState=true.

Nested graphs: navigation{} blocks create sub-graphs with their own start destination. Useful for auth flow (scope AuthViewModel to the auth graph) and feature modules. ViewModel scoped to graph: viewModel(viewModelStoreOwner = navController.getBackStackEntry("graphRoute")).

Must-Mention Points

  1. NavController + NavHost + NavGraph are the three core components.
  2. Type-safe navigation with @Serializable routes (Navigation 2.8+).
  3. popUpTo + inclusive for clearing back stack (logout, auth flows).
  4. Bottom navigation: popUpTo + launchSingleTop + saveState + restoreState.
  5. Nested navigation graphs for scoped ViewModels and feature isolation.
  6. Deep links via navDeepLink{} in composable declaration.
  7. Never pass complex objects — pass IDs only.

Likely Follow-up Questions

QuestionShort Answer
How do you share a ViewModel between screens in a flow?Scope the ViewModel to the nested navigation graph: viewModel(viewModelStoreOwner = navController.getBackStackEntry("checkoutGraph")). Both screens in the graph share the same instance; it's cleared when the graph is popped.
How do you handle back navigation from a composable?Use navController.navigateUp() (preferred — respects up navigation stack) or navController.popBackStack() (pops regardless). Pass the callback down as a lambda: onBack: () -> Unit = navController::navigateUp.
What's the difference between popBackStack and navigateUp?popBackStack() always pops the current destination. navigateUp() pops if there's a previous destination; otherwise delegates to the Activity's up navigation (useful for single-Activity with deep links).
How do deep links work in Navigation Compose?Declare navDeepLink { uriPattern = "https://..." } in composable(). Declare the intent-filter in AndroidManifest for the Activity. Navigation automatically routes the incoming Intent to the correct composable and extracts path parameters.

Senior-Level Insight

"The key advantage of Navigation Compose over Fragment Navigation is that there's no separate Fragment lifecycle — the composable back stack IS the navigation stack. There's no onCreateView/onDestroyView duality. State inside NavBackStackEntry persists across navigation (remember survives going back), and ViewModel scoping to a graph is cleaner than the Fragment activityViewModels() approach. The main trade-off is that Navigation Compose is less mature for very complex multi-module graphs — but Navigation 2.8's type-safe routes significantly close the gap, and I'd choose it for all new projects."

9 · Interview Questions (Self-Check)

Basic What are the three core components of Navigation Compose?
NavController (manages back stack state and provides navigate/popBackStack API), NavHost (Composable that renders the current destination from the back stack), NavGraph (the set of composable destinations and their routes, defined within the NavHost builder lambda).
Basic How do you pass an argument to a composable destination?
Declare the route with a placeholder: composable("product/{productId}", arguments = listOf(navArgument("productId") { type = NavType.StringType })) { backStackEntry -> val id = backStackEntry.arguments?.getString("productId") }. Navigate with: navController.navigate("product/abc123"). With Navigation 2.8+ typed routes: @Serializable data class ProductRoute(val productId: String), then navigate with navController.navigate(ProductRoute("abc123")) and val route: ProductRoute = backStackEntry.toRoute().
Basic How do you implement a logout flow that prevents the user from pressing Back to the home screen? 
navController.navigate(Route.Login) {
    popUpTo(0) { inclusive = true }  // clears entire back stack
}
popUpTo(0) removes all destinations back to the root (id=0). inclusive=true removes the start destination too. The user is left with only the Login screen and pressing Back exits the app.
Intermediate Explain the bottom navigation tab pattern with saveState and restoreState.
Without saveState/restoreState, switching tabs recreates the entire destination from scratch, losing scroll position and state. The pattern:
navController.navigate(tab.route) {
    popUpTo(navController.graph.findStartDestination().id) {
        saveState = true  // save the current tab's back stack
    }
    launchSingleTop = true  // don't stack duplicate
    restoreState = true     // restore previously saved state
}
This preserves each tab's individual state (scroll position, ViewModel state persists in memory) when switching between tabs.
Intermediate How do you scope a ViewModel to a nested navigation graph? 
// Define nested graph with a route
navigation(startDestination = "checkout_details", route = "checkout") {
    composable("checkout_details") { ... }
    composable("checkout_review") { ... }
    composable("checkout_payment") { ... }
}

// In any composable inside "checkout" graph:
val checkoutViewModel: CheckoutViewModel = viewModel(
    viewModelStoreOwner = remember(navController) {
        navController.getBackStackEntry("checkout")
    }
)
The ViewModel is created once and shared across all screens in the "checkout" graph. It's cleared when the entire graph is popped from the back stack.
Intermediate What is the difference between navigateUp() and popBackStack()?
popBackStack() always attempts to pop the current destination from the back stack, regardless of context. navigateUp() first tries to navigate up within the NavController's graph; if the back stack is empty, it delegates to the Activity's onSupportNavigateUp(), which handles system Up navigation (e.g., when the app was opened from a deep link and needs to go to a parent Activity). For in-app Back navigation, use navigateUp(). For programmatic navigation within flows, popBackStack() gives more control.
Intermediate How do you handle navigation events from a ViewModel safely?
Use a SharedFlow (or Channel as a Flow) to emit one-shot navigation events. Collect in the Composable with LaunchedEffect to ensure it only fires once even on recomposition:
// ViewModel
val navEvents = Channel<NavEvent>(Channel.BUFFERED)

// Composable
LaunchedEffect(Unit) {
    viewModel.navEvents.receiveAsFlow().collect { event ->
        when (event) {
            NavEvent.LoggedOut -> navController.navigate(Route.Login) {
                popUpTo(0) { inclusive = true }
            }
        }
    }
}
Using StateFlow for navigation events is a common mistake — it replays the last value on re-subscription, causing the navigation to fire again on recomposition.
Senior/Scenario [Scenario] After rotating the device mid-checkout (3 screens deep), the user is navigated back to the home screen. What went wrong?
The navigation event (e.g., navigate to home on auth state change) is being collected in a LaunchedEffect or from a StateFlow without lifecycle awareness, and fires again after rotation (because the state/event is still set). Specifically: if using StateFlow for a navigation event (instead of a one-shot Channel/SharedFlow), the last emitted value re-triggers on recomposition after rotation, causing an unintended navigation.

Fix: Use a Channel or SharedFlow(replay=0) for one-shot navigation events, not StateFlow. Alternatively, use ConsumedEvent wrappers or the official UiEvent pattern from Google's architecture samples. LaunchedEffect with a correct stable key (e.g., the event itself) ensures it only fires once per distinct event value.
Senior/Scenario [Coding] Implement a multi-module navigation setup where each feature module contributes its own NavGraph. 
// :core:navigation module
object AppRoutes {
    const val HOME_GRAPH = "home_graph"
    const val AUTH_GRAPH = "auth_graph"
}

// :feature:home module — extension function adds its destinations
fun NavGraphBuilder.homeGraph(navController: NavHostController) {
    navigation(startDestination = "home", route = AppRoutes.HOME_GRAPH) {
        composable("home") { HomeScreen(navController) }
        composable("product/{id}") { backStackEntry ->
            ProductScreen(backStackEntry.arguments?.getString("id")!!)
        }
    }
}

// :feature:auth module
fun NavGraphBuilder.authGraph(navController: NavHostController) {
    navigation(startDestination = "login", route = AppRoutes.AUTH_GRAPH) {
        composable("login") { LoginScreen(navController) }
        composable("register") { RegisterScreen(navController) }
    }
}

// :app module — assembles all graphs
@Composable
fun AppNavHost() {
    val navController = rememberNavController()
    NavHost(navController, startDestination = AppRoutes.HOME_GRAPH) {
        homeGraph(navController)
        authGraph(navController)
    }
}
Each feature module defines a NavGraphBuilder extension function. The :app module assembles them. No feature module depends on another feature module — they only depend on :core:navigation.
Senior/Scenario [Debug] Deep links from FCM notifications open the app but land on the wrong screen. What are the possible causes?
Common causes:
1. Wrong intent handling: The intent from the FCM PendingIntent is not being passed to the NavController. In a single-Activity setup, the NavController processes incoming Intents from handleDeepLink(intent) — this happens automatically if you use NavHost, but the Activity must call navController.handleDeepLink(intent) in onNewIntent().
2. Route mismatch: The URI pattern in navDeepLink{} doesn't match the URI in the notification exactly (trailing slash, query params, case sensitivity).
3. Missing intent-filter: The deep link intent-filter in AndroidManifest.xml doesn't match the URI scheme/host/path.
4. Auth state not ready: The NavHost starts with the unauthenticated start destination and navigates to login before the deep link is processed.
Fix: Add logging to navController.addOnDestinationChangedListener{} to trace every navigation. Verify URI patterns with adb: adb shell am start -W -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d "https://myapp.com/orders/123".

● Android Interview Prep

8A — Architecture Patterns

MVC, MVP, MVVM, MVI — what each solves and its trade-offs. Full layered architecture: UI → ViewModel → UseCase → Repository → Data Sources. When to use each pattern.

ID: 8A ⭐ Tier 1
🔍
1. Overview

Why architecture patterns matter

Architecture patterns solve the same fundamental problem: separation of concerns. In Android, without architecture, Activities and Fragments become God objects — containing business logic, UI code, data fetching, and state management all tangled together. The result: untestable, fragile, impossible-to-maintain code.

The evolution

  • MVC — classic pattern; Controller = Activity; View = XML; Model = data; Controller too big
  • MVP — Presenter separates logic; testable; but Presenter leaks View references; boilerplate
  • MVVM — ViewModel + LiveData/StateFlow; lifecycle-aware; two-way binding optional; Android recommended
  • MVI — strict UDF; immutable state; sealed Intents; single state object; most predictable
Senior Mental Model
In interviews, say: "We use MVVM with Clean Architecture layers — UI → ViewModel → UseCase → Repository → Remote/Local data sources. UseCases encapsulate single business rules, making them independently testable. Repository provides a single data access abstraction, hiding whether data comes from network or cache. We could layer MVI on top of MVVM if we need stricter state management."
⚙
2. MVC, MVP, MVVM

MVC — Model-View-Controller

LayerAndroid mappingResponsibility
ModelData classes, DB, APIBusiness data and logic
ViewXML layoutsDisplay only
ControllerActivity / FragmentGlue — handles events, updates View, calls Model

Problem: In Android, Activity is both Controller AND part of the lifecycle. Business logic in Activity = untestable. God Activity anti-pattern.

MVP — Model-View-Presenter

LayerAndroid mappingResponsibility
ModelRepository, data layerData and business logic
ViewActivity/Fragment (behind interface)UI only, delegates all logic
PresenterPlain Kotlin classBusiness logic, mediates between View and Model

Improvement: Presenter is testable (no Android deps). Problem: Presenter holds a View reference → memory leaks on rotation. Weak references or detach pattern needed. 1:1 Presenter-View coupling is boilerplate-heavy.

MVVM — Model-View-ViewModel

// View observes ViewModel state — no direct reference from VM to View
class OrderViewModel(
    private val placeOrder: PlaceOrderUseCase
) : ViewModel() {

    // ViewModel never holds a reference to View/Activity
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow(OrderState())
    val state: StateFlow<OrderState> = _state.asStateFlow()

    fun submitOrder(order: Order) {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            _state.update { it.copy(isLoading = true) }
            val result = placeOrder(order)
            _state.update { it.copy(isLoading = false, result = result) }
        }
    }
}
// View lifecycle: Activity destroyed → ViewModel survives rotation
// View lifecycle: navigated away → ViewModel.onCleared() called
⚗
3. MVI — Model-View-Intent

MVI takes UDF to its strictest form: a single immutable state object, sealed class Intents (user actions), and pure reducers that produce new state from old state + intent. No side effects in state — everything is explicit.

// Intent: sealed class representing all possible user actions
sealed class TransferIntent {
    data class AmountChanged(val amount: String) : TransferIntent()
    data class RecipientSelected(val id: String) : TransferIntent()
    object SubmitTransfer : TransferIntent()
}

// State: single immutable data class
data class TransferState(
    val amount: String = "",
    val recipientId: String? = null,
    val isLoading: Boolean = false,
    val error: String? = null,
    val isSuccess: Boolean = false
)

// ViewModel processes intents → produces new state
class TransferViewModel : ViewModel() {
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow(TransferState())
    val state = _state.asStateFlow()

    fun processIntent(intent: TransferIntent) {
        when (intent) {
            is TransferIntent.AmountChanged ->
                _state.update { it.copy(amount = intent.amount) }
            is TransferIntent.RecipientSelected ->
                _state.update { it.copy(recipientId = intent.id) }
            TransferIntent.SubmitTransfer -> submitTransfer()
        }
    }

    private fun submitTransfer() {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            _state.update { it.copy(isLoading = true) }
            // ... call use case
        }
    }
}
📊
4. Clean Architecture Layers
UI Layer (Compose Screens + ViewModels)
    ↕ StateFlow / Events
Domain Layer (UseCases / Interactors)
    ↕ suspend functions / Flow<T>
Data Layer (Repositories)
    ↕ suspend functions / Flow<T>
Data Sources (Remote API + Room DB + Preferences)

Each layer's responsibilities

// UI Layer: display state, forward events
@Composable
fun TransferScreen(viewModel: TransferViewModel) {
    val state by viewModel.state.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    /* render state, send intents to viewModel */
}

// Domain Layer: business rules, no Android deps
class ValidateTransferUseCase {
    operator fun invoke(
        amount: BigDecimal, balance: BigDecimal
    ): ValidationResult = when {
        amount <= BigDecimal.ZERO -> ValidationResult.InvalidAmount
        amount > balance -> ValidationResult.InsufficientFunds
        else -> ValidationResult.Valid
    }
}

class ExecuteTransferUseCase(
    private val repository: TransferRepository
) {
    suspend operator fun invoke(
        from: Account, to: Account, amount: BigDecimal
    ): Result<Transfer> = runCatching {
        repository.executeTransfer(from.id, to.id, amount)
    }
}

// Data Layer: data access abstraction
interface TransferRepository {
    suspend fun executeTransfer(fromId: String, toId: String, amount: BigDecimal): Transfer
}

class TransferRepositoryImpl(
    private val remoteApi: TransferApi,    // Retrofit
    private val localDao: TransferDao     // Room
) : TransferRepository {
    override suspend fun executeTransfer(fromId: String, toId: String, amount: BigDecimal): Transfer {
        val transfer = remoteApi.postTransfer(TransferRequest(fromId, toId, amount))
        localDao.insert(transfer.toEntity())
        return transfer
    }
}
🏭
5. Production Example

Banking: full transfer flow with all layers

// ViewModel: MVVM orchestrator
class TransferViewModel(
    private val validateTransfer: ValidateTransferUseCase,
    private val executeTransfer: ExecuteTransferUseCase,
    private val getAccount: GetAccountUseCase
) : ViewModel() {

    val uiState: StateFlow<TransferUiState> =
        getAccount()
            .map { account -> TransferUiState(balance = account.formattedBalance()) }
            .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), TransferUiState.Loading)

    private val _events = MutableSharedFlow<TransferEvent>(extraBufferCapacity = 1)
    val events = _events.asSharedFlow()

    fun submitTransfer(amount: BigDecimal, recipientId: String) {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            val account = (uiState.value as? TransferUiState.Ready)?.account ?: return@launch

            val validation = validateTransfer(amount, account.balance)
            if (validation != ValidationResult.Valid) {
                _events.emit(TransferEvent.ValidationError(validation))
                return@launch
            }

            executeTransfer(account, recipientId, amount)
                .onSuccess { _events.emit(TransferEvent.Success(it)) }
                .onFailure { _events.emit(TransferEvent.Error(it)) }
        }
    }
}

Comparison table — when to choose each

PatternTestabilityComplexityBest for
MVCPoor (logic in Activity)LowPrototypes only
MVPGood (Presenter pure)MediumLegacy codebases
MVVMExcellentMediumMost Android apps — Google recommended
MVIExcellent + auditableHighComplex flows with many state transitions (checkout, onboarding)
⚠
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1 — Fat ViewModel
Moving all business logic to the ViewModel without UseCases creates a "Fat ViewModel" anti-pattern — the same problem as Fat Controller in MVC, just moved. UseCases should encapsulate discrete business rules; the ViewModel should only orchestrate them.
Pitfall 2 — Repository doing too much
The Repository should be a clean data access abstraction — not the place for business logic. If a Repository method is called "validateAndSaveIfFundsAvailable", the validate part belongs in a UseCase, not the Repository.
Pitfall 3 — Domain layer depending on Android
UseCases should be pure Kotlin with zero Android dependencies — no Context, no ViewModel, no Room entities. This is what makes them unit-testable with JUnit without Robolectric.
Best Practice — Repository interface in domain layer
Define the Repository interface in the domain layer, implementation in the data layer. This inverts the dependency — data layer depends on domain, not the other way. Enables mocking in UseCase tests without a real DB or network.
🎯
7. Interview Framework

30-second answer

"We use MVVM with Clean Architecture. The UI layer has Compose composables and ViewModels. ViewModels expose StateFlow and receive events. The domain layer has UseCases — pure Kotlin, no Android deps, one business rule each. The data layer has Repositories that abstract Remote API and local Room database. Dependencies only flow inward: UI → Domain ← Data."

2-minute answer

"The architecture evolution: MVC had Activity as the Controller — god class, untestable. MVP extracted a Presenter but it held a View reference, causing memory leaks on rotation. MVVM solved this — ViewModel survives rotation, never holds a View reference, exposes observable state that the View subscribes to. Android Jetpack's ViewModel + LiveData/StateFlow makes MVVM lifecycle-safe.

On top of MVVM, Clean Architecture adds layers: UI calls UseCases, not Repositories directly. Each UseCase does one thing and is unit-testable without Robolectric. Repository interfaces live in the domain layer — implementations in the data layer — this inverts the dependency, enabling proper mocking in tests.

MVI adds stricter UDF on top: sealed class Intents describe all actions, a single immutable State describes all UI state, and a reducer maps Intent + State → new State. It's more boilerplate but makes complex checkout-style flows auditable — you can replay every state transition."

Must-mention points

1
MVVM + Clean Architecture = the Android standard; ViewModel has no View reference
2
UseCases = pure Kotlin — no Android deps, one business rule, independently testable
3
Repository interface in domain — dependency inversion; data layer depends on domain
4
MVI = strict UDF — sealed Intents, single immutable state, for complex flows
5
Layer diagram: UI → ViewModel → UseCase → Repository → API/DB

Follow-up Q&A

Q: "Why use a UseCase between ViewModel and Repository?"

A: Three reasons: (1) Testability — UseCases can be unit-tested with JUnit, injecting a mock Repository. (2) Reuse — multiple ViewModels can use the same UseCase without duplicating logic. (3) Single responsibility — each UseCase encapsulates exactly one business rule. Without UseCases, business logic leaks into ViewModels, making them fat and hard to test.

Q: "When would you choose MVI over MVVM?"

A: For complex, multi-step flows with many possible states and transitions — checkout flows, onboarding, complex forms with multiple validation rules. MVI's single state object and sealed Intents make the state machine explicit and auditable. You can log every Intent and replay the state transitions for debugging. For simpler screens (list + detail), MVVM is less boilerplate and equally appropriate.

Senior insight

Senior Insight
In a banking app, we use MVVM for most screens but MVI for the payment flow. The payment screen has 12+ possible states (form idle, amount entered, recipient selected, validating, payment pending, 3DS challenge, success, various error states). MVI's sealed state class makes every state explicit — no boolean flags, no "can this be null here?" guessing. The reducer is a pure function — testable with exhaustive when expressions. This is exactly the kind of complex flow where MVI pays its boilerplate cost.
📋

MVP:  Presenter + View interface

Layer diagram

     ↕ StateFlow
Domain: UseCase (pure Kotlin)
     ↕ interface
Data: RepositoryImpl
     ↕
Remote API + Room DB

UseCase pattern

class GetUserUseCase(
    private val repo: UserRepository // interface
) {
    suspend operator fun invoke(id: String) =
        repo.getUser(id)

sealed class Intent { ... }

❓
9. Interview Questions
What is the main problem with MVC in Android?
Basic⌄
In Android MVC, Activity/Fragment acts as the Controller. This creates a God Class — Activities handle button clicks, network calls, database queries, navigation, lifecycle management, and UI updates all in one place. The Controller is tightly coupled to Android SDK, making it untestable with JUnit. It's also lifecycle-unsafe: the Controller is destroyed on rotation, interrupting ongoing work.
What is the key difference between MVP and MVVM?
Basic⌄
In MVP, the Presenter holds a direct reference to the View interface and calls methods on it — tight coupling that requires careful lifecycle management (detach on destroy). In MVVM, the ViewModel exposes observable state (LiveData/StateFlow) and never holds a View reference. The View subscribes and unsubscribes independently. This makes MVVM lifecycle-safe automatically — ViewModel survives rotation, View re-subscribes on recreation.
Why use UseCases between ViewModel and Repository?
Basic⌄
Three reasons: (1) Single Responsibility — each UseCase encapsulates one business rule; (2) Testability — UseCases are pure Kotlin, no Android dependencies, unit-testable with JUnit using mock Repositories; (3) Reuse — multiple ViewModels can use the same UseCase. Without UseCases, business logic accumulates in ViewModels (Fat ViewModel anti-pattern) or Repositories.
What is MVI and how does it differ from MVVM?
Intermediate⌄
MVI (Model-View-Intent) enforces strict UDF with three components: sealed Intent class (all user actions explicit), immutable State data class (all UI state in one object), and a reducer (Intent + State → new State). Unlike MVVM where ViewModels may have multiple state flows and methods, MVI has one state object and one entry point (processIntent). This makes state transitions auditable and the complete state machine visible. Tradeoff: more boilerplate.
Where should the Repository interface be defined — in the domain layer or data layer?
Intermediate⌄
Domain layer. This is the Dependency Inversion Principle — the domain layer should not depend on the data layer. By defining the interface in domain and the implementation in data, the data layer depends on the domain (not the other way). This means UseCases can reference the interface without knowing about Retrofit or Room. In tests, you inject a fake Repository that implements the domain interface — zero Android SDK needed.
What dependencies should a UseCase have?
Intermediate⌄
Only Repository interfaces (defined in domain) and other UseCases or domain services. A UseCase should have zero Android SDK dependencies — no Context, no ViewModel, no Room entities, no Retrofit annotations. This purity makes it unit-testable with plain JUnit5. If you find yourself adding import android.* in a UseCase, that's a code smell — the logic probably belongs in the data layer or a domain-specific service.
When would you choose MVI over MVVM for a feature?
Intermediate⌄
Use MVI when a screen has many possible states and transitions that are hard to track with boolean flags across multiple StateFlows — checkout flows, complex onboarding, multi-step forms, game UIs. MVI's single state object makes every combination of booleans explicit; you can't have an "impossible state" (loading AND error simultaneously) if the State is a sealed class. Use MVVM for simpler screens — list/detail, settings, profile — where the overhead of sealed Intents and reducers isn't justified.
A junior dev put network retry logic in the ViewModel. Is this correct? Where should it go?
Senior⌄
Not correct for reusable retry logic. Network retry is a data-layer concern — it applies regardless of which screen triggers the request. Retry logic belongs in: (1) Repository (retryWhen on Flow, or manual retry in suspend function), or (2) a generic data source interceptor (OkHttp Interceptor for HTTP retries). The ViewModel should handle UI state for retries (show retry button, update loading state) but not implement the retry policy itself. If it's a business-level retry (e.g., retry payment only if network error, not if card declined), a UseCase can add retry semantics before calling the repository.
How would you test a UseCase that executes a bank transfer?
Senior⌄
class ExecuteTransferUseCaseTest { private val fakeRepo = FakeTransferRepository(); private val sut = ExecuteTransferUseCase(fakeRepo); @Test fun `transfer succeeds when funds available`() = runTest { val result = sut(fromAccount, toAccount, 100.toBigDecimal()); assertTrue(result.isSuccess); assertEquals(1, fakeRepo.recordedTransfers.size) }; @Test fun `transfer fails when API throws`() = runTest { fakeRepo.shouldThrow = IOException(); val result = sut(fromAccount, toAccount, 100.toBigDecimal()); assertTrue(result.isFailure) } }. FakeTransferRepository implements the domain interface — no Retrofit, no Room, no Hilt. Tests run on JVM in milliseconds.
Design the full architecture for a real-time price tracking screen in a banking app.
Senior⌄
UI: Compose screen collecting StateFlow. ViewModel: exposes PriceScreenState via stateIn(WhileSubscribed(5000)); uses SubscribeToPriceUpdatesUseCase. UseCase: SubscribeToPriceUpdatesUseCase(repo): returns Flow<PriceUpdate> — pure kotlin, composable with Flow operators. Repository interface (in domain): PriceRepository.observePrices(symbols): Flow<PriceUpdate>. Repository impl (in data): bridges WebSocket via callbackFlow; shareIn(appScope, WhileSubscribed(5000)) to share one socket among multiple subscribers. Local fallback: Room observeLatestPrices() on network error. Dependencies: ViewModel depends on UseCase; UseCase depends on Repository interface; RepositoryImpl depends on WebSocket client and Room DAO.
