16A — BroadcastReceiver

Inter-process and system event messaging: Static vs Dynamic receivers, modern API 26+ broadcast limits, receiver security permissions, ordered broadcasts, and goAsync().

ID: 16A ⭐ Tier 3 (System Components)
🚀
1. Overview & Receiver Types

A BroadcastReceiver is an Android system component that listens for system-wide broadcast announcements (e.g. battery low, screen on, boot completed) or custom inter-app / intra-app intents.

Static vs Dynamic Receivers
  • Static (Manifest-Declared): Declared in AndroidManifest.xml. The OS will instantiate the app process if needed to deliver the broadcast. Severely restricted since Android 8.0 (API 26) to prevent battery drain.
  • Dynamic (Context-Registered): Registered at runtime via context.registerReceiver() and tied to the lifecycle of the registering component (Activity, Service, or Application). Required on API 33+ to specify RECEIVER_EXPORTED or RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED.
⚙
2. How It Works Under the Hood

1. onReceive() Execution & Threading

BroadcastReceiver.onReceive(context, intent) runs synchronously on the Main Thread. The Android OS imposes a strict 10-second timeout before flagging the receiver with an ANR.

2. goAsync() for Background Work

If work cannot finish synchronously within milliseconds, call goAsync():

class HeavyBroadcastReceiver : BroadcastReceiver() {
    override fun onReceive(context: Context, intent: Intent) {
        val pendingResult: PendingResult = goAsync()
        CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO).launch {
            try {
                performShortWork()
            } finally {
                pendingResult.finish() // Must be called to release the WakeLock/receiver
            }
        }
    }
}

3. Ordered Broadcasts (sendOrderedBroadcast)

Broadcasts sent via sendOrderedBroadcast() are delivered to one receiver at a time in order of android:priority. A higher-priority receiver can:

  • Mutate broadcast extras via setResultData() or setResultExtras().
  • Completely terminate propagation via abortBroadcast().
🖈
3. Modern Restrictions & Security

Android 8.0 (API 26+) Implicit Broadcast Exceptions

Apps targeting API 26+ cannot register manifest receivers for implicit broadcasts, with few exceptions (e.g., ACTION_BOOT_COMPLETED, ACTION_LOCALE_CHANGED, ACTION_MY_PACKAGE_REPLACED). Broadcasts like CONNECTIVITY_ACTION must be registered dynamically or replaced with ConnectivityManager.NetworkCallback.

Android 13 (API 33+) Exported Receiver Flag

When calling registerReceiver(), you MUST pass either Context.RECEIVER_EXPORTED or Context.RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED. Omitting this flag throws a SecurityException.

Securing Broadcasts

  • Receiver Permission: Add android:permission="com.example.MY_PERMISSION" to restrict who can send intents to your receiver.
  • Sender Permission: Pass a permission string to sendBroadcast(intent, "com.example.MY_PERMISSION") to ensure only authorized apps receive it.
  • Intra-App State: For purely in-app events, replace broadcasts with Kotlin SharedFlow or Channel.
💻
4. Production Example (Dynamic Network / Airplane Mode Listener)
class ConnectivityMonitorActivity : ComponentActivity() {

    private val airplaneModeReceiver = object : BroadcastReceiver() {
        override fun onReceive(context: Context, intent: Intent) {
            val isAirplaneModeOn = intent.getBooleanExtra("state", false)
            updateAirplaneModeBanner(isAirplaneModeOn)
        }
    }

    override fun onStart() {
        super.onStart()
        val filter = IntentFilter(Intent.ACTION_AIRPLANE_MODE_CHANGED)
        if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= Build.VERSION_CODES.TIRAMISU) {
            registerReceiver(airplaneModeReceiver, filter, Context.RECEIVER_EXPORTED)
        } else {
            registerReceiver(airplaneModeReceiver, filter)
        }
    }

    override fun onStop() {
        super.onStop()
        unregisterReceiver(airplaneModeReceiver)
    }
}
⚖
5. Alternatives & Trade-offs
MechanismScopeSecurityModern Recommendation
Dynamic BroadcastReceiver System / Cross-app Requires flags / permissions Use for OS events (e.g. Battery, USB)
Static Manifest Receiver System (Boot/Package) Exported by default Use ONLY for BOOT_COMPLETED
SharedFlow / StateFlow In-app Process 100% private to JVM process Standard for intra-app events
NetworkCallback Network state Direct system callback Replaces CONNECTIVITY_ACTION
⚠
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1: Leaking Dynamic Receivers

Registering in onStart() without unregistering in onStop() (or onResume() / onPause()) causes an IntentReceiverLeaked error and keeps the surrounding Activity in memory.

Pitfall 2: Launching Async Coroutines without goAsync()

Once onReceive() returns, the Android OS considers the broadcast handled and reduces the process priority. Any background thread launched inside without goAsync() may be abruptly killed by the OS low memory killer.

Pitfall 3: Using LocalBroadcastManager (Deprecated)

LocalBroadcastManager was deprecated in Jetpack. For internal app messaging, use Kotlin Coroutines (SharedFlow, Channel, or EventBus pattern).

🎤
7. Interview Framework

30-Second Elevator Pitch

"BroadcastReceiver is an Android component for receiving system-wide or cross-app Intent broadcasts. Static receivers are declared in the manifest but restricted since API 26, while dynamic receivers are registered at runtime with mandatory RECEIVER_EXPORTED/NOT_EXPORTED flags in API 33+. onReceive runs on the main thread with a 10s timeout, extendable via goAsync()."

2-Minute Deep Dive

"BroadcastReceivers enable loosely coupled publish-subscribe messaging in Android. Under API 26 background execution limits, implicit broadcasts cannot be registered statically in the manifest, except for exempted actions like ACTION_BOOT_COMPLETED. For dynamic registration, API 33 requires explicitly specifying RECEIVER_EXPORTED or RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED for security.

onReceive() executes on the Main thread. If async work is needed, goAsync() returns a PendingResult, keeping the process alive until pendingResult.finish() is called. For ordered broadcasts, receivers process intents sequentially based on priority, allowing modifications via setResultData() or cancellation via abortBroadcast(). For intra-app communication, we favor Kotlin SharedFlow over deprecated LocalBroadcastManager."

Must-Mention Checklist

1
Static vs Dynamic: Manifest vs runtime registration lifecycles.
2
API 26 Restrictions: Prohibition of static implicit broadcasts.
3
API 33 Flags: RECEIVER_EXPORTED vs RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED.
4
Threading & goAsync(): 10s main thread limit and asynchronous delegation.
⚡
8. Quick Revision Sheet

RECEIVER BASICS

onReceive(context, intent) -> Main Thread
Timeout                    -> 10 seconds (ANR)
goAsync()                  -> Asynchronous extension
finish()                   -> Completes goAsync

API 33+ REGISTRATION

registerReceiver(
    receiver, filter,
    Context.RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED // Or EXPORTED
)

ORDERED BROADCASTS

sendOrderedBroadcast(intent, permission)
abortBroadcast()    // Stop propagation
setResultData()     // Alter downstream data
priority in filter  // Higher integer fires first

MODERN REPLACEMENTS

LocalBroadcastManager -> SharedFlow / Channel
CONNECTIVITY_ACTION   -> NetworkCallback
Static receivers      -> WorkManager / Dynamic
❓
9. Interview Questions (Self-Check)

Basic Questions

B1 — What is the execution time limit for BroadcastReceiver.onReceive()?
Easy▼
The execution time limit is 10 seconds on the main thread. If onReceive() blocks for more than 10 seconds, the Android OS flags the receiver with an Application Not Responding (ANR) dialog.
B2 — What is the difference between static and dynamic receivers?
Easy▼
Static receivers are declared in AndroidManifest.xml and can wake up a cold process when the broadcast fires. Dynamic receivers are registered at runtime using context.registerReceiver() and are only active during the lifecycle of the registering component.
B3 — What flag is required when dynamically registering a receiver on Android 13 (API 33)+?
Easy▼
You must pass either Context.RECEIVER_EXPORTED (if other apps can send broadcasts to it) or Context.RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED (if restricted to your app and the system). Omitting this parameter throws a runtime SecurityException.

Intermediate Questions

I1 — How does goAsync() work and why is it needed?
Medium▼
goAsync() returns a PendingResult object and informs the OS that the receiver intends to complete its work asynchronously on a background thread. This prevents the OS from considering the broadcast completed immediately upon onReceive() return and lowering process priority. Once work finishes, the worker must call pendingResult.finish().
I2 — Why can't you register a static receiver for CONNECTIVITY_ACTION on Android 8.0+?
Medium▼
Android 8.0 (API 26) introduced Background Execution Limits to prevent battery drain. Because network changes occur frequently, waking up hundreds of apps via static broadcast receivers caused severe battery depletion. Apps must use dynamic registration or ConnectivityManager.registerNetworkCallback() instead.
I3 — How do Ordered Broadcasts work?
Medium▼
Sent via sendOrderedBroadcast(), intents are delivered sequentially to receivers based on priority (defined in android:priority). Each receiver can read/modify results via getResultExtras() and setResultData(), or stop further delivery entirely by invoking abortBroadcast().
I4 — How do you restrict a broadcast so that only specific apps can receive it?
Medium▼
1. Define a custom permission in the sender app manifest (e.g. signature protection level).
2. Call sendBroadcast(intent, "com.example.CUSTOM_PERMISSION").
3. Receiver apps must declare <uses-permission android:name="com.example.CUSTOM_PERMISSION" /> signed with the same developer certificate.

Senior & Scenario Questions

S1 — How do you handle ACTION_BOOT_COMPLETED to schedule alarms in an Android 14 app?
HardScenario▼
1. Declare RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED permission in manifest.
2. Register static receiver for android.intent.action.BOOT_COMPLETED.
3. In onReceive(), call goAsync() or enqueue a WorkManager OneTimeWorkRequest to read scheduled alarms from Room DB and register them with AlarmManager. (WorkManager is preferred to avoid ANRs during heavy post-boot device load).
S2 — Why was LocalBroadcastManager deprecated and what is the modern Kotlin replacement?
HardScenario▼
LocalBroadcastManager was deprecated because it relied on global Intent serialization and Context references for what is fundamentally an in-process pub-sub pattern. The modern replacement is Kotlin Coroutines using MutableSharedFlow (or Channel for single-subscriber events), which provides compile-time type safety, zero IPC serialization overhead, and seamless lifecycle awareness.
S3 — An app receives an SMS broadcast via an ordered receiver to parse 2FA OTP. How do you prevent other apps from reading it?
HardScenario▼
Historically, apps used high-priority ordered receivers and called abortBroadcast(), but modern Android restricts SMS broadcast manipulation. The modern, secure Google-recommended solution is the SMS Retriever API (or SMS User Consent API), which delivers the 2FA SMS exclusively to your app without requiring the sensitive RECEIVE_SMS permission.

17A — ContentProvider

Secure inter-app data sharing, ContentResolver clients, URI syntax, MIME conventions, Binder IPC architecture, and FileProvider integration.

ID: 17A ⭐ Tier 3 (System Components)
🚀
1. Overview & Architecture

A ContentProvider encapsulates data and provides it to applications through a standardized, uniform interface. It is the primary Android abstraction for secure inter-process data sharing (e.g. Contacts, MediaStore, DocumentsProvider, FileProvider).

End-to-End IPC Architecture

App A (Client) → ContentResolver.query() → Binder IPC (IContentProvider) → App B (ContentProvider) → SQLite / File System

⚙
2. How It Works Under the Hood

1. Threading & Lifecycle

  • onCreate() runs on the Main Thread of the hosting process before Application.onCreate()! Keep it fast.
  • CRUD methods (query(), insert(), update(), delete(), call()) run on a Binder thread pool and MUST be thread-safe.

2. URI Structure & UriMatcher

content://com.example.bank.provider/accounts/1234
\_____/  \________________________/\_______/\___/
Scheme           Authority           Path    ID

3. Standard MIME Types (getType)

  • Directory / List: vnd.android.cursor.dir/vnd.com.example.account
  • Single Item: vnd.android.cursor.item/vnd.com.example.account

4. Cursor Iteration & Lifecycle

Always close cursors via use {} to prevent native memory leaks:

context.contentResolver.query(uri, projection, selection, args, sortOrder)?.use { cursor ->
    val idIndex = cursor.getColumnIndexOrThrow("_id")
    val nameIndex = cursor.getColumnIndexOrThrow("account_name")
    while (cursor.moveToNext()) {
        val id = cursor.getLong(idIndex)
        val name = cursor.getString(nameIndex)
    }
}
🖈
3. When to Use & FileProvider

When is a ContentProvider Required?

  • Sharing relational data or files with other external applications.
  • Providing custom search suggestions to Android System Search.
  • Exposing documents via DocumentsProvider (Storage Access Framework).
  • Sharing files securely (camera images, PDF exports) via FileProvider.

FileProvider: Secure File Sharing

Direct file:// URIs are forbidden since Android 7.0 (API 24) and throw FileUriExposedException. FileProvider creates temporary content:// URIs granted with transient read/write permissions via FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION.

💻
4. Production Example (FileProvider Camera & PDF Sharing)
// 1. res/xml/file_paths.xml
// <paths>
//     <cache-path name="shared_docs" path="reports/" />
// </paths>

// 2. Sharing a generated PDF invoice
fun sharePdfInvoice(context: Context, pdfFile: File) {
    val contentUri: Uri = FileProvider.getUriForFile(
        context,
        "${context.packageName}.fileprovider",
        pdfFile
    )

    val shareIntent = Intent(Intent.ACTION_SEND).apply {
        type = "application/pdf"
        putExtra(Intent.EXTRA_STREAM, contentUri)
        addFlags(Intent.FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION)
    }

    context.startActivity(Intent.createChooser(shareIntent, "Share Invoice"))
}
⚖
5. Alternatives & Trade-offs
ApproachIPC MechanismSecurityBest For
ContentProvider Binder (Shared memory / CursorWindow) URI & manifest permissions Structured relational data & system providers
FileProvider Binder with transient URI grants Scoped to granted URI Exporting images, PDF, documents
AIDL Bound Service Direct Binder IPC Signature permissions Method invocation / RPC streaming
Room DB (In-app) None (Process local) Private sandbox App internal persistent storage
⚠
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1: Slow Operations in onCreate() Delaying App Startup

ContentProviders are initialized BEFORE Application.onCreate(). Running heavy database migrations or network calls in ContentProvider.onCreate() will delay entire app launch and freeze cold starts.

Pitfall 2: Exported ContentProvider without Permissions

Setting android:exported="true" without android:readPermission / android:writePermission exposes private user data to every other app on the device (major security vulnerability).

Pitfall 3: CursorWindowAllocationException (1MB / 2MB Limit)

Android's Binder CursorWindow has a strict 2 MB memory buffer limit across IPC. Querying huge blobs or thousands of rows in one query throws a CursorWindowAllocationException. Always paginate with LIMIT and OFFSET.

🎤
7. Interview Framework

30-Second Elevator Pitch

"ContentProvider is Android's framework component for cross-process data and file sharing. Clients interact through ContentResolver using standardized URIs. Its onCreate runs on the main thread during startup, while query/insert/update/delete run on Binder worker threads. For secure file sharing, FileProvider generates scoped content URIs with transient read/write permissions."

2-Minute Deep Dive

"Architecturally, ContentProvider sits on top of Android Binder IPC. When an app calls ContentResolver.query(), the Binder marshals data through a shared memory CursorWindow (capped at 2MB). URIs follow the format content://authority/path/id and are matched via UriMatcher.

Security is enforced via android:readPermission, android:writePermission, and grantUriPermissions. Since Android 7.0 banned raw file:// URIs, FileProvider is the industry standard for sharing PDFs, camera photos, or cache files via Intent.FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION. For purely internal app storage, Room DB is preferred over building custom ContentProviders."

Must-Mention Checklist

1
IPC Flow: ContentResolver → Binder IPC → ContentProvider → SQLite/Disk.
2
FileProvider: Replaces file:// to prevent FileUriExposedException.
3
Cursor Management: use {} closure to prevent native memory leaks.
4
Threading Model: onCreate() on main thread; CRUD on Binder thread pool.
⚡
8. Quick Revision Sheet

URI ANATOMY

content://com.pkg.provider/table/1
Scheme   : content://
Authority: com.pkg.provider
Path     : table
ID       : 1

MIME PATTERNS

Directory -> vnd.android.cursor.dir/vnd.<auth>.<type>
Single    -> vnd.android.cursor.item/vnd.<auth>.<type>

FILEPROVIDER SETUP

1. file_paths.xml (cache-path, files-path)
2. <provider> in AndroidManifest
3. FileProvider.getUriForFile()
4. FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION

CORE PITFALLS

onCreate() runs before Application.onCreate()!
CursorWindow max 2 MB -> Always paginate!
Never leak Cursor -> use cursor.use { }
❓
9. Interview Questions (Self-Check)

Basic Questions

B1 — What is the primary purpose of a ContentProvider?
Easy▼
A ContentProvider manages access to a structured set of data and encapsulates data security. It is the standard Android mechanism for sharing data securely between different application processes (IPC) and with the Android OS (e.g., Contacts, MediaStore).
B2 — Why is FileProvider required on Android 7.0 (API 24)+?
Easy▼
Sharing raw file:// URIs across apps was prohibited in API 24 to prevent security vulnerabilities and throws a FileUriExposedException. FileProvider generates secure content:// URIs and grants temporary, scoped read/write permissions via Intent flags.
B3 — What does Cursor.use { } accomplish in Kotlin?
Easy▼
Cursor implements Closeable. The use { } inline extension executes the given block and guarantees that cursor.close() is called in a finally block, even if an exception occurs, preventing native cursor window memory leaks.

Intermediate Questions

I1 — On which thread does ContentProvider.onCreate() run vs query()?
Medium▼
onCreate() executes on the Main Thread of the application process when the provider is initialized. In contrast, query(), insert(), update(), and delete() run on Binder worker threads (from the IPC Binder thread pool) and must be implemented in a thread-safe manner.
I2 — What is the purpose of ContentProvider.getType(uri)?
Medium▼
getType(Uri) returns the MIME type of data associated with the given URI. By convention, returning a collection/list uses vnd.android.cursor.dir/..., while returning an individual row/item uses vnd.android.cursor.item/....
I3 — What causes a CursorWindowAllocationException?
Medium▼
When data is returned across process boundaries via Binder, it is copied into a shared memory buffer called CursorWindow, which has a default size limit of 2 MB. If a query attempts to load massive image blobs or unpaginated millions of rows exceeding this limit, the OS throws a CursorWindowAllocationException.
I4 — How does App Startup library utilize ContentProviders?
Medium▼
Because Android initializes ContentProviders before Application.onCreate(), libraries (like WorkManager or Firebase) historically used dummy ContentProviders for automatic zero-code initialization. Jetpack App Startup consolidates all library initializers into a single ContentProvider to eliminate startup overhead.

Senior & Scenario Questions

S1 — How do you notify UI observers when data in a ContentProvider changes?
HardScenario▼
1. In insert(), update(), and delete(), call context?.contentResolver?.notifyChange(uri, null) after mutating data.
2. In query(), call cursor.setNotificationUri(context?.contentResolver, uri).
3. The client can register a ContentObserver or use Room/Flow extensions to receive live updates whenever data matching that URI changes.
S2 — How do you securely export a ContentProvider to only apps with the same signing key?
HardScenario▼
1. Declare a custom permission in the provider app with android:protectionLevel="signature".
2. Apply android:permission="com.example.provider.READ_WRITE" to the <provider> tag in AndroidManifest.xml.
3. Any client app signed with the same developer signing certificate declaring <uses-permission> will automatically be granted access, while third-party apps will be blocked by the OS with a SecurityException.
S3 — Why shouldn't you use ContentProvider for purely internal app databases?
HardScenario▼
ContentProvider introduces significant overhead: Cursor abstraction, IPC marshalling, URI parsing via UriMatcher, and Binder transaction overhead. For in-process data management, Room Database directly returns strongly-typed Kotlin data classes and Flow streams with zero IPC overhead, full compile-time SQL query validation, and simpler testing.

18A — Navigation & Deep Linking

Jetpack Navigation Component, Compose NavHost, Type-Safe Safe Args, Deep Links vs Verified App Links, and Back Stack manipulation.

ID: 18A ⭐ Tier 2 (Core Architecture)
🚀
1. Overview & Architecture

The Jetpack Navigation Component provides a unified framework for in-app navigation, handling Fragment transactions, Compose destinations, deep linking, back stack consistency, and animations.

Three Pillars of Navigation Component
  • NavController: The central controller that tracks the current destination and swaps content.
  • NavHost: The UI container that hosts destinations (NavHostFragment in Views or NavHost() in Jetpack Compose).
  • NavGraph: The data structure defining all destinations, arguments, animations, and deep link paths.
⚙
2. How It Works Under the Hood

1. Back Stack Management (popUpTo, inclusive, launchSingleTop)

navController.navigate("home") {
    // Clears backstack up to "login", including "login" itself
    popUpTo("login") {
        inclusive = true
        saveState = true // Saves ViewModel/scroll state for bottom nav tabs
    }
    launchSingleTop = true // Avoids duplicate instances if already on top
    restoreState = true    // Restores saved state when returning
}

2. Deep Links: Implicit vs Android App Links

TypeSchemeDisambiguation Dialog?Verification
Custom Schememyapp://details/{id}Yes (if multiple apps claim)None
Web Deep Linkhttp://example.com/itemYes (prompts browser vs app)None
Android App Linkhttps://example.com/itemNo (opens app instantly)assetlinks.json on HTTPS domain
🖈
3. Compose Navigation & Type Safety

Modern Type-Safe Navigation in Compose (Navigation 2.8+)

Using Kotlin Serialization, destinations and arguments are defined as @Serializable objects or data classes instead of error-prone string URLs:

@Serializable
data class ProductDetailRoute(val productId: String, val isDiscounted: Boolean)

@Composable
fun AppNavGraph(navController: NavHostController) {
    NavHost(navController = navController, startDestination = "catalog") {
        composable<ProductDetailRoute> { backStackEntry ->
            val route: ProductDetailRoute = backStackEntry.toRoute()
            ProductDetailScreen(id = route.productId)
        }
    }
}

// Navigation call:
navController.navigate(ProductDetailRoute(productId = "SKU_450", isDiscounted = true))
💻
4. Production Example (Verified App Links & BottomNav)
// 1. AndroidManifest.xml App Link with autoVerify
// <intent-filter android:autoVerify="true">
//     <action android:name="android.intent.action.VIEW" />
//     <category android:name="android.intent.category.DEFAULT" />
//     <category android:name="android.intent.category.BROWSABLE" />
//     <data android:scheme="https" android:host="bank.example.com" android:pathPrefix="/account" />
// </intent-filter>

// 2. Compose NavHost with Deep Link Mapping
@Composable
fun BankNavHost(navController: NavHostController) {
    NavHost(navController = navController, startDestination = "dashboard") {
        composable(
            route = "account/{accountId}",
            arguments = listOf(navArgument("accountId") { type = NavType.StringType }),
            deepLinks = listOf(navDeepLink {
                uriPattern = "https://bank.example.com/account/{accountId}"
            })
        ) { backStackEntry ->
            val accountId = backStackEntry.arguments?.getString("accountId").orEmpty()
            AccountDetailsScreen(accountId = accountId)
        }
    }
}
⚖
5. Alternatives & Trade-offs
ArchitectureProsConsVerdict
Single-Activity + Jetpack Nav Unified back stack, shared ViewModels, smooth transition animations Requires discipline with NavGraph scope Industry Standard
Multi-Activity Architecture Clean OS-level separation, native task stacks High memory overhead, difficult shared transitions, fractured back stack Legacy / Rare
Custom Compose State Navigation Zero Jetpack Nav dependencies Manual back button handling, no deep linking, complex state restoration Only for micro-apps / SDKs
⚠
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1: Passing Large Complex Objects as Nav Arguments

Passing Parcelable objects or large lists in Navigation arguments violates Single Source of Truth and risks hitting the 1 MB Binder TransactionTooLargeException. Pass only entity IDs and fetch full state from the repository.

Pitfall 2: Forgetting autoVerify="true" for App Links

Without android:autoVerify="true" and a valid HTTPS /.well-known/assetlinks.json on the server domain, clicking your URL will trigger the Android system app chooser instead of opening your app directly.

Pitfall 3: Not using launchSingleTop on Tab Switches

Tapping bottom navigation tabs multiple times will pile duplicate instances of the same destination onto the back stack if launchSingleTop = true is omitted.

🎤
7. Interview Framework

30-Second Elevator Pitch

"Jetpack Navigation Component is the official framework for managing in-app routing and back stack transitions in Single-Activity and Jetpack Compose architectures. It standardizes fragment and composable routing, type-safe arguments (via Safe Args or Navigation 2.8+ @Serializable routes), bottom nav state restoration, and deep linking via verified Android App Links."

2-Minute Deep Dive

"Under the hood, Navigation relies on NavController, NavHost, and NavGraph. In Compose, NavHost maps routes to composables. Navigation 2.8 introduced compile-time type-safe navigation where routes are defined as Kotlin @Serializable classes, eliminating string parsing.

Back stack manipulation is managed via popUpTo with inclusive=true to prevent backstack memory accumulation (e.g., after login flow), along with saveState/restoreState and launchSingleTop for bottom navigation tabs. For external traffic, Android App Links (HTTPS with autoVerify='true' and assetlinks.json) open the app directly without disambiguation dialogs. We enforce passing only entity IDs through navigation arguments to respect Binder limits."

Must-Mention Checklist

1
Single-Activity Justification: Shared ViewModel scope, lighter lifecycle overhead.
2
Deep Links vs App Links: Custom scheme vs verified HTTPS assetlinks.json.
3
Back Stack DSL: popUpTo, inclusive, launchSingleTop, saveState.
4
Type Safety: Navigation 2.8+ @Serializable Kotlin routes.
⚡
8. Quick Revision Sheet

NAV OPTIONS DSL

popUpTo("login") { inclusive = true }
launchSingleTop = true
saveState = true
restoreState = true

APP LINKS VERIFICATION

1. https:// scheme only
2. android:autoVerify="true"
3. Domain hosts /.well-known/assetlinks.json
4. SHA-256 fingerprint matches app signing key

TYPE-SAFE COMPOSE NAV

@Serializable data class Route(val id: String)
composable<Route> { backStack ->
    val route: Route = backStack.toRoute()
}
navController.navigate(Route("123"))

CORE BEST PRACTICES

Pass IDs only (never Parcelables/Bitmaps)
Use single NavHost per feature or root
Share ViewModel via hiltNavGraphViewModel()
❓
9. Interview Questions (Self-Check)

Basic Questions

B1 — What is the role of NavController in Jetpack Navigation?
Easy▼
NavController is the central API that manages application navigation within a NavHost. It orchestrates the swapping of destination content, maintains the navigation back stack, and manages transitions and deep link routing.
B2 — What is the difference between popUpTo and inclusive = true?
Easy▼
popUpTo(destinationId) pops the back stack up to the specified destination. If inclusive = false (default), the target destination remains on top of the stack. If inclusive = true, the target destination is also popped off the stack.
B3 — What is the difference between a Deep Link and an Android App Link?
Easy▼
A Deep Link uses custom schemes (myapp://) or unverified HTTP/HTTPS URLs, which trigger a system disambiguation dialog asking the user to choose an app. An Android App Link is an HTTPS URL verified via a digital asset links JSON file on your domain, opening your app directly with zero disambiguation prompts.

Intermediate Questions

I1 — Why should you avoid passing complex objects (e.g. Parcelables) in Navigation arguments?
Medium▼
1. It violates Single Source of Truth (data becomes stale if updated elsewhere in DB).
2. It risks exceeding the Android 1MB Binder transaction buffer limit (TransactionTooLargeException).
3. URLs cannot easily encode large binary blobs for deep linking. Always pass unique IDs and load fresh data from the repository.
I2 — How does launchSingleTop = true protect the navigation back stack?
Medium▼
launchSingleTop = true ensures that if the destination you are navigating to is already at the top of the back stack, a new duplicate instance will not be created. This prevents rapid double-tap bugs and redundant screen stacking.
I3 — How is Type-Safe Navigation implemented in Navigation Compose 2.8+?
Medium▼
Navigation 2.8 uses Kotlinx Serialization. Instead of defining routes as strings ("detail/{id}"), routes are defined as @Serializable data classes or objects. composable<MyRoute>() generates the route schema automatically, and arguments are retrieved with backStackEntry.toRoute<MyRoute>().
I4 — What is the purpose of saveState and restoreState in NavOptions?
Medium▼
When switching between Bottom Navigation tabs, saveState = true saves the back stack and ViewModel state of the tab being left. When the user taps that tab again, restoreState = true restores its exact scroll position, back stack, and screen state.

Senior & Scenario Questions

S1 — How do you structure navigation across multiple feature modules in a modular Android project?
HardScenario▼
Create a shared :core:navigation module containing contract interfaces or @Serializable route definitions. Each feature module exposes a NavGraphBuilder.featureGraph(navController) extension function. The :app module orchestrates all feature graphs into the root NavHost, maintaining clean module decoupling and compilation independence.
S2 — How do you scope a ViewModel to a nested Navigation Graph in Jetpack Compose?
HardScenario▼
Obtain the NavBackStackEntry for the parent navigation graph using remember(backStackEntry) { navController.getBackStackEntry("parent_graph_route") }, and pass that parent entry as the ViewModelStoreOwner to hiltViewModel(parentEntry). All screens within that nested graph will share the exact same ViewModel instance until the parent graph is popped.
S3 — A user opens an App Link leading to a checkout screen when the app is closed. How do you construct the back stack so Back goes to Home?
HardScenario▼
Jetpack Navigation handles this automatically when deep links are defined inside the NavGraph or NavHost. When launched via a verified deep link Intent, Navigation creates a synthetic back stack by tracing the hierarchy from the graph's startDestination (e.g. Home) down to the target destination (Checkout), ensuring pressing Back navigates gracefully through Home before exiting.

19A — Data & Network Security

Android Sandbox, Hardware-Backed Keystore, EncryptedSharedPreferences, SQLCipher, TLS enforcement, Certificate Pinning, Network Security Config, and secrets handling.

ID: 19A ⭐ Tier 2 (Security Architecture)
🚀
1. Overview & Android Security Model

Android security relies on the Linux Application Sandbox. Each app runs with a distinct Linux User ID (UID) in its own process. By default, apps cannot access other apps' private data directories (/data/data/<package_name>).

Core Android Security Pillars
  • Hardware-Backed Keystore: Private keys and symmetric keys reside in a Secure Element / TEE (Trusted Execution Environment). Key material never enters the Android OS user space memory.
  • EncryptedSharedPreferences: AES-256 GCM encryption for key-value storage backed by a Keystore master key.
  • Network Security Config: Declarative XML rules enforcing HTTPS, disabling cleartext traffic, and configuring custom trust anchors.
  • Certificate Pinning: Restricts accepted TLS certificates to specific cryptographic public key hashes (SHA-256 pins).
⚙
2. How It Works Under the Hood

1. Android Keystore System

The Android Keystore lets apps create and use cryptographic keys without exposing key bytes to the app process or RAM. Operations (signing, decryption) are executed inside the secure hardware (TEE/StrongBox):

val keyGenerator = KeyGenerator.getInstance(
    KeyProperties.KEY_ALGORITHM_AES,
    "AndroidKeyStore"
)
val spec = KeyGenParameterSpec.Builder(
    "MyMasterKeyAlias",
    KeyProperties.PURPOSE_ENCRYPT or KeyProperties.PURPOSE_DECRYPT
)
    .setBlockModes(KeyProperties.BLOCK_MODE_GCM)
    .setEncryptionPaddings(KeyProperties.ENCRYPTION_PADDING_NONE)
    .setKeySize(256)
    .build()

keyGenerator.init(spec)
keyGenerator.generateKey()

2. EncryptedSharedPreferences (Jetpack Security)

Uses a two-tier key scheme: A Master Key stored in the Android Keystore encrypts keyset subkeys (using Tink), which encrypt the SharedPreferences values via AES-256 GCM and keys via AES-256 SIV.

🖈
3. Network Security & Certificate Pinning

1. Network Security Config (res/xml/network_security_config.xml)

<!-- Disallow all cleartext HTTP and enforce TLS -->
<network-security-config>
    <base-config cleartextTrafficPermitted="false">
        <trust-anchors>
            <certificates src="system" />
        </trust-anchors>
    </base-config>
    <domain-config>
        <domain includeSubdomains="true">api.bank.com</domain>
        <pin-set expiration="2026-12-31">
            <pin digest="SHA-256">k2v657xBsOwg11+/sgYDnU542/gGHPQFiXZq5PCmj0=</pin>
            <!-- Backup pin required for certificate rotation -->
            <pin digest="SHA-256">0Z/WvNvqA9oPj1m12Y2F4Q1aK0bFqW8lG5E4Q3P2A1=</pin>
        </pin-set>
    </domain-config>
</network-security-config>

2. OkHttp CertificatePinner

val certPinner = CertificatePinner.Builder()
    .add("api.bank.com", "sha256/k2v657xBsOwg11+/sgYDnU542/gGHPQFiXZq5PCmj0=")
    .add("api.bank.com", "sha256/0Z/WvNvqA9oPj1m12Y2F4Q1aK0bFqW8lG5E4Q3P2A1=") // Backup pin
    .build()

val okHttpClient = OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .certificatePinner(certPinner)
    .build()
💻
4. Production Example (Secure Auth Token Storage)
class SecureTokenStorage(context: Context) {

    private val masterKey = MasterKey.Builder(context)
        .setKeyScheme(MasterKey.KeyScheme.AES256_GCM)
        .build()

    private val sharedPreferences = EncryptedSharedPreferences.create(
        context,
        "secure_bank_prefs",
        masterKey,
        EncryptedSharedPreferences.PrefKeyEncryptionScheme.AES256_SIV,
        EncryptedSharedPreferences.PrefValueEncryptionScheme.AES256_GCM
    )

    fun saveAuthToken(token: String) {
        sharedPreferences.edit().putString("AUTH_JWT", token).apply()
    }

    fun getAuthToken(): String? = sharedPreferences.getString("AUTH_JWT", null)

    fun clear() = sharedPreferences.edit().clear().apply()
}
⚖
5. Alternatives & Trade-offs
Storage MechanismEncryption LevelPerformanceBest For
EncryptedSharedPreferences Hardware Keystore + AES-256 Medium Auth JWTs, session tokens, user secrets
SQLCipher for Android Full DB page-level AES-256 Slight SQL overhead (5-15%) Encrypted offline financial / health records
Standard SharedPreferences None (Plaintext XML) Fastest Non-sensitive UI settings (dark mode, layout)
Raw Android Keystore AES Direct TEE encryption Fastest crypto Custom binary file encryption
⚠
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1: Hardcoding API Secrets & Private Keys in Kotlin Code

Strings in Kotlin source code or BuildConfig are trivially extracted in seconds via jadx-gui or strings classes.dex. Sensitive backend secrets must live on a backend proxy server; client-side keys should be obfuscated with NDK C++ JNI and protected via API gateway authentication.

Pitfall 2: Single Certificate Pin Brick Hazard

Pinning a single leaf certificate without configuring a backup pin (intermediate CA or backup public key) means your app will permanently fail to connect to your backend if your production certificate expires or is revoked, requiring an emergency Play Store update.

Pitfall 3: Sensitive Logging in Release Builds (Timber)

Logging user PII, credit card details, or auth tokens via Log.d() exposes them to Android Logcat. In production, use Timber with a release tree that strips debug and sensitive logs.

🎤
7. Interview Framework

30-Second Elevator Pitch

"Android security follows defense-in-depth: the Linux UID sandbox isolates private app storage, the hardware-backed Android Keystore generates and stores cryptographic keys inside the TEE/StrongBox so raw keys never enter RAM, and EncryptedSharedPreferences protects local auth tokens. Over the wire, Network Security Config enforces TLS, and OkHttp CertificatePinner prevents Man-in-the-Middle attacks."

2-Minute Deep Dive

"At rest, sensitive tokens and keys must never be stored in plain SharedPreferences. We use Jetpack Security's EncryptedSharedPreferences, which uses a 2-tier key model: a Keystore MasterKey encrypts keyset encryption subkeys via AES-256 GCM. For relational datasets, SQLCipher encrypts SQLite databases at the page level.

In transit, Android disables cleartext HTTP by default via Network Security Config. For high-security banking endpoints, we enforce Certificate Pinning on the SPKI public key hash. To prevent app brinking during certificate rotation, we always include primary and backup pins. In code, secrets are never hardcoded; Timber release trees strip Logcat logs, and sensitive crypto operations require biometric user presence."

Must-Mention Checklist

1
Android Keystore / TEE: Keys generated and stored in secure hardware; never leave TEE.
2
EncryptedSharedPreferences: MasterKey + AES-256 GCM / SIV.
3
Certificate Pinning: Public key SHA-256 pinning + mandatory backup pins.
4
Network Security Config: cleartextTrafficPermitted="false".
⚡
8. Quick Revision Sheet

DATA AT REST

Android Keystore -> TEE / StrongBox backed
EncryptedPrefs   -> AES-256 GCM + MasterKey
SQLCipher        -> Encrypted SQLite pages
Never store      -> Plain text tokens / passwords

DATA IN TRANSIT

NetworkSecurityConfig -> Disable cleartext
CertificatePinner    -> OkHttp SHA-256 pin
Backup Pin           -> Mandatory for rotation
TLS 1.3 / 1.2        -> Modern cipher suites

SECRETS & KEYS

BuildConfig / NDK   -> Obfuscation, not encryption
Backend Proxy       -> True secret isolation
Keystore Alias      -> Hardware key reference

LOGGING & PII

Timber.plant(ReleaseTree) -> Strip debug logs
FLAG_SECURE -> Prevent screenshots / recents preview
❓
9. Interview Questions (Self-Check)

Basic Questions

B1 — How does the Android Application Sandbox isolate app data?
Easy▼
Android assigns each installed application a unique Linux User ID (UID) and runs it in an isolated process. File system permissions ensure that private directories (/data/data/<package_name>) can only be read and written by that specific UID, preventing other apps from accessing private files.
B2 — What is the primary advantage of storing keys in the Android Keystore?
Easy▼
The Android Keystore protects key material from being extracted. Keys are generated and stored inside hardware-backed secure enclaves (TEE or StrongBox). Cryptographic operations (signing, decryption) are performed inside the hardware module; raw key bytes are never exposed in the application's RAM.
B3 — What is Certificate Pinning and why is it used?
Easy▼
Certificate Pinning is a security technique where the client app hardcodes or verifies the exact cryptographic public key hash (SPKI SHA-256) of the server's certificate. This protects against Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attacks where a compromised or rogue Certificate Authority (CA) issues fraudulent certificates.

Intermediate Questions

I1 — How does EncryptedSharedPreferences work under the hood?
Medium▼
It uses Google's Tink crypto library with a 2-tier key architecture: A hardware-backed MasterKey in the Android Keystore encrypts a local keyset. Key names are deterministically encrypted using AES-256 SIV (so keys can be queried), and key values are encrypted using AES-256 GCM authenticated encryption.
I2 — Why must you always configure a backup pin when using Certificate Pinning?
Medium▼
If you pin only one certificate/key and that certificate expires, is revoked, or the server rotates keys due to a compromise, your mobile app will reject the new server certificate and permanently fail all network calls. A backup pin ensures smooth rotation without breaking existing client apps.
I3 — What is SQLCipher and how does it differ from standard Room DB?
Medium▼
Standard Room DB stores SQLite database files in plaintext on disk. SQLCipher is an open-source extension providing transparent 256-bit AES page-level encryption for the entire SQLite database file, headers, and journal data. It integrates with Room using SupportFactory(passphrase).
I4 — How do you prevent sensitive screens from appearing in Android Recents / App Switcher?
Medium▼
Call window.setFlags(WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_SECURE, WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_SECURE) in the Activity's onCreate(). This instructs the OS to treat the window surface as secure, blocking screenshots, screen recordings, and masking the window preview in the recent apps task switcher.

Senior & Scenario Questions

S1 — How do you protect a third-party payment gateway API secret in a mobile client?
HardScenario▼
Never store master payment gateway private keys in the client app code or APK. The only secure architecture is a Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) proxy: The Android client authenticates against your own secure backend with a user JWT, your backend communicates with the payment gateway using the secret key, and passes a short-lived, scoped client token/intent back to the Android app.
S2 — How would you implement biometric-bound encryption for high-value banking transactions?
HardScenario▼
1. Generate an AES key in Keystore with setUserAuthenticationRequired(true) and setUserAuthenticationParameters(0, AUTH_BIOMETRIC_STRONG).
2. Initialize a Cipher in ENCRYPT_MODE.
3. Wrap the cipher in BiometricPrompt.CryptoObject(cipher).
4. Present BiometricPrompt.authenticate(promptInfo, cryptoObject).
5. In onAuthenticationSucceeded(), obtain the authenticated cipher from result.cryptoObject.cipher and encrypt transaction payload.
S3 — What happens to Keystore keys when the user changes or removes their device lock screen PIN/biometrics?
HardScenario▼
If a key is generated with setInvalidatedByBiometricEnrollment(true) or bound to user authentication, enrolling a new fingerprint or disabling the lock screen permanently invalidates the key in the TEE. Attempting to use the key throws a KeyPermanentlyInvalidatedException. The app must detect this exception, clear local credentials, and force the user to re-authenticate with server credentials.

19B — App Hardening & Auth

BiometricPrompt, Play Integrity API, Root/Hook detection limitations, R8 code shrinking and obfuscation, WebView security, Intent hardening, and OWASP MASVS.

ID: 19B ⭐ Tier 2 (Security Architecture)
🚀
1. Overview & Threat Model

Application hardening protects Android binaries against reverse engineering, runtime tampering (Frida, Xposed), unauthorized cloning, and compromised OS environments (rooted devices, Magisk/Zygisk).

OWASP MASVS (Mobile Application Security Verification Standard)
  • MASVS-STORAGE: Protection of sensitive data at rest.
  • MASVS-CRYPTO: Proper use of cryptography (hardware keys, modern algorithms).
  • MASVS-AUTH: Robust authentication and session management.
  • MASVS-NETWORK: Secure TLS communication and certificate validation.
  • MASVS-RESILIENCE: Obfuscation, anti-tampering, root detection, and device integrity verification.
⚙
2. How It Works Under the Hood

1. BiometricPrompt API

BiometricPrompt provides a uniform system UI for fingerprint, face, and iris authentication. Authenticators are classified by BiometricManager.Authenticators:

  • BIOMETRIC_STRONG: Hardware-backed TEE evaluation with <1% Spoof Acceptance Rate (SAR). Required for CryptoObject cryptographic signing.
  • BIOMETRIC_WEAK: Software or low-assurance biometrics. Cannot unlock Keystore CryptoObjects.
  • DEVICE_CREDENTIAL: Device PIN, pattern, or password.

2. Play Integrity API (Replaces SafetyNet)

Google Play Integrity verifies that your app binary is unmodified, running on a genuine certified Android device, and licensed from Google Play:

Verdict FieldPossible ValuesMeaning
appLicensingVerdictLICENSED / UNLICENSEDInstalled from Google Play
appRecognitionVerdictPLAY_RECOGNIZEDBinary matches official developer signature
deviceRecognitionVerdictMEETS_STRONG_INTEGRITYHardware-backed verified boot + locked bootloader
deviceRecognitionVerdictMEETS_DEVICE_INTEGRITYCertified Android device running Google Play services
deviceRecognitionVerdictMEETS_BASIC_INTEGRITYBasic device without known emulators / obvious root
🖈
3. R8 Obfuscation & Component Hardening

1. R8 (Replaced ProGuard)

R8 performs 4 optimizations: Shrinking (removes unused code/classes), Optimization (inlining, removing dead code branches), Obfuscation (renames classes/fields/methods to a.b.c), and D8 Desugaring.

# proguard-rules.pro
-keepattributes *Annotation*, Signature, InnerClasses
-keepclassmembers enum * { *; }

# Keep data models used by Kotlin Serialization or Retrofit
-keep class com.example.model.** { *; }
-dontwarn okio.**

2. WebView Security Hardening

  • Never enable setAllowFileAccessFromFileURLs(true) or setAllowUniversalAccessFromFileURLs(true).
  • Only call setJavaScriptEnabled(true) when strictly necessary.
  • Validate all URLs in shouldOverrideUrlLoading() before navigating.
  • Prevent JavaScript interface reflection attacks on older Android versions.
💻
4. Production Example (Biometric Auth with CryptoObject)
class BiometricAuthenticator(
    private val activity: FragmentActivity,
    private val onAuthenticated: (Cipher) -> Unit,
    private val onError: (String) -> Unit
) {
    fun authenticateWithCrypto(cipher: Cipher) {
        val executor = ContextCompat.getMainExecutor(activity)
        val prompt = BiometricPrompt(activity, executor, object : BiometricPrompt.AuthenticationCallback() {
            override fun onAuthenticationSucceeded(result: BiometricPrompt.AuthenticationResult) {
                result.cryptoObject?.cipher?.let(onAuthenticated)
                    ?: onError("CryptoObject was null")
            }
            override fun onAuthenticationError(errorCode: Int, errString: CharSequence) {
                onError(errString.toString())
            }
        })

        val promptInfo = BiometricPrompt.PromptInfo.Builder()
            .setTitle("Confirm Payment")
            .setSubtitle("Authenticate via biometric sensor")
            .setNegativeButtonText("Cancel")
            .setAllowedAuthenticators(BiometricManager.Authenticators.BIOMETRIC_STRONG)
            .build()

        prompt.authenticate(promptInfo, BiometricPrompt.CryptoObject(cipher))
    }
}
⚖
5. Alternatives & Trade-offs
MechanismStrengthsWeaknessesSenior Reality
Client-side Root Check (RootBeer) Instant client-side feedback Trivially bypassed via Frida hook or Magisk hide Defense-in-depth only; never rely on it solely
Play Integrity API Cryptographically signed token verified on backend Requires network call and server token validation Gold standard for server integrity
R8 Obfuscation Built-in, zero cost, shrinks APK size Does not encrypt logic or strings; only renames Mandatory baseline for all release builds
Commercial RASP (DexGuard) String encryption, control flow flattening, active anti-debug Expensive licensing, builds slower Required for top-tier banking & defense apps
⚠
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1: Verifying Play Integrity Tokens on the Client Device

Decodes and checks Play Integrity tokens directly inside the Android app can be easily bypassed by attackers hooking the validation method using Frida. The token MUST be sent to your secure backend server and verified using Google's verification API.

Pitfall 2: Exported Components without android:exported="false"

Activities, Services, or Receivers with <intent-filter> are exported by default on older Android versions. Failing to set android:exported="false" allows malicious apps to launch private admin activities or trigger internal services directly.

Pitfall 3: Assuming Client-Side Anti-Tamper is 100% Unbreakable

Any code running on a device owned by an attacker can ultimately be reverse-engineered or hooked. High-value authorization decisions must always be made by the backend server.

🎤
7. Interview Framework

30-Second Elevator Pitch

"App hardening combines build-time optimizations and runtime integrity checks. R8 handles shrinking, dead code elimination, and symbol obfuscation. For authentication, BiometricPrompt paired with Keystore CryptoObject ensures cryptographic proof of user presence. To detect rooted or tampered devices, we use Google Play Integrity API with server-side token validation following OWASP MASVS standards."

2-Minute Deep Dive

"Client-side hardening is an exercise in defense-in-depth because client-side root checks (like RootBeer or file checks for /system/bin/su) can be bypassed by Magisk/Frida hooks. Therefore, true security relies on the Google Play Integrity API. The client requests an integrity token with a server nonce, and the backend verifies the signed JWT against Google's servers to confirm MEETS_STRONG_INTEGRITY and app licensing.

For authentication, BiometricPrompt enforces BIOMETRIC_STRONG with a Cipher CryptoObject. On the build side, R8 shrinks and obfuscates bytecode while stripping unused code. For component security, all non-public Android components explicitly declare android:exported='false', WebViews disable local file access, and sensitive activities enforce FLAG_SECURE."

Must-Mention Checklist

1
Play Integrity vs SafetyNet: Deprecated SafetyNet replaced by Play Integrity with server-side validation.
2
BiometricPrompt + CryptoObject: Hardware TEE authorization for sensitive crypto.
3
R8 Pipeline: Shrinking + Optimization + Obfuscation + Desugaring.
4
Root Detection Limitations: Why client checks fail and backend validation is mandatory.
⚡
8. Quick Revision Sheet

BIOMETRICS

BIOMETRIC_STRONG -> TEE hardware (<1% SAR)
BIOMETRIC_WEAK   -> 2D Face / Software
DEVICE_CREDENTIAL-> PIN / Pattern / Password
CryptoObject     -> Wraps Cipher / Signature

PLAY INTEGRITY VERDICTS

MEETS_STRONG_INTEGRITY -> Hardware backed boot
MEETS_DEVICE_INTEGRITY -> Certified Android OS
MEETS_BASIC_INTEGRITY  -> No known emulators
PLAY_RECOGNIZED        -> Legitimate app binary

R8 / PROGUARD

minifyEnabled true -> Enables R8
shrinkResources true -> Drops unused assets
-keep -> Protects reflection / models

COMPONENT HARDENING

android:exported="false" -> Protect components
FLAG_SECURE -> Mask previews in Recents
WebView -> Disable file access & validate URLs
❓
9. Interview Questions (Self-Check)

Basic Questions

B1 — What is the difference between ProGuard and R8?
Easy▼
ProGuard was a separate standalone Java bytecode optimizer that ran before the Android dex compiler (D8). R8 is Google's all-in-one replacement that combines shrinking, optimization, obfuscation, and DEX compilation into a single, faster step while using the same ProGuard keep rules syntax.
B2 — What is the purpose of BiometricPrompt.CryptoObject?
Easy▼
A CryptoObject wraps a cryptographic Cipher, Signature, or Mac initialized with a hardware-backed Keystore key requiring biometric authentication. Successful authentication unlocks the cipher inside the secure hardware to complete sensitive operations (e.g. authorizing a money transfer).
B3 — What does android:exported="false" do?
Easy▼
It ensures that an Android component (Activity, Service, or BroadcastReceiver) can only be launched by components belonging to the same application or the Android system (UID match), preventing external third-party apps from launching private internal screens or services.

Intermediate Questions

I1 — Why are client-side root detection libraries (like RootBeer) insufficient on their own?
Medium▼
Client-side root detection checks for su binaries, specific packages, or build tags. Attackers using tools like Magisk (Zygisk), Shamiko, or Frida can easily hook and override these check functions to always return false. Client checks serve only as a minor deterrent and must be backed by remote attestation (Play Integrity API).
I2 — What are the 3 device integrity levels in Google Play Integrity API?
Medium▼
1. MEETS_BASIC_INTEGRITY: Device passes basic system checks (not a recognized malicious emulator).
2. MEETS_DEVICE_INTEGRITY: Device is a certified Android device running Google Play services and passes CTS tests.
3. MEETS_STRONG_INTEGRITY: Device has hardware-backed verified boot with a locked bootloader and uncompromised OS key.
I3 — What security precautions must be taken when using WebViews?
Medium▼
1. Disable file access: setAllowFileAccess(false).
2. Disable universal/file access from file URLs.
3. Enable JavaScript only when required.
4. Validate domains in shouldOverrideUrlLoading().
5. Never expose sensitive Native Java interfaces via addJavascriptInterface to untrusted web content.
I4 — What is OWASP MASVS and why is it important?
Medium▼
The Mobile Application Security Verification Standard (MASVS) by OWASP defines industry-standard security requirements across mobile architecture, data storage, cryptography, authentication, network communication, platform interaction, code quality, and resilience. It serves as the official security compliance baseline for banking and enterprise apps.

Senior & Scenario Questions

S1 — How do you design an end-to-end anti-tamper architecture for a banking transaction?
HardScenario▼
1. Client requests a cryptographic nonce from the backend server.
2. Client invokes Play Integrity API passing the nonce to generate a signed integrity token.
3. User authorizes transaction via BiometricPrompt with a TEE Keystore CryptoObject, signing transaction details.
4. Client transmits the signature, transaction payload, and Play Integrity token to backend.
5. Backend decrypts Play Integrity token directly with Google API to verify device and app authenticity, validates the nonce, and verifies the TEE signature before committing funds.
S2 — Why did your app crash with ClassNotFoundException only in the Release build?
HardScenario▼
In Release builds, R8 shrinking and obfuscation is active (minifyEnabled true). If a class (e.g., a Retrofit JSON model or dynamically loaded class via reflection) is not explicitly referenced in static bytecode, R8 strips it or renames its fields. Fix: Add appropriate @Keep annotations or configure -keep class com.example.model.** { *; } in proguard-rules.pro.
S3 — How do you prevent Tapjacking / Overlay attacks on sensitive payment buttons?
HardScenario▼
Set android:filterTouchesWhenObscured="true" on the sensitive Button / View in XML or call view.setFilterTouchesWhenObscured(true). In Jetpack Compose, inspect touch event flags or set View.setFilterTouchesWhenObscured(true) on the ComposeView. This discards motion events when another window (e.g. a malicious system overlay) obscures the screen.
