22A — Memory Management & Leaks

JVM/ART Memory Model, Generational Garbage Collection, Reference Types (Strong, Weak, Soft, Phantom), the 7 Classic Android Leaks, and LeakCanary heap analysis.

ID: 22A ⭐ Tier 2 (Core System Optimization)
🚀
1. Overview & ART Memory Model

Android applications execute on the Android Runtime (ART). Understanding how memory is partitioned between thread execution and object allocation is essential to preventing OutOfMemoryErrors (OOM) and memory leaks.

JVM / ART Memory Structure
  • Stack Memory: Stores primitive local variables and method call stack frames. Allocated per thread; automatically reclaimed when a function frame pops.
  • Heap Memory: Stores all allocated objects (Bitmaps, Activities, ViewBindings, Singletons). Managed by ART Garbage Collection (GC).
  • GC Root: Objects that are guaranteed to be alive (static variables, running thread stacks, JNI global references). Anything unreachable from GC Roots is eligible for garbage collection.
⚙
2. How It Works: GC & Reference Types

1. The 4 Object Reference Types

Reference TypeGC BehaviorTypical Use Case
Strong Reference val obj = MyClass(). Never collected as long as reachable from a GC root. Standard variables, business models, ViewModels.
WeakReference WeakReference(activity). Reclaimed immediately on the very next GC cycle if no strong references exist. Listeners, static Handlers holding Activity context.
SoftReference Reclaimed only when the JVM is low on memory before throwing OOM. Memory-sensitive bitmap/file caches (rarely used modernly).
PhantomReference Enqueued in a ReferenceQueue after finalization. Low-level native cleanup (used internally by LeakCanary).

2. ART Garbage Collection Algorithms

ART uses Concurrent Copying (CC) and Generational Mark-and-Sweep. Young objects allocate into the nursery (Eden). Surviving objects promote to the Old generation. Garbage collection runs concurrently without freezing UI threads for long pause times.

🖈
3. The 7 Classic Android Memory Leaks
1. Activity Context in Singleton

Passing an Activity Context to a Singleton outlives the Activity's lifecycle. Fix: Pass context.applicationContext.

2. Static Reference to View or Activity

companion object { var currentView: View? = null }. The static GC root holds the View and its entire Activity context tree forever. Fix: Never store Views/Activities in static fields.

3. Anonymous Inner Class / Non-Static Inner Class

Non-static inner classes hold an implicit reference to the enclosing Activity (this$0). Fix: Use top-level classes, static nested classes, or Kotlin standalone functions.

4. Handler PostDelayed Holding Activity

A message posted via handler.postDelayed({ ... }, 60_000) places a Message in the Main Looper.MessageQueue holding an implicit reference to the target runnable and Activity. Fix: Call handler.removeCallbacksAndMessages(null) in onDestroy().

5. Uncancelled Coroutine in GlobalScope

Launching a coroutine in GlobalScope or non-lifecycle scope referencing Activity properties keeps the Activity alive in RAM until the job finishes. Fix: Use lifecycleScope or viewModelScope.

6. Unregistered Callback / Listener

Registering LocationManager.requestLocationUpdates() or a custom EventBus without calling removeUpdates() in onStop() / onDestroy() keeps the listener and Activity retained in the system service.

7. Fragment ViewBinding Not Nulled in onDestroyView

A Fragment's View lifecycle is shorter than the Fragment instance lifecycle (e.g. when placed on the back stack). Failing to set _binding = null in onDestroyView() retains the entire View hierarchy in memory.

💻
4. Production Example (Fixing Leaks & LeakCanary)

1. Proper Fragment ViewBinding Lifecycle

class TransactionDetailsFragment : Fragment(R.layout.fragment_details) {

    private var _binding: FragmentDetailsBinding? = null
    private val binding get() = _binding!!

    override fun onViewCreated(view: View, savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onViewCreated(view, savedInstanceState)
        _binding = FragmentDetailsBinding.bind(view)
        binding.titleText.text = "Transaction History"
    }

    override fun onDestroyView() {
        super.onDestroyView()
        // MUST nullify to prevent view leak while Fragment is on back stack
        _binding = null
    }
}

2. How LeakCanary Works Under the Hood

  1. Registers an ActivityLifecycleCallbacks listener.
  2. When an Activity reaches onDestroy(), LeakCanary wraps it in a KeyedWeakReference associated with an internal ReferenceQueue.
  3. Waits 5 seconds, forces GC, and checks if the weak reference was cleared.
  4. If still reachable from a GC root, it dumps the heap (.hprof), parses it using Shark, and prints the exact leak trace path.
⚖
5. Detection Tools & Trade-offs
ToolDetection MechanismWhen to UseOverhead
LeakCanary Automatic WeakReference + Shark Hprof parser Debug builds during daily development Minimal (pauses ~1s only when dumping heap)
Android Studio Memory Profiler Live heap dump, allocation tracking, shallow vs retained size Deep-dive investigation of Bitmap & native memory Requires active USB debugging
StrictMode (VmPolicy) Detects leaked Closable/SQLite cursors Automated debug logcat warnings Zero overhead
⚠
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1: Retaining ViewModel in Static / Long-Lived Scope

ViewModels are intended to survive configuration changes, but NOT app process scope. Storing a ViewModel in a static cache will leak the entire ViewModel and any Activity/Context callbacks attached to it.

Pitfall 2: Including LeakCanary in Release Builds

Never include LeakCanary in release production builds (debugImplementation 'com.squareup.leakcanary:leakcanary-android:...'). Heap dumping freezes the UI and leaks user PII stored in memory to disk.

Pitfall 3: Shallow Size vs Retained Size Confusion

Shallow Size is the memory consumed by the object itself (e.g. 32 bytes). Retained Size is the total memory freed if this object is garbage collected (including all dependent objects it holds, which can be 50+ MB for an Activity).

🎤
7. Interview Framework

30-Second Elevator Pitch

"Memory management on Android is handled by ART Generational Garbage Collection. A memory leak occurs when an unused object is prevented from being garbage collected because a surviving GC root (like a singleton, static field, running coroutine, or looper message) retains a strong reference to it. We catch leaks automatically using LeakCanary in debug and Memory Profiler in Android Studio."

2-Minute Deep Dive

"In the ART memory model, local variables live on the Stack while objects occupy the Heap. An object is eligible for GC when it has no strong reference chain leading back to a GC root.

The 7 classic leaks are:
1. Activity context passed to a Singleton instead of applicationContext.
2. Static references to Views or Activities.
3. Non-static inner classes holding an implicit reference to the outer Activity.
4. Handler.postDelayed messages lingering in the Looper MessageQueue.
5. Coroutines launched in unmanaged scopes like GlobalScope.
6. System service callbacks (LocationManager) registered without unregistering.
7. Fragment ViewBinding properties not nulled in onDestroyView.

LeakCanary detects leaks by attaching KeyedWeakReferences to destroyed Activities and watching a ReferenceQueue after a 5s forced GC. If retained, it parses the HPROF heap dump using Shark to produce an actionable leak trace."

Must-Mention Checklist

1
GC Roots: Static fields, thread stacks, JNI globals.
2
Reference Types: Strong vs Weak vs Soft vs Phantom.
3
The 7 Leaks: Context in singleton, static View, inner class, Handler, coroutine, listeners, Fragment binding.
4
LeakCanary Mechanism: KeyedWeakReference + ReferenceQueue + Shark heap dump.
⚡
8. Quick Revision Sheet

REFERENCE TYPES

Strong  -> Never collected if reachable
Weak    -> Collected on next GC
Soft    -> Collected only before OOM
Phantom -> Post-finalization cleanup

TOP 3 LEAK FIXES

Singleton -> Pass context.applicationContext
Fragment  -> _binding = null in onDestroyView
Handler   -> removeCallbacksAndMessages(null)

LEAKCANARY FLOW

1. Activity onDestroy() called
2. Wrapped in KeyedWeakReference
3. Wait 5s + trigger GC
4. Shark parses .hprof leak trace

PROFILER TERMS

Shallow Size  -> Size of object only
Retained Size -> Size freed if object is GC'd
GC Root       -> Active Thread / Static reference
❓
9. Interview Questions (Self-Check)

Basic Questions

B1 — What is a memory leak in Android?
Easy▼
A memory leak occurs when an object that is no longer needed by the application (such as an Activity that has finished and called onDestroy()) cannot be garbage collected because another surviving object with a longer lifecycle holds a strong reference to it. Over time, accumulated leaks exhaust available heap space and cause an OutOfMemoryError (OOM).
B2 — What is the difference between StrongReference and WeakReference?
Easy▼
A StrongReference is the default reference type in Kotlin/Java; as long as an object has a strong reference chain from a GC root, it will never be collected. A WeakReference does not prevent its referent from being collected; on the very next GC cycle, if no strong references remain, the GC immediately reclaims the object.
B3 — Why should you pass applicationContext instead of Activity context to a Singleton?
Easy▼
A Singleton lives for the entire lifetime of the application process. If you pass an Activity Context to a Singleton, that Singleton retains a strong reference to the Activity even after the user closes it, leaking the Activity, its View hierarchy, Bitmaps, and resources permanently. applicationContext is tied to the Application lifecycle and is safe for singletons.

Intermediate Questions

I1 — Why must Fragment ViewBinding be set to null in onDestroyView()?
Medium▼
In Android, a Fragment instance outlives its View hierarchy (e.g., when a Fragment transaction is added to the back stack). When navigating away, onDestroyView() is called and the View is destroyed, but the Fragment instance remains in memory. If _binding is not set to null, the binding property retains strong references to all inflated Views, creating a view hierarchy leak on the back stack.
I2 — How does LeakCanary detect memory leaks automatically?
Medium▼
1. LeakCanary registers ActivityLifecycleCallbacks and FragmentLifecycleCallbacks.
2. When an Activity/Fragment reaches onDestroy(), LeakCanary passes it to an AppWatcher that wraps it in a KeyedWeakReference linked to a ReferenceQueue.
3. After a 5-second delay, it forces a GC check. If the object has not appeared in the ReferenceQueue, it is considered retained.
4. It dumps the heap into a .hprof file and uses Shark parser to find the shortest path from GC roots to the leaking object.
I3 — How can Handler.postDelayed() cause an Activity memory leak?
Medium▼
When you post a runnable via handler.postDelayed(runnable, delay), the Android Looper.MessageQueue holds a Message containing a reference to the Runnable, which has an implicit reference to the outer Activity (if written as an anonymous class or lambda). The Looper is a static GC root, so the Activity cannot be garbage collected until the delay expires and the message is processed.
I4 — What is the difference between Shallow Size and Retained Size in memory profiling?
Medium▼
Shallow Size is the memory allocated to hold the object itself (its fields and header), excluding references to other objects. Retained Size is the total amount of memory that would be freed if this specific object were garbage collected, including all downstream child objects that are exclusively reachable from it.

Senior & Scenario Questions

S1 — How do Kotlin Coroutines prevent memory leaks compared to RxJava or Java Threads?
HardScenario▼
Kotlin Coroutines utilize Structured Concurrency. Scopes like lifecycleScope and viewModelScope are directly bound to the lifecycle of the host component (Activity, Fragment, or ViewModel). When the host is destroyed (e.g. onDestroy() or onCleared()), the scope automatically cancels its parent Job, which recursively cancels all child coroutines and releases object references. In contrast, RxJava requires manual compositeDisposable.clear() and raw Java Threads have no lifecycle integration.
S2 — Android Profiler shows native memory continuously climbing after loading high-res images in a RecyclerView. What is the root cause?
HardScenario▼
Since Android 8.0 (API 26), Bitmap pixel byte buffers are allocated in Native C++ memory (via GraphicBuffer/HardwareBuffer) rather than JVM Java heap. If images are not downsampled (using inSampleSize) and image views retain bitmaps in memory or custom caches without recycling, native memory balloons until ART triggers an OOM. Fix: Use an image loading library like Coil/Glide configured with strict memory cache limits and bitmap pooling.
S3 — How do you diagnose and fix a native cursor window leak reported by StrictMode?
HardScenario▼
StrictMode.VmPolicy.detectLeakedSqlLiteObjects() flags instances where a database Cursor or SQLiteDatabase connection was finalized without calling close(). The root cause is queries opened without try-finally or Kotlin's use {} block. Fix: Wrap all direct Cursor queries in cursor.use { cursor -> ... } or migrate entirely to Room Database, which manages cursor lifecycles automatically.

23A — Gradle / Build System

Gradle lifecycle, Android Gradle Plugin, build types, product flavors, version catalogs, KAPT vs KSP, and build performance — everything a senior Android engineer must know about the build system.

ID: 23A ★ Tier 3
🔍
1. Overview

What this unit covers

  • Gradle lifecycle: initialization → configuration → execution phases
  • Android Gradle Plugin (AGP): what it adds on top of Gradle
  • Build files: build.gradle.kts, settings.gradle.kts, libs.versions.toml
  • Build types & product flavors: debug/release, free/paid, variants
  • Annotation processing: KAPT vs KSP
  • Build performance: build cache, incremental builds, common tasks
Senior Mental Model
Gradle is a programmatic build system, not declarative like Make. Every build.gradle.kts is Kotlin code executed at configuration time. Understanding the three phases (init → config → exec) is essential for writing correct, fast build scripts and debugging mysterious build failures.
⚙
2. Gradle Lifecycle

Three Phases

PhaseWhat happensWhen it runs
InitializationGradle reads settings.gradle.kts; discovers which projects existEvery build
ConfigurationAll build.gradle.kts scripts execute top-to-bottom; task graph builtEvery build (even ./gradlew help)
ExecutionOnly the requested tasks run in dependency orderOnly needed tasks
Common Mistake
Code at the top level of build.gradle.kts runs at configuration time — even if you never run that task. Heavy I/O or network calls in configuration scripts slow every single Gradle invocation. Always put work inside task actions.

settings.gradle.kts

// settings.gradle.kts — root project file (must exist)
pluginManagement {
    repositories {
        google(); mavenCentral(); gradlePluginPortal()
    }
}
dependencyResolutionManagement {
    repositoriesMode.set(RepositoriesMode.FAIL_ON_PROJECT_REPOS)
    repositories { google(); mavenCentral() }
}
rootProject.name = "MyApp"
include(":app", ":core:network", ":feature:home")

Task Graph & Dependency

// Tasks form a directed acyclic graph (DAG)
// ./gradlew assembleDebug runs:
//   compileDebugKotlin → processDebugResources → mergeDebugAssets
//   → packageDebugResources → dexBuilderDebug → packageDebug

// Common tasks:
// assemble[Variant]     — builds APK
// bundle[Variant]       — builds AAB
// test[Variant]         — unit tests
// connected[Variant]    — instrumented tests
// lint[Variant]         — runs lint
// clean                 — deletes build/ directories
📄
3. AGP & Build Files

Android Gradle Plugin (AGP)

AGP is a Gradle plugin (applied as com.android.application or com.android.library) that adds Android-specific tasks: resource merging, manifest merging, DEX compilation, signing, and more. It wraps D8 (dexer) and R8 (shrinker/minifier).

// build.gradle.kts (app module)
plugins {
    alias(libs.plugins.android.application)
    alias(libs.plugins.kotlin.android)
    alias(libs.plugins.hilt)
    alias(libs.plugins.ksp)
}
android {
    namespace = "com.example.myapp"
    compileSdk = 35
    defaultConfig {
        applicationId = "com.example.myapp"
        minSdk = 26; targetSdk = 35
        versionCode = 1; versionName = "1.0.0"
    }
}

Version Catalog — libs.versions.toml

Introduced in Gradle 7.4 / AGP 7.x. Centralizes all dependency versions and library aliases in one file.

# gradle/libs.versions.toml
[versions]
kotlin = "2.0.0"
agp    = "8.5.0"
hilt   = "2.51"
room   = "2.6.1"

[libraries]
hilt-android         = { group = "com.google.dagger", name = "hilt-android",         version.ref = "hilt" }
hilt-compiler        = { group = "com.google.dagger", name = "hilt-compiler",        version.ref = "hilt" }
room-runtime         = { group = "androidx.room",     name = "room-runtime",         version.ref = "room" }

[plugins]
android-application  = { id = "com.android.application", version.ref = "agp"    }
kotlin-android       = { id = "org.jetbrains.kotlin.android", version.ref = "kotlin" }
hilt                 = { id = "com.google.dagger.hilt.android", version.ref = "hilt" }
ksp                  = { id = "com.google.devtools.ksp", version.ref = "ksp" }

# Usage in build.gradle.kts:
# implementation(libs.hilt.android)
# ksp(libs.hilt.compiler)

build.gradle.kts vs build.gradle (Groovy)

FeatureKotlin Script (.kts)Groovy (.gradle)
IDE supportFull auto-complete, type safetyLimited, dynamic typing
PerformanceSlightly slower first compile (cached)Faster to parse
Google recommendation✅ PreferredLegacy
RefactoringSafe refactoring via IDEText-based only
🆕
4. Build Variants & Signing

Build Types

buildTypes {
    debug {
        applicationIdSuffix = ".debug"
        isDebuggable = true
        isMinifyEnabled = false
    }
    release {
        isMinifyEnabled = true       // enables R8 shrinking + obfuscation
        isShrinkResources = true
        proguardFiles(
            getDefaultProguardFile("proguard-android-optimize.txt"),
            "proguard-rules.pro"
        )
        signingConfig = signingConfigs.getByName("release")
    }
}

Product Flavors

flavorDimensions += "env"
productFlavors {
    create("dev") {
        dimension = "env"
        applicationIdSuffix = ".dev"
        buildConfigField("String", "BASE_URL", "\"https://dev.api.example.com\"")
    }
    create("prod") {
        dimension = "env"
        buildConfigField("String", "BASE_URL", "\"https://api.example.com\"")
    }
}
// Variants: devDebug, devRelease, prodDebug, prodRelease

Signing Configuration

signingConfigs {
    create("release") {
        // Read from environment variables or local.properties (NEVER commit keystore)
        storeFile = file(System.getenv("KEYSTORE_PATH") ?: "keystore/debug.jks")
        storePassword = System.getenv("STORE_PASSWORD")
        keyAlias = System.getenv("KEY_ALIAS")
        keyPassword = System.getenv("KEY_PASSWORD")
    }
}
Security Warning
Never commit your .jks keystore or plaintext passwords to version control. Use environment variables (for CI) or local.properties (gitignored) for local development.
⚡
5. KAPT vs KSP & Caching

KAPT vs KSP

FeatureKAPTKSP
SpeedSlow — converts Kotlin to Java stubs first~2× faster — processes Kotlin symbols directly
Language awareJava-centric (annotation processing API)Kotlin-native, understands suspend, sealed, etc.
IncrementalLimited incremental supportFull incremental processing
SupportDeprecated in AGP 8+Recommended going forward
UsersHilt (old), Room (old), MoshiHilt, Room, Retrofit KSP, Moshi KSP
// build.gradle.kts — switching from KAPT to KSP
plugins {
    id("com.google.devtools.ksp") version "2.0.0-1.0.21"
}
dependencies {
    // KAPT (old):
    // kapt(libs.hilt.compiler)
    // kapt(libs.room.compiler)

    // KSP (new):
    ksp(libs.hilt.compiler)
    ksp(libs.room.compiler)
}

Build Cache

# gradle.properties — enable build cache
org.gradle.caching=true
org.gradle.parallel=true
org.gradle.configureondemand=true
org.gradle.jvmargs=-Xmx4g -XX:+UseG1GC

# Local build cache: ~/.gradle/caches/build-cache/
# Remote build cache: configure in settings.gradle.kts
buildCache {
    remote(HttpBuildCache::class) {
        url = uri("https://your-build-cache-server/")
        isPush = System.getenv("CI") != null   // only push from CI
    }
}

Incremental Builds

Gradle tracks task inputs and outputs. If inputs haven't changed since last run, tasks are UP-TO-DATE and skipped. KSP supports incremental annotation processing — only re-processes files that changed.

Performance Tips
Use ./gradlew assembleDebug --scan to get a build scan URL showing which tasks are slow. Common culprits: KAPT on large projects, full recompilation due to ABI changes, and disabled build cache.
⚠
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

Common Pitfalls

  • Slow configuration: network/file I/O at top level of build script — wrap in task actions
  • api vs implementation: using api() leaks transitive dependencies to consumers, increasing compilation scope. Use implementation() by default.
  • Not using Version Catalog: version duplication across modules causes drift. Adopt libs.versions.toml.
  • Committed keystore or passwords: security risk. Use environment variables or Gradle secrets plugins.
  • KAPT in new projects: adds ~30–60 sec to large project builds. Migrate to KSP.
  • Missing proguard rules: R8 may strip classes used via reflection (Retrofit, Gson, Moshi). Add keep rules.

Best Practices

PracticeWhy
Use libs.versions.tomlSingle source of truth for all versions
Prefer KSP over KAPT2× faster, incremental, Kotlin-native
Enable build cache + parallelDramatically reduces CI build time
Use implementation not apiReduces recompilation scope across modules
Put signing creds in env varsSecurity — never commit credentials
Profile with --scanIdentify slow tasks before optimizing
🏆
7. Interview Framework

30-Second Answer

"Gradle has three phases: initialization reads settings.gradle, configuration executes all build scripts and builds the task graph, execution runs only the requested tasks. AGP adds Android-specific tasks on top. For performance I use KSP instead of KAPT — roughly 2× faster — along with build cache and parallel execution enabled in gradle.properties. Dependencies are centralized in libs.versions.toml."

2-Minute Answer

"The Gradle lifecycle is init → config → execute. A critical detail is that configuration runs on every Gradle invocation, so heavy work in build scripts always hurts. AGP wraps D8 and R8: D8 converts bytecode to DEX, R8 shrinks and obfuscates for release builds. I structure build variants with build types (debug/release) and product flavors (dev/staging/prod), giving me a matrix of variants. For annotation processing, KSP is the modern choice — it processes Kotlin symbols directly without the Java stub generation step KAPT requires. For large multi-module projects, enabling org.gradle.caching=true and parallel=true in gradle.properties can cut CI build time by 40–60% when combined with a remote build cache. Signing credentials never go in the repository; they come from environment variables in CI and local.properties locally."

Must-Mention Points

1
Three Gradle phases: initialization, configuration, execution — configuration runs every time
2
AGP adds D8 (DEX compiler) + R8 (shrinker/obfuscator) — R8 enabled only in release builds
3
KSP over KAPT: 2× faster, incremental, Kotlin-native — KAPT deprecated in AGP 8+
4
Version Catalog (libs.versions.toml) — single source of truth for all dependency versions
5
Build cache + parallel compilation — critical for multi-module project build speed

Do NOT Go Deeper On

  • Custom Gradle plugin development (unless interviewer asks)
  • Internal Gradle daemon implementation details
  • ProGuard rule syntax details (mention R8 uses it, don't recite rules)

Follow-up Q&A

QuestionKey Answer
What's the difference between api and implementation?api exposes transitive deps to consumers (use for libraries); implementation hides them (default for apps)
How do you speed up slow builds?Enable build cache, parallel, migrate to KSP, run --scan to profile
What does R8 do?Shrinks (removes unused code), obfuscates (renames symbols), optimizes bytecode — all in one pass
How do you handle different API endpoints per environment?Product flavors with buildConfigField — devDebug, stagingRelease, prodRelease variants

Senior Insight

Senior Differentiator
Know that configuration-time performance matters: a slow build script slows every IDE sync and every CI pipeline check. Migrate KAPT → KSP, enable remote build cache, and use --configuration-cache (Gradle 8+) to serialize the task graph. This is the difference between a 2-minute CI build and an 8-minute one.
⚡
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Gradle Phases

Init    → settings.gradle.kts
Config  → all build scripts run
Execute → only requested tasks

gradle.properties

org.gradle.caching=true
org.gradle.parallel=true
org.gradle.jvmargs=-Xmx4g

KSP vs KAPT

KAPT: Java stubs → slow
KSP:  Kotlin symbols → 2× faster
      incremental, Kotlin-native

Variant Matrix

flavors: dev | prod
types:  debug | release
→ devDebug, devRelease,
  prodDebug, prodRelease

Key Terms

TermMeaning
AGPAndroid Gradle Plugin — adds Android build tasks
D8DEX compiler — converts .class → .dex
R8Shrinker + obfuscator + optimizer (release only)
KSPKotlin Symbol Processing — fast annotation processing
Version Cataloglibs.versions.toml — centralized dependency management
Build cacheReuse task outputs across builds/machines
Build variantflavor × buildType combination (e.g. prodRelease)
🅾
9. Interview Questions
1. What are the three phases of Gradle's build lifecycle?
Basic⌄
Initialization (reads settings.gradle, discovers projects), Configuration (executes all build scripts, builds the task graph — runs every time), Execution (runs only the requested tasks in dependency order). Key point: configuration always runs, so heavy work there slows every Gradle invocation.
2. What is a build variant and how is it formed?
Basic⌄
A build variant is the cross-product of a product flavor and a build type. If you have flavors [dev, prod] and types [debug, release], you get four variants: devDebug, devRelease, prodDebug, prodRelease. Each variant can have its own source set, resources, and BuildConfig values.
3. What is the Version Catalog (libs.versions.toml) and why use it?
Basic⌄
A TOML file in the gradle/ directory that centralizes all dependency versions, library coordinates, and plugin IDs. Modules reference them as libs.hilt.android or libs.plugins.ksp. Benefits: single source of truth for versions, no drift across modules, IDE auto-complete, and bundle grouping.
4. What is the difference between KAPT and KSP?
Intermediate⌄
KAPT (Kotlin Annotation Processing Tool) converts Kotlin source to Java stubs before running Java annotation processors — this stub generation adds significant overhead. KSP (Kotlin Symbol Processing) processes Kotlin symbols directly, making it ~2× faster, fully incremental, and Kotlin-aware (understands suspend functions, sealed classes, etc.). KAPT is deprecated in AGP 8+. Migrate Room and Hilt to KSP.
5. What does R8 do and when does it run?
Intermediate⌄
R8 is Google's code shrinker/obfuscator. It runs in a single pass doing tree-shaking (removes unused classes/methods), obfuscation (renames symbols to short names), and bytecode optimization. It only runs when isMinifyEnabled = true, typically for release builds. D8 converts bytecode to DEX; R8 is an enhanced D8 that also shrinks.
6. What is the difference between api() and implementation() in Gradle dependencies?
Intermediate⌄
api() exposes the dependency on the compile classpath of consumers — it leaks transitively. implementation() hides it from consumers — they can't see or reference that dependency. In modules: use implementation by default to minimize recompilation scope. Use api only when the dependency is part of your module's public API surface (e.g., a library module returning types from that dependency).
7. How do you handle release signing securely in CI?
Intermediate⌄
Store the keystore as a base64-encoded secret in CI (e.g. GitHub Secrets). In the CI pipeline, decode it to a file, then pass keystore path, alias, and passwords as environment variables. In build.gradle.kts, read them via System.getenv(). Never commit the .jks file or plain-text credentials. Alternatively, use the Gradle Secrets Plugin which reads from local.properties (gitignored) for local dev.
8. Your CI build takes 12 minutes. How do you diagnose and fix it?
Senior⌄
1) Run ./gradlew assembleDebug --scan to get a build scan — shows per-task timings. 2) Check if build cache is enabled (org.gradle.caching=true) and whether tasks are UP-TO-DATE or FROM-CACHE. 3) Identify KAPT tasks — evaluate KSP for supported processors and measure the result. 4) Enable parallel execution (org.gradle.parallel=true). 5) Set up a remote build cache server so CI agents share cached task outputs. 6) Use configuration cache when the project’s Gradle version and plugins support it to skip configuration phase on unchanged builds. Measure the impact on your own project; no fixed speedup is guaranteed.
9. Why does configuration time matter even when you're not building?
Senior⌄
Configuration runs on every Gradle invocation — for task graph calculation unless a compatible configuration-cache entry is reused. IDE sync is separate and does not use the configuration cache. If build scripts do file I/O, network calls, or expensive computation at the top level (outside task actions), they slow every developer interaction. This is why lazy task configuration (tasks.register instead of tasks.create) and configuration cache exist. The configuration cache serializes the task graph and skips re-configuration when inputs are unchanged.
10. How does the Gradle build cache differ from UP-TO-DATE checks?
Scenario⌄
UP-TO-DATE: task skipped because its inputs/outputs haven't changed on the same machine since last run — it checks the local output directory. Build cache: task outputs stored by a hash of the inputs — can be reused across machines (remote cache) or after a clean. After ./gradlew clean, UP-TO-DATE won't help, but the build cache will still restore outputs FROM-CACHE. Remote build cache is essential for CI where workspaces are fresh each run.
10. Practical Lab: Diagnose a Slow Build

Goal: explain a build failure or performance change with measurements, not assumed speedups. Use a sample Android project and record its Gradle, AGP, Kotlin and JDK versions before changing anything.

1. Reproduce with the project's wrapper

./gradlew --version
./gradlew :app:assembleDebug --profile
./gradlew :app:assembleDebug --profile
./gradlew :app:dependencyInsight --dependency kotlinx-coroutines --configuration debugRuntimeClasspath

Compare first and warm builds in the same environment. Record configuration time, slow tasks, and UP-TO-DATE or FROM-CACHE outcomes. The local profile report is under build/reports/profile. A Build Scan can provide more detail but publishes build information to a service; review what your organization permits before using --scan.

2. Compare the caches correctly

MechanismWhat it reusesWhat to inspect
UP-TO-DATEExisting task outputs in this workspaceDid task inputs or outputs change?
Build cacheCacheable task outputsAre inputs declared correctly and outputs reusable?
Configuration cacheConfigured task graphAre plugins and build logic compatible? Why was the entry invalidated?
./gradlew :app:assembleDebug --configuration-cache
./gradlew :app:assembleDebug --configuration-cache

Read any compatibility report and fix the cause before enabling this permanently. Configuration cache does not accelerate IDE sync. Avoid measuring every run after clean, which removes workspace outputs and changes the comparison.

3. Reproducibility and dependency trust

Commit the wrapper and reviewed dependency versions. Check the AGP/Gradle/JDK compatibility matrix rather than upgrading each independently. A version catalog centralizes declarations; dependency locking and dependency verification solve different problems. A wrapper distribution checksum protects the downloaded distribution; verification metadata checks dependency artifacts. Review generated checksums against trusted upstream information before committing them.

Practice and interview checkpoint

  1. Capture two baseline timings and make one change.
  2. Compare timings and correctness; do not promise a universal percentage improvement.
  3. Explain why a cache miss happened and how you would detect it in CI.
  4. Describe how you would investigate a dependency-version conflict with dependencyInsight.

References: Configuration cache, Build cache, Dependency verification, Gradle Wrapper.

24A — Modularization

Why to modularize, module types and responsibilities, dependency rules, api vs implementation, dynamic feature modules, build performance benefits, and inter-module communication patterns.

ID: 24A ★★ Tier 2
🔍
1. Overview

Why Modularize?

  • Build speed: Gradle can compile modules in parallel; unchanged modules are skipped (build cache)
  • Feature isolation: each feature module owns its own code, resources, and tests
  • Team scalability: teams own their modules independently — fewer merge conflicts
  • Reusability: :core:ui shared across all features; :core:network shared across all data layers
  • Dynamic delivery: Dynamic Feature Modules downloaded on demand — reduces initial APK size
Senior Mental Model
Modularization is primarily a build-time and team-scale concern, not a runtime concern. The main benefit is faster incremental builds and the ability for teams to work in parallel without blocking each other. For a 2-person team on a small app, modularization is overhead. For 20+ engineers on a large app, it's essential.
📂
2. Module Types

Recommended Module Structure

MyApp/
├── app/                      # Entry point — thin, just wires things together
├── feature/
│   ├── home/                 # Vertical feature slice — UI + ViewModel + UseCase
│   ├── product/
│   ├── cart/
│   └── checkout/
└── core/
    ├── network/              # Retrofit, OkHttp, interceptors
    ├── database/             # Room, DAOs
    ├── ui/                   # Shared composables, themes, design tokens
    ├── common/               # Utility extensions, base classes
    └── domain/               # Entities, repository interfaces, use case base
ModulePluginResponsibility
:appcom.android.applicationSingle entry point, DI graph root, navigation host
:feature:Xcom.android.libraryVertical slice: Screen + ViewModel + UseCase for feature X
:core:networkcom.android.libraryRetrofit, OkHttp, interceptors, token refresh
:core:databasecom.android.libraryRoom database, DAOs, migrations
:core:uicom.android.libraryShared Composables, themes, Material tokens
:core:commonkotlin (pure JVM)Extensions, utils, no Android deps
Tip
:core:common should ideally be a pure Kotlin module (kotlin("jvm") plugin) — no Android dependencies. This makes it fastest to compile and testable on the JVM without an emulator.
➛
3. Dependency Rules

Dependency Direction

// Allowed dependency directions:
//   :app → :feature:home → :core:network
//   :app → :feature:cart → :core:database
//   :feature:X → :core:ui, :core:common, :core:domain
//
// FORBIDDEN:
//   :feature:home → :feature:cart   (features must NOT depend on each other)
//   :core:network → :feature:X       (core must NOT depend on features)
//   Circular dependencies            (Gradle will fail)

api vs implementation in Library Modules

// :core:network/build.gradle.kts
dependencies {
    // implementation — hidden from consumers of :core:network
    implementation(libs.retrofit)          // OK: internal detail
    implementation(libs.okhttp.logging)    // OK: internal

    // api — exposed on compile classpath of consumers
    api(libs.retrofit.converter.gson)      // Only if consumers use Gson types directly
}
// Prefer implementation — reduces recompilation scope
// When :core:network's implementation dep changes, only :core:network recompiles
// If api dep changes, ALL modules depending on :core:network must recompile
Key Rule
Use api() only when the dependency's types appear in the module's public API (function signatures, return types). Everything else uses implementation(). Incorrect api() usage is the #1 cause of unnecessarily slow incremental builds in modularized projects.
⚡
4. Build Performance Benefits

Parallel Compilation

With org.gradle.parallel=true, Gradle compiles independent modules concurrently. In a monolith, everything is sequential. In a modular app with 10 feature modules all depending on shared cores, the features can all compile in parallel after the cores finish.

# Monolith build (sequential):          Modular build (parallel):
# compile → 8 minutes                   :core:* → 2 min
#                                        :feature:* (parallel) → +2 min
#                                        :app link → +30 sec
#                                        Total: ~4.5 minutes

Build Cache Per Module

Gradle caches task outputs per module based on a hash of inputs. If you change only :feature:cart, only that module recompiles. All other module caches are valid. In a monolith, any change recompiles everything.

ABI Changes

An ABI (Application Binary Interface) change is when a module's public API changes (adding/removing/changing a public method). This forces all dependent modules to recompile. Internal (private/internal) changes are non-ABI and don't trigger downstream recompilation. This is why good encapsulation in Kotlin (using internal) directly improves build speed.

Build Speed Rule of Thumb
Changing a private or internal function → only that module recompiles. Changing a public function → all dependent modules recompile. Maximize use of internal in library modules.
🚀
5. Dynamic Feature Modules

What Are They?

Dynamic Feature Modules (DFM) are Android library modules whose code and resources are not included in the base APK. They are downloaded on demand from the Play Store using the Play Core library. This reduces initial install size.

// :feature:ar-scanner/build.gradle.kts (Dynamic Feature Module)
plugins {
    id("com.android.dynamic-feature")
}
android {
    // No applicationId — inherits from :app
    // minSdk must match :app's minSdk
}
dependencies {
    implementation(project(":app"))  // DFM depends on :app, not the other way
}
// Requesting a Dynamic Feature at runtime
val splitInstallManager = SplitInstallManagerFactory.create(context)
val request = SplitInstallRequest.newBuilder()
    .addModule("ar_scanner")
    .build()
splitInstallManager.startInstall(request)
    .addOnSuccessListener { /* navigate to AR scanner */ }
    .addOnFailureListener { e -> /* handle error */ }
FeatureDetail
On-demand deliveryDownloaded when user first accesses the feature
Install-time deliveryDownloaded at install but packaged separately (faster update)
Conditional deliveryOnly on devices meeting criteria (country, API level, hardware)
Dependency directionDFM → :app (reversed from regular modules)
🔁
6. Module Communication Patterns

The Problem

Feature modules cannot depend on each other. But they often need to communicate — e.g., :feature:cart needs to know the user logged in (event from :feature:auth). Three patterns solve this:

1. Shared ViewModel via NavBackStackEntry

// Scoped ViewModel shared across feature screens via the nav graph
// Both features define the nav graph in :app — they share a parent entry
@Composable
fun CheckoutScreen(navController: NavController) {
    val parentEntry = remember(navController) {
        navController.getBackStackEntry("checkout_graph")
    }
    val sharedVm: SharedCartViewModel = hiltViewModel(parentEntry)
}

2. SharedFlow Event Bus via :core:common

// :core:common — defines the event contract (no feature dependencies)
sealed class AppEvent {
    data class UserLoggedIn(val userId: String) : AppEvent()
    object CartCleared : AppEvent()
}

// :core:common — EventBus singleton
object AppEventBus {
    private val _events = MutableSharedFlow<AppEvent>()
    val events: SharedFlow<AppEvent> = _events.asSharedFlow()
    suspend fun emit(event: AppEvent) = _events.emit(event)
}

3. Service Interface via Hilt (Preferred)

// :core:domain — interface (no feature deps)
interface CartRepository {
    suspend fun addItem(item: CartItem)
    fun getCartFlow(): Flow<List<CartItem>>
}

// :feature:cart — implementation (depends on :core:domain, :core:database)
class CartRepositoryImpl @Inject constructor(
    private val cartDao: CartDao
) : CartRepository { ... }

// :app — Hilt binding wires interface to implementation
@Binds abstract fun bindCartRepo(impl: CartRepositoryImpl): CartRepository
🏆
7. Interview Framework

30-Second Answer

"Modularization splits the app into :app, :feature:X vertical slices, and :core:* shared layers. The main benefits are faster incremental builds through parallel compilation and Gradle's build cache, plus team scalability. Features depend on core modules but never on each other — this enforces isolation. I use implementation() not api() for dependencies to minimize recompilation scope."

2-Minute Answer

"The standard structure is :app as the thin entry point, feature modules as vertical slices owning their own UI, ViewModels, and use cases, and core modules for shared infrastructure like :core:network, :core:database, :core:ui. The dependency rule is strict: app → features → core, and features never depend on each other. For build performance, parallel compilation means independent modules build concurrently, and Gradle's build cache means unchanged modules are skipped. Using implementation() instead of api() minimizes ABI surface — only ABI changes trigger downstream recompilation. For inter-module communication, I use shared ViewModels via NavBackStackEntry for co-located screens, SharedFlow event bus in core:common for cross-feature events, or best of all — define repository interfaces in :core:domain and bind implementations in :app via Hilt, so features depend only on contracts."

Must-Mention Points

1
Dependency direction: :app → :feature → :core — features NEVER depend on each other
2
api() vs implementation(): implementation hides transitives, prevents unnecessary recompilation
3
Build performance: parallel compilation + cache — changing one feature only recompiles that feature
4
Communication: interface in :core:domain, implementation in feature, binding in :app via Hilt
5
Dynamic Feature Modules: downloaded on demand, DFM depends on :app (reversed dependency)

Do NOT Go Deeper On

  • Navigation deep links between DFMs (complex, mention it exists)
  • Gradle composite builds (advanced, separate topic)
  • Specific module counts — it depends on team/app size

Senior Insight

Senior Differentiator
The real value of modularization shows at scale. In a monolith, every developer touching any file triggers full recompilation for everyone. In a well-modularized app, a developer on the :feature:checkout module can iterate in seconds because only that module recompiles. The architecture discipline (features not depending on each other) is what enables this — and it's enforced by Gradle, not just convention.
⚡
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Module Structure

:app (entry point)
:feature:home, :cart, :checkout
:core:network, :database
:core:ui, :common, :domain

Dependency Direction

:app → :feature:X → :core:*
Features NEVER depend on each other
:core:common = pure Kotlin (JVM)

api vs implementation

implementation → hidden, faster
api → leaks to consumers
Rule: use implementation by default

Communication Patterns

1. NavBackStackEntry ViewModel
2. SharedFlow event bus
3. Hilt interface binding (best)

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Vertical sliceFeature module containing all layers (UI, domain, data) for one feature
ABI changePublic API change that forces dependent modules to recompile
DFMDynamic Feature Module — downloaded on demand at runtime
api()Exposes dependency transitively to module consumers
implementation()Hides dependency from consumers — preferred default
🅾
9. Interview Questions
1. What are the main reasons to modularize an Android app?
Basic⌄
Build speed (parallel compilation, build cache), feature isolation (each feature owns its code), team scalability (teams work in independent modules), reusability (core modules shared), and dynamic delivery (Dynamic Feature Modules reduce install size).
2. What dependency direction rule must modules follow?
Basic⌄
:app → :feature:X → :core:*. Feature modules must NEVER depend on other feature modules. Core modules must never depend on feature modules. This one-way flow ensures isolation and allows parallel compilation.
3. What is an ABI change and why does it matter for build speed?
Basic⌄
An ABI (Application Binary Interface) change is a modification to a module's public API — adding, removing, or changing a public function or class. ABI changes force all dependent modules to recompile. Non-ABI changes (private/internal modifications) only recompile the changed module. Maximizing use of internal visibility directly improves build speed.
4. When would you use api() instead of implementation() in a module's dependency?
Intermediate⌄
Only when the dependency's types appear in the module's public API surface — function parameters, return types, or properties that consumers need to interact with. Example: if :core:network exposes a function returning a Retrofit Response<T>, then Retrofit needs to be api(). Everything else (OkHttp internals, logging interceptors) stays implementation(). Using api() unnecessarily increases the compilation scope for all consumers.
5. How do feature modules communicate without depending on each other?
Intermediate⌄
Three patterns: (1) Shared ViewModel scoped to a navigation graph entry — both features access the same ViewModel via NavBackStackEntry. (2) SharedFlow event bus defined in :core:common — features emit and collect events without knowing about each other. (3) Best: define interface contracts in :core:domain, implement them in feature/data modules, and bind them in :app via Hilt — features depend only on the interface, never the implementation.
6. What is a Dynamic Feature Module and when would you use one?
Intermediate⌄
A DFM is a module whose code/resources are NOT in the base APK. They're downloaded on demand via Play Store using SplitInstallManager. Use them for optional features (AR scanner, premium features, rarely-used tools) to reduce the initial install size. Note the reversed dependency: DFM depends on :app, not the other way. Requires app to be an AAB distributed via Play Store.
7. How does parallel Gradle build work with modules?
Intermediate⌄
With org.gradle.parallel=true, Gradle compiles modules concurrently as long as they have no dependency relationship between them. All :feature:* modules can compile in parallel once :core:* modules finish. In a monolith, compilation is sequential. A well-modularized app with 10 feature modules effectively parallelizes across CPU cores, cutting build time proportionally.
8. You inherit a monolith Android app with 300K LOC. How do you start modularizing it?
Senior⌄
Start bottom-up: (1) Extract :core:common first (utilities, extensions — lowest coupling). (2) Extract :core:network (Retrofit setup). (3) Extract :core:database (Room). (4) Extract :core:domain (entities, repository interfaces). (5) Then extract feature modules one at a time, starting with the most isolated feature. Never try to extract a feature before its dependencies are modularized. Use Dependency Analysis Gradle Plugin to detect illegal dependencies before they block extraction.
9. What is the role of :app in a modularized architecture?
Senior⌄
:app should be a thin orchestration layer — it declares the main Application class, the root Hilt component, the root NavHost, and Hilt module bindings that wire interface to implementation across modules. It doesn't contain business logic. Its build.gradle.kts is the only place that depends on all feature modules. This makes :app the most frequently recompiled module, so keep it minimal.
10. How does modularization affect Hilt dependency injection?
Scenario⌄
Each module can have its own @InstallIn Hilt modules. Feature modules install their bindings in the appropriate component (SingletonComponent for singletons, ViewModelComponent for VMs). The Hilt annotation processor in :app aggregates all @HiltAndroidApp, @InstallIn, and @AndroidEntryPoint components from all modules at compile time. Interfaces are typically defined in :core:domain, implemented in the feature module, and bound via @Binds in the feature's Hilt module.

25A — CI/CD

Git branching strategies, GitHub Actions pipelines, build signing in CI, Fastlane, Play Store deployment via AAB, Firebase App Distribution, and test coverage reporting.

ID: 25A ★★ Tier 2
🔍
1. Overview

What is CI/CD for Android?

Continuous Integration (CI): every code change triggers automated lint, tests, and builds — catching regressions before they reach main. Continuous Delivery (CD): tested builds are automatically packaged and distributed to testers or the Play Store.

  • Pipeline stages: push → lint → unit tests → build → UI tests → sign → distribute
  • GitHub Actions: YAML-based workflow files in .github/workflows/
  • Fastlane: Ruby-based automation for building, testing, and deploying iOS and Android apps
  • AAB: Android App Bundle — required for Play Store; Google generates optimized APKs per device
Senior Mental Model
CI/CD is a quality gate, not just automation. Every merge to main should be guaranteed to be shippable. The pipeline should fail fast — lint and unit tests first (cheap), then build, then UI tests (expensive). Never merge red builds.
🌿
2. Git Branching Strategies
StrategyDescriptionBest for
GitFlowmain + develop + feature/* + release/* + hotfix/*Scheduled releases, multiple live versions
GitHub Flowmain + feature branches, deploy from mainContinuous deployment, web apps
Trunk-BasedEveryone commits to main (or short-lived branches <1 day)High-velocity teams, feature flags for incomplete work

Pull Request Best Practices

  • Small PRs: <400 LOC changed — easier to review, less likely to break things
  • Required CI pass: lint + unit tests must pass before merge
  • Required reviewers: at least 1–2 approvals from team members
  • Automated checks: lint, test coverage threshold, static analysis
  • Branch protection: protect main from direct pushes
Android Team Recommendation
Most Android teams use a trunk-based approach with feature flags for incomplete features. Release branches are cut when preparing a Play Store submission. Hotfixes are cherry-picked from the release branch back to main.
⚙
3. GitHub Actions Pipeline

Android Pull Request Verification Example

Adapt the JDK, SDK packages and action versions to your project. Tags below are illustrative; pin reviewed production actions to full commit SHAs. Signing and publishing belong in a separate protected release workflow.

# .github/workflows/android-ci.yml
name: Android CI
permissions:
  contents: read
on:
  push:
    branches: [ main, develop ]
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  lint-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up JDK 17
        uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with:
          java-version: '17'
          distribution: 'temurin'

      - name: Setup Gradle
        uses: gradle/actions/setup-gradle@v3
        with:
          cache-encryption-key: ${{ secrets.GRADLE_ENCRYPTION_KEY }}

      - name: Run Lint
        run: ./gradlew lintDebug

      - name: Run Unit Tests
        run: ./gradlew testDebugUnitTest

      - name: Upload Test Results
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: test-results
          path: '**/build/reports/tests/'

  build:
    needs: lint-and-test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with: { java-version: '17', distribution: 'temurin' }
      - uses: gradle/actions/setup-gradle@v3
      - name: Build Debug APK
        run: ./gradlew :app:assembleDebug
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: debug-apk
          path: app/build/outputs/apk/debug/*.apk
Key Actions
gradle/actions/setup-gradle@v3 provides Gradle caching out of the box — it caches the Gradle wrapper, dependencies, and build cache between runs, dramatically reducing CI build time.
🔑
4. Signing & Distribution

Secure Signing in CI

  1. Base64-encode your keystore: base64 -i release.jks | pbcopy
  2. Add to GitHub Secrets: KEYSTORE_BASE64, STORE_PASSWORD, KEY_ALIAS, KEY_PASSWORD
  3. In CI: decode keystore to a temp file, pass path + creds as env vars to Gradle
  4. Delete temp keystore file after signing (or use tmpfs)
Security Rules
Never commit .jks files to the repo. Never log credentials. Never print env vars. Use GitHub Secrets (encrypted at rest, masked in logs). Rotate keys if accidentally exposed.

Distribution Channels

ChannelUse caseHow
Firebase App DistributionInternal testers / QAFastlane firebase_app_distribution plugin or GitHub Action
Play Store Internal TestingInternal team testing via PlayAAB uploaded to Play Console internal track
Play Store Alpha/BetaStaged rollout to opt-in usersPromote from internal → alpha → beta in Play Console
Play Store ProductionAll usersGradual rollout (1% → 10% → 100%) or full rollout

APK vs AAB

FormatContentsWhen to use
APKAll resources for all devicesDirect install, Firebase distribution, testing
AABSplit by ABI + density + languagePlay Store only — Google generates per-device APKs

AABs are 20–30% smaller on device because Google strips unnecessary resources for each device config.

🚀
5. Fastlane & Play Store

Fastlane for Android

Fastlane is a Ruby-based automation tool. Its Fastfile defines lanes — sequences of actions for building, testing, and deploying.

# fastlane/Fastfile
default_platform(:android)

platform :android do
  lane :test do
    gradle(task: "test", build_type: "Debug")
  end

  lane :beta do
    gradle(
      task: "bundle",
      build_type: "Release",
      properties: {
        "android.injected.signing.store.file" => ENV["KEYSTORE_PATH"],
        "android.injected.signing.store.password" => ENV["STORE_PASSWORD"],
        "android.injected.signing.key.alias" => ENV["KEY_ALIAS"],
        "android.injected.signing.key.password" => ENV["KEY_PASSWORD"],
      }
    )
    upload_to_play_store(
      track: "internal",
      aab: "app/build/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab"
    )
  end

  lane :deploy do
    upload_to_play_store(
      track: "beta",
      track_promote_to: "production",
      rollout: "0.1"   # 10% rollout
    )
  end
end

Test Coverage Reporting

# build.gradle.kts — enable JaCoCo coverage
android {
    buildTypes {
        debug {
            enableAndroidTestCoverage = true
            enableUnitTestCoverage = true
        }
    }
}
# Run: ./gradlew jacocoTestReport
# Reports: build/reports/jacoco/
# Upload to Codecov or SonarQube in CI
⚠
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

Common Pitfalls

  • Committing keystore/passwords: irreversible security breach. Use GitHub Secrets only.
  • Slow CI due to no caching: always use gradle/actions/setup-gradle for Gradle caching
  • Running UI tests on every PR: expensive. Run unit tests on PR, UI tests only on merge to main or nightly
  • No branch protection: developers can push broken code directly to main. Enforce CI pass + reviews.
  • Uploading APK to Play Store: Play Store requires AAB since August 2021 for new apps
  • Forgetting versionCode increment: Play Store rejects uploads with duplicate versionCode. Automate with CI build number.

Best Practices

PracticeWhy
Fail fast: lint before buildCatch cheap issues early, don't waste build minutes
Cache Gradle dependenciesSaves 3–5 min per CI run
Use GitHub EnvironmentsRequire manual approval before deploying to production
Automate versionCode from CIUse GITHUB_RUN_NUMBER as versionCode to avoid duplicates
Use AAB for Play Store20–30% smaller downloads vs APK
Stage production rolloutStart at 1–10%, monitor crash rate, then expand
🏆
7. Interview Framework

30-Second Answer

"Our CI pipeline runs on GitHub Actions: every PR triggers lint and unit tests, merge to main triggers a full build, signs an AAB with credentials from GitHub Secrets, and distributes to Firebase App Distribution for QA. Production deployments go through Fastlane with a staged rollout. Signing credentials are stored as base64-encoded secrets — the keystore is never committed."

2-Minute Answer

"For branching I prefer trunk-based development with short-lived feature branches and feature flags for incomplete work. The CI pipeline has two stages: lint + unit tests run on every PR (fast, catches most issues), and the full build + UI tests run on merge to main. GitHub Actions with gradle/actions/setup-gradle provides Gradle caching so dependencies and build cache are shared between runs, keeping build times under 5 minutes. For release: the AAB is built with R8 minification enabled, signed using a keystore decoded from base64-encoded GitHub Secret, and uploaded to Play Store's internal track via Fastlane. Production uses a staged rollout starting at 10%. I also set up JaCoCo coverage reports uploaded to Codecov to track test coverage trends over time."

Must-Mention Points

1
Signing credentials from GitHub Secrets — keystore base64-encoded, never committed
2
Fail fast: lint → unit tests → build → UI tests — don't run expensive steps before cheap ones pass
3
AAB for Play Store — 20–30% smaller, Google generates per-device APKs
4
Gradle caching in CI via gradle/actions/setup-gradle — saves minutes per run
5
Staged rollout — 10% → monitor crash rate → expand, can halt if issues found

Senior Insight

Senior Differentiator
Beyond the pipeline, discuss quality gates: minimum test coverage thresholds (fail if coverage drops below 80%), Lint baseline files so new lint issues block PRs without fixing legacy issues, and automated version code management using CI run numbers so versionCode is always unique. Also mention monitoring post-deploy: Firebase Crashlytics alerts on spike in crash rate within hours of a new rollout.
⚡

Pipeline Stages

push → lint → unit tests
→ build → UI tests
→ sign AAB → distribute

Key Actions

🅾
9. Interview Questions
1. What is the difference between an APK and an AAB?
Basic⌄
An APK (Android Package) contains all resources for all device configurations in one file — large download. An AAB (Android App Bundle) contains split code and resources for all configurations; Google Play generates device-specific APKs from it at download time, reducing install size by 20–30%. Play Store requires AAB for new apps since August 2021. APKs are still used for direct installs and Firebase App Distribution.
2. How do you securely handle the release keystore in CI?
Basic⌄
Base64-encode the keystore file and store it as a CI secret (e.g. KEYSTORE_BASE64 in GitHub Secrets). In the CI workflow, decode it: echo "$KEYSTORE_BASE64" | base64 -d > keystore.jks. Pass the path and credentials (STORE_PASSWORD, KEY_ALIAS, KEY_PASSWORD) as environment variables to the Gradle build. Never commit the .jks file or print env vars in logs.
3. What Play Store tracks are available for staged deployment?
Basic⌄
Internal testing (up to 100 testers, instant publish), Closed testing / Alpha (specific user groups), Open testing / Beta (any opted-in user), Production (all users, supports gradual rollout percentage). Standard flow: Internal → Alpha → Beta → Production at 10% → 50% → 100%.
4. What GitHub Actions steps are essential for an Android CI pipeline?
Intermediate⌄
actions/checkout (clone repo), actions/setup-java with JDK 17 (Temurin distribution), gradle/actions/setup-gradle (Gradle wrapper + dependency + build cache), then Gradle tasks: lintDebug, testDebugUnitTest, bundleRelease. For UI tests: need Android emulator action. Caching via gradle/actions/setup-gradle saves 3–5 min per run.
5. Compare GitFlow, GitHub Flow, and trunk-based development.
Intermediate⌄
GitFlow: main + develop + feature/* + release/* + hotfix/* — structured, good for scheduled releases. GitHub Flow: main + short-lived feature branches, deploy from main — simpler, continuous deployment. Trunk-based: everyone commits to main (or branches <1 day old), incomplete features hidden behind feature flags — best for high-velocity teams, minimizes merge conflicts. Most Android teams use trunk-based or GitHub Flow with Play Store release branches cut periodically.
6. How would you prevent a duplicate versionCode upload to Play Store in CI?
Intermediate⌄
Use the CI build number as the versionCode: in GitHub Actions, GITHUB_RUN_NUMBER is a monotonically increasing integer. Inject it into Gradle: android { defaultConfig { versionCode = System.getenv("GITHUB_RUN_NUMBER")?.toIntOrNull() ?: 1 } }. This guarantees each CI-built AAB has a unique versionCode. Local developer builds use 1 as the fallback.
7. Your CI pipeline takes 20 minutes. How do you optimize it?
Intermediate⌄
1) Enable gradle/actions/setup-gradle for dependency and build cache. 2) Split pipeline into parallel jobs: lint, unit tests, and instrumented tests can run simultaneously. 3) Run UI tests only on main merges, not every PR. 4) Use larger GitHub Actions runners for faster hardware. 5) Enable Gradle configuration cache. 6) Migrate KAPT to KSP. 7) Modularize so only changed modules recompile. Targeting 5–8 min for PR builds is reasonable.
8. What is a staged rollout and why is it important?
Senior⌄
A staged rollout releases a new version to a percentage of users first. Start at 1–10%, monitor crash rates in Firebase Crashlytics and ANR rates in Play Console for 24–48 hours, then expand to 50% then 100%. If crash rate spikes, halt the rollout and the previous version remains for un-updated users. This limits blast radius of production bugs. Always have monitoring set up BEFORE initiating a rollout — you need real-time crash alerts.
9. How does Fastlane's supply action work with Play Store?
Senior⌄
Fastlane's supply uses the Google Play Android Developer API. You create a service account in Google Cloud Console, grant it access to Play Console, download the JSON key, and store it as a secret. upload_to_play_store uses this JSON to authenticate and upload AABs. It supports specifying track (internal/alpha/beta/production), rollout percentage, changelogs, and screenshots. Can also promote between tracks without uploading a new binary.
10. How do you set up test coverage enforcement in CI?
Scenario⌄
Enable JaCoCo in Android build config. Run ./gradlew jacocoTestReport in CI. Upload the XML report to Codecov or SonarQube. In SonarQube, configure a quality gate that fails if coverage drops below the threshold (e.g., 75%). In GitHub Actions, the Codecov action posts coverage % as a PR comment and can fail the check on coverage decrease. This creates a ratchet — coverage can only stay the same or improve over time.
10. Practical Lab: Design a Reliable Android Pipeline

Goal: draw the path from a pull request to a releasable artifact, including failures and recovery. Apply the commands to a sample Android repository; this study website itself is not an Android build.

Separate verification from release

StageChecks and outputsTrust boundary
Pull requestLint, JVM tests, debug build; preserve reports even after failureNo signing or publishing credentials; read-only repository permissions
IntegrationEmulator/device tests for important journeys; defined API levelsUse synthetic test accounts and controlled services
ReleaseApproved commit, signed AAB, version checks, staged rolloutProtected environment and reviewed approval policy
./gradlew :app:lintDebug :app:testDebugUnitTest :app:assembleDebug
# Requires a running emulator or attached test device:
./gradlew :app:connectedDebugAndroidTest

Passing a debug build does not prove release behavior: test the release variant's shrinking, manifests and configuration before distribution. Retain lint/test reports, commit identity and artifact provenance. Choose report retention deliberately instead of keeping artifacts indefinitely.

Diagnose failures, not just retry them

  • Works locally, fails on CI: compare the wrapper, JDK, SDK packages, environment variables and task names.
  • Fork pull request fails to sign: signing does not belong in its verification job. Keep release credentials in the trusted release workflow.
  • Flaky emulator test: collect logs and failure evidence; replace fixed sleeps with synchronization. Track flakiness rather than rerunning until green.
  • Cache makes an incorrect build pass: compare against a fresh run, inspect inputs and restrict who can write shared caches.
  • Rollout regression: halt expansion, investigate crash/ANR and functional signals, and prepare a tested replacement. Do not assume users can automatically downgrade an installed version.

Pipeline safety and efficiency

Use pull_request for untrusted PR checks. Do not execute untrusted PR code in a privileged pull_request_target workflow. Review action sources and pin production actions to reviewed full commit SHAs. Set bounded job timeouts, cancel superseded verification runs, and upload diagnostics with if: always(). Gradle's setup action manages Gradle caching; avoid stacking multiple cache owners for the same directory.

Interview exercise

A team has a 15-minute pipeline and frequent release incidents. Propose measurable improvements: fail fast on cheap checks, identify the slowest stage, split verification and publishing, define release gates, and track queue time, duration, flake rate and escaped defects. Explain the trade-off before adding parallel jobs or broad caches.

References: Gradle on GitHub Actions, GitHub Actions security.

26A — Code Quality

Android Lint, Detekt, Ktlint, SonarQube, JaCoCo coverage, technical debt management, code review best practices, and Lint baseline files for legacy codebases.

ID: 26A ★★ Tier 2
🔍
1. Overview

The Code Quality Toolchain

ToolTypeWhat it checks
Android LintBuilt-in static analysisAndroid-specific issues, API level, performance, security
DetektKotlin static analysisComplexity, style, naming, potential bugs
KtlintKotlin formatterCode formatting only — enforces Kotlin style guide
SonarQubeQuality gate platformCoverage, duplication, debt, all tool reports aggregated
JaCoCoCoverage measurementUnit test line/branch/instruction coverage
Senior Mental Model
These tools form layers: Ktlint enforces formatting (no subjective debates in PR reviews), Detekt catches code smells, Lint catches Android-specific bugs, JaCoCo measures test coverage, and SonarQube tracks all of it over time with quality gates. Each serves a distinct role.
🔎
2. Android Lint

What Lint Checks

  • API level: using APIs not available on minSdk
  • Performance: unused resources, overdraw warnings
  • Security: hardcoded API keys, world-readable files
  • Correctness: wrong XML attribute usage, missing translations
  • Accessibility: missing content descriptions on ImageViews
// Running lint:
// ./gradlew lintDebug
// Report: app/build/reports/lint-results-debug.html

// Suppressing a single lint warning:
@SuppressLint("SetJavaScriptEnabled")
fun setupWebView(webView: WebView) {
    webView.settings.javaScriptEnabled = true  // intentional
}

// Suppressing in XML:
// tools:ignore="ContentDescription"

Lint Baseline File

For legacy codebases with hundreds of existing lint issues, a baseline file lets you suppress all current issues and only fail on new ones introduced after the baseline was created.

// Generate a baseline:
// ./gradlew lintDebug -Dlint.baselines.continue=true
// Creates: app/lint-baseline.xml

// Enable in build.gradle.kts:
android {
    lint {
        baseline = file("lint-baseline.xml")
        warningsAsErrors = true
        abortOnError = true
    }
}
// Now CI fails only on NEW lint issues — a ratchet pattern

Custom Lint Rules

// Custom Lint rule — detects direct use of android.util.Log in production code
class NoDirectLogDetector : Detector(), UastScanner {
    override fun getApplicableMethodNames() = listOf("d", "e", "i", "w", "v")
    override fun visitMethodCall(context: JavaContext, node: UCallExpression, method: PsiMethod) {
        if (context.evaluator.isMemberInClass(method, "android.util.Log")) {
            context.report(ISSUE, node, context.getLocation(node),
                "Use Timber instead of android.util.Log")
        }
    }
}
📋
3. Detekt & Ktlint

Detekt — Kotlin Static Analysis

// build.gradle.kts (root)
plugins {
    id("io.gitlab.arturbosch.detekt") version "1.23.6"
}
detekt {
    config.setFrom("config/detekt.yml")
    baseline = file("config/detekt-baseline.xml")
    buildUponDefaultConfig = true
}
# config/detekt.yml — example rules
complexity:
  LongMethod:
    active: true
    threshold: 60         # fail if method > 60 lines
  ComplexMethod:
    active: true
    threshold: 15         # cyclomatic complexity
naming:
  FunctionNaming:
    active: true
style:
  MagicNumber:
    active: true
    ignoreNumbers: ['-1','0','1','2']

Ktlint — Formatting Only

// Using ktlint via Gradle plugin
plugins {
    id("org.jlleitschuh.gradle.ktlint") version "12.1.0"
}
ktlint {
    version.set("1.2.1")
    android.set(true)
    reporters {
        reporter(ReporterType.PLAIN)
        reporter(ReporterType.CHECKSTYLE)
    }
}
// ./gradlew ktlintCheck  — checks formatting
// ./gradlew ktlintFormat — auto-fixes formatting
ToolDetektKtlint
PurposeCode smells, complexity, potential bugsFormatting only
ConfigYAML rule config.editorconfig
Auto-fixLimitedktlintFormat fixes all
Use together?Yes — they complement each other
📊
4. SonarQube & Coverage

SonarQube / SonarCloud

SonarQube aggregates lint, coverage, duplication, and complexity into a single dashboard with quality gates. SonarCloud is the hosted version — easier to set up for open source and small teams.

MetricWhat it measuresThreshold example
Coverage% of code covered by tests≥ 80% on new code
Duplications% of duplicated code blocks≤ 3%
Technical debtEstimated hours to fix all issuesDebt ratio ≤ 5%
Reliability ratingBug count → A/B/C/D/E≥ A (0 bugs)
Security ratingVulnerability count → A/B/C/D/E≥ A (0 vulnerabilities)

JaCoCo Setup

// build.gradle.kts
android {
    buildTypes {
        debug {
            enableUnitTestCoverage = true
        }
    }
}
// Run: ./gradlew testDebugUnitTest jacocoTestReport
// Output: build/reports/jacoco/testDebugUnitTestCoverage/

// SonarQube integration in GitHub Actions:
// - name: SonarCloud Scan
//   uses: SonarSource/sonarcloud-github-action@master
//   env:
//     GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
//     SONAR_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SONAR_TOKEN }}
Quality Gate
A quality gate is a threshold that must pass for a build to be considered "green." SonarQube's default quality gate fails if: new code coverage < 80%, new code has any blocker/critical bugs, or reliability rating is worse than A. This is the definition of "done" for a story or PR.
👁
5. Code Review Practices

What to Check in a Code Review

CategoryWhat to look for
Logic correctnessDoes the code do what it claims? Edge cases handled? Off-by-one errors?
NamingDescriptive names? No cryptic abbreviations? Consistent with codebase style?
Test coverageAre new code paths tested? Happy path + error path + edge cases?
PerformanceN+1 queries? Blocking main thread? Memory leaks?
SecurityHardcoded secrets? SQL injection? Insecure network? Sensitive data logged?
ArchitectureCorrect layer? ViewModel not touching View? Repository not calling ViewModel?
Android-specificContext leaks? Wrong lifecycle scope? Background work on main thread?

What NOT to do in Code Review

  • Don't debate formatting — that's Ktlint's job (automate it)
  • Don't nitpick style preferences — configure them in Detekt/Ktlint once
  • Don't approve PRs with failing CI — CI must be green before merge
  • Don't leave vague comments — be specific about what to change and why
Review Efficiency Tip
Automate everything that can be automated (formatting, lint, style) so human reviewers focus on what machines can't check: logic correctness, architecture decisions, test quality, and security.
📈
6. Technical Debt Management

What is Technical Debt?

Technical debt is the implied cost of future rework caused by choosing a fast/easy solution now instead of the better approach. SonarQube estimates it in hours based on issue count and complexity.

Debt Prioritization

SeverityPriorityExamples
BlockerFix immediately — don't shipNullPointerException risk, data corruption
CriticalFix in current sprintSecurity vulnerability, major performance issue
MajorSchedule in backlogComplex method, code duplication, missing test
Minor/InfoFix opportunisticallyNaming issues, formatting, minor style

Managing Legacy Debt

  • Lint baseline: suppress existing issues, fail only on new ones (ratchet pattern)
  • Detekt baseline: same approach for Detekt issues
  • Boy Scout Rule: leave every file you touch slightly better than you found it
  • Refactor sprints: schedule periodic debt-reduction work alongside features
  • Debt ratio tracking: SonarQube shows debt ratio over time — ensure it trends down
🏆
7. Interview Framework

30-Second Answer

"We use a layered quality toolchain: Ktlint for formatting (no debates in PR reviews), Detekt for Kotlin static analysis, Android Lint with a baseline file for legacy issues, JaCoCo for test coverage, and SonarQube as the aggregation platform with quality gates. Every PR must pass all tools before merge."

2-Minute Answer

"Code quality tools each serve a distinct role. Ktlint enforces formatting automatically — it removes subjective style debates from code reviews. Detekt catches code smells: overly complex methods, magic numbers, naming violations. Android Lint catches Android-specific issues like missing translations, deprecated APIs, and security issues. For legacy codebases, I use Lint and Detekt baseline files — these suppress existing issues so CI only fails on new ones, creating a ratchet that prevents regression without requiring a big-bang cleanup. JaCoCo measures test coverage, and I target 80% on new code. SonarQube or SonarCloud aggregates all of this with quality gates — a PR can't merge if it introduces bugs or drops coverage below the threshold. Code reviews then focus on what tools can't check: logic correctness, architecture adherence, security, and test quality."

Must-Mention Points

1
Each tool has a distinct role: Ktlint (format) → Detekt (code smells) → Lint (Android issues) → JaCoCo (coverage) → SonarQube (aggregate)
2
Lint baseline files — suppress legacy issues, fail only on new ones (ratchet pattern)
3
Quality gates in SonarQube — definition of "done" for code changes
4
Automate formatting/style so human reviews focus on logic, architecture, security

Senior Insight

Senior Differentiator
Custom Lint rules are a senior-level skill. When your team repeatedly makes the same mistake (e.g., calling android.util.Log directly, using hardcoded color values instead of theme attributes), write a custom Lint rule that fails CI. This is infinitely more effective than adding it to the code review checklist.
⚡
