9. Interview Questions
1. What is the difference between Android Lint, Detekt, and Ktlint?
Basic⌄
Android Lint: built-in, finds Android-specific issues (wrong API level, missing translations, security). Detekt: Kotlin static analysis for code quality — complexity, naming, style, potential bugs. Ktlint: formatting ONLY — enforces the Kotlin style guide (indentation, spacing, trailing commas). All three complement each other and should run in CI.
2. What is a Lint baseline file and why is it useful?
Basic⌄
A baseline file records all existing Lint issues at a point in time. CI is then configured to suppress all baselined issues and fail only when NEW issues are introduced. This is the "ratchet" pattern — it lets you adopt strict Lint enforcement in a legacy codebase without requiring a big-bang cleanup. Over time, fix issues and regenerate the baseline to shrink it.
3. What is a SonarQube quality gate?
Basic⌄
A quality gate is a set of conditions that code must meet to be considered releasable. Default conditions: new code coverage ≥ 80%, 0 new blocker or critical issues, reliability rating A, duplication ≤ 3%. If any condition fails, the SonarQube status is "failed" and CI can be configured to block the PR merge.
4. How do you measure test coverage in Android?
Intermediate⌄
Enable JaCoCo in Android build config: enableUnitTestCoverage = true in the debug buildType. Run ./gradlew testDebugUnitTest jacocoTestReport. This generates XML + HTML reports in build/reports/jacoco/. Upload the XML report to SonarQube or Codecov for tracking and quality gate enforcement. Note: JaCoCo measures unit test coverage; instrumented test coverage requires a separate configuration.
5. What should code reviewers focus on vs what should be automated?
Intermediate⌄
Automate: formatting (Ktlint), code style (Detekt), Android-specific issues (Lint), test coverage thresholds (JaCoCo/SonarQube). Human reviewers should focus on: logic correctness, edge cases, security, architecture adherence, test quality (are the right things tested?), naming clarity, and performance pitfalls. Never debate tabs vs spaces in reviews — configure it once in Ktlint.
6. How do you manage technical debt in a large codebase?
Intermediate⌄
Use SonarQube debt ratio to track total debt over time. Prioritize: fix blockers immediately, schedule criticals this sprint, major debt goes in the backlog. Use Lint/Detekt baselines as a ratchet — prevent new debt while gradually clearing old debt. Apply the Boy Scout Rule — leave code better than you found it. Periodically schedule refactor sprints alongside feature work. Never let debt ratio increase sprint over sprint.
7. How do you write a custom Android Lint rule?
Intermediate⌄
Create a separate Java/Kotlin module with lint-api dependency. Extend Detector and implement the appropriate Scanner interface (UastScanner for Kotlin/Java code, XmlScanner for XML). Override getApplicableMethodNames() or getApplicableElements() to specify what to analyze. In visitMethodCall() or visitElement(), use context.report() to flag issues. Define an Issue object with id, description, severity, and category. Register the rule in a custom IssueRegistry. Include the module as a lintChecks dependency.
8. You join a team with 500 Lint warnings. How do you introduce strict Lint enforcement without blocking the team?
Senior⌄
1) Generate a Lint baseline file today: ./gradlew lintDebug -Dlint.baselines.continue=true. 2) Add the baseline.xml to source control. 3) Enable lint { warningsAsErrors = true; abortOnError = true } in build.gradle.kts. 4) CI now only fails on new issues — existing 500 are suppressed. 5) In backlog, schedule sprints to fix high-severity issues and shrink the baseline. 6) Track baseline issue count in SonarQube over time — ensure it trends to zero.
9. What Detekt rules are most valuable for Android Kotlin code?
Senior⌄
Most valuable: LongMethod (methods over ~40-60 lines are hard to test), ComplexMethod (cyclomatic complexity > 10 indicates need to split), MagicNumber (unexplained literals should be named constants), UnusedPrivateMember (dead code), SwallowedException (catch blocks that ignore exceptions hide bugs), ForbiddenComment (TODO/FIXME tracking), and TooManyFunctions (class doing too much — SRP violation). Configure thresholds in detekt.yml to match team standards.
10. How does code coverage differ from code quality?
Scenario⌄
Coverage measures what percentage of code is executed by tests. Quality measures whether tests are meaningful. 100% coverage can coexist with terrible tests — if tests have no assertions, every line is "covered" but nothing is verified. Good tests: test behavior not implementation, cover happy + error + edge paths, are deterministic, and fail meaningfully when production code breaks. Coverage is a necessary but not sufficient indicator of quality. Aim for high coverage AND meaningful assertions — code review of tests is as important as code review of production code.

27A — Permissions

Normal vs dangerous permissions, runtime permissions flow with ActivityResultContracts, one-time permissions, location levels, notification permissions (API 33+), storage evolution, and Android permission behavior changes across versions.

ID: 27A ★ Tier 3
🔍
1. Overview

Permission Types

TypeGrant mechanismExamples
NormalAuto-granted at install timeINTERNET, ACCESS_NETWORK_STATE, VIBRATE, RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED
DangerousRequires runtime request from userCAMERA, RECORD_AUDIO, READ_CONTACTS, ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION
SignatureAuto-granted if same signing certUsed for inter-app communication between your own apps
Key Rule
Always declare permissions in AndroidManifest.xml regardless of type. Normal permissions are auto-granted — you don't need to request them at runtime. Dangerous permissions must be requested at runtime on API 23+ (Android 6.0). Always check before use with ContextCompat.checkSelfPermission().
🔒
2. Normal vs Dangerous

Normal Permissions (auto-granted)

<!-- AndroidManifest.xml — declare, no runtime request needed -->
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.INTERNET" />
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_NETWORK_STATE" />
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.VIBRATE" />
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.WAKE_LOCK" />

Dangerous Permissions — must declare AND request

<!-- AndroidManifest.xml -->
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.CAMERA" />
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.RECORD_AUDIO" />
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION" />
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.READ_CONTACTS" />
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.POST_NOTIFICATIONS" /> <!-- API 33+ -->

Permission Groups

Dangerous permissions belong to groups. Granting one permission in a group may auto-grant others in the same group. However, always request each individual permission — don't rely on group behavior.

GroupPermissions
LOCATIONACCESS_COARSE_LOCATION, ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION, ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION
CAMERACAMERA
MICROPHONERECORD_AUDIO
CONTACTSREAD_CONTACTS, WRITE_CONTACTS, GET_ACCOUNTS
NOTIFICATIONSPOST_NOTIFICATIONS (API 33+)
⚙
3. Runtime Permissions Flow

Complete Permission Request Flow

class CameraFragment : Fragment() {

    // Register launcher BEFORE fragment/activity is created
    private val requestPermissionLauncher = registerForActivityResult(
        ActivityResultContracts.RequestPermission()
    ) { isGranted ->
        if (isGranted) {
            openCamera()
        } else {
            showPermissionDeniedMessage()
        }
    }

    fun checkAndRequestCamera() {
        when {
            // 1. Already granted — proceed
            ContextCompat.checkSelfPermission(
                requireContext(), Manifest.permission.CAMERA
            ) == PackageManager.PERMISSION_GRANTED -> openCamera()

            // 2. Show rationale — user previously denied
            shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale(Manifest.permission.CAMERA) -> {
                showRationaleDialog {
                    requestPermissionLauncher.launch(Manifest.permission.CAMERA)
                }
            }

            // 3. Request permission — first time or after "don't ask again"
            else -> requestPermissionLauncher.launch(Manifest.permission.CAMERA)
        }
    }
}

shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale()

StateReturnsMeaning
First time askingfalseShow dialog directly, no rationale needed
User denied oncetrueShow rationale explaining why permission is needed
User checked "Don't ask again"falseDirect to Settings — can't request again programmatically
Permission grantedfalseAlready have permission

Multiple Permissions

private val multiplePermissionsLauncher = registerForActivityResult(
    ActivityResultContracts.RequestMultiplePermissions()
) { permissions ->
    val cameraGranted = permissions[Manifest.permission.CAMERA] == true
    val audioGranted = permissions[Manifest.permission.RECORD_AUDIO] == true
    if (cameraGranted && audioGranted) startVideoRecording()
}
multiplePermissionsLauncher.launch(arrayOf(
    Manifest.permission.CAMERA,
    Manifest.permission.RECORD_AUDIO
))
📍
4. Location & Notification Permissions

Location Permission Levels

PermissionAccuracyAPINotes
ACCESS_COARSE_LOCATION~1 km (cell/WiFi)1+Low precision, minimal privacy impact
ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION~10 m (GPS)1+High precision, runtime request
ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATIONEither29+Separate request — must request foreground first, then background. Play Store requires justification.
// Android 10+ (API 29+): background location is a SEPARATE permission
// Step 1: request foreground location first
requestPermissionLauncher.launch(Manifest.permission.ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION)

// Step 2: ONLY after foreground is granted, request background
// This shows a different system dialog on Android 11+
requestPermissionLauncher.launch(Manifest.permission.ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION)
// Android 11: system redirects user to Settings for background permission

Notification Permission (POST_NOTIFICATIONS — API 33+)

<!-- AndroidManifest.xml -->
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.POST_NOTIFICATIONS" />

// Runtime request on Android 13+ (API 33+)
// On Android 12 and below: notifications are auto-granted
if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= Build.VERSION_CODES.TIRAMISU) {
    requestPermissionLauncher.launch(Manifest.permission.POST_NOTIFICATIONS)
}

// One-time permissions (Android 11+)
// User can grant camera/mic/location "only this time"
// App loses permission when it goes to background
// No code change needed — system handles it; just check permission before use
One-Time Permissions (API 30+)
Android 11 introduced "Only this time" for CAMERA, RECORD_AUDIO, and location. The permission is automatically revoked when the app goes to background. You don't need to handle this specially — just always call checkSelfPermission() before using sensitive features, even if you thought you had permission.
📁
5. Storage Permissions

Storage Evolution

ApproachWhen to useAPI
MediaStore APIImages, videos, audio files in shared media collectionsAll, best on 29+
SAF (Storage Access Framework)User picks any file type via system file picker19+
MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGEFile manager apps — broad access; Play Store review required30+
READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGELegacy — deprecated on API 33+Legacy
READ_MEDIA_IMAGES, READ_MEDIA_VIDEO, READ_MEDIA_AUDIOGranular media access on API 33+33+

Modern Storage Approach

// Modern approach: scoped storage (Android 10+)
// Apps can read/write their own files WITHOUT permissions
// To access OTHER apps' media: request specific media permission

// Android 13+ granular media permissions
val mediaPermissions = if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 33) {
    arrayOf(
        Manifest.permission.READ_MEDIA_IMAGES,
        Manifest.permission.READ_MEDIA_VIDEO
    )
} else {
    arrayOf(Manifest.permission.READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE)
}
multiplePermissionsLauncher.launch(mediaPermissions)

// SAF — user picks file, you get a Uri (no storage permission needed)
val openDocument = registerForActivityResult(ActivityResultContracts.OpenDocument()) { uri ->
    uri?.let { /* process the file */ }
}
openDocument.launch(arrayOf("application/pdf", "image/*"))
📋
6. Android Version Evolution
Android VersionAPIPermission Changes
Android 6.0 Marshmallow23Runtime permissions introduced — dangerous perms must be requested at runtime
Android 10 Q29Scoped storage; background location separate permission; ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION added
Android 11 R30One-time permissions (camera, mic, location); background location: system redirects to Settings; MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE added; auto-reset permissions for unused apps
Android 12 S31/32Approximate vs precise location: user can grant coarse instead of fine; Bluetooth permissions split (BLUETOOTH_SCAN, BLUETOOTH_CONNECT)
Android 13 T33POST_NOTIFICATIONS required at runtime; granular media permissions (READ_MEDIA_IMAGES, READ_MEDIA_VIDEO, READ_MEDIA_AUDIO) replace READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE; nearby WiFi permission
Android 14 U34Photo picker: partial media access — user grants specific photos not all; READ_MEDIA_VISUAL_USER_SELECTED for partial access
Senior Mental Model
Android permissions have evolved toward granularity and transparency. Each version restricts more and gives users more control. Always check the target API level and use Build.VERSION.SDK_INT to handle different permission models. Compile against the latest targetSdk so your app gets the new privacy features.
🏆
7. Interview Framework

30-Second Answer

"Normal permissions are auto-granted at install. Dangerous permissions require runtime requests via ActivityResultContracts.RequestPermission. The flow is: check if granted → show rationale if previously denied (shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale) → request → handle result. Always check before use, especially with one-time permissions on Android 11+."

2-Minute Answer

"Permissions split into normal (auto-granted, like INTERNET) and dangerous (require runtime request, like CAMERA). The modern way is ActivityResultContracts — register the launcher before the fragment starts, then when needed: check if already granted, check shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale to decide whether to show rationale UI, then launch the request. For location: coarse and fine are one-step; background location is a SEPARATE request on API 29+ and must happen after foreground is granted. Android 11 added one-time permissions — apps lose access when backgrounded. API 33 added POST_NOTIFICATIONS as a required runtime permission, so notification apps must request it on Android 13+. For storage: scoped storage on API 29+, granular media permissions on API 33+, and SAF for user-picked files with no permission needed."

Must-Mention Points

1
ActivityResultContracts.RequestPermission — modern API; must register before fragment/activity created
2
shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale() — shows rationale after first denial, returns false after "don't ask again"
3
Background location (API 29+) — SEPARATE request, must have foreground first
4
POST_NOTIFICATIONS required on API 33+ — needs runtime request
5
One-time permissions (API 30+) — revoked when app goes background; always check before use

Senior Insight

Senior Differentiator
Understand that "don't ask again" can never be detected directly (shouldShowRationale returns false for both first-time and permanently denied). The pattern to detect "permanently denied": track whether you've asked before using SharedPreferences. If you asked before AND shouldShowRationale is false AND permission is denied → permanently denied → direct to Settings via Intent(Settings.ACTION_APPLICATION_DETAILS_SETTINGS).

9. Interview Questions
1. What is the difference between normal and dangerous permissions?
Basic⌄
Normal permissions (like INTERNET, VIBRATE) are automatically granted at install time — no user interaction needed. Dangerous permissions (like CAMERA, LOCATION, READ_CONTACTS) can access sensitive user data or device features, so they must be declared in the manifest AND explicitly requested at runtime on Android 6+ (API 23). The user must grant them; they can be revoked at any time.
2. What does shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale() return in each state?
Basic⌄
First time asking: false (no rationale needed, show dialog). User denied once: true (show rationale UI explaining why you need it). User checked "Don't ask again": false (same as first time — can't distinguish programmatically). Permission already granted: false. The key gotcha: false doesn't tell you whether it's first-time or permanently denied — you must track "has the user been asked before" separately.
3. What changed about notifications in Android 13?
Basic⌄
Android 13 (API 33) made POST_NOTIFICATIONS a dangerous permission requiring a runtime request. On Android 12 and below, apps could post notifications without permission. Apps targeting API 33+ must declare the permission in the manifest and request it at runtime. The user can deny it, in which case all notifications from the app are blocked. Apps upgraded from lower target SDK get a one-time automatic grant prompt.
4. How do you request background location on Android 10+?
Intermediate⌄
Two separate requests: Step 1: request ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION (or COARSE). Wait for it to be granted. Step 2: only after foreground is granted, request ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION. On Android 11+, the system dialog for background location has no "Allow all the time" option — it redirects the user to Settings where they manually select "Allow all the time." Request both permissions in separate user actions, not simultaneously. Play Store requires a declaration explaining why you need background location.
5. What are one-time permissions and how do they affect your app?
Intermediate⌄
Introduced in Android 11. Users can grant CAMERA, RECORD_AUDIO, and location permissions "Only this time." The permission is automatically revoked when the app goes to background or the user switches away. No code change required — your app doesn't know it's a one-time grant. The implication: always call checkSelfPermission() before using these features, even mid-session. If the user put your app in background while recording, you might lose the permission when returning.
6. What is scoped storage and which permissions does it affect?
Intermediate⌄
Scoped storage (Android 10+) gives each app its own private storage area it can read/write without permissions, and limits access to shared storage. Apps can access their own app-specific directory (getFilesDir()) freely. For shared media: use MediaStore API. For arbitrary files: use SAF (user picks via system file picker, no permission needed). MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE grants broad access but requires Play Store justification. On API 33+, READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE is split into READ_MEDIA_IMAGES, READ_MEDIA_VIDEO, READ_MEDIA_AUDIO.
7. How do you handle the "permanently denied" (Don't ask again) case?
Intermediate⌄
You can't directly detect "don't ask again" since shouldShowRationale returns false for both first-time and permanently denied. Pattern: store a boolean (e.g., "hasAskedForCamera") in SharedPreferences. If hasAskedForCamera is true AND shouldShowRationale returns false AND permission is DENIED → permanently denied. Show a dialog explaining the situation and open Settings: Intent(Settings.ACTION_APPLICATION_DETAILS_SETTINGS, Uri.parse("package:" + packageName)).
8. Walk through the full permission request flow for a camera feature in a Compose app.
Senior⌄
In Compose, use rememberLauncherForActivityResult(ActivityResultContracts.RequestPermission()). On button tap: 1) Check ContextCompat.checkSelfPermission — if GRANTED, open camera. 2) Check shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale — if true, show rationale dialog with "OK" button that triggers launcher.launch(CAMERA). 3) Otherwise, launch directly. In result callback: if granted → open camera; if denied → check if permanently denied (using stored pref), if so show Settings dialog. Handle lifecycle correctly — the launcher must be registered at composition time, not in a click handler.
9. What is the Storage Access Framework (SAF) and when do you use it?
Senior⌄
SAF lets users pick files from any location (local storage, Google Drive, Dropbox) via the system file picker. The app receives a content URI — no storage permissions needed. Use SAF when users need to select arbitrary file types (PDFs, documents, custom formats). Use ActivityResultContracts.OpenDocument for single file, OpenMultipleDocuments for multiple. The returned URI has persisted permissions (take persistable URI permission for across-session access). Contrast with MediaStore (media collections only) and direct file access (app-private directory only).
10. How does Android 12's approximate location affect your app?
Scenario⌄
Android 12 (API 31) lets users grant only approximate location (COARSE) even when your app requests precise (FINE). The permission dialog shows "Precise" vs "Approximate" options. Your app must handle receiving COARSE when it requested FINE. Design: if the feature genuinely requires precise GPS, check that ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION is granted — don't just check that any location permission is granted. If the user chose approximate, show UI explaining why precise is needed for this specific feature, or degrade gracefully to coarse-based functionality.

28A — RecyclerView

RecyclerView architecture, ViewHolder pattern, DiffUtil, ListAdapter, LayoutManagers, ItemDecoration, nested RecyclerViews with RecycledViewPool, and performance optimization techniques.

ID: 28A ★ Tier 3
🔍
1. Overview

RecyclerView Architecture

RecyclerView
  ├── LayoutManager       — decides where items go (linear, grid, staggered)
  ├── Adapter             — creates and binds ViewHolders
  │   └── ViewHolder      — wraps a single item View
  ├── RecycledViewPool    — cache of recycled ViewHolders by viewType
  ├── ItemDecoration      — draws dividers, spacing, overlays
  └── ItemAnimator        — animates add/remove/change
Senior Mental Model
RecyclerView's core innovation is view recycling. Instead of inflating a new View for every list item, it reuses off-screen ViewHolders (via the RecycledViewPool). The ViewHolder caches view references — no findViewById in onBindViewHolder. DiffUtil calculates minimal diff on a background thread, delivering smooth animations without full dataset reloads.
⚙
2. Architecture & ViewHolder Pattern

Adapter Lifecycle

class ProductAdapter : RecyclerView.Adapter<ProductAdapter.ProductViewHolder>() {

    private val items = mutableListOf<Product>()

    // 1. inflate — called only when no recycled view available
    override fun onCreateViewHolder(parent: ViewGroup, viewType: Int): ProductViewHolder {
        val binding = ItemProductBinding.inflate(
            LayoutInflater.from(parent.context), parent, false
        )
        return ProductViewHolder(binding)
    }

    // 2. bind — called every time a ViewHolder is (re)used for an item
    // NEVER do findViewById here — use ViewBinding instead
    override fun onBindViewHolder(holder: ProductViewHolder, position: Int) {
        holder.bind(items[position])
    }

    override fun getItemCount() = items.size

    // ViewHolder — view references cached as constructor properties
    class ProductViewHolder(
        private val binding: ItemProductBinding
    ) : RecyclerView.ViewHolder(binding.root) {

        fun bind(product: Product) {
            binding.nameText.text = product.name
            binding.priceText.text = product.formattedPrice()
            Glide.with(binding.root)
                .load(product.imageUrl)
                .into(binding.productImage)
        }
    }
}
ViewHolder Pattern
The ViewHolder pattern avoids repeated findViewById() calls during scrolling. With ViewBinding, view references are auto-generated as properties of the binding class and cached in the ViewHolder instance. onBindViewHolder is called frequently during scroll — keep it fast.
↻
3. DiffUtil & ListAdapter

DiffUtil.Callback

class ProductDiffCallback : DiffUtil.ItemCallback<Product>() {

    // Are these the same item? (same identity — used for move animations)
    override fun areItemsTheSame(oldItem: Product, newItem: Product): Boolean =
        oldItem.id == newItem.id

    // Are the contents identical? (used to decide if binding is needed)
    override fun areContentsTheSame(oldItem: Product, newItem: Product): Boolean =
        oldItem == newItem  // data class equals() compares all fields

    // Optional: return specific changed payload for partial binding
    override fun getChangePayload(oldItem: Product, newItem: Product): Any? {
        return if (oldItem.price != newItem.price) "PRICE_CHANGED" else null
    }
}

ListAdapter — the recommended approach

// ListAdapter wraps DiffUtil with AsyncListDiffer
// Diff calculation happens on a background thread
class ProductAdapter : ListAdapter<Product, ProductAdapter.ProductViewHolder>(
    ProductDiffCallback()
) {
    override fun onCreateViewHolder(parent: ViewGroup, viewType: Int) = ...
    override fun onBindViewHolder(holder: ProductViewHolder, position: Int) {
        holder.bind(getItem(position))  // use getItem(), not external list
    }
}

// Submit a new list — diff calculated in background, then dispatched
// Only items that actually changed get animated/rebound
adapter.submitList(newProducts)

// Important: always submit a NEW list, not mutate the existing one
// DiffUtil compares old vs new — mutating in place skips the diff
Common Mistake
Never call adapter.submitList(list) with the same list reference you mutated. AsyncListDiffer compares the new list object to the internally stored one — if it's the same reference, it skips the diff. Always create a new list: submitList(currentList.toMutableList().also { it.add(item) }) or work with immutable state.
🎺
4. LayoutManagers
LayoutManagerLayoutUse case
LinearLayoutManagerSingle column/rowChat messages, news feed, settings list
GridLayoutManagerFixed column gridPhoto grid, product catalog
StaggeredGridLayoutManagerVariable height gridPinterest-style, masonry layout
// LinearLayoutManager — vertical (default) or horizontal
recyclerView.layoutManager = LinearLayoutManager(context)
recyclerView.layoutManager = LinearLayoutManager(context, LinearLayoutManager.HORIZONTAL, false)

// GridLayoutManager — 2 columns, with span customization
val gridLM = GridLayoutManager(context, 2).apply {
    spanSizeLookup = object : GridLayoutManager.SpanSizeLookup() {
        override fun getSpanSize(position: Int) =
            if (adapter.getItemViewType(position) == HEADER) 2 else 1
    }
}

// StaggeredGridLayoutManager
recyclerView.layoutManager = StaggeredGridLayoutManager(2, StaggeredGridLayoutManager.VERTICAL)
🎨
5. ItemDecoration & Nested RecyclerViews

ItemDecoration

// Add spacing between items
class SpaceItemDecoration(private val spacing: Int) : RecyclerView.ItemDecoration() {
    override fun getItemOffsets(
        outRect: Rect, view: View,
        parent: RecyclerView, state: RecyclerView.State
    ) {
        val position = parent.getChildAdapterPosition(view)
        if (position != RecyclerView.NO_ID) {
            outRect.bottom = spacing
            if (position == 0) outRect.top = spacing
        }
    }
}
recyclerView.addItemDecoration(SpaceItemDecoration(spacing = 16))

Nested RecyclerViews with RecycledViewPool

// Problem: each horizontal RV inside a vertical RV has its own ViewPool
// → ViewHolders are not shared, causing excessive inflation

// Solution: share RecycledViewPool between all nested horizontal RVs
val sharedPool = RecyclerView.RecycledViewPool()
sharedPool.setMaxRecycledViews(VIEW_TYPE_PRODUCT, 20)  // pool 20 items

// In the outer adapter's onCreateViewHolder:
class CategoryViewHolder(binding: ItemCategoryBinding) : RecyclerView.ViewHolder(binding.root) {
    val productsRV: RecyclerView = binding.productsRecyclerView

    fun bind(category: Category, sharedPool: RecyclerView.RecycledViewPool) {
        productsRV.setRecycledViewPool(sharedPool)
        productsRV.setHasFixedSize(true)
        (productsRV.layoutManager as? LinearLayoutManager)
            ?.initialPrefetchItemCount = 4
    }
}
⚡
6. Performance Optimization
OptimizationHowEffect
setHasFixedSize(true)recyclerView.setHasFixedSize(true)Skips requestLayout() on data change if size doesn't change
setItemViewCacheSizerecyclerView.setItemViewCacheSize(20)Off-screen cache before ViewHolder goes to pool — avoids rebind
setInitialPrefetchItemCountOn nested RV's LinearLayoutManagerPrefetches N items of nested RV during parent scroll
Stable IDssetHasStableIds(true) + override getItemId()DiffUtil can optimize rebinding with stable IDs
ViewType separationSeparate viewTypes for different item layoutsViewHolder pool separated per type — no wrong-type binding
Avoid heavy work in bindDon't decode bitmaps in onBindViewHolder — use Glide/CoilPrevents jank during scroll
// Performance checklist:
recyclerView.setHasFixedSize(true)
recyclerView.setItemViewCacheSize(20)
recyclerView.recycledViewPool.setMaxRecycledViews(0, 20)

// In the adapter:
init { setHasStableIds(true) }
override fun getItemId(position: Int): Long = getItem(position).id.hashCode().toLong()

// Avoid in onBindViewHolder:
// ❌ Bitmap.decodeResource() — use Glide/Coil
// ❌ Network requests — data should come from ViewModel
// ❌ Creating new listeners each bind — set listener in ViewHolder constructor
🏆
7. Interview Framework

30-Second Answer

"RecyclerView uses the ViewHolder pattern to cache view references and recycle off-screen views. I use ListAdapter built on DiffUtil's AsyncListDiffer — it calculates the diff on a background thread and dispatches minimal updates with animations. For performance: setHasFixedSize(true), use stable IDs, share RecycledViewPool for nested RecyclerViews, and avoid expensive work in onBindViewHolder."

2-Minute Answer

"RecyclerView separates concerns: the LayoutManager decides positioning, the Adapter creates and binds ViewHolders, and the RecycledViewPool caches off-screen ViewHolders for reuse. The ViewHolder pattern caches view references — with ViewBinding, references are typed properties so no findViewByld is ever needed in bind(). For efficient updates I use ListAdapter, which wraps AsyncListDiffer. DiffUtil requires implementing areItemsTheSame (identity check — usually ID) and areContentsTheSame (equality check — data class equals works). The diff runs on a background thread and dispatches precise insert/remove/change/move animations. Critical mistake: never submit a mutated list — always submit a new list instance. For nested RecyclerViews (e.g. horizontal carousels inside vertical feed), sharing a RecycledViewPool dramatically reduces inflation overhead. And setHasFixedSize(true) skips unnecessary layout passes when item count changes but container size doesn't."

Must-Mention Points

1
ViewHolder pattern — caches view refs; onCreateViewHolder (inflate once), onBindViewHolder (bind frequently)
2
ListAdapter + DiffUtil — async diff on background thread, minimal updates, smooth animations
3
areItemsTheSame (identity/ID) vs areContentsTheSame (data equality)
4
Never submit the same list reference mutated — DiffUtil compares references first
5
Shared RecycledViewPool for nested RVs — prevents excessive inflation

Senior Insight

Senior Differentiator
Know the full RecycledViewPool hierarchy: scrap cache (just off screen, rebind happens but not reinflate) → RecycledViewPool (pooled by viewType, must rebind). For nested RecyclerViews, understand that without a shared pool, each row creates its own pool — if 20 rows each inflate 5 items that's 100 inflations vs sharing a pool of 20. Also know when NOT to use RecyclerView — for <10 static items, a simple Column in Compose or LinearLayout is cheaper.
⚡

9. Interview Questions
1. Why is the ViewHolder pattern important?
Basic⌄
ViewHolder caches view references. Without it, onBindViewHolder would call findViewById() on every scroll event — an expensive tree traversal. The ViewHolder stores all view references as properties, created once in onCreateViewHolder. With ViewBinding, references are auto-generated as typed properties — cleaner and null-safe. The key insight: onCreateViewHolder is called rarely (only when no recycled view is available), but onBindViewHolder is called on every visible item during scroll.
2. What is the difference between areItemsTheSame and areContentsTheSame?
Basic⌄
areItemsTheSame checks identity — are these two items representing the same entity? Usually compares unique IDs. areContentsTheSame checks equality — do both items have the same data to display? Usually uses data class equals() or field-by-field comparison. If areItemsTheSame is false: item is added/removed (insert/delete animation). If true but areContentsTheSame is false: item is updated (change animation). Both true: no change, skip rebind.
3. What is ListAdapter and how does it improve on plain RecyclerView.Adapter?
Basic⌄
ListAdapter wraps AsyncListDiffer which runs DiffUtil.calculateDiff() on a background thread. Plain adapter requires calling notifyDataSetChanged() (expensive — rebinds everything) or manually calling notifyItemInserted/Removed (error-prone). ListAdapter.submitList() automatically diffs old vs new list and dispatches precise updates with animations. It also stores the current list internally — use getItem(position) in onBindViewHolder.
4. Why can't you submit the same mutated list to ListAdapter?
Intermediate⌄
AsyncListDiffer stores a reference to the last submitted list. When submitList is called, it first checks if oldList === newList (same reference). If yes, it bails out without diffing — even if you mutated the contents. This is why you must always create a new list: currentList.toMutableList().also { it.add(item) }. Functional/immutable state management (like Kotlin's plus operator on lists) naturally avoids this problem.
5. When would you use multiple view types in an adapter?
Intermediate⌄
When list items have different layouts: header + items, loading footer, ads between items, different item styles in the same feed. Override getItemViewType() to return a unique Int per type. Create separate ViewHolder classes per type. In onCreateViewHolder, inflate based on viewType. In onBindViewHolder, cast to the correct ViewHolder type. Each viewType gets its own RecycledViewPool bucket — ViewHolders are never reused across types.
6. How do shared RecycledViewPool and prefetching help nested RecyclerViews?
Intermediate⌄
In a vertical RV where each row has a horizontal RV (e.g. category rows): by default each horizontal RV has its own ViewPool — ViewHolders aren't shared. Shared RecycledViewPool lets all horizontal RVs share one pool, dramatically reducing inflation when scrolling vertically. Set initialPrefetchItemCount on the horizontal LinearLayoutManager so the RenderThread prefetches items for new rows before they appear, reducing jank.
7. What does setHasFixedSize(true) do?
Intermediate⌄
When set to true, RecyclerView skips calling requestLayout() on the parent when the adapter notifies data changes. requestLayout() is an expensive re-measure/re-layout pass. If your RecyclerView's size doesn't change when items are added/removed (e.g., it's match_parent in both dimensions), this is always safe to enable and avoids unnecessary layout work during updates.
8. Your list has janky scrolling. How do you diagnose and fix it?
Senior⌄
1) Use Android Studio's CPU Profiler to find which methods are slow. 2) Check onBindViewHolder — is it doing heavy work? (bitmap decode, network, JSON parsing) Move to Glide/background. 3) Check for synchronous notifyDataSetChanged() calls — switch to ListAdapter. 4) Check overdraw with "Show GPU Overdraw" in developer options. 5) Check if views have complex layouts — flatten with ConstraintLayout. 6) Add setHasFixedSize(true) and stable IDs. 7) For nested RVs, add shared RecycledViewPool and initialPrefetchItemCount.
9. How does getChangePayload() improve partial binding?
Senior⌄
When areItemsTheSame is true but areContentsTheSame is false, DiffUtil calls getChangePayload() to return a description of what changed. This payload is passed to onBindViewHolder(holder, position, payloads). Instead of rebinding the entire item, you can update only the changed views. Example: if only the price changed, update just the price TextView instead of rebinding the image and name. Reduces unnecessary Glide reloads and prevents image flicker on partial updates.
10. How does RecyclerView's recycling work internally?
Scenario⌄
RecyclerView has multiple caches: (1) Attached/detached scrap — ViewHolders that are still in the layout but being re-laid out; retrieved without rebinding. (2) Cache (default size 2) — recently off-screen ViewHolders cached by position; retrieved without rebinding if the same position comes back. (3) RecycledViewPool — typed ViewHolders for reuse; must rebind when retrieved. (4) ViewCacheExtension — custom cache layer. Order of retrieval: scrap → cache → pool → onCreateViewHolder. setItemViewCacheSize increases the size of the cache layer, reducing rebinds for recently-off-screen items.

28B — Legacy UI

ViewBinding, DataBinding, ConstraintLayout, Custom Views (onMeasure/onDraw), XML layout techniques (include/merge/ViewStub), and why Jetpack Compose is replacing all of this.

ID: 28B ★ Tier 3
🔍
1. Overview

The Legacy UI Toolkit

Android's original UI toolkit uses XML layout files inflated into View objects. Jetpack Compose is the modern replacement, but legacy UI knowledge is essential for maintaining existing apps and understanding the limitations Compose was designed to solve.

TechnologyPurposeStatus
ViewBindingType-safe view access — replaces findViewById✅ Recommended when not using Compose
DataBindingTwo-way binding between XML and data⚠️ Works but adds complexity — prefer ViewModel + ViewBinding
ConstraintLayoutFlat, flexible layout✅ Best XML layout manager
Custom ViewsFully custom rendering via Canvas✅ Still needed for complex custom components
ViewStub/merge/includeLayout optimization techniques✅ Still used in XML-based apps
Senior Mental Model
Know legacy UI well enough to maintain and migrate it. In interviews, acknowledge that Compose solves the fundamental problems of XML UI (no type safety, manual state management, complex custom rendering) while still demonstrating mastery of the legacy stack for the millions of existing Android apps.
🔗
2. ViewBinding & DataBinding

ViewBinding

// Enable in build.gradle.kts:
android { buildFeatures { viewBinding = true } }

// Fragment — proper lifecycle management
class ProductFragment : Fragment(R.layout.fragment_product) {

    private var _binding: FragmentProductBinding? = null
    private val binding get() = _binding!!

    override fun onCreateView(inflater: LayoutInflater, container: ViewGroup?, savedInstanceState: Bundle?) =
        FragmentProductBinding.inflate(inflater, container, false).also { _binding = it }.root

    override fun onDestroyView() {
        super.onDestroyView()
        _binding = null  // IMPORTANT: prevent memory leak
    }
}
Memory Leak Warning
In Fragments, the View can be destroyed while the Fragment instance lives on (e.g., in the back stack). Always null out the binding reference in onDestroyView() to prevent the binding (and all its view references) from leaking.

DataBinding

// Enable:
android { buildFeatures { dataBinding = true } }

<!-- XML layout wrapped in <layout> tag -->
<layout>
    <data>
        <variable name="product" type="com.example.Product" />
        <variable name="viewModel" type="com.example.ProductViewModel" />
    </data>
    <TextView
        android:text="@{product.name}"
        android:onClick="@{() -> viewModel.onProductClicked(product)}" />
    <!-- Two-way binding: -->
    <EditText android:text="@={viewModel.searchQuery}" />
</layout>
FeatureViewBindingDataBinding
Type safety✅ Full✅ Full
Build speedFaster (no annotation processing)Slower (KSP/KAPT needed)
XML expressions❌ No✅ @{}, @={} expressions
Two-way binding❌ No✅ @={}
Kotlin syntheticsDeprecated — removed in Kotlin 1.8

Recommendation: Use ViewBinding for simple view access. DataBinding for two-way binding — but be aware of hidden complexity (hard-to-debug XML expressions, build time overhead). Prefer ViewModel + ViewBinding + manual observation over DataBinding expressions.

📍
3. ConstraintLayout

ConstraintLayout produces a flat view hierarchy — all views at the same level with positional relationships defined by constraints. This eliminates deeply nested LinearLayouts/RelativeLayouts, reducing measure/layout passes.

Key Concepts

ConceptDescription
ConstraintsAttach view edges to parent, other views, or guidelines
ChainsLinked group of views sharing space — spread, packed, or weighted
BarrierVirtual guide that tracks the extremity of multiple views
GuidelineFixed or percentage-based position line for alignment
GroupControl visibility of multiple views together
MotionLayoutSubclass for complex animations between two ConstraintSets
<!-- Typical ConstraintLayout card -->
<androidx.constraintlayout.widget.ConstraintLayout>

    <ImageView
        android:id="@+id/avatar"
        app:layout_constraintTop_toTopOf="parent"
        app:layout_constraintStart_toStartOf="parent" />

    <TextView
        android:id="@+id/nameText"
        app:layout_constraintTop_toTopOf="@id/avatar"
        app:layout_constraintStart_toEndOf="@id/avatar"
        app:layout_constraintEnd_toEndOf="parent" />

    <!-- Barrier — follows the longer of name or subtitle -->
    <androidx.constraintlayout.widget.Barrier
        android:id="@+id/textBarrier"
        app:barrierDirection="bottom"
        app:constraint_referenced_ids="nameText,subtitleText" />

</androidx.constraintlayout.widget.ConstraintLayout>

ConstraintSet for Programmatic Changes

val constraintSet = ConstraintSet()
constraintSet.clone(constraintLayout)
constraintSet.connect(R.id.view, ConstraintSet.TOP, R.id.anchor, ConstraintSet.BOTTOM, 16)
// Apply with animation:
TransitionManager.beginDelayedTransition(constraintLayout)
constraintSet.applyTo(constraintLayout)
🎨
4. Custom Views

Custom View Lifecycle

class CircleProgressView @JvmOverloads constructor(
    context: Context,
    attrs: AttributeSet? = null,
    defStyleAttr: Int = 0
) : View(context, attrs, defStyleAttr) {

    private val paint = Paint(Paint.ANTI_ALIAS_FLAG).apply {
        color = Color.BLUE
        style = Paint.Style.STROKE
        strokeWidth = 8f
    }
    private val oval = RectF()
    var progress: Float = 0f
        set(value) { field = value.coerceIn(0f, 1f); invalidate() }

    // onMeasure: define the view's size
    override fun onMeasure(widthMeasureSpec: Int, heightMeasureSpec: Int) {
        val size = resolveSize(200, widthMeasureSpec).coerceAtLeast(
            resolveSize(200, heightMeasureSpec)
        )
        setMeasuredDimension(size, size)
    }

    // onLayout: position children (for ViewGroups only)

    // onDraw: render to Canvas — called every invalidate()
    override fun onDraw(canvas: Canvas) {
        val padding = paint.strokeWidth / 2
        oval.set(padding, padding, width - padding, height - padding)
        canvas.drawArc(oval, -90f, progress * 360f, false, paint)
    }
}

Custom XML Attributes

<!-- res/values/attrs.xml -->
<declare-styleable name="CircleProgressView">
    <attr name="progressColor" format="color" />
    <attr name="strokeWidth" format="dimension" />
</declare-styleable>

// Read in constructor:
init {
    context.obtainStyledAttributes(attrs, R.styleable.CircleProgressView).use { ta ->
        paint.color = ta.getColor(R.styleable.CircleProgressView_progressColor, Color.BLUE)
        paint.strokeWidth = ta.getDimension(R.styleable.CircleProgressView_strokeWidth, 8f)
    }
}
Performance Warning
Never allocate Paint, RectF, or other objects inside onDraw() — it runs 60+ times per second and triggers GC pressure. Create all objects in the constructor or as class fields.
📄
5. XML Layout Techniques

include — reuse layout files

<!-- Reuse a common toolbar layout -->
<include
    layout="@layout/toolbar_main"
    android:id="@+id/toolbar"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content" />

merge — eliminate root ViewGroup

<!-- Without merge: include adds toolbar_main's root FrameLayout into parent -->
<!-- With merge: children merge directly into include location -->
<merge xmlns:android="...">
    <!-- Children are merged into the parent container directly -->
    <TextView android:id="@+id/label" ... />
    <ImageView android:id="@+id/icon" ... />
</merge>
<!-- Use when the included layout's root type matches the parent container -->

ViewStub — lazy inflation

<!-- ViewStub: 0x0 placeholder — not inflated until needed -->
<ViewStub
    android:id="@+id/errorStub"
    android:layout="@layout/layout_error"
    android:inflatedId="@+id/errorView"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content" />

// Inflate on demand:
val stub = binding.errorStub
if (stub.parent != null) {  // check not already inflated
    stub.inflate()
}
// After inflation, stub is removed from hierarchy and replaced by the layout
// Ideal for error states, onboarding screens, rare UI paths
TechniqueWhen to useBenefit
includeReusing common layouts (toolbar, footer)DRY, maintainability
mergeWhen included layout root matches parentRemoves extra nesting level
ViewStubLayouts used conditionally (error, empty, overlay)Reduces initial inflation cost
🚀
6. Migration to Compose

Why Compose Replaces All of This

Legacy ProblemCompose Solution
Manual state management (setText, setVisibility)State-driven UI — recompose on state change automatically
No type safety in XML attributesPure Kotlin — compile-time type checking everywhere
Complex two-way binding with DataBindingrememberSaveable + ViewModel.uiState — simple and explicit
onMeasure/onDraw boilerplate for custom renderingCanvas in DrawScope, Modifier.drawBehind — Kotlin DSL
Nested layouts causing measure overheadIntrinsic measurements, single-pass layout
ViewStub for conditional inflationif/when expressions — lazy evaluation by default

Incremental Migration Strategy

// Step 1: Add Compose to a Fragment with ComposeView
class ProductFragment : Fragment() {
    override fun onCreateView(...) = ComposeView(requireContext()).apply {
        setViewCompositionStrategy(ViewCompositionStrategy.DisposeOnViewTreeLifecycleDestroyed)
        setContent {
            MyAppTheme { ProductScreen(viewModel = hiltViewModel()) }
        }
    }
}

// Step 2: Embed legacy View in Compose with AndroidView
@Composable
fun LegacyMapView() {
    AndroidView(factory = { context -> MapView(context).apply { ... } })
}

// Step 3: Full migration — replace Fragment with a NavHost entry
🏆
7. Interview Framework

30-Second Answer

"For legacy XML-based UI: ViewBinding for type-safe view access (replacing kotlin synthetics which are removed), ConstraintLayout for flat hierarchies, ViewStub for lazy inflation of conditional UI. DataBinding is an option for two-way binding but I prefer ViewModel + ViewBinding due to lower complexity. Custom Views use onMeasure → onDraw with Canvas. Compose replaces all of this with state-driven, type-safe, declarative UI."

2-Minute Answer

"ViewBinding generates a typed binding class from each XML layout — fragment_product.xml becomes FragmentProductBinding. The critical Fragment pattern is nulling out the binding in onDestroyView() to prevent memory leaks since the Fragment lives longer than its View. DataBinding adds @{} XML expressions and @={} two-way binding — it works but adds build overhead and hard-to-debug XML logic; I prefer keeping logic in the ViewModel and using ViewBinding for view access. ConstraintLayout produces flat hierarchies via constraints, barriers, and chains — it's the best XML layout manager. For custom rendering, Custom Views override onMeasure (size) and onDraw (Canvas rendering) — never allocate objects in onDraw or you'll cause GC pressure during animation. ViewStub defers inflation until needed — useful for error/empty states. Compose replaces all of this: state-driven recomposition instead of manual setText/setVisibility, pure Kotlin type safety, and intrinsic measurements instead of multi-pass layout."

Must-Mention Points

1
ViewBinding: null _binding in onDestroyView() — Fragment View lifecycle is shorter than Fragment lifecycle
2
Kotlin synthetics removed in Kotlin 1.8 — ViewBinding is the replacement
3
Custom Views: no object allocation in onDraw — 60fps means Paint/RectF in constructor
4
ViewStub: lazy inflation — 0 cost until inflate() called
5
ComposeView + AndroidView — the bridge for incremental migration

Senior Insight

Senior Differentiator
Understand the View measurement system: measure() → onMeasure() → layout() → onLayout() → draw() → onDraw(). Every parent calls measure on all children before laying them out. Deeply nested layouts cause O(n²) measure passes. ConstraintLayout reduces this to O(n) by solving constraints in one pass. Compose's Intrinsics API provides similar benefits with explicit opt-in.
⚡

ViewBinding Fragment

9. Interview Questions
1. What is ViewBinding and how does it differ from DataBinding?
Basic⌄
ViewBinding generates a typed class for each XML layout file — provides null-safe, type-safe access to views. It replaces findViewByld and Kotlin synthetics. DataBinding also generates typed classes but additionally supports @{} expressions in XML for data binding and @={} for two-way binding. ViewBinding is faster to compile (no annotation processing), simpler to debug (no XML expressions), and preferred for most cases. Use DataBinding only when two-way XML binding is genuinely needed.
2. Why must you null the binding reference in Fragment.onDestroyView()?
Basic⌄
Fragments have two lifetimes: the Fragment itself (created to destroyed) and the Fragment's View (onCreateView to onDestroyView). When the Fragment is on the back stack, its View is destroyed but the Fragment instance lives on. The binding holds references to all Views in the destroyed layout. If not nulled, this constitutes a memory leak — the Fragment keeps the entire View hierarchy alive. Always: onDestroyView() { super.onDestroyView(); _binding = null }.
3. What are the key advantages of ConstraintLayout over LinearLayout/RelativeLayout?
Basic⌄
Flat hierarchy — all views at one level, no nested containers. This reduces measure/layout passes (nested LinearLayouts require O(n²) measurement). ConstraintLayout can express any layout that would require nested LinearLayouts + RelativeLayouts in a single flat structure. Additional features: chains (spread/pack weight distribution), barriers (dynamic alignment), groups (visibility control), guidelines, and MotionLayout for animations.
4. What is ViewStub and when is it useful?
Intermediate⌄
ViewStub is a zero-size, zero-draw placeholder in the layout hierarchy. It takes up no memory or draw time until inflate() is called. On inflate, the ViewStub is replaced in the view tree by the specified layout. Useful for: error states (only shown when network fails), onboarding overlays (shown once), premium features UI (shown only to paid users), complex UI that's rarely needed. It reduces initial inflation and layout costs for these conditional views.
5. What are the lifecycle methods of a Custom View and when does each run?
Intermediate⌄
onMeasure(widthSpec, heightSpec): called by parent to determine this View's size. Must call setMeasuredDimension(). onLayout(changed, l, t, r, b): called to position children (ViewGroups only). onDraw(canvas): render the view. Called on every invalidate() — runs at 60fps during animations. invalidate(): schedules a redraw (calls onDraw). requestLayout(): schedules re-measure + re-layout + redraw. Call invalidate() for visual changes, requestLayout() when size might change.
6. Why shouldn't you allocate objects in onDraw()?
Intermediate⌄
onDraw() runs 60+ times per second during animations and scrolling. Allocating Paint, RectF, Path, or other objects in onDraw() creates thousands of objects per second. Each allocation eventually triggers garbage collection — GC pauses can cause visible jank (frame drops). Allocate all drawing objects in the constructor or as class-level fields. Reuse and update them (e.g., rect.set() instead of new RectF()). Android Lint has a "DrawAllocation" check that flags this pattern.
7. How does the merge tag work with include?
Intermediate⌄
Normally, <include> embeds the entire XML including its root ViewGroup. A <FrameLayout> wrapper in the included file becomes an extra nested view. Using <merge> as the root of the included layout tells the inflater to merge the children directly into the parent at the include insertion point — the <merge> tag itself is not a View. This removes one level of nesting. Use merge when the included layout's content type matches the parent container (e.g., including into a LinearLayout when merge contains LinearLayout children).
8. How do you incrementally migrate XML-based UI to Compose?
Senior⌄
Strategy: start with new screens in Compose, don't rewrite working screens. For existing screens: use ComposeView inside Fragment.onCreateView() — the Fragment container becomes a thin shell hosting Compose UI. Set ViewCompositionStrategy.DisposeOnViewTreeLifecycleDestroyed for correct lifecycle. Use AndroidView for embedding legacy Views that have no Compose equivalent (MapView, WebView). Gradually replace Fragment-by-Fragment, then remove Fragment dependencies as screens become fully Compose. The ViewModel layer remains untouched throughout migration.
9. When would you still write a Custom View in a Compose-first project?
Senior⌄
Custom Views are still warranted for: third-party SDKs that provide custom View subclasses (Maps, AR, camera preview), extremely complex custom rendering that's better expressed with Canvas API than Compose's DrawScope, and integration with accessibility frameworks that work better with View. In Compose, Canvas {} composable and Modifier.drawBehind cover 95% of custom drawing needs. For the remaining 5%, use AndroidView to embed the custom View in Compose with full lifecycle management.
10. What are ConstraintLayout chains and when do you use them?
Scenario⌄
A chain is a group of views linked bi-directionally. Chain styles: spread (equal spacing between views), spread_inside (equal spacing but no outer margin), packed (views clustered together with bias). Weighted chains allow LinearLayout-style weight distribution in ConstraintLayout. Use chains when multiple views share horizontal or vertical space and need to distribute it. Example: three buttons sharing the bottom of a form — create a horizontal chain with spread_inside to space them evenly without nested LinearLayout.

29A — Paging 3

PagingSource, Pager configuration, PagingData streams, RemoteMediator for offline-first paging, Room + Paging integration, LazyPagingItems in Compose, and API pagination design.

ID: 29A ★ Tier 3
🔍
1. Overview

Paging 3 Architecture

Repository layer:
  PagingSource<Key, Value>  ← single data source (network OR database)
  RemoteMediator             ← network + database (offline-first)
  Pager(config, source)     ← orchestrates loading
    └── Flow<PagingData<T>> ← stream of paginated data

ViewModel layer:
  Flow<PagingData<T>>.cachedIn(viewModelScope)

UI layer:
  LazyPagingItems<T>         ← Compose
  PagingDataAdapter           ← RecyclerView
Senior Mental Model
Paging 3 is a reactive pagination library. The UI never directly requests pages — it signals loading triggers (prefetch distance reached), and the Pager + PagingSource respond asynchronously. The key design: PagingSource for single source, RemoteMediator for network+database (offline-first). Room automatically generates PagingSource from @Query — no manual implementation needed.
⚙
2. PagingSource
// PagingSource<Key, Value>
// Key: type of page key (Int for offset, String for cursor)
// Value: type of data items
class ProductPagingSource(
    private val api: ProductApiService
) : PagingSource<Int, Product>() {

    override suspend fun load(params: LoadParams<Int>): LoadResult<Int, Product> {
        val page = params.key ?: 1  // default to first page
        return try {
            val response = api.getProducts(page = page, pageSize = params.loadSize)
            LoadResult.Page(
                data = response.products,
                prevKey = if (page == 1) null else page - 1,
                nextKey = if (response.isLastPage) null else page + 1
            )
        } catch (e: Exception) {
            LoadResult.Error(e)
        }
    }

    // Called when data is invalidated (refresh signal)
    override fun getRefreshKey(state: PagingState<Int, Product>): Int? {
        // Return the page key for the anchor position (item closest to viewport center)
        return state.anchorPosition?.let { anchor ->
            state.closestPageToPosition(anchor)?.let { page ->
                page.prevKey?.plus(1) ?: page.nextKey?.minus(1)
            }
        }
    }
}

LoadResult Types

TypeMeaning
LoadResult.Page(data, prevKey, nextKey)Successful page load. null prevKey = no more previous pages. null nextKey = no more next pages.
LoadResult.Error(throwable)Load failed. Paging delivers CombinedLoadStates.append/prepend.error to the UI.
LoadResult.InvalidSource invalidated — Pager will create a new PagingSource
🆕
3. Pager & PagingData

Repository — creating the paged stream

class ProductRepository @Inject constructor(
    private val api: ProductApiService
) {
    fun getProductsPaged(): Flow<PagingData<Product>> = Pager(
        config = PagingConfig(
            pageSize = 20,             // items per page
            prefetchDistance = 5,       // load next page when 5 items from end
            initialLoadSize = 40,       // first load: 2× pageSize for faster initial display
            enablePlaceholders = false  // set true for known total count
        ),
        pagingSourceFactory = { ProductPagingSource(api) }
    ).flow
}

ViewModel — cache the flow

@HiltViewModel
class ProductViewModel @Inject constructor(
    repository: ProductRepository
) : ViewModel() {

    val products: Flow<PagingData<Product>> = repository
        .getProductsPaged()
        .cachedIn(viewModelScope)  // IMPORTANT: cache survives rotation
}
cachedIn is Required
Without .cachedIn(viewModelScope), every collector (including rotation) restarts the flow from scratch — losing loaded pages. cachedIn stores the last emitted PagingData in the ViewModel scope, surviving recomposition and configuration changes.
🔁
4. RemoteMediator (Offline-First)

Architecture: Network + Database Paging

// RemoteMediator fetches from network, stores in Room
// The UI always reads from Room (single source of truth)
// RemoteMediator is the "middleware" that keeps Room fresh

@OptIn(ExperimentalPagingApi::class)
class ProductRemoteMediator(
    private val api: ProductApiService,
    private val db: AppDatabase
) : RemoteMediator<Int, ProductEntity>() {

    override suspend fun load(
        loadType: LoadType,        // REFRESH, PREPEND, or APPEND
        state: PagingState<Int, ProductEntity>
    ): MediatorResult {
        return try {
            val page = when (loadType) {
                LoadType.REFRESH -> 1     // start from beginning
                LoadType.PREPEND -> return MediatorResult.Success(endOfPaginationReached = true)
                LoadType.APPEND -> {
                    val lastKey = db.remoteKeysDao().getLastKey()
                        ?: return MediatorResult.Success(endOfPaginationReached = true)
                    lastKey + 1
                }
            }
            val response = api.getProducts(page, state.config.pageSize)
            db.withTransaction {
                if (loadType == LoadType.REFRESH) {
                    db.productDao().clearAll()   // fresh data on refresh
                    db.remoteKeysDao().clearAll()
                }
                db.productDao().insertAll(response.products.map { it.toEntity() })
                db.remoteKeysDao().insert(RemoteKey(page))
            }
            MediatorResult.Success(endOfPaginationReached = response.isLastPage)
        } catch (e: Exception) {
            MediatorResult.Error(e)
        }
    }
}
LoadType Meanings
REFRESH: initial load or explicit refresh (e.g., swipe-to-refresh). Clear old data. PREPEND: load pages before the start. Typically return Success(endOfPaginationReached = true) for typical APIs. APPEND: load next page when user scrolls to end.
📌
5. Room + Paging Integration

Room Auto-generates PagingSource

// Room DAO — return PagingSource directly
@Dao
interface ProductDao {
    @Query("SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY name ASC")
    fun getProductsPaged(): PagingSource<Int, ProductEntity>
    // Room generates the PagingSource implementation — no code needed
}

// Repository — combine Pager + RemoteMediator + Room
@OptIn(ExperimentalPagingApi::class)
fun getProductsPaged(): Flow<PagingData<Product>> = Pager(
    config = PagingConfig(pageSize = 20),
    remoteMediator = ProductRemoteMediator(api, db),
    pagingSourceFactory = { db.productDao().getProductsPaged() }
).flow
    .map { pagingData -> pagingData.map { it.toDomain() } }

Data Flow with RemoteMediator

User scrolls → Pager signals prefetch
  → Room PagingSource serves cached items immediately (offline)
  → RemoteMediator.load(APPEND) called
      → Fetch from API
      → Store in Room (transaction)
      → Room PagingSource auto-invalidates
      → UI receives new PagingData from Room
🚀
6. Compose & API Pagination Design

LazyPagingItems in Compose

@Composable
fun ProductListScreen(viewModel: ProductViewModel = hiltViewModel()) {
    val lazyItems = viewModel.products.collectAsLazyPagingItems()

    LazyColumn {
        items(
            count = lazyItems.itemCount,
            key = lazyItems.itemKey { it.id }
        ) { index ->
            val product = lazyItems[index]  // triggers load if null (placeholder)
            if (product != null) {
                ProductItem(product = product)
            }
        }

        // Handle load states
        when (val loadState = lazyItems.loadState.append) {
            is LoadState.Loading -> item { LoadingSpinner() }
            is LoadState.Error  -> item { ErrorRetryItem { lazyItems.retry() } }
            else -> {}
        }
    }
}

API Pagination Design

StyleKeyProsCons
Offset-basedpage=2&size=20Simple, jump to any pageData shift on insert/delete — items skipped or duplicated
Cursor-basedafter=cursor_tokenConsistent — no skips with real-time dataCan't jump to arbitrary page

For real-time feeds (chat, social, catalog updates) cursor-based is strongly preferred — an item inserted at position 5 between page requests won't cause page 2 to duplicate the item that shifted from page 1.

🏆
7. Interview Framework

30-Second Answer

"Paging 3 has three core pieces: PagingSource defines how to load a page of data, Pager orchestrates loading based on config (pageSize, prefetchDistance), and PagingData is the immutable snapshot streamed as a Flow. For offline-first, RemoteMediator fetches from network, writes to Room, and Room's auto-generated PagingSource serves the UI. The ViewModel caches the flow with cachedIn(viewModelScope) so rotation doesn't reset pagination."

2-Minute Answer

"PagingSource.load() is given LoadParams (key = current page, loadSize = how many to load) and returns LoadResult.Page(data, prevKey, nextKey) or LoadResult.Error. Pager wraps it with a PagingConfig — pageSize controls items per page, prefetchDistance triggers loading N items before the visible end, initialLoadSize is typically 2× pageSize for faster initial fill. For offline-first paging, RemoteMediator handles the network+database cycle: on REFRESH it clears Room and reloads; on APPEND it fetches the next page from API and inserts into Room. Room auto-generates PagingSource from a @Query returning PagingSource<Int, Entity> — when RemoteMediator writes new rows, Room invalidates the PagingSource and new data flows to the UI. In Compose, collectAsLazyPagingItems() + LazyColumn items(count) handles display including load state monitoring for spinners and retry buttons. Always use .cachedIn(viewModelScope) in the ViewModel — without it, every new subscriber (including orientation change) restarts paging from page 1."

Must-Mention Points

1
PagingSource.load() → LoadResult.Page(data, prevKey=null at start, nextKey=null at end)
2
cachedIn(viewModelScope) — survives rotation, prevents re-pagination
3
RemoteMediator = network + Room; pagingSourceFactory = Room's auto-generated PagingSource
4
LoadType: REFRESH (clear + reload), APPEND (next page), PREPEND (usually end-of-pagination)
5
Cursor-based pagination preferred for real-time data — offset-based causes duplicates/skips

Senior Insight

Senior Differentiator
Understand that Room's PagingSource auto-invalidates when the database changes. This is the key to RemoteMediator working: you don't need to manually signal the UI to refresh — writing new rows to Room triggers PagingSource.invalidate(), which causes Pager to create a new PagingSource and the new data flows automatically. This is the reactive backbone of offline-first paging.
⚡
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Paging Components

PagingSource  → load one page
Pager         → orchestrates
PagingData    → immutable snapshot
RemoteMediator → net + db

prefetchDistance = 5
initialLoadSize  = 40
enablePlaceholders = false

  .getProductsPaged()
  .cachedIn(viewModelScope)

  .collectAsLazyPagingItems()
LazyColumn {
  items(items.itemCount) { i ->
    items[i]?.let { ProductItem(it) }
  }

🅾
9. Interview Questions
1. What are the three main components of Paging 3?
Basic⌄
PagingSource: defines how to load a single page of data — takes LoadParams (key, loadSize) and returns LoadResult.Page or LoadResult.Error. Pager: orchestrates loading, manages the RecycledViewPool, and emits Flow<PagingData<T>>. PagingData: an immutable snapshot of a page — consumed by LazyPagingItems in Compose or PagingDataAdapter in RecyclerView. RemoteMediator is optional — adds network+database (offline-first) support.
2. What does prevKey and nextKey represent in LoadResult.Page?
Basic⌄
prevKey: the key to load the page BEFORE this one. null = no more previous pages (start of data). nextKey: the key to load the page AFTER this one. null = no more next pages (end of data). For offset-based: prevKey = page - 1, nextKey = page + 1. When nextKey is null, Pager stops appending and marks endOfPaginationReached = true.
3. Why is cachedIn(viewModelScope) necessary?
Basic⌄
Without cachedIn, each new collector of the Flow starts fresh — meaning every screen rotation restarts paging from page 1. cachedIn stores the latest PagingData in the ViewModel's scope. New collectors (after rotation or recomposition) immediately receive the cached PagingData — the user stays on their position in the list. It's the equivalent of calling cachedIn that creates an ActiveFlow that survives config changes.
4. What is RemoteMediator and how does it differ from PagingSource?
Intermediate⌄
PagingSource is a single data source — either network or database. RemoteMediator is the bridge between network and local database for offline-first: it fetches from the network, stores in Room, and the PagingSource reads from Room. The UI always reads from Room (single source of truth). RemoteMediator is triggered by Pager when more data is needed (based on distance to end). Room's PagingSource auto-invalidates when RemoteMediator writes new rows.
5. How does Room auto-generate PagingSource?
Intermediate⌄
Room's annotation processor generates a PagingSource implementation when a @Query method returns PagingSource<Int, Entity>. Room's implementation wraps the query in a paging strategy that: reads one page at a time (keyed by offset), observes the database for changes using InvalidationTracker, and calls PagingSource.invalidate() when the queried table changes. This auto-invalidation is what makes RemoteMediator + Room work — no manual notification required.
6. What are the three LoadType values in RemoteMediator and when does each trigger?
Intermediate⌄
REFRESH: triggered on initial load or explicit refresh (swipe-to-refresh, invalidate()). Clear existing Room data and load page 1. APPEND: triggered when the user scrolls near the end of the list (within prefetchDistance items). Load the next page, append to Room. PREPEND: triggered when scrolling near the start. For most use cases, return MediatorResult.Success(endOfPaginationReached = true) since APIs typically don't support backward pagination.
7. How do you display loading and error states in Compose with Paging 3?
Intermediate⌄
LazyPagingItems exposes loadState: CombinedLoadStates with three properties: refresh (initial load), prepend (loading more at start), append (loading more at end). Each is a LoadState: Loading, NotLoading, or Error. In LazyColumn: observe lazyItems.loadState.refresh for initial loading spinners/errors. Add an item {} inside LazyColumn for append states — LoadState.Loading shows a spinner at the bottom; LoadState.Error shows a retry button that calls lazyItems.retry().
8. Why is cursor-based pagination better than offset-based for real-time data?
Senior⌄
Offset-based: page 2 = items 21-40. If a new item is inserted at position 5 between loading page 1 and page 2, every item shifts by 1. The old item 20 is now item 21 — the first item of page 2, duplicating it. Or if an item is deleted, page 2 skips an item. Cursor-based: page 2 = "items after cursor X" where X is the ID/timestamp of the last item on page 1. Insertions elsewhere don't affect the cursor — you always get the next items relative to the stable anchor point. Essential for chat, social feeds, and any dataset with real-time mutations.
9. How do you implement swipe-to-refresh with Paging 3?
Senior⌄
Call lazyItems.refresh() to signal REFRESH to both the PagingSource and RemoteMediator. In Compose, wrap LazyColumn with PullToRefreshBox (Material3) or SwipeRefresh, binding isRefreshing to lazyItems.loadState.refresh is LoadState.Loading. The refresh() call triggers RemoteMediator.load(LoadType.REFRESH) → clears Room → fetches page 1 from API → Room auto-invalidates PagingSource → new data flows to UI. The isRefreshing indicator should go false when loadState.refresh is not Loading.
10. What is PagingConfig.enablePlaceholders and when should you enable it?
Scenario⌄
When enablePlaceholders = true, Paging shows null items for positions that haven't loaded yet — the list appears full-length immediately with skeleton/shimmer items. Requires knowing the total item count (PagingSource must set itemsBefore/itemsAfter in LoadResult.Page). When false (default), the list grows as new pages are loaded — no placeholders. Enable placeholders when: total count is known from API, items have fixed height, and you want to show scrollbar position accurately. Disable when: total count is unknown, items have variable height, or you prefer growing lists.

30A — Offline-First Product Catalog

Design an Android product catalog with offline browsing, search, pagination, and background sync — a complete senior-level system design answer covering architecture, data flow, trade-offs, and failure handling.

ID: 30A ★ Senior Differentiator
🔍
1. Problem Statement

Requirements

Functional

  • Browse product catalog with infinite scroll / pagination
  • Search products by name, category, or price range
  • View product detail (images, description, price, availability)
  • Offline access: catalog usable without internet connection
  • Push catalog updates: price changes, new arrivals visible on next launch

Non-Functional

  • Fast initial load — no blank screen while fetching
  • No duplicate products on pagination
  • Battery efficient background sync
  • Handle device variety: low-end phones with limited storage

Constraints & Assumptions

  • REST API for product catalog (cursor-based pagination)
  • ~10,000 products total, 20 per page
  • Catalog updated daily by backend team
  • Users expected to browse offline in areas with poor connectivity
🏛
2. Architecture & Components
