3. Data Flow

Online Flow — First Launch

App launch
  → CatalogViewModel creates Flow<PagingData>
  → Pager emits initial load request
  → RemoteMediator.load(REFRESH)
      → Fetch products/page=1 from API
      → Insert into Room (transaction: clear + insert)
  → Room PagingSource auto-invalidates
  → UI receives PagingData from Room → displays products
  → User scrolls near end
  → RemoteMediator.load(APPEND)
      → Fetch page 2 from API → insert into Room
  → UI updates with new items

Offline Flow

App launch (no internet)
  → RemoteMediator.load(REFRESH) fails
  → Returns MediatorResult.Error(NetworkException)
  → Room PagingSource serves existing cached data immediately
  → UI shows: "Showing cached data" banner
  → NetworkConnectivityObserver emits true (connected)
  → App triggers refresh() on PagingData
  → RemoteMediator.load(REFRESH) succeeds → fresh data

Background Sync Flow

WorkManager PeriodicWorkRequest (every 6 hours, on WiFi + charging)
  → CatalogSyncWorker.doWork()
      → Fetch updated catalog from API
      → Insert/update products in Room
      → Room invalidates PagingSource
      → If app is in foreground: UI auto-updates
      → If app is in background: fresh cache ready on next launch

Search Flow

User types in search box
  → searchQuery StateFlow debounced (300ms)
  → flatMapLatest: new Pager with search query param
  → ProductApi.search(query, page) → new RemoteMediator
  → OR: local Room FTS5 search for offline search
⚙
4. Key Design Decisions

1. Single Source of Truth = Room

The UI never reads directly from the network. Retrofit data goes to Room, and Room feeds the UI via PagingSource. This ensures offline reads are seamless and the UI always has consistent data regardless of network state.

2. Stale-While-Revalidate Pattern

Show cached data immediately on launch, then fetch fresh data in background. Users see content instantly — the catalog updates underneath. Implemented via: Room PagingSource loads immediately while RemoteMediator refreshes asynchronously.

3. WorkManager for Background Sync

val constraints = Constraints.Builder()
    .setRequiredNetworkType(NetworkType.CONNECTED)
    .setRequiresBatteryNotLow(true)
    .build()

val syncWork = PeriodicWorkRequestBuilder<CatalogSyncWorker>(6, TimeUnit.HOURS)
    .setConstraints(constraints)
    .setBackoffCriteria(BackoffPolicy.EXPONENTIAL, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .build()

WorkManager.getInstance(context).enqueueUniquePeriodicWork(
    "catalog_sync",
    ExistingPeriodicWorkPolicy.KEEP,
    syncWork
)

4. NetworkConnectivityObserver

class NetworkConnectivityObserver @Inject constructor(
    @ApplicationContext context: Context
) {
    private val connectivityManager =
        context.getSystemService(ConnectivityManager::class.java)

    val isConnected: Flow<Boolean> = callbackFlow {
        val callback = object : ConnectivityManager.NetworkCallback() {
            override fun onAvailable(network: Network) { trySend(true) }
            override fun onLost(network: Network) { trySend(false) }
        }
        connectivityManager.registerDefaultNetworkCallback(callback)
        awaitClose { connectivityManager.unregisterNetworkCallback(callback) }
    }.distinctUntilChanged()
}
⚖
5. Trade-offs & Failure Handling

Trade-offs

DecisionChosen ApproachAlternativeWhy Chosen
Sync strategyWorkManager periodic syncPush via FCM + on-demandBattery efficient; acceptable for daily catalog updates
SearchAPI search + Room FTS5 offlineAPI search onlyOffline search requires local FTS; minor storage overhead
PaginationCursor-based API + Paging3Offset-basedConsistent results when catalog updates between pages
Cache strategyStale-while-revalidateNetwork-first / cache-firstBest UX — instant display + fresh data
StorageRoom (SQLite)DataStore, file cacheQueryable, paging-integrated, relational

Failure Scenarios

FailureHandling
Network unavailableRemoteMediator returns Error; Room PagingSource still serves cache; UI shows offline banner
API returns 5xxRemoteMediator returns MediatorResult.Error; Paging shows retry button; no data loss from cache
Room database corruptRoom allows destructive migration; re-sync from API on next launch
WorkManager failsExponential backoff retry; also sync on app foreground
Stale data too oldTrack last_sync timestamp in Room; show "Last updated X hours ago" warning
📈
6. Scalability & Failure Handling

Scaling to Larger Catalogs

  • Storage pruning: Don't store entire 10K catalog on device. Store last N pages viewed (keep 100 most recent items, prune on sync). Use Room entity with last_accessed timestamp.
  • Partial sync: API supports ?updated_after=timestamp — sync only changed products, not full catalog
  • Category-based prefetch: Pre-sync only the category the user most recently viewed
  • Image caching: Coil's disk cache handles product images; set max disk cache size per available storage

Multi-Module Architecture

:feature:catalog  → CatalogScreen, CatalogViewModel
:feature:search   → SearchScreen, SearchViewModel
:core:product     → ProductRepository, ProductApi, ProductDao, RemoteMediator
:core:database    → Room setup, AppDatabase
:core:network     → Retrofit, OkHttp, interceptors
:core:sync        → CatalogSyncWorker, NetworkConnectivityObserver

Testing Strategy

  • Unit tests: ProductRepository with FakeProductApi + in-memory Room
  • PagingSource tests: TestPagingDataDiffer to collect paginated items
  • RemoteMediator tests: Mock API responses, verify Room state after each LoadType
  • E2E tests: Maestro or Espresso for offline catalog browsing flow
🏆
7. Interview Framework

30-Second Answer

"I'd use an offline-first architecture with Room as the single source of truth. Retrofit fetches from the API via a RemoteMediator, writes to Room, and the UI reads from Room via Paging 3's PagingSource — so it always has data even offline. Background sync runs via WorkManager on a 6-hour schedule when connected. Network state is observed as a Flow to show offline banners and trigger re-sync when reconnected."

2-Minute Answer

"The key insight is stale-while-revalidate: show cached data immediately, refresh in the background. Architecture: Compose UI → CatalogViewModel → GetProductsUseCase → ProductRepository. The repository creates a Pager with a RemoteMediator and Room's auto-generated PagingSource. RemoteMediator handles network: on REFRESH it clears Room and loads page 1; on APPEND it loads the next page and inserts. Room's InvalidationTracker auto-invalidates the PagingSource when RemoteMediator writes, so the UI updates automatically. For offline: if RemoteMediator fails, Room still serves the last cached data — the user sees products with an 'offline' banner. Search works both online (API query) and offline (Room FTS5). Background sync via WorkManager with constraints: connected, battery not low — keeps catalog fresh without draining battery. NetworkConnectivityObserver as a Flow<Boolean> triggers refresh when connectivity returns."

Must-Mention Points

1
Room = single source of truth; UI never reads from network directly
2
RemoteMediator: REFRESH clears + reloads; APPEND fetches next page + inserts
3
Stale-while-revalidate: show cache immediately, refresh in background
4
WorkManager for battery-efficient background sync (constraints: connected, not low battery)
5
NetworkConnectivityObserver as Flow<Boolean> — reactive offline detection

Follow-up Q&A

QuestionKey Answer
How do you handle stale data?Track last_sync_at timestamp in Room; show "last updated" UI; WorkManager ensures max staleness is 6h
What if the catalog has 1M products?Prune local cache to last N viewed; partial sync with updated_after timestamp; server-side search instead of local FTS
How do you test offline behavior?MockWebServer returning errors, in-memory Room, TestPagingDataDiffer to verify loaded items

Senior Insight

Senior Differentiator
Proactively mention that Room's PagingSource auto-invalidates when data is written — this is not obvious and shows deep understanding. Also mention the RemoteKeys table pattern: to track which page corresponds to which cursor/offset across app restarts, store page keys in a separate Room table. Without this, APPEND after app restart restarts from page 1.
⚡

→ UseCase → Repository
→ RemoteMediator + Room
→ Retrofit (API)

9. Interview Questions
1. What does "single source of truth" mean in offline-first architecture?
Basic⌄
Room (local database) is the only source the UI reads from. The network is a supplier of data INTO Room, not a direct source for the UI. This ensures: (a) offline works — Room always has data, (b) UI is consistent — no race between network response and cache, (c) reactivity — Room's LiveData/Flow notifies UI when data changes from any source. Network data → Room → UI (always via Room).
2. How does RemoteMediator know which page to load next after app restart?
Basic⌄
RemoteKeys table in Room stores the last fetched page key (cursor or offset). On APPEND, RemoteMediator reads the last key from RemoteKeysDao.getLastKey() to determine which page to fetch next. On REFRESH, it clears the RemoteKeys table along with the product data. Without this table, after app restart APPEND would have no idea where pagination left off and would restart from page 1.
3. What is the stale-while-revalidate pattern?
Basic⌄
Show cached (potentially stale) data immediately to the user, then fetch fresh data in the background and update the UI when it arrives. Users see content instantly — no empty screen. The catalog may be hours old on first render, but updates within seconds as the background fetch completes. This is the best pattern for catalogs: it optimizes perceived performance while ensuring data freshness.
4. How do you implement offline search?
Intermediate⌄
Room supports FTS5 (Full Text Search) virtual tables. Define a @Fts4 or @Fts5 entity and create a shadow FTS table. ProductFts entity with content relationship to Product. Room generates efficient full-text search queries using MATCH operator. For online search: use API search endpoint. Strategy: if connected, use API search for fresh results; if offline, fall back to Room FTS search on cached data. Show "searching cached data" indicator when offline.
5. How do you detect when the device goes offline and comes back online?
Intermediate⌄
Use ConnectivityManager.registerDefaultNetworkCallback() wrapped in a callbackFlow. Emit true in onAvailable, false in onLost. Use distinctUntilChanged() to avoid duplicate emissions. Expose as Flow<Boolean> from a singleton NetworkConnectivityObserver (Hilt @Singleton). In ViewModel: collect isConnected, when it transitions to true call pagingData.refresh(). In UI: show/hide offline banner based on connectivity state.
6. What WorkManager constraints would you use for catalog sync?
Intermediate⌄
setRequiredNetworkType(NetworkType.CONNECTED) — don't sync without network. setRequiresBatteryNotLow(true) — don't drain low battery. Optional: setRequiresCharging(true) for large syncs only. Use PeriodicWorkRequest with 6-hour interval for catalog freshness. Use ExistingPeriodicWorkPolicy.KEEP to prevent duplicate schedules. Add exponential backoff for retry on failure. For immediate sync on reconnect, schedule a OneTimeWorkRequest with the same worker when connectivity is restored.
7. How would you handle a product catalog of 1 million items on a mobile device?
Senior⌄
Don't cache 1M items locally — that's 100MB+. Instead: (1) Cache only recently viewed categories/pages (LRU eviction policy in Room — prune items not accessed in 7 days). (2) Use partial sync: API endpoint GET /catalog?updated_after={timestamp} — only sync changed items. (3) Use server-side search — don't build local FTS for 1M items. (4) Category-level caching: user's most-browsed categories get deeper local cache; others get minimal cache. (5) Track storage budget: check available device storage, reduce cache size if low.
8. Design the Room schema for this system.
Senior⌄
Tables: (1) products(id, name, description, price, category, image_url, last_synced_at) — main catalog. (2) remote_keys(id, prev_key, next_key) — pagination state for RemoteMediator. (3) categories(id, name) — for category filter. (4) product_fts USING fts5(content=products) — virtual FTS table for offline search. (5) sync_metadata(key, last_sync_at) — track when last sync occurred. Indices: products(category), products(last_synced_at) for pruning queries.
9. How do you show "last updated X minutes ago" to the user?
Scenario⌄
Store last_sync_at timestamp in Room (a sync_metadata table or SharedPreferences). Expose it as Flow<Long?> from a SyncMetadataRepository. In ViewModel: combine isConnected flow with lastSyncAt flow → compute age string ("Last updated 3 min ago", "Offline — last updated 2 hours ago"). Update last_sync_at in RemoteMediator after successful REFRESH. If last_sync_at is null: never synced (first install). Show "Loading..." until first sync completes.
10. Walk through what happens when a user opens the app in airplane mode for the first time.
Scenario⌄
First install, airplane mode: (1) CatalogViewModel starts flow. (2) Pager triggers RemoteMediator.load(REFRESH). (3) RemoteMediator tries API → IOException. Returns MediatorResult.Error. (4) Room PagingSource has zero items (empty database). (5) UI receives empty PagingData + loadState.refresh is Error. (6) Show empty state screen: "No internet connection. Please connect to load the catalog." with a "Retry" button. (7) User turns off airplane mode → NetworkConnectivityObserver emits true → ViewModel calls refresh() → RemoteMediator succeeds → products appear. This is the correct UX — graceful empty state, not a crash.

30B — Login / Authentication System

Design a complete authentication system: email/password login, OAuth, biometric, JWT token management, silent refresh via OkHttp interceptor, secure storage, and session lifecycle.

ID: 30B ★ Senior Differentiator
🔍
1. Problem Statement

Requirements

Functional

  • Email/password login and registration
  • OAuth 2.0 / social login (Google, Apple)
  • Biometric authentication (fingerprint, face)
  • Remember me / persistent sessions
  • Secure token storage and automatic token refresh
  • Logout — clear all session data, navigate to login

Non-Functional

  • Tokens never stored in plaintext or SharedPreferences
  • Silent token refresh — user never sees "session expired" unexpectedly
  • Biometric enrollment tied to security key — re-enrollment required if biometrics change
  • Thread-safe token refresh (concurrent requests during refresh must wait, not each refresh independently)
🏛

3. Data Flow

Login Flow

User enters email + password → taps Login
  → AuthViewModel.onLoginClicked()
  → LoginUseCase.invoke(email, password)
  → AuthRepository.login(email, password)
  → Retrofit POST /auth/login
  → Response: { access_token, refresh_token, expires_in }
  → TokenStorage.save(accessToken, refreshToken, expiry)
  → AuthRepository emits Success(AuthSession)
  → AuthViewModel updates uiState = LoggedIn
  → NavController navigates to HomeScreen
    (FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TASK clears login back stack)

Automatic Token Refresh Flow

App makes any API request
  → TokenRefreshInterceptor adds Authorization: Bearer {accessToken}
  → Server returns 401 Unauthorized (token expired)
  → OkHttp Authenticator is called
  → Checks refreshToken exists
  → Calls AuthApi.refreshToken(refreshToken) synchronously
  → (Thread-safe: Mutex prevents concurrent refreshes)
  → On success: save new accessToken + refreshToken
  → Retry original request with new accessToken
  → On refresh failure (401 on refresh):
      → TokenStorage.clear()
      → Emit session expired event
      → Navigate to LoginScreen

Biometric Auth Flow

Biometric Login button tapped
  → BiometricUseCase creates CryptoObject
      (Cipher initialized with Keystore key)
  → BiometricPrompt.authenticate(cryptoObject)
  → User authenticates with fingerprint/face
  → OnSuccess callback: CryptoObject has authenticated Cipher
  → Decrypt stored refresh_token using Cipher
  → AuthRepository.refreshToken(decryptedRefreshToken)
  → Navigate to HomeScreen

Logout Flow

Logout tapped / session expired
  → LogoutUseCase.invoke()
  → AuthRepository.logout()
      → API POST /auth/logout (invalidate server-side)
      → TokenStorage.clear()
  → AuthViewModel emits LoggedOut state
  → NavController navigate to LoginScreen with:
      Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TASK or
      NavOptions popUpTo(root) inclusive=true
⚙
4. Key Design Decisions

1. Token Storage — EncryptedSharedPreferences vs Keystore

OptionSecurityUse When
SharedPreferences (plain)❌ Plaintext on rooted deviceNever for tokens
EncryptedSharedPreferences✅ AES-256 encrypted, Keystore-backed keyAccess + refresh tokens — standard choice
Android Keystore directly✅✅ Hardware-backed, key never leaves KeystoreKeys for biometric binding — highest security
In-memory only✅ Wiped on process killAccess token only (short-lived)

2. JWT Strategy

// Access token: short-lived (15 min)
// • Stored in memory (most secure) OR EncryptedSharedPreferences
// • Sent in every API request as Bearer token
// • If it expires: use refresh token to get a new one silently

// Refresh token: long-lived (30 days)
// • Stored in EncryptedSharedPreferences only
// • Used only to get a new access token
// • Rotated on each refresh (server issues new refresh token)
// • On refresh failure: session expired → force login

3. Thread-Safe Token Refresh

class TokenRefreshAuthenticator @Inject constructor(
    private val authRepository: AuthRepository
) : Authenticator {

    private val refreshMutex = Mutex()

    override fun authenticate(route: Route?, response: Response): Request? {
        if (response.code != 401) return null
        // runBlocking here because OkHttp Authenticator is synchronous
        return runBlocking {
            refreshMutex.withLock {
                // Check if another thread already refreshed while we waited
                val currentToken = authRepository.getAccessToken()
                val requestToken = response.request.header("Authorization")
                    ?.removePrefix("Bearer ")
                if (currentToken != requestToken) {
                    // Token already refreshed by another request
                    return@runBlocking response.request.newBuilder()
                        .header("Authorization", "Bearer $currentToken")
                        .build()
                }
                val result = authRepository.refreshToken()
                result.getOrNull()?.let { session ->
                    response.request.newBuilder()
                        .header("Authorization", "Bearer ${session.accessToken}")
                        .build()
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

4. Biometric Binding

// Keystore key tied to biometric enrollment
// Key is invalidated if biometrics change (new fingerprint added)
val keyGenSpec = KeyGenParameterSpec.Builder(
    "biometric_key",
    KeyProperties.PURPOSE_ENCRYPT or KeyProperties.PURPOSE_DECRYPT
).apply {
    setBlockModes(KeyProperties.BLOCK_MODE_CBC)
    setEncryptionPaddings(KeyProperties.ENCRYPTION_PADDING_PKCS7)
    setUserAuthenticationRequired(true)
    setInvalidatedByBiometricEnrollment(true)  // KEY SECURITY FEATURE
}.build()
KeyGenerator.getInstance(KeyProperties.KEY_ALGORITHM_AES, "AndroidKeyStore")
    .also { it.init(keyGenSpec) }
    .generateKey()
⚖
5. Trade-offs & Failure Handling

Trade-offs

DecisionChosenAlternativeReason
Token storageEncryptedSharedPreferencesPlain SharedPreferences, DataStoreAES-256 Keystore-backed, easy API
Refresh mechanismOkHttp AuthenticatorManual expiry check before each callTransparent to callers, handles concurrent requests
Access token locationEncryptedSharedPreferencesIn-memory onlySurvives process death; in-memory needs refresh on every cold start
Biometric bindingKeystore + setInvalidatedByBiometricEnrollmentStore biometric hashHardware-backed, cryptographically tied to enrollment

Failure Scenarios

FailureHandling
Login API failsShow specific error message (wrong password vs network); never log credentials
Refresh token expiredClear all tokens, emit SessionExpired event, navigate to login with message
Biometric key invalidatedCatch KeyPermanentlyInvalidatedException, delete key, prompt re-enrollment
Concurrent 401s during token refreshMutex ensures only one refresh — others wait and use the new token
Device compromised (root)EncryptedSharedPreferences relies on Keystore — hardware-backed keys resist extraction

Multi-Account Support

7. Interview Framework

30-Second Answer

"The auth system has three layers: a LoginScreen with AuthViewModel, AuthRepository handling API calls, and TokenStorage using EncryptedSharedPreferences for secure persistence. Access tokens are short-lived (15 min), refresh tokens long-lived (30 days). An OkHttp Authenticator handles silent refresh on 401 — thread-safe via Mutex so concurrent requests don't each trigger their own refresh. Biometrics use a Keystore key with setInvalidatedByBiometricEnrollment — re-enrollment required if fingerprints change."

2-Minute Answer

"Login flow: email/password → AuthRepository.login() → Retrofit POST /auth/login → tokens stored in EncryptedSharedPreferences (AES-256, Keystore-backed). JWT strategy: access token is short-lived (15 min), refresh token is long-lived (30 days) and rotated on use. Token refresh is completely transparent via OkHttp Authenticator: on 401, it calls /auth/refresh synchronously, saves new tokens, and retries the original request. Mutex ensures only one refresh runs — if 5 concurrent requests all get 401, only one refresh happens and the others reuse the result. Biometric: the Keystore key has setInvalidatedByBiometricEnrollment(true) — if the user adds a new fingerprint, the key is invalidated and we catch KeyPermanentlyInvalidatedException to force re-enrollment. Logout clears all tokens and navigates with FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TASK so the back stack contains only the login screen. For OAuth, use AppAuth library with PKCE — never implement OAuth manually."

Must-Mention Points

1
EncryptedSharedPreferences for tokens — never plain SharedPreferences
2
OkHttp Authenticator for silent token refresh on 401 — transparent to all callers
3
Mutex in Authenticator — prevents 5 concurrent 401s each triggering independent refreshes
4
setInvalidatedByBiometricEnrollment(true) — biometric key invalidated if enrollment changes
5
Logout: clear tokens + FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TASK — back button cannot return to authenticated screens

Senior Insight

Senior Differentiator
The concurrent token refresh problem is a classic. Without Mutex: 5 simultaneous API calls all get 401, all call refreshToken() concurrently, the server issues 5 new tokens but only one is stored. The other 4 refresh tokens are now invalid — user gets logged out unnecessarily. The fix: check whether the token has already changed before using your result (another thread may have already refreshed). This "check-after-lock" pattern is the correct solution.
⚡

9. Interview Questions
1. Where should you store JWT tokens on Android?
Basic⌄
EncryptedSharedPreferences backed by Android Keystore. It uses AES-256-GCM encryption with the key stored in the hardware-backed Keystore — the key cannot be extracted from the device. Never use plain SharedPreferences (plaintext on rooted devices), DataStore (not designed for tokens), or external storage. For extra security: keep access token in memory only (wiped on process kill) and only persist refresh token in EncryptedSharedPreferences.
2. How does OkHttp Authenticator differ from an Interceptor for token refresh?
Basic⌄
Interceptor runs before every request — you'd need to check token expiry time and refresh proactively. This can miss edge cases (clock skew, server-side revocation). Authenticator is triggered reactively by the server's 401 response — always accurate. OkHttp calls authenticate() exactly when authentication is needed, passes the failed response, and returns a new Request with updated credentials. Much cleaner and accurate than timestamp-based proactive refresh.
3. What is the "concurrent token refresh" problem and how do you solve it?
Basic⌄
Problem: 5 simultaneous API calls all get 401. All 5 call refreshToken() concurrently. Server issues 5 tokens — but each refresh token can only be used once (server rotates them). 4 of the 5 refresh attempts fail → user force-logged-out. Solution: Mutex in the Authenticator. Only one thread refreshes at a time. Threads 2-5 wait for the Mutex. When they get the lock, they check: is the current stored token different from what was in our failed request? If yes, another thread already refreshed — just retry with the new token without calling refresh again.
4. How does setInvalidatedByBiometricEnrollment(true) work?
Intermediate⌄
When creating a Keystore key with setInvalidatedByBiometricEnrollment(true), Android invalidates the key if the device's biometric enrollment changes — e.g., a new fingerprint is added. The next time the app tries to use the key, it gets KeyPermanentlyInvalidatedException. This prevents an attacker from adding their fingerprint and accessing the app's biometric-locked data. On exception: catch it, delete the key, show "biometric re-enrollment required" dialog, and generate a new key after re-authentication.
5. Walk through the biometric authentication flow.
Intermediate⌄
Setup (once): Generate Keystore key. Encrypt refresh_token with the key. Store encrypted token in EncryptedSharedPreferences. Login flow: Get Cipher from Keystore key in DECRYPT mode. Wrap in CryptoObject. Call BiometricPrompt.authenticate(cryptoObject). User authenticates. onAuthenticationSucceeded provides authenticated CryptoObject. Use Cipher to decrypt refresh_token. Call AuthRepository.refreshToken(decryptedToken). Navigate to home on success. The private key never leaves the Keystore — biometric authentication unlocks the hardware key operation.
6. How do you implement "remember me" functionality securely?
Intermediate⌄
Store the refresh_token in EncryptedSharedPreferences on successful login. On next app launch: check if refresh_token exists → call /auth/refresh → if successful, user is silently logged in. If refresh fails (token expired): clear tokens, show login screen. For "remember me" toggle: if unchecked, only store tokens in memory — they're lost on process kill. If checked, persist in EncryptedSharedPreferences. Distinguish between session timeout (acceptable UX warning) vs force logout (security event requiring re-auth).
7. How do you ensure the back stack is clean after logout?
Intermediate⌄
Two approaches: (1) Activity-based: startActivity(loginIntent.apply { flags = Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK or Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TASK }) — clears entire back stack, makes login the only activity. (2) Navigation Component: navController.navigate(loginRoute) { popUpTo(navGraph.startDestinationId) { inclusive = true } } — clears entire nav back stack to root. After this, pressing back exits the app rather than returning to authenticated screens. Also check AuthState on every screen's onResume to catch token expiry across deep links.
8. How would you implement OAuth 2.0 login (Google Sign-In) securely?
Senior⌄
Use AppAuth-Android library with PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange). Never implement OAuth manually. Flow: (1) Create AuthorizationRequest with code_verifier (random). Send authorization_code request to provider. (2) Receive authorization code via custom URI scheme or App Link callback. (3) Exchange code for tokens using code_verifier (server-side PKCE validation). (4) Send ID token to your backend for validation → your backend issues your app's JWT pair. Never use the OAuth provider's access token directly with your backend — always exchange for your own tokens.
9. How do you detect and handle session expiry across different app states?
Senior⌄
Multiple detection points: (1) Foreground API call gets 401 and refresh fails → Authenticator emits sessionExpiredFlow. (2) App resumes from background → check token expiry timestamp in EncryptedSharedPreferences — if expired, trigger refresh or show re-auth. (3) WorkManager background task gets 401 → emit session event. Handle via: a SharedFlow<Unit> sessionExpiredFlow in AuthRepository. Collect in RootComposable or Application.onCreate with a ProcessLifecycleOwner. On emission: clear tokens, navigate to login. UX: show "Your session expired. Please log in again." — don't silently lose user state.
10. What security risks exist in mobile auth and how do you mitigate them?
Scenario⌄
Risks: (1) Token in plaintext storage → Mitigation: EncryptedSharedPreferences. (2) Token in logs → Mitigation: never log auth headers; okhttp.log level = BASIC not HEADERS. (3) SSL stripping → Mitigation: Certificate pinning (OkHttp CertificatePinner). (4) Biometric bypass → Mitigation: setInvalidatedByBiometricEnrollment + CryptoObject binding — biometric without crypto is weaker. (5) Refresh token reuse attack → Mitigation: refresh token rotation — server invalidates old refresh token on use. (6) Backup/restore exposes tokens → Mitigation: android:allowBackup="false" or exclude EncryptedSharedPreferences file from backup rules.

30C — Shopping Cart

Design an Android shopping cart: local Room persistence, server sync, optimistic updates, guest-to-auth migration, conflict resolution, promo codes, and order placement flow.

ID: 30C ★ Senior Differentiator
🔍
1. Problem Statement

Requirements

Functional

  • Add, remove, update item quantity in cart
  • Cart persists across app restarts and device reboots
  • Cart syncs with backend for cross-device access
  • Guest cart (not logged in) → migrates to authenticated cart on login
  • Apply discount/promo codes
  • Place order from cart

Non-Functional

  • Instant UI feedback — optimistic updates (don't wait for network)
  • Cart badge count visible on bottom nav
  • Handle concurrent edits (phone + web)
  • No duplicate items — quantity update, not double-add
🏛
2. Architecture & Components

ASCII Architecture Diagram

Room Schema

@Entity(tableName = "cart_items")
data class CartItemEntity(
    @PrimaryKey val productId: String,
    val quantity: Int,
    val price: Double,
    val productName: String,
    val imageUrl: String,
    val syncStatus: SyncStatus = SyncStatus.PENDING,
    val localUpdatedAt: Long = System.currentTimeMillis()
)
enum class SyncStatus { PENDING, SYNCED, FAILED }
→
3. Data Flow

Add to Cart — Optimistic Update

User taps "Add to Cart"
  → CartViewModel.onAddItem(product)
  → AddToCartUseCase.invoke(product)
  → CartRepository.addItem(product)
      1. Write to Room immediately (syncStatus = PENDING)
         → UI updates instantly via Flow (optimistic)
      2. Enqueue SyncCartWorker in background
      3. SyncCartWorker calls CartApi.addItem()
      4. On success: update Room (syncStatus = SYNCED)
      5. On failure: mark FAILED, show retry banner

Cart Badge Count

// Always from Room — instant, no network needed
val cartItemCount: Flow<Int> = cartDao.getTotalItemCount()
// Collect in AppViewModel (singleton) → display on bottom nav badge

Guest Cart → Auth Cart Migration

Guest user adds items → stored in Room with userId = "guest"
User logs in:
  → AuthRepository emits LoginSuccess event
  → CartRepository.migrateGuestCart()
      1. Read all guest cart items from Room
      2. POST /cart/guest-merge with all items + auth token
      3. Server merges: sum quantities for duplicate items,
         or overwrite with auth cart if server is source of truth
      4. Receive merged cart from server
      5. Clear guest items in Room
      6. Save merged cart in Room (userId = authenticated userId)
  → UI shows merged cart

Promo Code Flow

User enters promo code → taps Apply
  → CartViewModel.onApplyPromo(code)
  → ApplyPromoUseCase.invoke(code)
  → CartApi.applyPromo(cartId, code)
  → Response: { discount_amount, discount_type, error? }
  → On success: save promo to Room, recalculate CartSummary
  → On failure: show "Invalid code" error in UiState
  → CartSummary = subtotal - discount + tax

Order Placement

User taps "Place Order"
  → Validate: cart not empty, items still in stock (server check)
  → Show payment selection (Stripe/PayPal intent)
  → POST /orders with: cart_id, payment_method_id, address
  → Response: { order_id, status: "PROCESSING" }
  → Clear local cart (Room.clearAll())
  → Navigate to OrderConfirmationScreen(orderId)
  → Track order status via GET /orders/{id} polling or WebSocket
⚙
4. Key Design Decisions

1. Optimistic Updates Pattern

Update Room immediately, sync in background. Users see instant feedback — the cart count and items update without waiting for the server. If the sync fails: show a non-intrusive error banner ("Some changes couldn't sync — tap to retry").

suspend fun addItem(item: CartItem) {
    // 1. Optimistic: update local immediately
    cartDao.insertOrUpdate(item.toEntity(SyncStatus.PENDING))

    // 2. Background sync (don't await — fire and forget)
    val syncWork = OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<SyncCartWorker>().build()
    workManager.enqueue(syncWork)
}

2. Conflict Resolution

StrategyDescriptionWhen to use
Server winsServer state always overrides local on syncSimple; good for high-trust server-side inventory
Last-write-winsMost recent update (by timestamp) winsMulti-device sync with timestamps
Merge / unionGuest cart + auth cart quantities are summedGuest cart migration

Recommendation: Use server wins for quantity conflicts (prevents overselling inventory). Use merge for guest → auth migration (users expect their guest items to survive login).

3. Debounced Quantity Updates

// Stepper: +/- rapid taps should not fire 10 API calls
private val quantityUpdateFlow = MutableSharedFlow<Pair<String, Int>>()

init {
    quantityUpdateFlow
        .debounce(500)       // wait 500ms after last tap
        .flatMapLatest { (productId, qty) ->
            cartRepository.updateQuantity(productId, qty)
        }
        .launchIn(viewModelScope)
}
⚖
5. Trade-offs & Failure Handling

Trade-offs

DecisionChosenAlternativeReason
Local-firstRoom as source of truth + background syncNetwork-only (no local storage)Instant UI, works offline
Sync mechanismWorkManager + syncStatus fieldImmediate sync, fail hardBattery efficient, resilient to network gaps
Conflict resolutionServer wins on inventory conflictsLast-write-wins everywherePrevents overselling
Guest cartRoom + migration on loginSession-only (lost on logout)Better UX — users expect cart to survive login

Failure Scenarios

FailureHandling
Network unavailable on addSaved locally as PENDING; synced when back online via WorkManager
Item out of stock at checkoutServer returns 409 Conflict; show inline error on item; offer removal or waiting list
Promo code expiredServer 400 response; show "Code expired" inline error; remove discount from UI
Sync fails repeatedlyAfter 3 failures: show persistent banner "Cart sync failed — changes may be lost"; offer retry
Order placement failsDon't clear cart; show error with retry; ensure idempotency key so duplicate requests are safe
📈
6. Scalability

Real-time Cart Updates

For cross-device sync (phone + web): use WebSocket or Server-Sent Events to push cart changes. CartViewModel subscribes to websocket flow; when server emits a cart update event, merge with local Room data (server wins for conflicts).

// WebSocket cart update handler
webSocketFlow
    .filterIsInstance<CartUpdatedEvent>()
    .onEach { event ->
        // Server data overrides local for server-authoritative fields
        cartDao.merge(event.items)
    }
    .launchIn(viewModelScope)

Item Quantity Limits

// Validate client-side AND server-side
fun onUpdateQty(productId: String, newQty: Int) {
    if (newQty > MAX_QUANTITY_PER_ITEM) {
        _uiState.update { it.copy(error = "Max $MAX_QUANTITY_PER_ITEM per item") }
        return
    }
    if (newQty <= 0) { onRemoveItem(productId); return }
    quantityUpdateFlow.tryEmit(productId to newQty)
}
🏆
7. Interview Framework

30-Second Answer

"The cart uses Room as local storage with a sync_status field. When users add/update/remove items, Room updates immediately (optimistic update) — the UI responds instantly. A WorkManager job syncs PENDING items to the backend. Server wins on conflicts to prevent inventory overselling. Guest cart items migrate to the authenticated cart on login. Debounced quantity updates prevent API spam from rapid taps."

2-Minute Answer

"Architecture: CartScreen → CartViewModel → CartUseCase → CartRepository → Room + Retrofit. The key design is optimistic updates: user taps '+1' → Room updates immediately with syncStatus = PENDING → WorkManager enqueues a background sync → CartApi call → on success mark SYNCED. This gives instant UI without waiting for the network. For quantity stepper: debounce 500ms so rapid taps don't generate 10 API calls — only the final quantity syncs. Guest cart: items stored in Room with userId='guest'. On login, migrateGuestCart() merges guest items with the server cart (quantities summed for duplicate products). Conflict resolution: server wins for inventory-sensitive fields to prevent overselling; we use last-write-wins (localUpdatedAt timestamp) for ordering non-inventory details. For order placement: validate stock with server → payment intent → POST /orders with idempotency key (prevents duplicate orders from retries) → clear cart only on success → navigate to confirmation."

Must-Mention Points

1
Optimistic updates: Room first (syncStatus = PENDING), background sync via WorkManager
2
Server wins for inventory conflicts — prevents overselling
3
Guest → auth migration: merge on login (sum quantities for duplicates)
4
Debounce quantity updates — prevent API spam from stepper taps
5
Idempotency key for order placement — safe to retry without duplicate orders

Senior Insight

Senior Differentiator
Idempotency keys for order placement: generate a UUID when the user taps "Place Order", include it as X-Idempotency-Key header. If the network drops after the server processes the order but before the response arrives, the client retries with the same key — the server detects the duplicate and returns the already-created order rather than creating a second one. This prevents double-charging.
⚡

9. Interview Questions
1. What are optimistic updates and why use them for a cart?
Basic⌄
Optimistic updates means updating the local UI immediately (as if the server accepted the change) and then syncing in the background. For a cart: user taps "+1" → quantity shows 3 instantly → network sync happens asynchronously. This feels snappy and responsive. If sync fails, show an error and optionally roll back. Contrast with pessimistic updates: wait for server confirmation before updating UI — laggy, especially on poor connections.
2. How do you migrate a guest cart to an authenticated cart?
Basic⌄
Store guest cart in Room with userId="guest". On successful login: read all guest items from Room, call POST /cart/guest-merge with items + auth token. Server applies merge strategy: sum quantities for duplicate products (product in both guest + existing auth cart), keep auth-only items, keep guest-only items. Response: merged cart. Client: clear guest items in Room, save merged cart as authenticated user's cart. Show "Your cart has been merged" notification.
3. What is an idempotency key and why is it critical for order placement?
Basic⌄
An idempotency key is a unique identifier (UUID) that the client generates before placing an order and includes in the request header (X-Idempotency-Key). If the same key is sent twice, the server returns the existing response instead of creating a duplicate. This handles the "network dropped after server processed but before client received response" scenario — client retries, server detects duplicate key → returns existing order → no double charge. Generate the UUID when the user confirms the order, not on button tap (to survive navigation).
4. How do you prevent API spam from a quantity stepper?
Intermediate⌄
Debounce: each stepper tap emits to a SharedFlow. Use .debounce(500ms) to wait 500ms after the last tap before calling the API. If the user taps + five times in 400ms, only one API call fires. Additionally: cancel the previous pending request if a new one arrives before it completes (flatMapLatest). This is the standard pattern for quantity inputs, search fields, and any rapid-fire user input.
5. How do you handle a "product is now out of stock" error during checkout?
Intermediate⌄
Server returns HTTP 409 Conflict with a payload indicating which products are out of stock. Client: don't clear the cart. Show inline errors on the affected cart items ("No longer available"). Offer options: remove item from cart, or save to wishlist for later. Don't place the order until the problematic items are resolved. Consider a "Validate Cart" step before showing the checkout button — call GET /cart/validate to check stock before showing the payment screen.
6. How do you handle cart badge count across the entire app?
Intermediate⌄
CartCountRepository provides Flow<Int> from Room's cartDao.getTotalItemCount(). This query returns the sum of quantities instantly from the local database. Inject CartCountRepository into a Hilt-scoped ViewModel or share it via the Application's Hilt SingletonComponent. In MainActivity's composable root: collect cartCount and pass to BottomNavigation badge. Because it's Room, it updates reactively whenever items are added/removed — no manual refresh needed.
7. How do you design the sync mechanism for PENDING cart items?
Intermediate⌄
SyncCartWorker (WorkManager) with constraints: requires network. On run: query Room for all items where syncStatus = PENDING. For each: call the appropriate API (add/update/delete based on operation type — add an operation enum to the entity). On success: update syncStatus = SYNCED. On failure: increment retryCount, WorkManager's retry/backoff handles re-runs. After max retries: mark FAILED, show persistent sync error banner. Use FAILED status to prevent infinite retry loops.
8. How would you handle real-time cart updates across devices?
Senior⌄
WebSocket or Server-Sent Events (SSE) connection per authenticated session. Server pushes CartUpdatedEvent when the cart changes from any device. Client receives event, applies server-wins merge to local Room data (update quantities, add new items, remove deleted items). Use a version number or timestamp per cart to detect stale updates. Show brief "Cart updated from another device" snackbar. Handle reconnection with exponential backoff and replay last event to avoid missing updates during reconnection gap.
9. Design the order placement flow with payment integration.
Senior⌄
Flow: (1) "Checkout" tapped → validate cart (stock check). (2) Show address selection + payment method. (3) Request payment intent from backend (POST /payment/create-intent) → returns client_secret. (4) Present Stripe/PayPal SDK with client_secret. (5) On payment confirmation: POST /orders { cart_id, payment_intent_id, idempotency_key, address_id }. (6) On 200: clear cart from Room, navigate to OrderConfirmationScreen. (7) On failure: keep cart, show error, allow retry with same idempotency_key. Never process payment entirely client-side — always via server-issued payment intents.
10. What would change in your design if the cart required strict consistency (no optimistic updates)?
Scenario⌄
Drop local Room as source of truth. Each cart action calls the API first and waits for confirmation: show loading indicator, then update UI with server response. UiState has explicit Loading/Error states for each operation. Pros: always consistent, no conflicts, no sync complexity. Cons: poor UX on slow connections, unusable offline. This model is appropriate for high-value items (luxury goods, limited edition) where overselling risk outweighs UX concerns. You could also use a hybrid: optimistic updates but with server-side locks that reject conflicting changes and trigger a cart refresh.

30D — Chat Application

Design a real-time chat app: WebSocket connection management, message delivery states, offline message queue, cursor-based pagination for history, push notifications, and media sharing.

ID: 30D ★ Senior Differentiator
🔍
1. Problem Statement

Requirements

Functional

  • Real-time messaging between users (1:1 and group)
  • Offline support: compose and queue messages when disconnected
  • Read receipts: sent → delivered → read indicators
  • Typing indicators
  • Message history pagination (load older messages)
  • Push notifications for new messages when app is in background
  • Media sharing (images, files)

Non-Functional

  • Sub-second message delivery when connected
  • Message ordering guaranteed (no out-of-order display)
  • No duplicate messages on reconnect
  • Battery-efficient connection management
🏛

3. Data Flow

Send Message Flow

User types message → taps Send
  → ChatViewModel.onSendMessage(text)
  → Create Message(id=UUID, status=SENDING)
  → Insert into Room immediately (optimistic)
    → UI shows message with "sending" indicator
  → WebSocket.send(message JSON)
  → Server ACK: { message_id, status: "SENT", timestamp }
  → Update Room: status=SENT, serverId=message_id
    → UI shows single checkmark (sent)
  → Recipient receives message
  → Server pushes: { type: "DELIVERED", message_id }
  → Update Room: status=DELIVERED
    → UI shows double checkmark (delivered)
  → Recipient opens chat
  → Server pushes: { type: "READ", message_id }
  → Update Room: status=READ
    → UI shows blue double checkmark (read)

Offline Message Queue

User sends message while offline
  → Create Message(status=SENDING, localOnly=true)
  → Save to Room
  → WebSocket send fails (not connected)
  → Message stays in Room with status=SENDING
  → NetworkConnectivityObserver detects online
  → WebSocketManager reconnects
  → MessageRepository.flushPendingMessages()
      → Query Room: messages WHERE localOnly=true ORDER BY timestamp
      → Send each via WebSocket in order
      → On ACK: update status=SENT, localOnly=false

Load Message History

User scrolls to top of chat
  → ChatViewModel.onLoadMore()
  → Fetch oldest message timestamp in Room
  → GET /messages?chatId={id}&before={timestamp}&limit=30
  → Insert into Room (don't clear existing)
  → Room Flow auto-updates — messages appear above
  → Cursor-based ensures no duplicates or gaps

Typing Indicator

// Typing: lightweight WebSocket events (NOT stored in Room)
User starts typing
  → debounce 1s → send { type: "TYPING", chatId }
  → WebSocket broadcasts to conversation participants
  → Received by other device: show "{name} is typing..."
  → Auto-clear after 3s of no new TYPING event from that user

// Implementation in ViewModel:
private val typingFlow = MutableSharedFlow<Unit>()
init {
    typingFlow.debounce(1000)
        .onEach { webSocket.sendTypingEvent(chatId) }
        .launchIn(viewModelScope)
}
⚙
4. Key Design Decisions

1. WebSocket Connection Management

class WebSocketManager @Inject constructor(
    private val okHttpClient: OkHttpClient
) {
    private var webSocket: WebSocket? = null
    private val reconnectDelay = listOf(1, 2, 4, 8, 16)  // exponential backoff in seconds

    val messageFlow: SharedFlow<ChatEvent> = callbackFlow {
        val request = Request.Builder().url("wss://api.example.com/ws").build()
        webSocket = okHttpClient.newWebSocket(request, object : WebSocketListener() {
            override fun onMessage(ws: WebSocket, text: String) {
                trySend(parseChatEvent(text))
            }
            override fun onFailure(ws: WebSocket, t: Throwable, r: Response?) {
                // Reconnect with backoff
            }
            override fun onClosed(ws: WebSocket, code: Int, reason: String) {
                close()
            }
        })
        awaitClose { webSocket?.close(1000, "Client closing") }
    }.shareIn(scope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed())

    // Heartbeat — keep connection alive, detect silent failures
    private fun startHeartbeat() {
        scope.launch {
            while (true) {
                delay(30_000)  // ping every 30 seconds
                webSocket?.send("""{"type":"ping"}""")
            }
        }
    }
}

2. Message Delivery States

StateIconMeaningWhen set
SENDINGClockSaved locally, WebSocket not yet ACKedImmediately on send
SENTSingle checkServer received and storedServer ACK via WebSocket
DELIVEREDDouble checkRecipient's device receivedServer push when recipient online
READBlue double checkRecipient opened the conversationServer push when recipient reads
FAILEDRed exclamationSend failed — tap to retryWebSocket error + retries exhausted

3. Preventing Duplicate Messages on Reconnect

// Client-generated UUID for each message
// Server deduplicates by UUID — idempotent
// On reconnect: server sends last N missed events
// Client checks Room: if message UUID exists, skip insert

Trade-offs

DecisionChosenAlternativeReason

6. Scalability

Push Notifications for Background Messages

// When app is in background: WebSocket is closed
// Server sends FCM data message (not notification message)
// App's FirebaseMessagingService.onMessageReceived() handles it:
override fun onMessageReceived(message: RemoteMessage) {
    val chatMessage = parseChatMessage(message.data)
    // Save to Room
    CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO).launch {
        messageDao.insert(chatMessage.toEntity())
    }
    // Show notification
    showMessageNotification(chatMessage)
}

Media Sharing Flow

User picks image
  → Compress image (max 1MB) using Compressor library
  → Upload to CDN: POST /media/upload (multipart)
  → Response: { cdn_url, thumbnail_url }
  → Send message via WebSocket: { type: "IMAGE", url: cdn_url }
  → Store in Room with cdn_url
  → UI shows: image thumbnail (loaded via Coil)
  → While uploading: show progress indicator on message bubble

Group Chats and Channels

  • ConversationEntity with participants list and metadata
  • WebSocket subscribes to conversation channels by ID
  • Message delivery tracking per participant (delivered/read per user in group)
  • Group typing: "Alice, Bob are typing..." (aggregate multiple TYPING events)

App Lifecycle and WebSocket

// Connect when app is foregrounded
// Disconnect when app is backgrounded (after grace period)
// Use ProcessLifecycleOwner to detect foreground/background
ProcessLifecycleOwner.get().lifecycle.addObserver(object : DefaultLifecycleObserver {
    override fun onStart(owner: LifecycleOwner) = webSocketManager.connect()
    override fun onStop(owner: LifecycleOwner) = webSocketManager.disconnect()
})
🏆
7. Interview Framework

30-Second Answer

"The chat uses OkHttp WebSocket for real-time messaging. Messages are saved to Room immediately on send (SENDING state) for offline support. The WebSocket pipeline is: send → server ACK → SENT → recipient online → DELIVERED → recipient reads → READ. Reconnection uses exponential backoff. Offline messages queue in Room and flush when the WebSocket reconnects. History uses cursor-based pagination to avoid gaps when new messages arrive."

2-Minute Answer

"Architecture: ChatScreen → ChatViewModel → MessageRepository → Room + WebSocketManager. The WebSocket is managed as a callbackFlow — events are emitted and observed reactively. Messages go through four delivery states: SENDING (local only), SENT (server ACKed), DELIVERED (recipient device received), READ (recipient opened). All states stored in Room — the message list is a Flow<List<Message>> from Room, always up-to-date. For offline: messages with localOnly=true wait in Room; when WebSocket reconnects, flushPendingMessages() sends them in order. Duplicate prevention: every message has a client-generated UUID; Room uses INSERT OR IGNORE; server also deduplicates by UUID. Heartbeat pings every 30 seconds detect silent connection failures before users notice. When backgrounded, WebSocket disconnects and FCM data messages handle incoming notifications — onMessageReceived() saves the message to Room and shows a notification. History loads via GET /messages?before={timestamp} — cursor-based so new messages mid-scroll don't shift older pages."

Must-Mention Points

1
WebSocket lifecycle: connect on foreground, disconnect on background; heartbeat every 30s
2
Message delivery: SENDING → SENT → DELIVERED → READ — all stored in Room
3
Offline queue: localOnly messages flushed on reconnect in timestamp order
4
Duplicate prevention: client UUID + INSERT OR IGNORE in Room
5
Background: FCM data message → onMessageReceived → Room + notification

Senior Insight

Senior Differentiator
The WebSocket reconnection gap is a classic problem: what happens to messages sent to you while the connection was broken? Solution: on reconnect, send the server your last received message timestamp. Server replies with all events since that timestamp (missed messages, status updates). Client inserts them with INSERT OR IGNORE to deduplicate. This gap-fill pattern is what separates a production chat system from a demo.
⚡

  flushPendingMessages()
  → send in timestamp order
  → on ACK: localOnly=false

Background Messages

FCM data message
→ onMessageReceived()
→ insert to Room
→ show notification
→ user opens: already in Room
🅾
9. Interview Questions
1. Why use WebSocket over HTTP polling for real-time chat?
Basic⌄
WebSocket: persistent bidirectional connection, sub-second delivery, server pushes without client request, minimal overhead (no HTTP headers per message). HTTP polling: client polls every N seconds — higher latency (up to N seconds), higher battery drain, higher server load (N clients × 1/poll_interval requests/second). SSE (Server-Sent Events): server-to-client only, not bidirectional — can't easily send messages. WebSocket is the standard for full-duplex real-time communication like chat.
2. What are the four message delivery states and when does each apply?
Basic⌄
SENDING: message saved locally, WebSocket send not yet acknowledged. Shows clock icon. SENT: server received and stored — confirmed by server ACK. Single checkmark. DELIVERED: recipient device received (recipient online, device received). Double checkmark. READ: recipient opened the conversation. Blue double checkmark. FAILED: send failed after retries — red error icon with "tap to retry".
3. How do you prevent duplicate messages when the WebSocket reconnects?
Basic⌄
Two layers: (1) Every message has a client-generated UUID. Room uses INSERT OR IGNORE (or REPLACE with conflict strategy). If the server replays a message the client already has, the insert is silently ignored. (2) Server-side deduplication: server tracks message UUIDs and ignores duplicate sends from the client (important for the offline flush queue). Also: on reconnect, send lastReceivedTimestamp to server → server sends only events after that timestamp, minimizing the replay set.
4. How does the offline message queue work?
Intermediate⌄
Messages sent while offline are saved to Room with localOnly=true and status=SENDING. They display in the chat immediately (optimistic). When NetworkConnectivityObserver emits connected=true AND WebSocket reconnects: call flushPendingMessages() — query Room for messages WHERE localOnly=true ORDER BY timestamp ASC. Send each via WebSocket in timestamp order (critical — messages must arrive in the order they were composed). On ACK per message: set localOnly=false, status=SENT.
5. How do you handle messages received while the app is in the background?
Intermediate⌄
When the app is backgrounded, the WebSocket connection is closed. The server sends an FCM data message (not notification message — you want to handle it yourself). FirebaseMessagingService.onMessageReceived() runs in the background: parse the message, insert into Room, build and show a notification. When the user opens the app from the notification: ChatScreen collects from Room's Flow — the message is already there. No additional API call needed. The chat opens showing the new message seamlessly.
6. How do you implement typing indicators efficiently?
Intermediate⌄
Typing is ephemeral — never stored in Room. On each keystroke: emit to a SharedFlow → debounce(1000ms) → send {type:"TYPING", chatId} via WebSocket. Debounce prevents N messages for N keystrokes. Receiver side: maintain a typingUsers: Map<userId, Long> where Long is the last TYPING event timestamp. Every second: remove users whose last TYPING was more than 3 seconds ago. UI shows "Alice is typing..." while her userId is in the map. Auto-clear handles the case where the WebSocket drops mid-typing.
7. How do you implement WebSocket reconnection with backoff?
Intermediate⌄
On WebSocketListener.onFailure() or onClosed(): use exponential backoff. delays = [1s, 2s, 4s, 8s, 16s, max 60s]. Increment attempt counter on each failure. If reconnect succeeds: reset counter. If NetworkConnectivityObserver emits offline: stop retrying — restart only when it emits online. Show "Reconnecting..." in the connection status banner. Cap at 60 seconds to prevent 10+ minute gaps. On successful reconnect: send gap-fill request (lastTimestamp) before resuming normal operation.
8. How do you handle the "gap" in messages during a WebSocket disconnect?
Senior⌄
On reconnect: client sends {type:"SYNC", lastTimestamp: T} where T = max(createdAt) of messages in Room. Server responds with all events from T to now (missed messages + status updates). Client processes each: INSERT OR IGNORE for messages (dedup), UPDATE for status changes. This gap-fill ensures no messages are lost during disconnects. Server should have a reasonable limit (e.g., events from last 24h max) to prevent massive replays. For longer gaps: trigger a full refresh of recent message history.
9. Design the media sharing flow for images.
Senior⌄
Flow: (1) User picks image. (2) Compress to ≤1MB (Compressor library or Bitmap.compress). (3) Show sending state with progress indicator on the message bubble. (4) POST /media/upload (multipart/form-data) → response {cdn_url, thumbnail_url}. (5) On upload complete: send WebSocket message {type:"IMAGE", cdnUrl, thumbnailUrl, localId}. (6) Insert to Room with cdnUrl. (7) UI loads thumbnail via Coil. Handle upload failures: retry button on the message; don't retry automatically to avoid multiple uploads. Never send binary images via WebSocket — use CDN.
10. How do you load older message history without disrupting the current view?
Scenario⌄
LazyColumn in reverse order (reverseLayout=true) — newest messages at bottom, user scrolls up for older. On reaching top (first item becomes visible): trigger onLoadMore(). Fetch GET /messages?chatId={id}&before={oldestTimestamp}&limit=30. Insert into Room. Room Flow emits new list — old messages appear above. Maintain scroll position: save the firstVisibleItemIndex and scroll offset before update, restore after. This is the standard pattern for chat — new messages auto-scroll to bottom via LazyListState.scrollToItem(0). Cursor-based ensures no page gaps or duplicates when new messages arrive during history loading.

● Android Interview Prep · Senior System Design

30E — Push Notification System

Design a complete Android push notification system: FCM architecture, token management, data vs notification messages, custom notification channels, deep link handling, grouping, foreground handling, and delivery receipts.

ID: 30E ★ Senior Differentiator
🔍
1. Problem Statement

Requirements

Functional

  • Transactional alerts: order shipped, payment confirmed, security alerts
  • Marketing / promotional: new deals, personalized recommendations
  • Deep link handling: notification tap opens the correct in-app screen
  • Notification grouping: multiple messages bundled under one summary
  • Handle notification when app is in foreground (don't show system notification)
  • Delivery receipts: know whether the user received/tapped the notification

Non-Functional

  • No notification for revoked consent (POST_NOTIFICATIONS permission denied)
  • Token refresh handled automatically — server always has valid token
  • Correct channel importance — transactional uses HIGH, marketing uses DEFAULT
  • Works on all Android versions from API 26+
🏛
2. Architecture & Components

FCM Architecture — ASCII Diagram

└─────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────┘
                      │  POST https://fcm.googleapis.com/v1/...
                      ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  FIREBASE CLOUD MESSAGING                    │
│   Routes message to the correct device via Google's          │

                      │
                      ▼

3. Data Flow

FCM Token Registration Flow

App starts for first time
  → FirebaseMessaging.getInstance().getToken()
  → Token generated by Firebase
  → FirebaseMessagingService.onNewToken(token) called
  → Store token in SharedPreferences (local)
  → POST /notifications/register { token, deviceId, platform: "android" }
  → Server stores: userId → [token1(phone), token2(tablet)]

Token refresh (rare, but must handle):
  → FCM rotates token if: app reinstalled, data cleared, new device
  → onNewToken() called again with new token
  → Same flow: POST /notifications/register with new token
  → Server upserts token for this deviceId

Notification Message Delivery

Backend sends order shipped notification:
  → FCM HTTP v1 POST with { token, notification: {title, body}, data: {...} }

Case 1: App in BACKGROUND
  → System shows notification automatically (from `notification` field)
  → User taps notification
  → Intent with data payload delivered to MainActivity
  → NavController.handleDeepLink(intent)

Case 2: App in FOREGROUND
  → System does NOT show notification (if `notification` field present)
  → onMessageReceived() called
  → App shows in-app snackbar / banner
  → OR: build and show notification manually from onMessageReceived()

Case 3: Data-only message (no `notification` field)
  → onMessageReceived() always called (foreground AND background)
  → App handles display entirely — full control
  → This is the RECOMMENDED pattern for apps wanting full control

Deep Link Handling

// In AndroidManifest.xml — declare intent filter for notification deep links
<activity android:name=".MainActivity">
    <intent-filter android:autoVerify="true">
        <action android:name="android.intent.action.VIEW" />
        <category android:name="android.intent.category.DEFAULT" />
        <data android:scheme="https" android:host="app.example.com" />
    </intent-filter>
</activity>

// In onMessageReceived() — build PendingIntent with deep link
val deepLinkUri = Uri.parse(message.data["deep_link"])
val intent = NavDeepLinkBuilder(context)
    .setGraph(R.navigation.nav_graph)
    .setDestination(R.id.orderDetailFragment)
    .setArguments(bundleOf("orderId" to message.data["order_id"]))
    .createPendingIntent()

// TaskStackBuilder for proper back stack
val stackBuilder = TaskStackBuilder.create(context)
stackBuilder.addNextIntentWithParentStack(Intent(context, MainActivity::class.java))
val pendingIntent = stackBuilder.getPendingIntent(0, PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE)
⚙
4. Key Design Decisions

1. Data Message vs Notification Message

TypeWhen deliveredWho shows notificationUse when
Notification messageBackground: always. Foreground: onMessageReceived onlySystem (background), App (foreground)Simple notifications, don't need foreground handling
Data messageAlways (foreground + background)App always (onMessageReceived)Full control, rich notifications, foreground handling needed
Both (data + notification)System shows notification in backgroundSystem (background), App (foreground)Fallback behavior in background, custom in foreground
Recommendation
Use data-only messages for full control. Always show notifications manually in onMessageReceived(). This ensures consistent behavior in foreground and background, and allows custom notification styling.

2. Notification Channels

// Create channels in Application.onCreate() — idempotent
fun createNotificationChannels(context: Context) {
    if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT < Build.VERSION_CODES.O) return
    val manager = context.getSystemService(NotificationManager::class.java)

    // Transactional: HIGH importance — makes sound, pops up
    manager.createNotificationChannel(NotificationChannel(
        "transactional", "Orders & Payments",
        NotificationManager.IMPORTANCE_HIGH
    ).apply { description = "Order updates, payment confirmations, security alerts" })

    // Marketing: DEFAULT importance — silent, no popup
    manager.createNotificationChannel(NotificationChannel(
        "marketing", "Promotions",
        NotificationManager.IMPORTANCE_DEFAULT
    ).apply { description = "Deals, offers, and personalized recommendations" })
}

3. Notification Grouping

// Multiple chat messages → group under conversation summary
val GROUP_KEY = "com.example.CHAT_MESSAGES"

// Individual notifications (each message)
val msgNotification = NotificationCompat.Builder(context, "chat")
    .setContentTitle("Alice")
    .setContentText(messageText)
    .setGroup(GROUP_KEY)
    .build()

// Summary notification (required for grouping on Android 7+)
val summaryNotification = NotificationCompat.Builder(context, "chat")
    .setStyle(NotificationCompat.InboxStyle()
        .setSummaryText("3 new messages"))
    .setGroup(GROUP_KEY)
    .setGroupSummary(true)
    .build()

notificationManager.notify(messageId, msgNotification)
notificationManager.notify(SUMMARY_ID, summaryNotification)
⚖
5. Trade-offs & Failure Handling

Trade-offs

DecisionChosenAlternativeReason
Message typeData-only messagesNotification messagesFull control in all app states
Token storageSharedPreferences + server DBServer onlyQuick local check; server for targeting
Deep linksNavDeepLinkBuilder + TaskStackBuilderCustom Activity flagsCorrect back stack, integrates with NavComponent
Foreground handlingonMessageReceived → show custom bannerLet system show notificationBetter UX — contextual in-app alert instead of interrupting notification

Failure Scenarios

FailureHandling
INVALID_REGISTRATION from FCMRemove this token from server DB — device uninstalled or cleared app data
NOT_REGISTERED from FCMSame as above — unregister token
Token not registered on serverOn launch: always re-register token even if it seems the same; server upserts
User denied POST_NOTIFICATIONS (API 33+)Server still sends FCM; onMessageReceived runs; just don't call notificationManager.notify()
High-priority message not deliveredFCM guarantees best-effort; for critical: also check via WebSocket or polling fallback
📈
6. Scalability

Delivery Receipts

// When notification is delivered:
override fun onMessageReceived(message: RemoteMessage) {
    val notifId = message.data["notification_id"] ?: return
    // Send delivery receipt to backend
    CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO).launch {
        notificationApi.sendReceipt(DeliveryReceipt(
            notificationId = notifId,
            status = "DELIVERED",
            timestamp = System.currentTimeMillis()
        ))
    }
    showNotification(message)
}

// When user taps notification — track "opened"
// In the Activity/Composable that receives the deep link intent:
intent.extras?.getString("notification_id")?.let { notifId ->
    notificationApi.sendReceipt(DeliveryReceipt(notifId, "OPENED", ...))
}

Multi-device Token Management

// Server schema: user_notification_tokens
// user_id | device_id | token      | platform | created_at | last_active
// Send to ALL active tokens for a user (multi-device support)
// On INVALID_REGISTRATION: delete the specific token (not all tokens)
// Prune tokens not seen in 60 days: DELETE WHERE last_active < NOW - 60d

Topic-Based Notifications

Use FCM Topics for broadcast notifications (e.g., "new_sale" topic sent to all users who subscribed). Subscribe in app: FirebaseMessaging.getInstance().subscribeToTopic("new_sale"). Use for marketing pushes — no individual token management needed.

NotificationCompat Foreground Service

// Long-running operations (download, upload) require foreground service notification
val notification = NotificationCompat.Builder(this, "downloads")
    .setContentTitle("Downloading...")
    .setProgress(100, progress, false)
    .setOngoing(true)  // can't be dismissed
    .build()
startForeground(NOTIF_ID, notification)
🏆
7. Interview Framework

30-Second Answer

"The system uses FCM for delivery. The app registers its FCM token on launch and whenever onNewToken() fires — token sent to the backend and stored per userId+deviceId. I use data-only messages so onMessageReceived() always runs, giving full control in foreground and background. Notification channels separate transactional (IMPORTANCE_HIGH) from marketing (IMPORTANCE_DEFAULT). Deep links use NavDeepLinkBuilder + TaskStackBuilder for correct back stack. Groups bundle related notifications with a summary notification."

2-Minute Answer

"FCM architecture: app → Firebase → FCM → device. Token lifecycle: onNewToken() sends the token to our backend. Always re-register on every app start (server upserts) to handle reinstalls. For message types: data-only messages are preferred over notification messages — onMessageReceived() fires regardless of app state, giving us full rendering control. For importance: transactional notifications (orders, security alerts) use NotificationChannel with IMPORTANCE_HIGH — they pop over other apps and make sound. Marketing uses IMPORTANCE_DEFAULT — delivered silently to the notification shade. For deep links: NavDeepLinkBuilder creates an intent that navigates to the right screen with proper arguments, and TaskStackBuilder ensures back button works correctly. For notification grouping: set the same GROUP_KEY on individual notifications and add a summary notification with setGroupSummary(true). To handle notifications in foreground: detect in onMessageReceived() whether the chat screen is currently visible — if yes, show an in-app banner instead of a system notification. Delivery receipts: POST /notifications/{id}/receipt when onMessageReceived fires (DELIVERED) and again when the user taps (OPENED). Handle invalid tokens: FCM returns INVALID_REGISTRATION for uninstalled devices — server must delete that token."

Must-Mention Points

1
FCM flow: app → Firebase → FCM → device; token registered per userId+deviceId on server
2
Data-only messages → onMessageReceived always fires; full app control in all states
3
Notification channels: IMPORTANCE_HIGH (transactional) vs IMPORTANCE_DEFAULT (marketing)
4
Deep links: NavDeepLinkBuilder + TaskStackBuilder for correct back stack
5
Handle INVALID_REGISTRATION → delete stale token from server to prevent sending to uninstalled apps

Senior Insight

Senior Differentiator
Know that notification messages in the background are shown by the system — your onMessageReceived() is NOT called if the app is in the background and the payload has a notification field. The data in the data field is put in the activity's intent when the user taps. This is the #1 source of confusion in FCM integration: developers assume onMessageReceived always fires, but it doesn't for notification messages in the background. Use data-only to avoid this asymmetry.
⚡
8. Quick Revision Sheet

FCM Flow

App → Firebase → FCM → Device
onNewToken() → POST /register
Token per userId + deviceId
Re-register on every launch

notification msg → system shows BG
                   app shows FG
data msg → onMessageReceived ALWAYS
→ Prefer data-only for full control

Channels

IMPORTANCE_HIGH  → transactional
  heads-up, sound, vibrate
IMPORTANCE_DEFAULT → marketing
  silent, shade only

Deep Links

NavDeepLinkBuilder → destination
TaskStackBuilder → back stack
PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE
Target: specific Fragment + args
🅾
9. Interview Questions
1. What is an FCM token and when does it change?
Basic⌄
An FCM token is a unique identifier for an app installation on a specific device. FCM uses it to route messages. The token changes when: app is uninstalled and reinstalled, user clears app data, app is restored to a new device. When it changes, onNewToken(newToken) is called — you must send the new token to your server. Always call FirebaseMessaging.getInstance().getToken() on app launch and register it (server upserts) to ensure the server has the current token.
2. What is the difference between notification messages and data messages in FCM?
Basic⌄
Notification messages: have a "notification" JSON field (title, body). In background: system shows the notification automatically. onMessageReceived is NOT called when in background. In foreground: onMessageReceived is called, system does NOT show notification. Data messages: only have a "data" field. onMessageReceived is ALWAYS called regardless of app state. App handles all display logic. Recommendation: use data-only messages for consistent behavior — always goes through onMessageReceived in all app states.
3. What are notification channels and why were they introduced?
Basic⌄
NotificationChannels (API 26+) let users control notification behavior per category instead of per app. Apps define channels with importance levels: IMPORTANCE_HIGH (heads-up, sound), DEFAULT (sound only), LOW (silent), MIN (no visual). Users can disable specific channels without disabling all notifications. Required since API 26 — notifications without a valid channel are silently dropped. Create channels in Application.onCreate() — creation is idempotent (safe to call multiple times).
4. How do you handle a notification tap that should open a specific screen?
Intermediate⌄
Use NavDeepLinkBuilder to create a PendingIntent pointing to a specific NavGraph destination with arguments. Wrap with TaskStackBuilder to ensure the back stack is correct (Back button returns to the parent screen, not exits the app). Attach this PendingIntent to the notification's setContentIntent(). When the user taps: PendingIntent fires, MainActivity opens (or resumes), NavController navigates to the destination. Handle the case where MainActivity was already running: check getIntent() in onNewIntent() for the deep link data.
5. How do you handle a notification when the app is in the foreground?
Intermediate⌄
With data-only messages, onMessageReceived() fires in foreground. Decide based on context: if the user is already on the chat screen where the notification applies, show a subtle in-app banner (Snackbar, custom composable toast) rather than interrupting with a system notification. If they're on a different screen, show a normal notification or an in-app heads-up. Implement by: checking the current NavDestination ID against the notification's target screen. If match → show in-app UI. If not → show system notification.
6. How do you implement notification grouping?
Intermediate⌄
Set .setGroup(GROUP_KEY) on each notification with a consistent group key per category (e.g., per chat conversation). Create a separate summary notification with .setGroup(GROUP_KEY) and .setGroupSummary(true). Style the summary with NotificationCompat.InboxStyle(). Android bundles all notifications with the same GROUP_KEY under the summary. Required: show the summary notification alongside individual notifications. On Android 7+, system auto-groups if there are 4+ notifications with the same group key, but explicitly setting the summary ensures control over the summary text.
7. How do you handle stale/invalid FCM tokens?
Intermediate⌄
FCM HTTP API returns error codes for invalid tokens: INVALID_REGISTRATION (token format invalid), NOT_REGISTERED (app uninstalled or token revoked). Server must: detect these error codes in FCM API responses, immediately delete the corresponding token from the database, not retry sending to that token. If sending to multiple tokens for a user (multi-device), remove only the failed token — not all tokens. Also: prune tokens not active in 60+ days as a maintenance policy. Client: always re-register on launch to replace stale tokens.
8. How do you implement notification delivery receipts?
Senior⌄
Two events to track: DELIVERED (device received it) and OPENED (user tapped). DELIVERED: POST receipt in onMessageReceived() with notification_id from the data payload. Fire and forget — use a background coroutine. OPENED: attach the notification_id to the PendingIntent's data. When MainActivity receives the intent (from notification tap), extract notification_id and POST OPENED receipt. Be careful: if the app is killed and relaunched from the notification, handle this in onCreate() too. Store receipts locally if offline (Room) and flush when connected.
9. How does POST_NOTIFICATIONS permission on Android 13+ affect your system?
Senior⌄
Android 13 (API 33) requires POST_NOTIFICATIONS runtime permission. On API 33+: must declare <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.POST_NOTIFICATIONS"/> and request at runtime. Without permission: NotificationManager.notify() silently does nothing. FCM still delivers the data message (onMessageReceived fires) — the permission only affects showing system notifications. Approach: request permission on first launch or when the user first accesses a feature that needs notifications. Show rationale explaining value. If denied: suppress all notification display, but FCM data messages still arrive for in-app banners.
10. Design a notification system that distinguishes transactional from marketing pushes.
Scenario⌄
Server: tag every notification with a type field in the data payload (type: "ORDER_SHIPPED" vs "PROMO_DEAL"). Client: in onMessageReceived(), route to the correct channel based on type. Transactional → channel "transactional" (IMPORTANCE_HIGH: heads-up notification, sound, vibration). Marketing → channel "marketing" (IMPORTANCE_DEFAULT: silent). Users can disable the "marketing" channel in Settings without losing order updates. Backend: respect opt-out preferences — don't send marketing to users who unsubscribed (check marketing_consent before sending). Include campaign_id in data payload for analytics tracking.
