● System Design

30F — System Design: Image-heavy Feed

Design an infinite-scroll image feed for Android — Paging 3, Coil, three-level cache, offline support, 60fps smoothness. Senior differentiator unit.

ID: 30F ⭐ Senior Differentiator
🔍
1. Problem Statement

Scenario

Design an Android client for an image-heavy social feed (think Instagram-style) that scrolls infinitely, loads images fast, works offline, and maintains 60fps throughout.

Functional Requirements

  • Infinite scroll — load next page as user approaches end of list
  • Fast image loading with progressive reveal (no pop-in jank)
  • Offline support — users must see cached content with no internet
  • Smooth 60fps / 120fps scroll under load
  • Like/comment counts update in real-time (WebSocket or polling)

Non-Functional Requirements

  • Performance: image load <100ms from cache, <500ms from CDN
  • Memory: no OOM on 2GB RAM devices; evict images when not visible
  • Battery: batch network requests; cancel requests when item scrolls off screen
  • Bandwidth: serve thumbnails first, full-res on demand / WiFi
Clarifying Questions to Ask
(1) Is the feed real-time or pull-to-refresh? (2) What image sizes — fixed aspect ratio or variable? (3) Is there a CDN? (4) Do we need Stories/Reels or just feed? (5) What's the p50/p99 feed latency from backend?
🏛
2. Architecture

Layer Breakdown

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ UI Layer (Compose) │ │ FeedScreen (LazyColumn) ← PagingData<FeedItem> │ └──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘ │ collectAsLazyPagingItems() ┌──────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────┐ │ ViewModel Layer │ │ FeedViewModel → Pager(config, remoteMediator) │ └──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘ │ Flow<PagingData<FeedItem>> ┌──────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────┐ │ Domain Layer │ │ GetFeedUseCase (optional) │ └──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘ │ ┌──────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────┐ │ Data Layer │ │ FeedRepository ← FeedRemoteMediator │ │ ↓ Room (FeedItemEntity) │ │ ↓ Retrofit (FeedItemDto) │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ Image Loading (Coil): AsyncImage → MemoryCache (LRU) → DiskCache → Network (CDN)

Key Components

  • FeedScreen — Compose LazyColumn with items(lazyPagingItems); stable key = { it.id } for scroll position preservation
  • FeedViewModel — creates Pager, exposes Flow<PagingData> cached with .cachedIn(viewModelScope)
  • FeedRemoteMediator — Paging 3's offline-first bridge: loads from network, saves to Room, Room is single source of truth
  • FeedRepository — returns @PagingSource from Room; mediator handles network boundary
  • Coil — Compose-native, coroutine-based, handles memory + disk cache automatically

Domain Models

ModelLayerFields
FeedItemDomainid, authorId, imageUrl, thumbUrl, caption, likes, timestamp
FeedItemEntityRoomsame + page key for Paging
FeedItemDtoAPIsnake_case JSON; mapped to domain in repository
// ViewModel — Pager setup
class FeedViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val repository: FeedRepository
) : ViewModel() {

    val feedPagingData: Flow<PagingData<FeedItem>> = Pager(
        config = PagingConfig(
            pageSize = 20,
            prefetchDistance = 5,       // start loading 5 items before end
            enablePlaceholders = false
        ),
        remoteMediator = repository.remoteMediator(),
        pagingSourceFactory = { repository.pagingSource() }
    ).flow().cachedIn(viewModelScope)   // survive rotation
}
🔁
3. Data Flow

Paging 3 + RemoteMediator Flow

User scrolls near end │ ▼ PagingSource exhausted (no more local data) │ ▼ RemoteMediator.load(LoadType.APPEND, state) │ ├─── Fetch page from Retrofit API │ (cursor = lastItem.cursor) │ ├─── Map Dto → Entity │ ├─── Room.withTransaction { │ if REFRESH: delete old rows │ insert new FeedItemEntity rows │ } │ └─── return MediatorResult.Success(endOfPaginationReached) │ ▼ Room PagingSource automatically invalidated → emits new data → UI updates

Image Loading Flow

AsyncImage(model = item.imageUrl) │ ▼ MemoryCache (LRU, ~20% heap by default in Coil) │ MISS ▼ DiskCache (up to 250MB on disk, LRU) │ MISS ▼ Network request to CDN URL │ ▼ Decode in background thread (IO dispatcher) │ ▼ Store in Disk + Memory cache │ ▼ Display with crossfade animation

Placeholder / Shimmer Strategy

AsyncImage(
    model = ImageRequest.Builder(context)
        .data(item.imageUrl)
        .crossfade(true)
        .size(Size.ORIGINAL)
        .build(),
    placeholder = painterResource(R.drawable.shimmer_placeholder),
    error = painterResource(R.drawable.ic_broken_image),
    contentDescription = item.caption,
    modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth().aspectRatio(1f)
)

Cursor-based Pagination

Real-time feeds should use cursor-based pagination (not offset-based). Reason: if 3 new items are inserted at top while user is on page 2, offset-based pagination skips or duplicates items. Cursor points to a specific item ID/timestamp — always consistent.

⚖
4. Key Decisions

Why Coil over Glide / Picasso?

  • Compose-native — AsyncImage composable with no XML
  • Coroutine-based cancellation — image load auto-cancels when composable leaves composition
  • Kotlin-first API, same coroutine dispatcher as the rest of the app
  • Built-in SVG, GIF, video frame support

Why Room as single source of truth?

  • Offline support is free — Room emits cached data even with no network
  • Paging 3 + RemoteMediator is purpose-built for this pattern
  • Single source of truth prevents UI/data inconsistency

Image Format Decision

FormatProsConsUse when
WebP25–35% smaller than JPEG same qualityOlder Android <4.0 no support (irrelevant now)Default for CDN
Progressive JPEGLow-res version loads first (visible fast)Larger than WebPFallback
AVIFBest compressionAndroid 12+ only, slow decodeFuture / high-end

Thumbnail vs Full-resolution Strategy

  • Feed row: load thumbnail URL (CDN resized to 400px width) — fast, cheap
  • Detail view: load full-res on demand
  • On WiFi: pre-fetch next 3 full-res images in background
  • On metered: thumbnail only unless user taps
// Check connection type before pre-fetching
val isWifi = connectivityManager
    .getNetworkCapabilities(connectivityManager.activeNetwork)
    ?.hasTransport(NetworkCapabilities.TRANSPORT_WIFI) == true

if (isWifi) {
    // pre-load full-res for next 3 items
    nextItems.take(3).forEach { item ->
        imageLoader.enqueue(ImageRequest.Builder(context).data(item.imageUrl).build())
    }
}
⚖
5. Trade-offs
DecisionChosenAlternativeWhy chosen
Pagination libraryPaging 3Manual offset pagingRemoteMediator handles offline-first; built-in loading states
Image loaderCoilGlideCompose-native, coroutine cancellation, Kotlin API
Pagination strategyCursor-basedOffset-basedStable under real-time insertions; no duplicate/skip
StorageRoom single source of truthIn-memory onlyOffline support; survives process death
Image cache sizeMemory: 20% heap, Disk: 250MBSmallerCoil defaults are sane; reducing causes re-downloads
List componentLazyColumnRecyclerViewCompose project; lazy recomposition with stable keys

Memory Pressure Trade-off

Coil evicts memory cache under low-memory conditions automatically (respects onLowMemory / ComponentCallbacks2). Disk cache persists across memory pressure — ensures images reload from disk not network after eviction.

Common Mistake
Loading full-resolution images (2000×2000px) into feed thumbnails. Coil's .size() modifier or ImageRequest.size() should be set to the display size. Decoding a 4K image into a 400px thumbnail wastes 10× memory and CPU.
📈
6. Scalability & Failure Modes

Failure Scenarios

FailureBehaviourSolution
No network on app launchRemoteMediator returns Error; PagingSource reads Room cacheShow cached data + error banner; retry button
Image CDN downCoil returns error drawableShow broken-image icon; disk cache still serves previously loaded images
API returns empty page prematurelyendOfPaginationReached=true too earlyValidate with backend; add retry with exponential backoff in mediator
OOM from image cacheCoil handles via ComponentCallbacks2Set memory cache max size explicitly; use thumbnail URLs in feed
Scroll jank on image decodeDecode blocks main threadCoil decodes on IO by default; ensure not calling on main thread manually

60fps Checklist

  • Stable key in LazyColumn — prevents full recomposition on data update
  • Use @Immutable or @Stable on FeedItem to tell Compose it won't change unexpectedly
  • Avoid allocating lambdas inside composable functions — hoist them to top level or remember
  • Fixed item height where possible — avoids measure passes
  • Pre-fetch distance = 5 items — network request starts before user reaches end
  • Avoid notifyDataSetChanged() equiv — Paging uses diffing internally
🏆
7. Interview Framework
10-Minute Answer Structure
1 min: Clarify requirements (real-time? offline needed? image sizes?) → 2 min: High-level architecture diagram (layers) → 3 min: Deep-dive Paging 3 + RemoteMediator → 2 min: Image loading + three-level cache → 1 min: Trade-offs → 1 min: Failure modes

Opening Statement

"I'd design this as an offline-first feed using Paging 3 with a RemoteMediator. Room is the single source of truth — the UI always reads from Room, and the mediator loads from network and writes to Room. For images, I'd use Coil with a three-level cache: memory LRU, disk up to 250MB, then CDN. The key senior decisions are cursor-based pagination for real-time correctness and serving thumbnail URLs in the feed to control memory pressure."

Must-mention Points (Senior Level)

  • Why cursor-based over offset-based pagination
  • Why cachedIn(viewModelScope) is critical (survives rotation without re-fetch)
  • Three-level cache: memory → disk → network and eviction policy
  • Stable keys in LazyColumn for scroll position + performance
  • Canceling image loads when composable leaves composition (Coil handles automatically)
  • Bandwidth strategy: thumbnails in feed, full-res on detail
⚡
8. Quick Revision Sheet
ConceptOne-liner
RemoteMediatorBridge between network and local DB; loads pages, saves to Room, Room is source of truth
cachedIn(viewModelScope)Prevents re-fetch on rotation; shares PagingData across collectors
Cursor paginationStable under real-time insertions; use lastItem.cursor not page offset
Coil three-level cacheMemoryCache (LRU ~20% heap) → DiskCache (250MB) → Network CDN

❓
9. Quiz
Why is cursor-based pagination preferred over offset-based for a real-time feed?
Medium▼
Offset-based pagination (page=2&size=20) breaks when new items are inserted at the top — page 2 now contains items that were on page 1. Cursor-based pagination points to a specific item (cursor = lastItem.id or timestamp), so the next page always starts after that item regardless of insertions above it.
What does cachedIn(viewModelScope) do and why is it critical?
Medium▼
It caches the PagingData Flow in the ViewModel's scope, so when the screen rotates (Fragment/Activity recreated), the new collector gets the same in-memory pages immediately — no network re-fetch and no scroll position loss. Without it, rotation triggers a full reload from RemoteMediator.
Describe Coil's three-level cache and when each level is hit.
Easy▼
1) MemoryCache — LRU in-process heap (~20% by default); fastest, cleared on process death. 2) DiskCache — stored as files on device (default 250MB); survives process restart, cleared by OS under storage pressure. 3) Network — CDN fetch; slowest, billed against data. Coil checks each level in order.
How does RemoteMediator enable offline-first behaviour?
Hard▼
The PagingSource always reads from Room. The RemoteMediator's job is to fill Room with data from the network. If the network is unavailable, load() returns MediatorResult.Error — but Room already has cached items, so the PagingSource keeps serving them. The UI shows stale data + an error banner. No blank screen.
Why use stable keys in LazyColumn and what happens without them?
Medium▼
Without stable keys (key = { item.id }), Compose uses list position as the key. When Paging 3 inserts items or the list is refreshed, items shift positions — causing Compose to recompose and re-measure all visible items, which causes jank. Stable keys let Compose diff by identity and only recompose changed items.
How does Coil automatically cancel image loads when items scroll off screen?
Medium▼
AsyncImage is a Composable that binds its image request to the composition lifecycle. When the composable leaves composition (item scrolled off screen and recycled by LazyColumn), the coroutine backing the image load is automatically cancelled. This prevents wasted network bandwidth and decoding CPU on off-screen items.
What image format would you use for a CDN serving an Android feed and why?
Easy▼
WebP — supported since Android 4.0, 25–35% smaller than JPEG at the same quality, lossless and lossy modes available. The CDN should serve WebP to Android clients (via Accept header negotiation) and fall back to JPEG for unsupported clients. AVIF offers even better compression but decoding is slow and Android 12+ only.
What is the role of @Immutable on FeedItem and how does it affect performance?
Hard▼
@Immutable tells the Compose compiler that none of FeedItem's public properties will change after construction. This enables "skippable" recomposition — if a FeedItem composable's parameters haven't changed (by reference), Compose skips recomposing it. Without @Immutable (or @Stable), Compose conservatively recomposes all items whenever the parent recomposes, causing jank.
How would you handle a user tapping "Like" while offline?
Hard▼
Optimistic update: immediately update Room (which flows to UI via PagingSource) and enqueue a WorkManager background task to sync the like to the server when network is available. If the server rejects the like, roll back the Room update and show an error. This gives instant feedback and survives app restart before sync.
What is prefetchDistance in PagingConfig and what value would you use?
Easy▼
prefetchDistance is how many items before the end of the loaded list Paging 3 starts loading the next page. A value of 5 means "start loading the next page when the user is 5 items from the bottom." Too small causes visible load indicators; too large wastes bandwidth. 3–10 is typical; tune based on network latency and scroll speed.

● System Design

30G — System Design: Large-scale Modular Android App

Architect an Android app for millions of users, 10+ feature teams, fast builds, A/B testing, and production reliability. The full senior system design answer.

ID: 30G ⭐ Senior Differentiator
🔍
1. Problem Statement

Scenario

Design the Android client architecture for a large-scale consumer app (banking / e-commerce / social) with millions of active users, 10+ independent feature teams, fast build times, A/B testing, staged rollouts, and a 99.5% crash-free session SLA.

Requirements

  • 10+ feature teams working independently without blocking each other
  • Fast local builds (<3 min incremental, <15 min clean build)
  • A/B testing and Feature Flags for gradual rollout
  • Multi-variant builds: free/premium, debug/staging/production
  • 99.5% crash-free session rate SLA
  • Startup time <2 seconds cold start
  • CI/CD pipeline with parallel testing, automated releases
Clarifying Questions
(1) Monorepo or multiple repos? (2) Is Jetpack Compose already adopted or migrating? (3) Do teams own backend APIs too? (4) What's the current crash-free rate and startup time? (5) Any existing DFM (Dynamic Feature Modules) usage?
🏛
2. Architecture

Module Graph

:app (thin shell, only navigation + DI graph wiring) │ ├── :feature:home (Home feed) ├── :feature:checkout (Checkout flow) ├── :feature:profile (User profile) ├── :feature:search (Search & discovery) │ each feature: UI + ViewModel + UseCases (no data layer) │ ├── :core:data (Repositories, Room, Retrofit, DataStore) ├── :core:domain (Use cases, domain models — pure Kotlin, no Android) ├── :core:ui (Design system: components, theme, typography) ├── :core:network (OkHttp, interceptors, auth token refresh) ├── :core:analytics (event tracking abstraction) ├── :core:featureflags (Remote Config wrapper, local fallback) └── :core:testing (test utilities, fakes, test rules) Dependency Rule: feature → core only. Features NEVER depend on other features.

Strict Dependency Rules

  • :feature:X can depend on any :core:Y
  • :feature:X must never depend on :feature:Z
  • :core:domain has NO Android dependencies — pure Kotlin/Java
  • :app depends on all features (for DI wiring) but features don't depend on :app
  • Enforce with forbiddenDependencies in Gradle scripts or Dependency Guard plugin

Dynamic Feature Modules (DFMs)

Optional heavy features (AR try-on, large onboarding flows) live in DFMs — they are not installed until needed, reducing APK size for users who never use them. DFMs are downloaded on demand via SplitInstallManager.

🔁
3. Data Flow

Feature Flag + A/B Flow

App launch │ ▼ RemoteConfig.fetchAndActivate() (async, non-blocking) │ ├── Success: live flag values cached locally └── Failure: local fallback defaults used FeatureFlag("new_checkout_ui").isEnabled() │ ├── true → show NewCheckoutScreen └── false → show LegacyCheckoutScreen A/B Experiment: RemoteConfig key = "checkout_cta_color" Variant A → "blue" (50% of users) Variant B → "green" (50% of users) Analytics.logEvent("cta_clicked", variant)

BFF Pattern (Backend for Frontend)

Each mobile platform (Android, iOS) has a dedicated BFF API gateway that aggregates multiple microservice calls and returns a single mobile-optimised response. The Android app doesn't call 5 microservices directly — it calls /mobile/v1/home and gets everything for the home screen in one request.

Multi-variant Build Flow

Gradle productFlavors: flavorDimensions: [tier, env] tier: free | premium env: debug | staging | production Variants generated: freeDebug, freeStagine, freeProduction premiumDebug, premiumStaging, premiumProduction Each variant: different base URL, signing config, analytics key, feature flag project
⚖
4. Key Decisions

Why Strict Modularization?

  • Build speed: Gradle only recompiles modules that changed. If :feature:profile changes, :feature:checkout doesn't recompile.
  • Team isolation: Teams own their module, set their own API surface. No merge conflicts with unrelated teams.
  • Testability: Each module tested in isolation with fake implementations of core modules.
  • Play Feature Delivery: Modules can become DFMs for optional delivery.

Feature Flags Strategy

interface FeatureFlagProvider {
    fun isEnabled(flag: FeatureFlag): Boolean
    fun getVariant(experiment: Experiment): String
}

// Production: backed by Firebase Remote Config
class RemoteConfigFlagProvider @Inject constructor(
    private val remoteConfig: FirebaseRemoteConfig
) : FeatureFlagProvider {
    override fun isEnabled(flag: FeatureFlag): Boolean =
        remoteConfig.getBoolean(flag.key)
}

// Test / debug: local override
class LocalFlagProvider(
    private val overrides: Map<FeatureFlag, Boolean> = emptyMap()
) : FeatureFlagProvider {
    override fun isEnabled(flag: FeatureFlag) = overrides[flag] ?: flag.defaultValue
}

CI/CD at Scale

  • Parallel test shards: split 2000 unit tests across 8 workers → 4× faster CI
  • Gradle Build Cache: remote cache (Gradle Enterprise) shares task outputs across machines
  • Incremental compile: only changed modules recompile
  • Automated version code: CI sets versionCode = CI_BUILD_NUMBER
  • Staged rollout: internal → alpha → beta → production 10% → 100%
⚖
5. Trade-offs
DecisionChosenAlternativeReason
ModularizationFeature + Core modulesSingle moduleBuild speed at scale, team isolation, DFM support
Feature FlagsFirebase Remote ConfigCustom server / LaunchDarklyFree, integrated with A/B testing, no extra infra
NavigationNavigation component with deep linksManual back stackType-safe args, deep links, back stack handled
DFMsOptional heavy features onlyAll features as DFMDFMs add install complexity; only worth it for large optional features
API layerBFF patternDirect microservice callsReduces round trips, mobile-optimised response shape, less client logic

Build Time vs Modularity Trade-off

Too many small modules can slow Gradle's configuration phase. Optimal: 15–30 modules at this scale. Group small utilities into a single :core:utils module rather than one module per utility.

Common Anti-patterns
(1) :app module contains business logic — makes testing impossible. (2) Feature modules depend on each other — creates tight coupling. (3) Feature flags checked directly in ViewModel — should be injected via abstraction. (4) Remote Config fetched synchronously at startup — blocks main thread.
📈
6. Scalability & Failure

Performance SLAs

MetricTargetTool
Cold start time<2 secondsFirebase Performance, Macrobenchmark
Crash-free sessions>99.5%Crashlytics dashboard
ANR rate<0.1%Play Console, ANR detection
Memory (p95)<200MB heapAndroid Profiler, Firebase Perf traces
CI build time<15 min cleanGradle Enterprise metrics

Emergency Halt

  • If a new release causes crash spike: Play Console → staged rollout halt → revert to previous version
  • Feature flags provide a kill switch: disable a feature remotely without a new release
  • Crashlytics alerts: if crash-free rate drops below 99%, PagerDuty alert fires

Startup Optimization

  • App Startup library: lazy-initialize SDKs that don't need to be ready at t=0
  • Baseline Profiles: ship pre-compiled code paths for critical user journeys (startup, checkout)
  • No blocking I/O in Application.onCreate() — defer to background coroutines
  • Splash screen API (Android 12+): smooth handoff from OS splash to app content
🏆
7. Interview Framework
10-Minute Presentation Structure
0–1 min: Clarify scale (users, teams, SLAs) → 1–3 min: Module graph + dependency rules → 3–5 min: Feature flags + A/B testing → 5–7 min: CI/CD + build optimization → 7–9 min: Monitoring + failure handling → 9–10 min: Trade-offs

Opening Statement

"I'd architect this as a strictly modular multi-module project with a :app shell, :feature:X modules owned by individual teams, and shared :core:Y modules. Teams can build and test their modules independently. Feature flags via Firebase Remote Config give us kill switches and A/B testing without new releases. Baseline Profiles plus lazy initialization keep startup under 2 seconds. Crashlytics + ANR monitoring with automated alerts maintain our 99.5% crash-free SLA."

Senior Differentiators

  • Enforcing dependency rules with Dependency Guard or Forbidden Dependencies plugin
  • Baseline Profiles for startup — most candidates don't mention this
  • BFF pattern — shows awareness of mobile-backend collaboration
  • Remote Config as kill switch, not just A/B testing
  • Team ownership model: who owns what module, how breaking changes are communicated
⚡

:core:domainPure Kotlin, no Android imports — fastest to compile, easiest to test
Feature FlagsRemote Config: remote kill switch + A/B; local fallback defaults for offline

9. Quiz
Why must feature modules never depend on other feature modules?
Medium▼
Feature-to-feature dependencies create tight coupling — changing :feature:profile breaks :feature:checkout. It also creates potential circular dependency cycles which Gradle cannot build. Cross-feature communication should go through :core:domain shared models or navigation events. This ensures teams can release independently.
What is a Baseline Profile and how does it reduce cold start time?
Hard▼
A Baseline Profile is a list of critical code paths (startup, key user journeys) that are pre-compiled to native code (AOT) during app installation. Without it, the JIT compiler compiles code at runtime during first run — causing slow startup. With Baseline Profiles, the critical path is already native code, reducing cold start by 30–40%.
How would you use Firebase Remote Config as a kill switch?
Easy▼
Define a boolean flag like "new_payment_ui_enabled = true". Wrap the new feature: if (flags.isEnabled(FeatureFlag.NEW_PAYMENT_UI)) { showNewUI() } else { showOldUI() }. If the new UI causes crashes in production, flip the flag to false in Remote Config console — takes effect within minutes without a Play Store release. Always have a local default (false) for offline scenarios.
What is the BFF pattern and why is it valuable for mobile?
Medium▼
Backend for Frontend (BFF) is a dedicated API gateway layer for each client type (Android, iOS, web). Instead of the mobile app calling 5 microservices to render a screen, the BFF aggregates those calls server-side and returns one mobile-optimised response. Benefits: fewer network round trips, response shape designed for mobile consumption, backend changes don't break mobile APIs directly.
How does the App Startup library help cold start time?
Medium▼
The App Startup library provides a single ContentProvider that initializes multiple SDKs sequentially or concurrently, replacing the pattern of each SDK having its own ContentProvider (which adds startup overhead). It allows lazy initialization — defer SDK initialization until it's first needed rather than blocking app startup. Especially important for analytics, crash reporting, and image loaders.
How do Dynamic Feature Modules (DFMs) reduce APK size?
Medium▼
DFMs are Gradle modules that are NOT bundled in the initial install. They're downloaded on demand via SplitInstallManager when the user accesses that feature for the first time. This keeps the initial download small. Good candidates: AR features, large PDF viewers, rarely-used admin tools. Poor candidates: core functionality users need immediately.
Describe the staged rollout process from internal to production.
Easy▼
Internal track → Alpha (opted-in testers) → Beta (larger group) → Production 10% rollout → Production 50% → Production 100%. Monitor crash-free rate and ANR rate at each stage. If crash-free rate drops below threshold at 10%, halt rollout and investigate before proceeding. Emergency halt is instant; revert to previous version if needed.
Why should :core:domain have no Android dependencies?
Hard▼
Pure Kotlin/Java modules compile faster (no Android toolchain) and can be tested with plain JUnit without an Android emulator or Robolectric. Domain use cases and models are business logic — they have no reason to depend on Android Context, Activity, or Android-specific APIs. This also makes the domain layer portable to other platforms (KMP).
How would you enforce module dependency rules automatically?
Hard▼
Use the Dependency Guard Gradle plugin — it generates a baseline of allowed dependencies and fails CI if any module adds a new unexpected dependency. Alternatively, write custom Gradle tasks that parse the dependency graph and assert no :feature:X → :feature:Y edges. Pair with PR review guidelines. Some teams use lint rules or the ArchUnit library for architectural constraint verification.
An A/B test shows variant B has 10% higher conversion but 2% higher crash rate. What do you recommend?
Hard▼
Do not ship variant B as-is. A 2% higher crash rate is unacceptable — if crash-free rate was 99.5%, this would drop it to 97.5%. First, identify the crash root cause from Crashlytics. Fix the crash in variant B. Re-run the A/B test with the fixed variant. Only ship when both metrics are satisfied: higher conversion AND same or better crash-free rate.

31A — Firebase

Auth, Firestore, Realtime DB, FCM, Crashlytics, Analytics, Remote Config, and Performance Monitoring — the complete Firebase interview guide for Android.

ID: 31A Tier 3
🔍
1. Overview

Firebase Services on Android

ServiceWhat it doesInterview frequency
AuthenticationEmail/password, Google, phone sign-in; manages tokensHigh
Cloud FirestoreNoSQL document database with real-time syncHigh

Senior Mental Model
Firebase is a backend-as-a-service that lets small teams ship quickly. The trade-off is vendor lock-in and limited query flexibility (Firestore can't do JOINs). At scale (>10M users), cost and query limitations push teams to custom backends. Know when to use Firebase vs custom backend.
🔒
2. Authentication & Firestore

Firebase Authentication

// Email/password sign-in
suspend fun signIn(email: String, password: String): FirebaseUser? {
    return try {
        val result = auth.signInWithEmailAndPassword(email, password).await()
        result.user
    } catch (e: FirebaseAuthInvalidCredentialsException) {
        null   // wrong password
    }
}

// Google Sign-In flow
val googleSignInClient = GoogleSignIn.getClient(context, gso)
val signInIntent = googleSignInClient.signInIntent
launcher.launch(signInIntent)  // in Activity/Fragment

// In callback: get credential and sign in to Firebase
val account = GoogleSignIn.getSignedInAccountFromIntent(data).getResult()
val credential = GoogleAuthProvider.getCredential(account.idToken, null)
auth.signInWithCredential(credential).await()

// Auth state listener — observe sign-in/out changes
auth.addAuthStateListener { firebaseAuth ->
    val user = firebaseAuth.currentUser
    // user != null → signed in; null → signed out
}

// Force token refresh (call when getting 401 from backend)
val idToken = auth.currentUser?.getIdToken(/* forceRefresh = */ true)?.await()?.token

Cloud Firestore

// Structure: /users/{userId}/orders/{orderId}
val db = FirebaseFirestore.getInstance()

// Write document
db.collection("users").document(userId)
    .set(userMap).await()

// Real-time listener (Flow wrapper)
fun userFlow(userId: String): Flow<User> = callbackFlow {
    val listener = db.collection("users").document(userId)
        .addSnapshotListener { snapshot, error ->
            if (error != null) { close(error); return@addSnapshotListener }
            snapshot?.toObject(User::class.java)?.let { trySend(it) }
        }
    awaitClose { listener.remove() }   // clean up on Flow cancellation
}

// Pagination with startAfter
val firstPage = db.collection("posts")
    .orderBy("timestamp", Query.Direction.DESCENDING)
    .limit(20)
    .get().await()

val lastDoc = firstPage.documents.last()
val nextPage = db.collection("posts")
    .orderBy("timestamp", Query.Direction.DESCENDING)
    .startAfter(lastDoc)
    .limit(20)
    .get().await()

Firestore Security Rules (must know)

rules_version = '2';
service cloud.firestore {
  match /databases/{database}/documents {
    match /users/{userId} {
      // Only authenticated user can read/write their own document
      allow read, write: if request.auth != null && request.auth.uid == userId;
    }
    match /posts/{postId} {
      allow read: if true;  // public read
      allow write: if request.auth != null && request.resource.data.authorId == request.auth.uid;
    }
  }
}
Firestore vs Realtime Database
Use Firestore for: structured data, complex queries, subcollections, offline support. Use Realtime Database for: simple data structures, very low latency (<10ms), presence (online/offline status). Firestore is the default for new apps.
📱
3. FCM & Realtime Database

Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM)

// FirebaseMessagingService — extend in your app
class MyFCMService : FirebaseMessagingService() {

    // Called when a message is received while app is in foreground
    override fun onMessageReceived(message: RemoteMessage) {
        val title = message.notification?.title
        val body  = message.notification?.body
        val data  = message.data   // Map<String, String> — custom payload
        showNotification(title, body)
    }

    // Called when FCM token is refreshed (or first time)
    override fun onNewToken(token: String) {
        // Send token to your backend so it can target this device
        sendTokenToServer(token)
    }
}

// Notification payload (handled by system, shown even in background)
// vs Data payload (always delivered to onMessageReceived)

Notification Channels (Android 8+, required)

val channel = NotificationChannel(
    "ORDERS", "Order Updates", NotificationManager.IMPORTANCE_HIGH
)
channel.description = "Notifications for order status changes"
notificationManager.createNotificationChannel(channel)
Payload typeForegroundBackgroundKilled
notification onlyonMessageReceived calledSystem shows notificationSystem shows notification
data onlyonMessageReceived calledonMessageReceived calledNOT delivered (use high priority)
notification + dataonMessageReceived calledSystem shows; data in intent extrasSystem shows; data in intent extras

Realtime Database

val database = FirebaseDatabase.getInstance()
val ref = database.getReference("users/$userId/status")

// One-time read
ref.get().await().getValue(String::class.java)

// Real-time listener
ref.addValueEventListener(object : ValueEventListener {
    override fun onDataChange(snapshot: DataSnapshot) {
        val status = snapshot.getValue(String::class.java)
    }
    override fun onCancelled(error: DatabaseError) { }
})
📉
4. Crashlytics & Analytics

Firebase Crashlytics

// Automatic crash reporting — no code needed after setup
// Add to gradle: implementation "com.google.firebase:firebase-crashlytics-ktx"

// Custom keys — add context to crash reports
FirebaseCrashlytics.getInstance().setCustomKey("user_id", userId)
FirebaseCrashlytics.getInstance().setCustomKey("screen", "checkout")
FirebaseCrashlytics.getInstance().setCustomKey("cart_size", cartItems.size)

// Custom log — breadcrumbs that appear in crash report
FirebaseCrashlytics.getInstance().log("User tapped checkout button")

// Non-fatal exception — record without crashing
try {
    riskyOperation()
} catch (e: Exception) {
    FirebaseCrashlytics.getInstance().recordException(e)
    // continue — non-fatal, just log it
}

// Set user ID for attribution
FirebaseCrashlytics.getInstance().setUserId(userId)
Crash-free Users Metric
Crashlytics tracks "crash-free users" — percentage of unique users who had NO crashes. This is the production SLA metric. A 99.5% crash-free rate means 5 in 1,000 users experienced a crash. Monitor this per version in the Crashlytics dashboard.

Firebase Analytics

val analytics = FirebaseAnalytics.getInstance(context)

// Log event
analytics.logEvent("add_to_cart") {
    param(FirebaseAnalytics.Param.ITEM_ID, productId)
    param(FirebaseAnalytics.Param.ITEM_NAME, productName)
    param(FirebaseAnalytics.Param.VALUE, price)
    param(FirebaseAnalytics.Param.CURRENCY, "USD")
}

// Screen tracking
analytics.logEvent(FirebaseAnalytics.Event.SCREEN_VIEW) {
    param(FirebaseAnalytics.Param.SCREEN_NAME, "ProductDetail")
    param(FirebaseAnalytics.Param.SCREEN_CLASS, "ProductDetailActivity")
}

// User properties — for segmentation and A/B test targeting
analytics.setUserProperty("subscription_tier", "premium")
analytics.setUserId(userId)
⚙
5. Remote Config & Performance

Firebase Remote Config

val remoteConfig = FirebaseRemoteConfig.getInstance()

// Set default values (used if fetch fails or before first fetch)
remoteConfig.setDefaultsAsync(R.xml.remote_config_defaults)

// Fetch and activate (MUST call before reading values)
suspend fun initRemoteConfig() {
    try {
        remoteConfig.fetchAndActivate().await()
    } catch (e: Exception) {
        // Network failure — defaults are active, safe to proceed
    }
}

// Read values
val isNewCheckoutEnabled = remoteConfig.getBoolean("new_checkout_enabled")
val heroColor = remoteConfig.getString("hero_banner_color")
val maxRetries = remoteConfig.getLong("api_max_retries").toInt()
Fetch Throttling
In production, Remote Config caches fetched values for 12 hours by default. Calls to fetch() more frequently return cached values. In debug builds, use setMinimumFetchIntervalInSeconds(0) for instant updates. Never call fetchAndActivate() on every screen because it's throttled.

Firebase Performance Monitoring

// Automatic traces: app start, activity transitions, HTTP requests

// Custom trace
val trace = FirebasePerformance.getInstance().newTrace("checkout_flow")
trace.start()
// ... checkout logic ...
trace.putAttribute("payment_method", "credit_card")
trace.putMetric("items_count", cartSize.toLong())
trace.stop()

// HTTP metric monitoring (automatic with OkHttp interceptor)
// Add: implementation "com.google.firebase:firebase-perf"
// Automatically tracks response time, payload size, status codes
⚠
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
PitfallFix
Reading Remote Config before fetchAndActivate()Defaults are served — always await fetchAndActivate() at startup
Firestore listener not removedStore ListenerRegistration, call remove() in onStop/onDestroy or awaitClose in callbackFlow
FCM token not refreshed on serverAlways implement onNewToken and update the server with the new token
Posting notification without channel on Android 8+Create NotificationChannel before building notification
Auth token not refreshed on 401Use OkHttp Authenticator to call getIdToken(forceRefresh=true) and retry
Writing sensitive data without security rulesAlways define and test Firestore security rules; default is deny-all after rules version 2
Crashlytics user ID containing PIIUse hashed or anonymous ID, not email/name in setUserId()

Offline Persistence

// Enable Firestore offline persistence (enabled by default on Android)
val settings = firestoreSettings {
    setPersistenceEnabled(true)
    setCacheSizeBytes(FirebaseFirestoreSettings.CACHE_SIZE_UNLIMITED)
}
db.firestoreSettings = settings

// Reads work offline — serve from local cache
// Writes are queued and synced when network returns
🏆
7. Interview Framework
How to Answer Firebase Questions
Structure: What it does → How to set it up → Production pattern → Pitfall to avoid. For any Firebase question, always mention the coroutine/Flow integration pattern.

Common Question Patterns

  • "How do you handle auth token expiry?" → OkHttp Authenticator intercepts 401, calls getIdToken(forceRefresh=true), retries with new token. Use Mutex to prevent concurrent refreshes.
  • "Firestore vs Realtime Database?" → Firestore: structured, better querying, offline, scales. RTDB: simpler, lower latency, presence tracking. Use Firestore for new apps.
  • "How do you handle FCM when app is killed?" → Use notification payload (not data-only) — the system delivers it even when app is killed. Data-only messages require high priority and may not be delivered on doze mode.
  • "What's a crash-free user rate?" → Percentage of users with zero crashes in the time window. Industry target: 99.5%+. Monitor per app version in Crashlytics dashboard.
⚡
8. Quick Revision Sheet
TopicKey API / Concept
Auth sign-insignInWithEmailAndPassword().await() — suspend-friendly with kotlinx coroutines
Auth token refreshcurrentUser?.getIdToken(forceRefresh=true)?.await()?.token
Auth stateaddAuthStateListener { user → } — observe sign-in/out changes
Firestore real-timeaddSnapshotListener wrapped in callbackFlow; remove listener in awaitClose
Firestore paginationstartAfter(lastDocument).limit(20)
FCM foregroundonMessageReceived() — show manual notification
FCM tokenonNewToken() — send to backend; token can change, always update
CrashlyticssetCustomKey, log (breadcrumbs), recordException (non-fatal), setUserId
Remote ConfigsetDefaultsAsync → fetchAndActivate() → getBoolean/getString/getLong
PerformancenewTrace("name").start() ... putMetric() ... stop()
❓
9. Interview Questions
How do you handle an expired Firebase auth token when making API calls?
Hard▼
Implement OkHttp Authenticator: when a 401 is received, call FirebaseAuth.currentUser?.getIdToken(forceRefresh=true)?.await()?.token. Use a Mutex to ensure only one refresh happens concurrently — if 5 requests fail with 401, only one should refresh and the others wait. Retry the failed request with the new token.
When would you choose Realtime Database over Firestore?
Medium▼
Realtime Database is better for: (1) Presence/online status tracking (built-in onDisconnect handlers), (2) Very simple flat data structures (JSON tree), (3) Ultra-low latency requirements (<10ms). Firestore is better for everything else: subcollections, complex queries, better offline support, scales horizontally. Use Firestore for new apps by default.
What is the difference between FCM notification payload and data payload?
Medium▼
Notification payload: handled by the FCM SDK automatically — shows a system notification when app is in background or killed. Data payload: always delivered to onMessageReceived() regardless of app state. Best practice: use notification+data payload so system handles display when backgrounded, and you also receive data in onMessageReceived() when foreground. Pure data messages need high priority for background delivery.
How do you prevent a Firestore memory leak from an unremoved snapshot listener?
Medium▼
Wrap the listener in callbackFlow { ... awaitClose { listener.remove() } }. The awaitClose block is called when the Flow is cancelled (collector's coroutine cancelled), which happens when the ViewModel is cleared. This automatically removes the Firestore listener. Never add a listener in Fragment without a corresponding remove() in onDestroyView().
What are Crashlytics custom keys used for?
Easy▼
Custom keys add context to crash reports — they appear in the Crashlytics dashboard alongside the stack trace. Examples: user's subscription tier, current screen name, feature flag values, cart size. This helps reproduce crashes by understanding the app state at the time. Limit: 64 custom keys, 1KB per value.
Why must fetchAndActivate() be called before reading Remote Config values?
Easy▼
Remote Config values are not automatically synced. The app has a local cache of fetched values. fetchAndActivate() fetches the latest values from the server AND activates them (makes them available to getBoolean/getString). Without this call, you read stale cached values or the default values you set in R.xml.remote_config_defaults. Always await this coroutine at startup before using any flag.
How does Firestore offline persistence work on Android?
Medium▼
Firestore caches all documents you've read in a local SQLite database. When offline, reads are served from this cache. Writes are added to a local queue and automatically synced when connectivity is restored. Snapshot listeners still fire with cached data. This is enabled by default on Android. Set setCacheSizeBytes to control storage usage.
How do you track screen views with Firebase Analytics in a Compose app?
Medium▼
In Compose there's no Activity lifecycle tied to screens, so you must log manually. Use a NavigationListener on NavController that fires on every destination change. In the listener, read the current destination route and log FirebaseAnalytics.Event.SCREEN_VIEW with SCREEN_NAME and SCREEN_CLASS params. This replaces the automatic Activity-based screen tracking.
What Firestore security rule would you write to allow a user to read/write only their own data?
Easy▼
allow read, write: if request.auth != null && request.auth.uid == userId; — where userId is the document ID wildcard. This checks that the requesting user is authenticated AND their auth UID matches the document path. Without this, any authenticated user could read all users' data.
How would you use Firebase Performance Monitoring to measure checkout speed?
Easy▼
Create a named trace: val trace = FirebasePerformance.getInstance().newTrace("checkout_complete"). Call trace.start() when user taps "Pay". Add attributes (payment method, item count). Call trace.stop() when the order confirmation is received. Firebase aggregates the duration across all users — you can view p50/p90/p99 in the Performance Monitoring console.

32A — Android App Release: End-to-End

The complete production release pipeline: from code freeze to live on Google Play — every step, every command, every config, with real-world examples from a fintech app.

ID: 32A ★ Tier 3 — Senior Must-Know
🔍
1. Overview — The Full Release Pipeline

Releasing an Android app is not just "clicking upload." It's an engineering pipeline with 13 discrete stages. Missing any one of them can mean a crash-heavy rollout, a rejected build, or a security vulnerability shipped to millions of devices.

ANDROID RELEASE PIPELINE — END TO END Code Freeze Build Sign Optimise │ │ │ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ ▼ ┌──────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌───────────────┐ ┌───────────────────┐ │ Merge to │──▶│ Gradle Release │─▶│ Keystore / │─▶│ R8 shrink+minify │ │ main / │ │ Build (AAB) │ │ Upload Key │ │ baseline profile │ │ release │ └─────────────────┘ └───────────────┘ └───────────────────┘ └──────────┘ │ ▼ QA Gate Upload Tracks Monitor │ │ │ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ ▼ ┌──────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌───────────────┐ ┌───────────────────┐ │ Internal │──▶│ Play Console │─▶│ Internal → │─▶│ Crashlytics ANR │ │ Testing │ │ AAB Upload │ │ Alpha → Beta │ │ Play vitals │ │ Track │ └─────────────────┘ │ → Production │ │ Force-stop rate │ └──────────┘ └───────────────┘ └───────────────────┘

The 13 stages — what can go wrong at each

#StageCommon failure
1Code freeze & version bumpWrong versionCode — Play rejects re-uploads with same or lower code
2Unit + integration tests passSkipping CI gate → regressions reach production
3Release build variantUsing debug signing accidentally; minifyEnabled false in release
4Keystore signingLost keystore = can never update the app; wrong alias/password
5R8 / ProGuard shrink & obfuscateMissing -keep rules crash app at runtime (reflection, serialisation)
6AAB generationAPK uploaded instead of AAB; split configs missing
7Play Console uploadManifest missing permissions; target SDK out of date; policy violation
8Internal test trackTesters not in group; wrong SHA-1 for Firebase integration
9Alpha / closed trackCrash rate too high — promote anyway and it becomes public
10Open beta trackForce-stop rate above Play threshold triggers automatic hold
11Staged production rolloutRollout at 100% immediately; can't halt quickly enough if P0 crash
12Post-launch monitoringNo Crashlytics alerts configured; ANR spike goes undetected for hours
13Hotfix processNo documented fast-track path; regression fix takes same 2-week cycle
✅
2. Pre-Release Checklist — What to Do Before Building

2.1 Version bump — the most critical step

Every Play Store upload must have a strictly increasing versionCode. versionName is what users see; versionCode is the integer Play uses to order releases. Using the same or lower code will hard-fail the upload.

// app/build.gradle.kts — production pattern
android {
    defaultConfig {
        // versionCode = CI build number (always incrementing)
        // GitHub Actions: System.getenv("GITHUB_RUN_NUMBER")?.toInt() ?: 1
        versionCode = System.getenv("VERSION_CODE")?.toInt() ?: 1
        versionName = "3.7.2"       // semantic: major.minor.patch
        minSdk = 26
        targetSdk = 35               // Must be current year's API or Play warns
        applicationId = "com.acme.bankapp"
    }
}

2.2 Mandatory pre-release checks

1

Run full test suite — unit + integration + UI

./gradlew testReleaseUnitTest connectedReleaseAndroidTest — must be green before any build is promoted.

2

Run Android Lint on release variant

./gradlew lintRelease — check for missing translations, deprecated API calls, hardcoded strings. Treat errors as build failures.

3

Check targetSdkVersion

Google Play requires new apps to target at minimum Android 14 (API 34) and existing apps must be updated by August of the following year. Failing this causes upload rejection.

4

Audit permissions in AndroidManifest.xml

Remove any permission not used in the release build. Play reviews permissions and will flag unused dangerous permissions.

5

Verify no debug flags in release

android:debuggable="true" in the manifest, BuildConfig.DEBUG checks, Stetho/Flipper interceptors — must all be release-guarded.

6

Verify no sensitive keys in code or git

API keys, Firebase credentials, and signing passwords must come from CI environment variables or local.properties (gitignored), never hardcoded.

Hard Stop — targetSdkVersion
As of 2025, Google Play requires targetSdkVersion ≥ 34 for all new app submissions and updates. Apps targeting API 33 or below get a hard rejection. Update targetSdk and test against the newer behaviour changes (photo picker, notification permission, predictive back gesture).
🔧
3. Build Variants & Product Flavours

Build types: debug vs release

// app/build.gradle.kts
android {
    buildTypes {
        debug {
            applicationIdSuffix(".debug")      // install alongside release
            isDebuggable = true
            isMinifyEnabled = false
            isShrinkResources = false
        }
        release {
            isMinifyEnabled = true           // R8 code shrinking
            isShrinkResources = true         // remove unused resources
            proguardFiles(
                getDefaultProguardFile("proguard-android-optimize.txt"),
                "proguard-rules.pro"
            )
            // Signing configured here or via signingConfigs block
            signingConfig = signingConfigs.getByName("release")
        }
    }
}

Product flavours — staging vs production

android {
    flavorDimensions("env")
    productFlavors {
        create("staging") {
            dimension = "env"
            applicationIdSuffix(".staging")
            buildConfigField("String", "API_BASE_URL", "\"https://api-staging.acme.com\"")
            buildConfigField("Boolean", "ENABLE_LOGS", "true")
        }
        create("production") {
            dimension = "env"
            buildConfigField("String", "API_BASE_URL", "\"https://api.acme.com\"")
            buildConfigField("Boolean", "ENABLE_LOGS", "false")
        }
    }
}
// This creates build variants:
// stagingDebug, stagingRelease, productionDebug, productionRelease
// Upload variant: productionRelease

Build the release AAB

# Build production release AAB (not APK — AAB is required for Play Store)
./gradlew bundleProductionRelease

# Output: app/build/outputs/bundle/productionRelease/app-production-release.aab

# Run lint before building — fail fast
./gradlew lintProductionRelease bundleProductionRelease
📜
4. APK vs AAB & App Signing

APK vs AAB — what's the difference

PropertyAPK (Android Package)AAB (Android App Bundle)
Required for Play Store❌ Rejected since Aug 2021✅ Mandatory for new apps
What it containsAll resources & code for all devicesSplit by ABI, screen density, language
Size on deviceFull size regardless of device15–40% smaller (Play serves device-specific splits)
SigningYou sign the APK directlyGoogle re-signs splits with your upload key
Direct installYes — sideload with adb installNo — must go through Play or bundletool
Dynamic features❌ Not supported✅ Dynamic Feature Modules

4.1 Keystore and signing — the most critical permanent decision

Irreversible — losing your keystore = losing your app
Your keystore is the permanent identity of your app. If you lose it and you don't use Play App Signing, you can never push another update to the same package name. Store it in: password manager + encrypted cloud backup + offline USB drive. Never store it in git.

Generate a new release keystore (one-time, production)

# Create keystore — do this ONCE and store it permanently
keytool -genkeypair \
  -alias acme-release-key \
  -keyalg RSA \
  -keysize 4096 \
  -validity 10000 \
  -keystore acme-release.keystore \
  -storepass '$STORE_PASSWORD' \
  -keypass  '$KEY_PASSWORD' \
  -dname "CN=Acme Corp, OU=Android, O=Acme, L=London, S=England, C=GB"

# Verify the keystore contents
keytool -list -v -keystore acme-release.keystore -storepass '$STORE_PASSWORD'

Configure signing in Gradle (secure CI pattern)

// app/build.gradle.kts — reads from environment variables (CI-safe)
android {
    signingConfigs {
        create("release") {
            storeFile   = file(System.getenv("KEYSTORE_PATH") ?: "../acme-release.keystore")
            storePassword = System.getenv("KEYSTORE_PASSWORD") ?: properties["KEYSTORE_PASSWORD"].toString()
            keyAlias    = System.getenv("KEY_ALIAS") ?: "acme-release-key"
            keyPassword = System.getenv("KEY_PASSWORD") ?: properties["KEY_PASSWORD"].toString()
        }
    }
    buildTypes {
        release {
            signingConfig = signingConfigs.getByName("release")
        }
    }
}

4.2 Play App Signing — the modern approach

Since 2021, Google Play manages two keys: the app signing key (held by Google, used to sign APK splits delivered to devices) and the upload key (you hold this to sign the AAB you upload).

KeyWho holds itWhat it signsIf lost
App signing keyGoogleAPK splits delivered to devicesGoogle can reset it via identity verification
Upload keyYouAAB you upload to Play ConsoleRequest an upload key reset from Google support
Best Practice — Always use Play App Signing
Enrol every new app in Play App Signing from the first upload. This decouples your upload key (which you can reset) from the actual signing key (held by Google). You get: key rotation support, smaller APKs, and safety against keystore loss.

Verify your signed AAB before uploading

# Use bundletool to test locally (download from github.com/google/bundletool)
java -jar bundletool.jar build-apks \
  --bundle=app-production-release.aab \
  --output=app.apks \
  --ks=acme-release.keystore \
  --ks-pass=pass:$KEYSTORE_PASSWORD \
  --ks-key-alias=acme-release-key \
  --key-pass=pass:$KEY_PASSWORD

# Install on connected device to verify before uploading to Play
java -jar bundletool.jar install-apks --apks=app.apks
📷
5. R8, ProGuard & Obfuscation

R8 is the compiler + shrinker + obfuscator + optimiser that runs during release builds. It replaces ProGuard. Understanding it prevents the most common release crash: "Class not found at runtime even though it compiled fine."

What R8 does — four passes

PassWhat it doesControlled by
Tree shakingRemoves unreachable classes, methods, fieldsminifyEnabled true
ObfuscationRenames classes/methods to a, b, c…minifyEnabled true
Resource shrinkingRemoves unused drawable, layout, string resourcesshrinkResources true
OptimisationInlines methods, removes dead code paths, constant propagationproguard-android-optimize.txt

Complete production ProGuard rules — proguard-rules.pro

##──────── Kotlin ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
-keepclassmembers class **$WhenMappings { <fields>; }
-keepclassmembers class ** implements kotlin.coroutines.CoroutineContext$Element { *; }
-keep class kotlin.** { *; }
-keep class kotlinx.** { *; }
-dontwarn kotlin.**

##──────── Retrofit + OkHttp ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
-keepattributes Signature, Exceptions, *Annotation*
-keepattributes EnclosingMethod
-keep,allowobfuscation,allowshrinking interface retrofit2.**
-keep class retrofit2.** { *; }
-keep class okhttp3.** { *; }
-dontwarn okhttp3.**

##──────── Gson / Moshi / Kotlinx Serialisation ──────────────────────────────
# Keep all data classes used in JSON serialisation (Gson uses reflection)
-keep class com.acme.bankapp.data.model.** { *; }
-keepclassmembers class ** {
    @com.google.gson.annotations.SerializedName <fields>;
}
# Moshi generated adapters
-keep class **JsonAdapter { *; }

##──────── Room ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
-keep class * extends androidx.room.RoomDatabase { *; }
-keep @androidx.room.Entity class * { *; }

##──────── Hilt / Dagger ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
-keep,allowobfuscation @dagger.hilt.android.HiltAndroidApp class *
-keep class dagger.** { *; }
-keep class javax.inject.** { *; }
-keep class * extends dagger.hilt.android.internal.managers.** { *; }

##──────── Firebase / Crashlytics ────────────────────────────────────────────
-keepattributes SourceFile,LineNumberTable
-keep public class * extends java.lang.Exception
-keep class com.google.firebase.** { *; }
-dontwarn com.google.firebase.**

##──────── Parcelable / Serializable ─────────────────────────────────────────
-keepclassmembers class * implements android.os.Parcelable {
    public static final android.os.Parcelable$Creator CREATOR;
}
-keepclassmembers class * implements java.io.Serializable {
    static final long serialVersionUID;
    private static final java.io.ObjectStreamField[] serialPersistentFields;
    private void writeObject(java.io.ObjectOutputStream);
    private void readObject(java.io.ObjectInputStream);
    java.lang.Object readResolve();
}

##──────── WebView / JS interface ─────────────────────────────────────────────
-keepclassmembers class * {
    @android.webkit.JavascriptInterface <methods>;
}

##──────── Enums ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
-keepclassmembers enum * {
    public static **[] values();
    public static ** valueOf(java.lang.String);
}

##──────── Keep mapping file for Crashlytics deobfuscation ───────────────────
-printmapping build/outputs/mapping/release/mapping.txt
Always upload mapping.txt to Crashlytics
R8 obfuscates stack traces. Without the mapping.txt file, your Crashlytics crashes show a.b.c() line 12 instead of real class names. Upload it automatically via ./gradlew uploadCrashlyticsProguardMappingProductionRelease or the Firebase Gradle plugin handles it automatically when firebaseCrashlytics { mappingFileUploadEnabled = true }.

Verify R8 output with apkanalyzer

# Check what's in your AAB / check which classes survived shrinking
$ANDROID_HOME/cmdline-tools/latest/bin/apkanalyzer dex packages \
  app/build/outputs/bundle/productionRelease/app-production-release.aab \
  | grep "com.acme"

# Check final APK size breakdown (after bundletool build-apks)
$ANDROID_HOME/cmdline-tools/latest/bin/apkanalyzer apk download-size app.apks
🚀
6. Play Console Upload — Step-by-Step

6.1 Manual upload via Play Console UI

1

Go to play.google.com/console → Your app → Release → Testing or Production

Choose the track: Internal testing → Closed testing (Alpha) → Open testing (Beta) → Production.

2

Create new release → Upload AAB

Drag and drop the .aab file. Play validates: package name, versionCode, signing certificate, minimum SDK, and target SDK. Any mismatch gives a hard rejection with a specific error code.

3

Fill release notes (What's new)

Required for production; optional for testing tracks. Supports 500 chars per locale. Must be filled for each locale your app supports.

4

Review → Save → Review release

Play runs pre-launch checks: screenshots, robo-test, policy scan, permission audit. Results appear in the Pre-launch report within 30–60 minutes.

5

Start rollout

For production: choose rollout percentage (1–100%). For internal/alpha/beta: 100% to all testers in the track group.

6.2 Automated upload via Play Developer API (Fastlane / CI)

# Using Fastlane supply — the standard CI upload tool
# Gemfile
gem "fastlane"

# fastlane/Fastfile
lane :deploy_production do
  # 1. Run tests
  gradle(task: "test", build_type: "Release", flavor: "Production")

  # 2. Build AAB
  gradle(
    task:        "bundle",
    build_type:  "Release",
    flavor:      "Production",
    properties: {
      "KEYSTORE_PATH"     => ENV["KEYSTORE_PATH"],
      "KEYSTORE_PASSWORD" => ENV["KEYSTORE_PASSWORD"],
      "KEY_ALIAS"         => ENV["KEY_ALIAS"],
      "KEY_PASSWORD"      => ENV["KEY_PASSWORD"]
    }
  )

  # 3. Upload to internal track first
  upload_to_play_store(
    track:               "internal",
    aab:                 "app/build/outputs/bundle/productionRelease/app-production-release.aab",
    json_key:            "fastlane/play-store-api-key.json",
    skip_upload_apk:     true,
    release_status:      "completed",
    version_name:        android_get_package_version_name()
  )
end

6.3 Common Play Console rejection reasons

ErrorCauseFix
VERSION_CODE_NOT_INCREMENTINGSame or lower versionCodeIncrement versionCode; use CI build number
APK_NOT_ZIP_ALIGNEDOld manual APK buildUse AAB; or zipalign before signing
INVALID_SIGNING_CERTIFICATEDifferent cert from enrolled upload keyUse the correct keystore; or request key reset
Policy violationUndeclared permissions, deceptive contentRemove unused permissions; update data safety form
TARGET_SDK_VERSION_TOO_LOWtargetSdk < minimum requiredUpdate to current requirement (API 34 as of 2025)
📊
7. Tracks & Staged Rollout Strategy

The four tracks — what each means

TrackWho sees itPurposeCrash rate threshold
Internal testingUp to 100 internal testers (email list)First smoke test after QA sign-offNo automatic hold
Closed testing (Alpha)Closed group — up to thousands; invite onlyBroader regression test with real devicesNo automatic hold
Open testing (Beta)Opt-in from Play Store page — publicGather real-world feedback before full launchPlay may flag >1.09% crash rate
ProductionAll usersLive release — partial rollout supportedPlay halts rollout at >1.09% crash rate

Staged rollout — the only safe way to release

Never push directly to 100% of production users. A staged rollout lets you monitor crash rate and vitals before the damage scales.

RECOMMENDED STAGED ROLLOUT TIMELINE Day 0 │ Internal track (100 testers) │ ✓ Zero P0 crashes → promote after 4h │ Day 1 │ Closed Alpha (2,000 testers) │ ✓ Crash rate < 0.5% → promote after 24h │ Day 2 │ Open Beta (opt-in, ~10,000 users) │ ✓ Crash rate < 0.8% → promote after 48h │ Day 4 │ Production rollout ── 1% │ Monitor 4h → crash rate? force-stop rate? │ ✓ Still below threshold → expand to 5% │ Day 5 │ Production ── 10% │ Monitor 8h → Play vitals still green? │ Day 6 │ Production ── 20% → 50% → 100% │ Automate with Fastlane promote lane or │ Play Developer API incremental_rollout

Programmatic staged rollout via Fastlane

# fastlane/Fastfile — promote lane
lane :promote_to_production do |options|
  upload_to_play_store(
    track:                    "beta",
    track_promote_to:         "production",
    rollout:                  options[:rollout] || "0.01",  # 1%
    json_key:                 "fastlane/play-store-api-key.json",
    skip_upload_aab:          true,
    skip_upload_apk:          true
  )
end

# Expand rollout
lane :expand_rollout do |options|
  upload_to_play_store(
    track:           "production",
    rollout:         options[:percentage].to_s,
    json_key:        "fastlane/play-store-api-key.json",
    skip_upload_aab: true,
    skip_upload_apk: true
  )
end

# Halt rollout (emergency stop)
lane :halt_rollout do
  upload_to_play_store(
    track:           "production",
    rollout:         "0",     # 0% halts new installs
    json_key:        "fastlane/play-store-api-key.json",
    skip_upload_aab: true
  )
end
Automatic Halt — Play Store safety net
If your app's crash rate exceeds 1.09% or ANR rate exceeds 0.47% on Android Vitals, Play Console displays a warning and can automatically pause the rollout. You'll see this as "Rollout paused due to Play policy". Fix the issue and manually resume — it does NOT auto-resume.
⚙
8. CI/CD Automation — Full GitHub Actions Pipeline

Complete production release workflow

# .github/workflows/release.yml
name: Release to Play Store
on:
  push:
    tags: [ 'v*.*.*' ]          # trigger on version tag e.g. v3.7.2

jobs:
  release:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # 1. Set up JDK
      - name: Set up JDK 17
        uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with: { java-version: '17', distribution: 'temurin' }

      # 2. Cache Gradle dependencies
      - name: Cache Gradle
        uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: |
            ~/.gradle/caches
            ~/.gradle/wrapper
          key: gradle-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('**/*.gradle*') }}

      # 3. Decode keystore from base64 secret
      - name: Decode Keystore
        run: |
          echo "${{ secrets.KEYSTORE_BASE64 }}" | base64 --decode \
            > $GITHUB_WORKSPACE/acme-release.keystore

      # 4. Run tests
      - name: Run Unit Tests
        run: ./gradlew testProductionReleaseUnitTest

      # 5. Run Lint
      - name: Run Lint
        run: ./gradlew lintProductionRelease

      # 6. Build AAB
      - name: Build Release AAB
        env:
          KEYSTORE_PATH: ${{ github.workspace }}/acme-release.keystore
          KEYSTORE_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.KEYSTORE_PASSWORD }}
          KEY_ALIAS: ${{ secrets.KEY_ALIAS }}
          KEY_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.KEY_PASSWORD }}
          VERSION_CODE: ${{ github.run_number }}
        run: ./gradlew bundleProductionRelease

      # 7. Upload AAB artifact
      - name: Upload AAB
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: release-aab
          path: app/build/outputs/bundle/productionRelease/

      # 8. Upload to Play Store internal track
      - name: Deploy to Play Store (Internal Track)
        uses: r0adkll/upload-google-play@v1
        with:
          serviceAccountJsonPlainText: ${{ secrets.PLAY_STORE_JSON_KEY }}
          packageName: com.acme.bankapp
          releaseFiles: app/build/outputs/bundle/productionRelease/app-production-release.aab
          track: internal
          status: completed
          whatsNewDirectory: fastlane/metadata/android/en-US/changelogs/

      # 9. Upload mapping.txt to Crashlytics
      - name: Upload Crashlytics Mapping
        env:
          GOOGLE_SERVICES_JSON: ${{ secrets.GOOGLE_SERVICES_JSON }}
        run: ./gradlew uploadCrashlyticsProguardMappingProductionRelease

# 1. IAM & Admin → Service Accounts → Create Service Account

# 2. Grant role: "Service Account User"
# 3. Keys → Add Key → JSON → Download
# 4. In Play Console: Setup → API access → Link to Google Cloud project

9. Post-Release Monitoring — What to Watch

The critical metrics in the first 24 hours

MetricGood thresholdDanger thresholdWhere to see it
Crash-free users rate> 99.5%< 98.9% → Play may pause rolloutFirebase Crashlytics + Play Vitals
ANR rate< 0.10%> 0.47% → Play policy thresholdPlay Console → Android Vitals
Force-stop rate< 0.20%> 1.09% → Rollout auto-pausedPlay Console → Android Vitals
Average rating changeStable or upDrop > 0.2 starsPlay Console → Ratings & Reviews
Core web vitals (startup)Cold start < 500ms> 1200msPlay Console → Performance

Firebase Crashlytics alert setup

// In your Application class — set up Crashlytics before any crash can occur
class BankApp : Application() {
    override fun onCreate() {
        super.onCreate()
        // Enable crash collection in release only
        FirebaseCrashlytics.getInstance()
            .setCrashlyticsCollectionEnabled(!BuildConfig.DEBUG)

        // Set user ID for better debugging (anonymised)
        FirebaseCrashlytics.getInstance().setUserId(
            getAnonymisedUserId()  // hash of real ID, never PII directly
        )
    }
}

// In build.gradle.kts — automatically upload mapping.txt on every release build
firebaseCrashlytics {
    mappingFileUploadEnabled = true   // auto-upload proguard mapping
    nativeSymbolUploadEnabled = false  // set true if using NDK/C++
}

Setting up Crashlytics alerts (Firebase Console)

1

Firebase Console → Crashlytics → Alerts

Set up: "Velocity alerts" — triggers when a new crash hits 0.1% of sessions within 1 hour.

2

Set regression alerts

Alerts when a previously resolved crash re-opens — catches regressions introduced by new releases immediately.

3

Connect to PagerDuty / Slack

Firebase → Project Settings → Integrations → PagerDuty or Slack webhook. Route P0 crashes directly to your on-call engineer.

4

Monitor Play Console Android Vitals daily

Play Console → Android Vitals → Core vitals. Set email digest. If ANR or crash rate crosses the "bad behaviour threshold," you receive an automated email from Play.

Hotfix decision tree

HOTFIX DECISION TREE Production crash detected │ ▼ Is crash rate > 1%? ├─ YES → HALT rollout immediately (Play Console → Halt rollout) │ │ │ └─ Can we fix in < 4h? → YES → hotfix branch → expedited review request │ → NO → rollback to previous version (Play Console) │ └─ NO → Is it a P0 security issue? ├─ YES → expedited hotfix + notify security team └─ NO → schedule normal patch release

10. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1 — Losing your keystore
Never store the keystore in git. Store it in a password manager + two separate encrypted cloud vaults. The only recovery is enrolling in Play App Signing before you lose it. Without it, your only option is to publish under a new package name (losing all your users and reviews).
Pitfall 2 — Skipping ProGuard -keep rules
R8 will shrink away classes referenced only via reflection (Gson models, Room entities, Parcelable classes, JS interfaces). The app compiles but crashes at runtime with ClassNotFoundException. Always test the release build on a real device before uploading.
Pitfall 3 — Uploading APK instead of AAB
Google Play has required AAB for all new apps since August 2021. An APK upload will fail with error UPLOAD_APK_FORBIDDEN_PACKAGE_NAME for new apps, and for existing apps it still works but misses on-demand delivery and significantly larger install sizes.
Pitfall 4 — Not testing the release build variant
Debug and release builds behave differently: R8 removes branches, ProGuard renames classes, signing is different. Always install productionRelease on a physical device and smoke-test the critical flows before uploading.
Pitfall 5 — Hardcoding API keys in code
R8 obfuscates method names but does NOT encrypt string literals. Any string in your code is visible via strings command on the APK. Use Google Cloud Secret Manager, remote config, or at minimum place keys in local.properties and inject them as BuildConfig fields — never commit them.
Best Practice — Baseline Profiles
Add a baseline-prof.txt generated by the Macrobenchmark library. It pre-compiles the hot startup paths (app startup, main screen rendering). Result: 15–30% faster cold start visible in Play Console Core Vitals. Must be regenerated for each release. 
./gradlew :app:generateBaselineProfile
🎯
11. Interview Framework

30-second answer — "Walk me through your release process"

"We follow a gated pipeline: code freeze on the release branch, full test suite and lint must pass in CI. We build a signed AAB using a Release build type with R8 enabled, sign it with our upload key via Play App Signing, upload to the internal track first, then promote through Alpha → Beta → Production with a staged rollout starting at 1%. We monitor Crashlytics and Play Vitals — if crash rate exceeds 0.5% we halt the rollout. Everything is automated via GitHub Actions and Fastlane."

2-minute answer — what separates seniors

"Beyond the basics, the senior-level considerations are: keystore management (Play App Signing so we can rotate the upload key), ProGuard/R8 keep rules (I've been burned by missing Gson model keeps causing runtime ClassNotFoundException), Baseline Profiles to maintain cold start SLA, and the monitoring setup — Crashlytics velocity alerts with PagerDuty integration so P0s page on-call within 60 seconds of hitting 0.1% of sessions. For versioning, we use the CI build number as versionCode so it's guaranteed to be monotonically increasing. And we never roll out to 100% immediately — 1% → 5% → 10% → 50% → 100% over 3–5 days."

Must mention — the examiner's checklist

  • AAB vs APK — AAB mandatory, Play re-signs the splits
  • Upload key vs signing key — Play App Signing manages the distinction
  • R8 keep rules — Gson/Retrofit/Parcelable all need explicit keeps
  • mapping.txt — must be uploaded to Crashlytics for readable stack traces
  • versionCode — must be strictly increasing; use CI build number
  • Staged rollout — 1% first, monitor vitals, expand over days
  • Play Vitals thresholds — 1.09% crash rate triggers automatic rollout halt

Follow-up: "What's the difference between versionCode and versionName?"

A: versionCode is an internal integer used by Play to order releases — must strictly increase with each upload. versionName is the human-readable string shown to users (e.g. "3.7.2") — semantic versioning convention, but Play doesn't enforce any format. You can have versionCode=1042 with versionName="3.7.2".

Follow-up: "How do you handle a P0 crash post-release?"

A: Immediately halt the rollout in Play Console (drops new installs to 0%). Assess if previous version should be rolled back — Play Console lets you re-publish the last release without re-uploading. Create a hotfix branch from the release tag, fix, fast-track through CI and expedited Play review (available for critical security/crash fixes), then resume rollout.

13. Interview Questions
What is the difference between APK and AAB, and which does Google Play require?
Basic⌄
AAB (Android App Bundle) is required for all new apps since August 2021. Unlike APK which bundles all code and resources for all device configurations, AAB is a publishing format — Google Play generates and delivers optimised APKs per device (correct ABI, screen density, language only). This makes installs 15–40% smaller. You cannot sideload an AAB directly; use bundletool to test locally.
You upload a new build and get "VERSION_CODE_NOT_INCREMENTING". What happened and how do you fix it?
Basic⌄
The new build has a versionCode equal to or lower than the last uploaded build. Play requires strictly increasing version codes. Fix: increment the versionCode in build.gradle.kts and rebuild. Production pattern: use the CI build number (System.getenv("GITHUB_RUN_NUMBER").toInt()) as the versionCode — it's guaranteed to increase with every CI run.
What is Play App Signing, and why should you use it?
Intermediate⌄
Play App Signing separates the upload key (you hold) from the app signing key (Google holds). You sign your AAB with the upload key before uploading. Google re-signs the APK splits it delivers to devices with the app signing key. Benefits: (1) if your upload key is lost, you can request a reset from Google support and your users are unaffected; (2) enables key rotation; (3) enables APK split optimisation. Without it, losing your keystore permanently blocks you from updating your app.
Your app crashes in production after enabling R8. The crash is ClassNotFoundException for a Gson model. What caused it and how do you fix it?
Intermediate⌄
R8 tree-shaking removed the Gson model class because it detected no direct code references (Gson accesses it via reflection, which R8 cannot see statically). Fix: add a ProGuard keep rule: -keep class com.acme.bankapp.data.model.** { *; } or more specifically -keepclassmembers class ** { @com.google.gson.annotations.SerializedName <fields>; }. After adding the rule, rebuild the release, install it on a device, and test the affected API call before re-uploading.
Walk through your complete staged rollout strategy for a major feature release.
Intermediate⌄
Internal track (100 internal testers, 4h, zero P0 crashes) → Closed Alpha (2,000 testers, 24h, crash rate <0.5%) → Open Beta (public opt-in, 48h, crash rate <0.8%) → Production 1% (4h monitor) → 5% (8h) → 10% (overnight) → 20% → 50% → 100%. At each production step: check Crashlytics crash-free session rate, Play Vitals ANR rate, and force-stop rate. If crash rate exceeds 1%, halt the rollout immediately and assess whether to fix-forward with a hotfix or roll back to the previous version.
Why is it important to upload the mapping.txt file to Crashlytics after each release?
Basic⌄
R8 obfuscates class and method names during release builds (e.g., MainActivity becomes a, fetchUser becomes b). Without the mapping.txt, Crashlytics stack traces show only obfuscated names — impossible to debug. The mapping.txt maps obfuscated names back to original names. It must be re-uploaded for every release since each build produces a different mapping. Enable automatic upload with firebaseCrashlytics { mappingFileUploadEnabled = true }.
A P0 crash is found 2 hours after rollout reaches 10% of production users. What do you do?
Senior⌄
1. Immediately halt the rollout in Play Console (sets rollout % to 0, stops new installs of the buggy version). 2. Assess scope: how many users affected, is it recoverable at runtime or data-corrupting? 3. If crash is isolated and fixable in <4h: create a hotfix branch off the release tag, fix, merge, trigger CI, upload to internal track for smoke test, then request expedited review from Google (available for critical bugs). 4. If fix will take >4h or is complex: roll back by promoting the previous production version (Play Console allows re-publishing without re-upload). 5. After hotfix is ready: resume rollout from 10% and monitor. Post-mortem within 48h.
How do you ensure secrets like API keys are not bundled in the release APK?
Senior⌄
Several layers: (1) Never hardcode secrets in source — R8 obfuscates method names but string literals remain readable via strings on the APK. (2) Use local.properties (gitignored) for local dev, inject as BuildConfig fields via Gradle — these are embedded in the binary but at least not in version control. (3) For production: use server-side secret delivery — app fetches config from a secure backend endpoint authenticated with an app attestation (Play Integrity API). (4) For keys that must be on-device (e.g., payment SDK): use Android Keystore-backed encrypted storage, never plain SharedPreferences. (5) Regularly rotate API keys in the backend, monitoring for unauthorized usage.
What are Baseline Profiles and how do they affect the release process?
Senior⌄
Baseline Profiles are a list of hot code paths (baseline-prof.txt) that tell the Android runtime (ART) to AOT-compile those methods ahead of time during app installation, instead of waiting for JIT compilation at first run. Generated by the Macrobenchmark library targeting real user startup flows. They reduce cold start time by 15–30% and eliminate initial jank. Release process impact: (1) They must be re-generated for each release because class/method references change. (2) They're included in the AAB automatically when using the androidx.profileinstaller library. (3) Results become visible in Play Console Core Vitals 7–14 days post-release as user install data accumulates.
Design an end-to-end release pipeline for a 10-million-user fintech app with a 2-week sprint cycle.
Senior⌄
Week 1: development + feature flags. Week 2 Day 1: code freeze on release branch, CI runs full test suite + lint + static analysis (Detekt). Day 2: Staging QA — internal track AAB built by CI, team smoke tests on physical devices including production-equivalent data. Day 3: Closed Alpha — ~500 beta users, 24h monitoring. Day 4: Open Beta (existing opted-in users). Day 5 (Monday): Production 1% rollout, Crashlytics alerts monitoring. Tue: 5%. Wed: 10% if vitals green. Thu: 25%. Fri: 50%. Following Mon: 100%. All promotions trigger Slack notification with crash-free rate metric. Play Vitals below threshold = auto-alert to release engineer. Keystore stored in HashiCorp Vault, injected as CI secret. mapping.txt auto-uploaded. Post-release retrospective at Day+7.
