33A — Debugging Scenarios

Six production debugging scenarios with root cause analysis, fixes, and prevention strategies. Each scenario: Problem → Clarifying Questions → Root Cause → Solution → Prevention.

ID: 33A ⭐ Senior Differentiator
🔍
1. Overview

Debugging Framework (use in interviews)

  1. Clarify: Ask when does it happen? Always or sometimes? Which devices? Which Android version? After rotation?
  2. Hypothesize: Form 2–3 root cause hypotheses based on symptoms
  3. Investigate: Name the tool you'd use (Logcat, Profiler, Compose metrics, LeakCanary)
  4. Root cause: Identify the exact cause
  5. Fix: Describe the code change
  6. Prevent: What process/pattern prevents this class of bug in future
Senior Signal
Juniors describe what happened. Seniors diagnose WHY it happened and add a prevention step. Always end your scenario answer with: "To prevent this in future, I would..."
🔁
2. API Called Twice After Rotation
1
Network call fires twice every time the screen rotates
Problem

User rotates the device. The loading indicator appears briefly, network call is made again, UI flickers. Happens every rotation.

Clarifying Questions
  • Is the network call in a ViewModel or in the Fragment/Activity directly?
  • Where exactly is the call triggered — onCreate, onStart, or in init?
  • Is it a Fragment or Activity?
Root Cause

The API call is made in Activity.onCreate() or Fragment.onViewCreated() directly — not in a ViewModel. On rotation, the Activity/Fragment is destroyed and recreated, so onCreate() runs again, triggering a new network call.

Solution
// ❌ Wrong — call in Activity/Fragment lifecycle
override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
    viewModel.loadUser()   // called AGAIN on every rotation
}

// ✅ Correct — call in ViewModel init{} (survives rotation)
class UserViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val repo: UserRepository
) : ViewModel() {

    val userState = MutableStateFlow<UiState<User>>(UiState.Loading)

    init {
        loadUser()  // called ONCE; ViewModel survives rotation
    }

    private fun loadUser() = viewModelScope.launch {
        userState.value = UiState.Loading
        userState.value = repo.getUser().fold(
            onSuccess = { UiState.Success(it) },
            onFailure = { UiState.Error(it.message) }
        )
    }
}

// Fragment observes — not triggers
viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
    repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
        viewModel.userState.collect { renderState(it) }
    }
}
Prevention
  • Code review rule: no network calls in Fragment/Activity lifecycle methods
  • All data loading happens in ViewModel init{} or in response to user actions
⚡
3. Compose Screen Continuously Recomposes
2
Compose screen flickers or Profiler shows constant recompositions
Problem

UI is janky. Compose Profiler shows 60+ recompositions per second even with no user interaction. Frame rate drops under scroll.

Clarifying Questions
  • What type is being passed as a parameter to the composable? Is it a List or custom class?
  • Are lambdas captured from the composition scope?
  • Is there a State that is being updated on every frame?
Root Cause

The composable parameter is an unstable type — Compose can't determine if it's changed, so it recomposes every time the parent recomposes. Common causes: passing a plain List<T> (mutable, considered unstable), a class without @Stable/@Immutable, or inline lambdas that are recreated every composition.

Solution
// ❌ Unstable — List is mutable, Compose marks it unstable
@Composable
fun FeedList(items: List<FeedItem>) { ... }

// ✅ Option 1: Wrap with ImmutableList (kotlinx.collections.immutable)
@Composable
fun FeedList(items: ImmutableList<FeedItem>) { ... }

// ✅ Option 2: Mark domain class @Immutable
@Immutable
data class FeedItem(val id: String, val title: String)

// ✅ Option 3: Wrapper class marked @Immutable
@Immutable
data class FeedUiState(val items: List<FeedItem> = emptyList())

// For lambdas — hoist out of composition or use remember
// ❌ New lambda instance every recomposition
FeedItem(onClick = { viewModel.onItemClick(item.id) })

// ✅ Stable lambda with rememberUpdatedState or function reference
val onClick = remember(item.id) { { viewModel.onItemClick(item.id) } }
Tools
  • Compose compiler metrics: freeCompilerArgs += "-P", "plugin:androidx.compose.compiler.plugins.kotlin:metricsDestination=..." — shows stable/unstable/skippable per class
  • Layout Inspector recomposition counts in Android Studio
Prevention
  • Mark all domain/UI state classes with @Immutable or use ImmutableList
  • Enable Compose compiler metrics in CI to catch unstable types before they merge
📉
4. App Crashes Only in Production
3
ClassNotFoundException or NullPointerException in production, not in debug
Problem

Crashlytics shows a crash affecting 3% of users. Stack trace points to a JSON parsing method. Works perfectly in debug and staging builds.

Clarifying Questions
  • Is minifyEnabled=true only in release builds?
  • Are any data classes used with Gson/Moshi for JSON parsing?
  • Was a new model class added recently without corresponding keep rules?
Root Cause

Missing R8 keep rules: R8 removed or renamed a data class used for JSON deserialization. Gson uses reflection to map JSON fields to class fields. When R8 renames userAddress to a, Gson can't find the field → NullPointerException or wrong data.

Solution
// Option 1: Add keep rule in proguard-rules.pro
-keep class com.myapp.data.model.** { *; }
-keepclassmembers class com.myapp.data.model.** { *; }

// Option 2: Annotate with @Keep
@Keep
data class UserDto(
    @SerializedName("user_address")
    val address: String
)

// Option 3: Switch to kotlinx.serialization (works with R8 without keep rules)
@Serializable
data class UserDto(val address: String)

// Debug the crash in release mode locally:
// adb shell setprop debug.viewAttributeInspectionEnabled true
// Or build a release APK locally and install via adb install -r app-release.apk
Other Causes of Prod-only Crashes
  • Different API levels — test against minimum supported API on a real device or emulator
  • Missing exception handling for edge cases that only occur with real data
  • Race conditions that only manifest under production load
Prevention
  • Run a release build smoke test before every production push
  • Add tests that instantiate all model classes via the serialization library
  • Use kotlinx.serialization instead of Gson — no reflection at runtime
🕐
5. App Startup Takes 5 Seconds
4
Cold start time is 5 seconds — users complain about slow launch
Problem

Firebase Performance shows p50 cold start = 5.2s. Target is <2s. App shows blank white screen for 3+ seconds before content appears.

Clarifying Questions
  • What SDK initializations happen in Application.onCreate()?
  • Is there any synchronous disk I/O or network call during startup?
  • How large is the database being opened at startup?
Root Cause Analysis

Common causes: (1) Heavy SDK init in Application.onCreate() — each SDK adding 100–300ms; (2) Blocking I/O on main thread — database open, SharedPreferences read, file access; (3) Synchronous network call before showing UI; (4) Large Activity/Fragment inflation with complex view hierarchy.

Solution
// ❌ Blocking Application.onCreate()
class App : Application() {
    override fun onCreate() {
        super.onCreate()
        Firebase.initializeApp(this)           // ok - fast
        heavyDatabase.initialize(this)       // ❌ blocking, 800ms
        analyticsLibrary.init(this)           // ❌ blocking, 400ms
        legacySharedPrefs.loadAll(this)      // ❌ disk I/O on main thread
    }
}

// ✅ App Startup library for lazy, ordered initialization
class AnalyticsInitializer : Initializer<Unit> {
    override fun create(context: Context) {
        // Runs on background thread via WorkManager startup
        analyticsLibrary.init(context)
    }
    override fun dependencies() = emptyList<Class<out Initializer<*>>>()
}

// ✅ Lazy inject: Room DB not opened until first query
val database: AppDatabase by lazy {
    Room.databaseBuilder(appContext, AppDatabase::class.java, "app.db").build()
}

// ✅ Baseline Profile — pre-compile critical startup code paths
// Generate with Macrobenchmark BaselineProfileRule
// Reduces JIT compilation overhead at startup by 30-40%
Measurement Tools
  • adb shell am start-activity -W — measures Time To Initial Display (TTID)
  • Android Studio Profiler → CPU → System Trace
  • Firebase Performance Monitoring — _app_start automatic trace
  • Macrobenchmark library for reliable CI measurement
Prevention
  • Rule: no blocking calls on main thread in Application.onCreate()
  • Macrobenchmark startup test in CI — fails if startup > 2s threshold
  • Baseline Profiles generated and shipped with every release
💧
6. Flow Collected Multiple Times
5
UI updates are duplicated or Flow emissions trigger actions multiple times
Problem

A toast appears twice for the same event. A navigation action triggers twice. A network request is fired multiple times for one user action.

Root Cause

The Flow is collected without repeatOnLifecycle in a Fragment. When the Fragment goes to background and returns, a new collector is created without cancelling the old one. Two collectors are now active for the same Flow.

Solution
// ❌ Wrong — creates new collector on each onStart(), old one still active
override fun onStart() {
    super.onStart()
    lifecycleScope.launch {
        viewModel.events.collect { handleEvent(it) }
        // This coroutine lives as long as lifecycleScope (until onDestroy)
        // but collect() is called AGAIN on next onStart()
    }
}

// ✅ Correct — exactly ONE collector active when STARTED, cancelled on STOPPED
override fun onViewCreated(view: View, savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
        viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
            viewModel.events.collect { handleEvent(it) }
            // Automatically cancelled when Fragment STOPPED, re-starts on STARTED
        }
    }
}

// For one-shot events: use SharedFlow with replay=0
val events = MutableSharedFlow<UiEvent>(replay = 0, extraBufferCapacity = 1)
// Emits to currently-active collectors only; no replaying on new collector
Prevention
  • Team convention: always use repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) in Fragments — never naked lifecycleScope.launch { flow.collect }
  • Lint rule: Android Studio provides a lint check for this exact pattern
🔥
7. Activity Leak + Interview Framework
6
Activity is leaking — LeakCanary reports Activity retained after finish()
Root Causes (Most Common)
CausePatternFix
Static referencecompanion object / object holds Activity referenceUse WeakReference or remove static reference
Anonymous inner classInner Runnable/Listener holds implicit outer class (Activity) referenceUse named static class or WeakReference
Unregistered listenerregisterX() without unregisterX() in onDestroyUnregister in onDestroy or use lifecycle-aware components
Handler with delayhandler.postDelayed({ ... }, 5000) — Activity destroyed before delay firesCancel in onDestroy: handler.removeCallbacks(runnable)
Application context missingSingleton holds Activity context — use applicationContextInject applicationContext in singletons, not activity context
// ❌ Handler leak
private val handler = Handler(Looper.getMainLooper())
private val runnable = Runnable { updateUI() }  // holds Activity ref
handler.postDelayed(runnable, 5000)

// ✅ Fix: cancel in onDestroy
override fun onDestroy() {
    super.onDestroy()
    handler.removeCallbacks(runnable)
}

// ✅ Better: use lifecycle-aware coroutine instead of Handler
lifecycleScope.launch {
    delay(5000)
    updateUI()
    // Auto-cancelled when lifecycle is destroyed
}

Interview Framework: Debugging

DRIDE Framework
Describe symptoms → Reproduce reliably → Isolate (binary search: which component? which state?) → Diagnose root cause → Eliminate + prevent recurrence
⚡

9. Practice Questions
How do you diagnose why a Compose screen is recomposing too frequently?
Hard▼
Step 1: Enable Layout Inspector in Android Studio → Show Recomposition Counts — this shows how many times each composable recomposed. Step 2: Enable Compose compiler metrics (freeCompilerArgs plugin args) — generates a report showing which classes are stable/unstable/skippable. Step 3: Look for parameters marked as "unstable" — these force recomposition. Fix: @Immutable annotation, ImmutableList, stable lambda references.
A colleague's code causes an Activity leak. How do you detect and fix it?
Medium▼
Detection: Add LeakCanary to the debug build — it automatically detects and reports retained objects with a full path to the leak root. Also check Android Profiler → Memory → Force GC → Heap Dump for Activity instances. Fix: look at the LeakCanary report path (static field → Activity, or anonymous class holding outer Activity), then apply: WeakReference for static refs, removeCallbacks for Handler, unregister listeners in onDestroy.
Why does repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) prevent double-collection in Fragments?
Hard▼
repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) creates a new coroutine block when the lifecycle reaches STARTED and cancels it when it drops below STARTED (i.e., STOPPED). This means: (1) Only one collection is active at a time. (2) When the Fragment returns to foreground, the old collection was already cancelled, so a fresh one starts. Without it, each call to launch { flow.collect } adds a permanent collector that survives background/foreground transitions.
How would you measure and improve cold start time to under 2 seconds?
Hard▼
Measure: adb shell am start-activity -W (TTID/TTFD), Firebase Performance _app_start trace, Macrobenchmark. Improve: (1) Profile Application.onCreate() — move heavy init off main thread via App Startup library; (2) Lazy initialization for Room DB, heavy singletons; (3) Reduce ContentProviders (each adds startup overhead); (4) Generate and ship Baseline Profiles — pre-compiles critical code paths, 30-40% faster startup; (5) Splash screen API to fill perceived wait with branded splash.
What is @Immutable in Compose and when is it not safe to use?
Hard▼
@Immutable is a contract you make to the Compose compiler saying "none of the public properties of this class will change after construction." It enables skippable recomposition. It is NOT safe to use if: the class has mutable properties (var), the class contains a mutable List or Map (even if the field is val), or you might mutate the object after passing it to a composable. Misusing @Immutable causes silent UI bugs where the UI doesn't update when data changes.
Name three patterns that cause Activity memory leaks and their fixes.
Medium▼
(1) Static reference: companion object holds Activity → use WeakReference or remove. (2) Handler with postDelayed: delayed runnable holds Activity reference → cancel with removeCallbacks in onDestroy, or replace with lifecycle-aware coroutine + delay(). (3) Unregistered listener: registerReceiver without unregister → use lifecycle-aware components (LifecycleObserver) that auto-unregister, or manually unregister in onStop/onDestroy.
How do you debug a crash that only happens in production and has an obfuscated stack trace?
Medium▼
Step 1: Check Crashlytics dashboard — if the firebase-crashlytics Gradle plugin uploaded the mapping.txt at build time, Crashlytics auto-symbolicated the trace. Step 2: If not, find the mapping.txt file at app/build/outputs/mapping/release/mapping.txt for that build (store in CI artifacts). Step 3: Run retrace mapping.txt obfuscated-trace.txt. Step 4: Reproduce locally with a release build (adb install -r app-release.apk). Step 5: Add missing keep rules for the affected class.
What tool would you use for each: memory leak, slow startup, Compose jank, network call frequency?
Easy▼
Memory leak → LeakCanary (debug) + Android Profiler Heap Dump. Slow startup → adb am start-activity -W + Macrobenchmark + Firebase Performance _app_start + Android Studio CPU System Trace. Compose jank → Layout Inspector Recomposition Counts + Compose compiler metrics report. Network call frequency → Android Studio Profiler Network tab + OkHttp logging interceptor in debug + Firebase Performance HTTP traces in production.
What is the App Startup library and how does it help?
Medium▼
The App Startup library provides a single ContentProvider (InitializationProvider) that replaces the pattern of each SDK registering its own ContentProvider. Each ContentProvider adds ~5ms startup overhead — with 10 SDKs that's 50ms. App Startup initializes them all through one ContentProvider. Additionally it supports: ordered initialization (Initializer dependencies), lazy initialization (on first use), and explicit initialization from code (useful for testing).
A user reports that tapping a button sends duplicate API requests. Walk through your debugging approach.
Hard▼
(1) Check if the Flow is collected multiple times — look for missing repeatOnLifecycle. (2) Check if the button click listener is set multiple times (e.g., in onViewCreated called multiple times without cleanup). (3) Check if the ViewModel launches without deduplication — add a loading guard: if (uiState.value is Loading) return. (4) Check for debounce — rapid taps can trigger multiple launches; add viewModelScope.launch with debounce or a flag. Fix: use a loading/in-progress state flag in the ViewModel to prevent concurrent requests.

33B — Data & Concurrency Scenarios

Five production concurrency and data scenarios: parallel APIs, sequential chaining, token refresh race condition, stale cache handling, and large list performance.

ID: 33B ⭐ Senior Differentiator
🔍
1. Overview

These scenarios test whether you understand coroutine structured concurrency, race conditions, and data layer patterns. They are the most common "whiteboard coding" scenarios at senior Android interviews.

ScenarioKey ConceptSenior Signal
Parallel APIsasync/await, awaitAllFailure handling — what if one fails?
Sequential APIswithContext(IO), sequential awaitError propagation chain
Token refresh raceMutex, OkHttp AuthenticatorPrevents duplicate refreshes
Stale cache + failUiState sealed class, error bannerNever show blank screen
10,000 itemsDiffUtil, Paging 3, LazyColumnNever notifyDataSetChanged()
⚡
2. Two APIs Run Simultaneously
1
Fetch user profile AND order history simultaneously, show both when both complete
Naive (Wrong) Approach
// ❌ Sequential — second call waits for first. 600ms total instead of 300ms
val user = api.getUser(userId)     // 300ms
val orders = api.getOrders(userId) // 300ms — waits for user to complete
Correct: async/await
// ✅ Parallel — both start immediately, total ~300ms (whichever is slower)
suspend fun loadProfilePage(userId: String): ProfilePage = coroutineScope {
    val userDeferred  = async(Dispatchers.IO) { api.getUser(userId) }
    val ordersDeferred = async(Dispatchers.IO) { api.getOrders(userId) }
    
    // Both start immediately; await blocks until each completes
    val user   = userDeferred.await()
    val orders = ordersDeferred.await()
    ProfilePage(user, orders)
}

// Or with awaitAll for a list of deferred values
val results = listOf(d1, d2, d3).awaitAll()  // waits for all, fails fast if any fails
Failure Handling (Senior differentiator)
// What if orders fails but user succeeds? Show partial data
suspend fun loadProfilePagePartial(userId: String): ProfilePage = coroutineScope {
    val userDeferred   = async(Dispatchers.IO) {
        runCatching { api.getUser(userId) }
    }
    val ordersDeferred = async(Dispatchers.IO) {
        runCatching { api.getOrders(userId) }
    }
    ProfilePage(
        user   = userDeferred.await().getOrNull(),
        orders = ordersDeferred.await().getOrNull() ?: emptyList()
    )
}
🔁
3. API B Depends on API A Result
2
Fetch product details, then use productId to fetch recommendations
// ✅ Sequential — await result of A before calling B
suspend fun loadProductWithRecs(productId: String): ProductPageData =
    withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {
        val product = api.getProduct(productId)          // Step 1: fetch product
        val recs    = api.getRecommendations(product.category) // Step 2: uses category from step 1
        ProductPageData(product, recs)
    }

// Error propagation: if getProduct() throws, getRecommendations is never called
// Exception propagates up to the caller — handle at ViewModel level

// In ViewModel:
fun loadProduct(productId: String) {
    viewModelScope.launch {
        uiState.value = UiState.Loading
        uiState.value = runCatching {
            repository.loadProductWithRecs(productId)
        }.fold(
            onSuccess = { UiState.Success(it) },
            onFailure = { UiState.Error("Failed to load product: ${it.message}") }
        )
    }
}
Partial failure variant
// Recommendations are optional — show product even if recs fail
suspend fun loadProductWithOptionalRecs(productId: String): ProductPageData =
    withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {
        val product = api.getProduct(productId)   // must succeed
        val recs = runCatching {
            api.getRecommendations(product.category)
        }.getOrDefault(emptyList())              // optional — empty on failure
        ProductPageData(product, recs)
    }
🔒
4. Token Refresh Race Condition
3
5 coroutines make API calls simultaneously. Token expires. All 5 get 401. How do you prevent 5 concurrent token refreshes?
Problem

Without coordination, all 5 coroutines call refreshToken() simultaneously. This causes: multiple refresh requests to the server, race conditions on token storage, previous tokens invalidated mid-request.

Solution: Mutex
// In your TokenManager / AuthRepository
class TokenManager @Inject constructor(private val api: AuthApi) {

    private val mutex = Mutex()   // Only ONE coroutine refreshes at a time
    private var cachedToken: String? = null

    suspend fun getValidToken(): String {
        cachedToken?.let { if (!isExpired(it)) return it }

        // Lock: only one coroutine enters; others wait
        mutex.withLock {
            // Double-check: another coroutine may have refreshed while we waited
            cachedToken?.let { if (!isExpired(it)) return it }

            // Actually refresh
            val newToken = api.refreshToken()
            cachedToken = newToken.accessToken
            return newToken.accessToken
        }
    }
}
OkHttp Authenticator Pattern
class TokenAuthenticator @Inject constructor(
    private val tokenManager: TokenManager
) : Authenticator {

    override fun authenticate(route: Route?, response: Response): Request? {
        // Called by OkHttp when it receives a 401
        if (response.responseCount() >= 2) return null  // stop after 1 retry
        
        val newToken = runBlocking {          // OkHttp is sync; runBlocking here is ok
            tokenManager.getValidToken()    // Mutex ensures only 1 refresh
        }
        
        return response.request.newBuilder()
            .header("Authorization", "Bearer $newToken")
            .build()
    }

    private fun Response.responseCount(): Int {
        var result = 1
        var prior = priorResponse
        while (prior != null) { result++; prior = prior.priorResponse }
        return result
    }
}
📁
5. Room Has Stale Data but API Fails
4
User has cached data in Room. Network request fails. What should the UI show?
Wrong Behaviour

Show a blank error screen, discarding the cached data. This is the worst UX — user sees nothing instead of slightly-stale data.

Correct UiState Design
// UiState models all combinations
sealed class FeedUiState {
    object Loading : FeedUiState()
    data class Success(val items: List<FeedItem>, val isStale: Boolean = false) : FeedUiState()
    data class Error(val message: String, val cachedItems: List<FeedItem>? = null) : FeedUiState()
}

// Repository: emit cache first, then try network
fun getFeed(): Flow<FeedUiState> = flow {
    // 1. Emit cached data immediately (fast)
    val cached = db.feedDao().getAllItems()
    if (cached.isNotEmpty()) {
        emit(FeedUiState.Success(cached, isStale = true))
    } else {
        emit(FeedUiState.Loading)
    }
    
    // 2. Try to refresh from network
    runCatching { api.getFeed() }
        .onSuccess { fresh ->
            db.withTransaction { db.feedDao().replaceAll(fresh) }
            emit(FeedUiState.Success(fresh, isStale = false))
        }
        .onFailure { error ->
            // Network failed — show stale data with error indicator
            emit(FeedUiState.Error(
                message = error.message ?: "Failed to refresh",
                cachedItems = cached.ifEmpty { null }
            ))
        }
}.flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)
UI Rendering
when (val state = uiState) {
    is FeedUiState.Loading  -> ShowShimmer()
    is FeedUiState.Success  -> {
        FeedList(state.items)
        if (state.isStale) StaleDataBanner()   // subtle "Last updated 5 min ago"
    }
    is FeedUiState.Error -> {
        state.cachedItems?.let { FeedList(it) }   // show stale data if available
        ErrorBanner(state.message)                 // "Couldn't refresh — pull to retry"
    }
}
📊
6. RecyclerView with 10,000 Items
5
A list of 10,000 items needs to update efficiently. Scrolling is janky.
Anti-patterns to avoid
  • notifyDataSetChanged() — rebinds ALL items, O(n) work even if 1 item changed
  • Holding all 10,000 items in memory at once without pagination
  • Complex item view that measures multiple times (nested weights, wrap_content chains)
Efficient Solutions
// 1. DiffUtil + ListAdapter (for manageable lists)
class FeedAdapter : ListAdapter<FeedItem, FeedViewHolder>(
    object : DiffUtil.ItemCallback<FeedItem>() {
        override fun areItemsTheSame(old: FeedItem, new: FeedItem) = old.id == new.id
        override fun areContentsTheSame(old: FeedItem, new: FeedItem) = old == new
    }
) { ... }

// 2. Paging 3 — don't load all 10,000 at once
// Load 20 at a time, Room + RemoteMediator pattern (see 30F)

// 3. LazyColumn with stable keys (Compose)
LazyColumn {
    items(items, key = { it.id }) { item ->   // stable key = no recompose on unrelated changes
        FeedItemRow(item)
    }
}

// 4. Fixed item size — avoid remeasuring every scroll
// RecyclerView: setHasFixedSize(true) if item heights are uniform
// Compose: use height(Dp) instead of wrapContentHeight() where possible
DiffUtil Algorithm

DiffUtil uses Eugene Myers' diff algorithm (O(N+D²) where D = number of changes). For large lists (>1000 items), compute the diff on a background thread and submit to the adapter on main thread — ListAdapter does this automatically.

🏆
7. Interview Framework
Concurrency Question Framework
When asked "how do you make two API calls", always address: 1) The happy path (async/await) → 2) What if one fails? (runCatching, partial result) → 3) Cancellation (coroutineScope auto-cancels siblings on failure). This shows senior-level thinking.

Token Refresh: The Key Insight

The critical insight is the double-check pattern inside the Mutex: when 5 coroutines are waiting for the lock and coroutine #1 refreshes the token, the other 4 should NOT refresh again. After acquiring the lock, check if the token is now valid — if so, return immediately without refreshing.

Stale Cache: The Golden Rule

"Never show a blank screen when you have cached data." Always prefer showing stale data with an error indicator over an empty screen. The user's goal is to see data — stale data with a "refresh failed" banner is far better than nothing.

9. Practice Questions
Write Kotlin code to fetch user profile and orders in parallel. Handle the case where orders fail but user succeeds.
Hard▼
coroutineScope { val userD = async(IO) { runCatching { api.getUser(id) } }; val ordersD = async(IO) { runCatching { api.getOrders(id) } }; ProfilePage(user = userD.await().getOrThrow(), orders = ordersD.await().getOrDefault(emptyList())) }. Key: wrap each async in runCatching for independent failure handling. userD.await().getOrThrow() propagates user failure; ordersD.await().getOrDefault(emptyList()) shows empty orders on failure.
Why is the double-check pattern inside a Mutex critical for token refresh?
Hard▼
When 5 coroutines all find the token expired and race to acquire the Mutex, only one enters the lock first and refreshes the token. When the remaining 4 acquire the lock sequentially, the token is now valid. Without the double-check, all 4 would refresh again unnecessarily (and potentially invalidate the token refreshed by #1). The double-check: if (!isExpired(cachedToken)) return cachedToken — exit early after acquiring lock if already fresh.
What is the difference between async + awaitAll vs coroutineScope + launch + join?
Medium▼
async{} returns a Deferred which carries the result — you call await() to get the value. awaitAll(d1, d2) waits for all and returns a List of results. launch{} + join() only synchronizes completion — launch doesn't return a value. Use async/await when you need results. Use launch/join when you just need completion (fire and forget side effects). awaitAll() also fails fast — if any async throws, awaitAll throws immediately.
Design a UiState sealed class that handles loading, success, stale success, and error with partial data.
Medium▼
sealed class UiState<T> { object Loading : UiState<Nothing>(); data class Success(val data: T, val isStale: Boolean = false) : UiState<T>(); data class Error(val message: String, val partialData: T? = null) : UiState<T>() }. The Error state carries partialData so the UI can show stale content + error banner simultaneously. isStale on Success allows a subtle "last updated" indicator without hiding data.
Why should you never call notifyDataSetChanged() for large list updates?
Easy▼
notifyDataSetChanged() tells RecyclerView that every item has potentially changed. RecyclerView then rebinds all visible items — O(visible items) work even if only 1 item changed. It also destroys all recycled views, losing scroll state. DiffUtil computes the minimal diff (which items changed, added, removed) and only rebinds changed items. For a 10,000-item list where 1 item changed, DiffUtil rebinds 1 item; notifyDataSetChanged() rebinds ~15 visible items and invalidates the full internal state.
When would you use coroutineScope{} vs supervisorScope{} for parallel calls?
Hard▼
coroutineScope{}: if any child fails, ALL siblings are cancelled immediately. Use when all results are required — a failure in one means the whole operation fails. supervisorScope{}: children fail independently — one failure doesn't cancel others. Use when children are independent and partial results are acceptable (e.g., loading 5 widgets on a dashboard where each is independent). For the profile page example: if user fetch is required but orders are optional, use supervisorScope + runCatching on the optional async.
How does DiffUtil's areItemsTheSame differ from areContentsTheSame?
Easy▼
areItemsTheSame: checks if two items represent the same entity (same ID). This determines the structural diff — moves, insertions, deletions. Returns true if it's the "same item" even if the content changed. areContentsTheSame: only called when areItemsTheSame returns true. Checks if the item's visual content has changed — determines whether to call onBindViewHolder. Return old == new (data class equality). Example: areItemsTheSame(old, new) = old.id == new.id; areContentsTheSame(old, new) = old == new.
What happens if you call await() on a Deferred that threw an exception?
Medium▼
Calling await() on a failed Deferred re-throws the exception at the await() call site. This is the mechanism for propagating errors from async back to the parent. If you call awaitAll() on a list that contains a failed Deferred, it throws the first exception it encounters. Wrap in runCatching { deferred.await() } to handle per-request errors without cancelling the parent scope.
How would you implement a "refresh" button in a stale-data scenario?
Medium▼
Add a refresh() function in the ViewModel that: (1) Sets state to Loading (or Success(stale=true) to keep showing data), (2) Calls the repository network refresh explicitly, (3) Updates state on success/failure. Use a MutableStateFlow for the refresh trigger or just call a suspend function. Don't re-collect the repository Flow — call a dedicated refresh method that bypasses cache and goes straight to network, then updates Room, which triggers the existing Flow from Room.
How do you prevent a user from rapidly tapping a button to trigger multiple concurrent API calls?
Medium▼
In the ViewModel, check for an in-progress state before launching: if (_uiState.value is Loading) return. This prevents concurrent launches. Alternatively, use a loading flag: private var isLoading = false; fun onSubmit() { if (isLoading) return; isLoading = true; viewModelScope.launch { try { ... } finally { isLoading = false } } }. In Compose, disable the button when loading: Button(enabled = uiState !is Loading, onClick = {...}).

33C — Platform & Scale Scenarios

Two senior scenarios: diagnosing API-level breakage (Android 12 → 15/16 regressions) and architecting for millions of users. Complete system design answer included.

ID: 33C ⭐ Senior Differentiator
🔍
1. Overview

Platform compatibility and scale architecture are the two areas that most clearly separate senior engineers from mid-level. These questions require breadth across the Android platform and depth on architectural trade-offs.

ScenarioKey TopicsSenior Signal
Android version regressionIntent mutability, exact alarms, FGS types, exported components, photo pickerSystematic debugging process, not random guessing
Architect for millionsModularization, offline-first, feature flags, CI/CD, monitoringTeam structure + production reliability, not just technical patterns
⚠
2. App Works on Android 12 but Fails on Android 15/16
1
App works perfectly on Android 12 but crashes or misbehaves on Android 15+
Common Root Causes by Area
AreaAndroid 12+ ChangeFix
PendingIntentMust specify FLAG_IMMUTABLE or FLAG_MUTABLE explicitlyAdd PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE to all PendingIntent calls
Exact AlarmsAndroid 12+ requires SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM permission; Android 13+ user must grant itCheck canScheduleExactAlarms() before calling setExact(); use inexact alarms or WorkManager instead
Exported ComponentsActivities/Services/Receivers with intent-filters must declare android:exported explicitlyAdd android:exported="true/false" to each component with intent-filter
Foreground Service TypesAndroid 14+ requires android:foregroundServiceType in manifestDeclare type: location, camera, mediaPlayback, health, etc.
Notification permissionAndroid 13+ requires POST_NOTIFICATIONS runtime permissionRequest POST_NOTIFICATIONS permission before showing notifications
Photo PickerAndroid 13+ introduces Photo Picker API; old ACTION_PICK may behave differentlyUse ActivityResultContracts.PickVisualMedia for Android 13+
Background start restrictionsAndroid 12+ stricter limits on starting activities from backgroundShow notification instead; only start Activity from user-visible context
Predictive backAndroid 13+ adds predictive back gesture; custom back handling may breakMigrate to OnBackPressedCallback or predictive back APIs
// ✅ PendingIntent — always specify mutability
val pendingIntent = PendingIntent.getActivity(
    context, requestCode, intent,
    PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT or PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE
)

// ✅ Exact alarms — check permission first (Android 12+)
if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= Build.VERSION_CODES.S) {
    val alarmManager = getSystemService(AlarmManager::class.java)
    if (alarmManager.canScheduleExactAlarms()) {
        alarmManager.setExact(...)
    } else {
        // Redirect to exact alarm settings or use setWindow()
    }
}

// ✅ Notification permission (Android 13+)
if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 33) {
    requestPermissions(arrayOf(Manifest.permission.POST_NOTIFICATIONS), RC_NOTIF)
}
📊
3. Systematic Debug Approach for Version Regressions

Step-by-Step Process

  1. Reproduce on a specific API level — use emulator with Android 15/16 API. Note the exact error in Logcat.
  2. Check the Android behavior changes page — developer.android.com/about/versions/15/behavior-changes. New versions document all breaking changes.
  3. Binary search API levels — does it fail on Android 14? 13? Narrow down which version introduced the break.
  4. Check Logcat for security exceptions or permission denials — these have specific messages pointing to the issue.
  5. Search Crashlytics by OS version filter — compare crash rates by Android version to confirm which versions are affected.
  6. Check targetSdkVersion — some changes only apply when targetSdk is ≥ a certain level.
// Common log messages that identify the cause
// "SecurityException: Permission Denial" → missing permission or exported flag
// "IllegalArgumentException: Receiver not registered" → lifecycle mismatch
// "ActivityNotFoundException" → intent-filter or exported=false issue
// "Foreground service did not call startForeground" → FGS type change

// Runtime permission check pattern
fun hasNotificationPermission(): Boolean =
    if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 33) {
        checkSelfPermission(Manifest.permission.POST_NOTIFICATIONS) ==
            PackageManager.PERMISSION_GRANTED
    } else true  // pre-Android 13: always granted
Senior Signal
Mention that you'd set up CI testing on multiple API levels (16, 23, 26, 28, 33, latest) using Firebase Test Lab or emulator matrix. This prevents version regressions from reaching production.
🏛
4. Architect an Android App for Millions of Users
2
Design an Android client architecture for a consumer app with millions of daily active users
Architecture Overview
:app (shell — navigation + DI)
  └─ :feature:home, :feature:checkout, :feature:profile (10+ feature modules)
  └─ :core:data, :core:domain, :core:ui, :core:network, :core:featureflags
Offline-first
  • Room as single source of truth for all persistent data
  • Network is a cache-refresh mechanism, not the primary data source
  • WorkManager for background sync (survives app death)
  • Optimistic updates for user actions (like, add to cart) — sync later
Feature Flags + A/B Testing
  • Firebase Remote Config for all feature flags — kill switch for any feature
  • A/B experiments through Remote Config parameters with user targeting
  • All flags have local defaults (work offline, on first launch before fetch)
  • Staged rollout: internal → 10% → 50% → 100%
Performance at Scale
  • Cold start target <2s: Baseline Profiles + App Startup library
  • Crash-free sessions >99.5%: Crashlytics alerts at 99%
  • ANR rate <0.1%: strict no-main-thread-I/O enforcement
  • Memory <200MB p95: Coil with size limits, no bitmap leaks
CI/CD Pipeline
  • Every PR: unit tests + lint + Detekt + Compose metrics check
  • Every merge to main: instrumented tests on Firebase Test Lab (API matrix)
  • Nightly: full regression suite + startup benchmark
  • Release: automatic Play Console upload to internal track
📈
5. Monitoring & Reliability

Observability Stack

SignalToolAlert Threshold
Crash-free sessionsCrashlytics<99% → PagerDuty alert
ANR ratePlay Console + Crashlytics ANR detection>0.1% → alert
App startup timeFirebase Performance _app_start tracep95 >3s → alert
HTTP error rateFirebase Performance HTTP metrics>1% 5xx → alert
Custom tracesFirebase Performance custom tracesPer feature: checkout_complete p95 >5s
MemoryFirebase Performance memory metricp95 >200MB → investigate

Progressive Delivery

  • Staged rollout to 10% users → monitor 48 hours → expand
  • Feature flags as kill switch — no emergency release needed for most issues
  • Version targeting — can force users on old versions to update if critical security fix
  • Play In-App Updates API — prompt users to update from within the app
⚖
6. Trade-offs & Team Structure

Key Trade-offs

DecisionTrade-off
ModularizationFaster incremental builds & team isolation vs initial setup complexity and Gradle config overhead
Offline-first (Room)Better UX & resilience vs more complex sync logic and potential data staleness
Feature flags everywhereEasy rollback & experiments vs configuration complexity, stale flag cleanup debt
Optimistic updatesInstant UI feedback vs rollback complexity on sync failure
DFMs for optional featuresSmaller initial install vs install friction when feature is first accessed

Team Ownership Model

  • Each feature team owns its :feature:X module end-to-end (UI → ViewModel → UseCase)
  • :core:Y modules owned by a platform team (no feature team modifies core without review)
  • Breaking changes to core require RFC (Request for Comment) with affected teams
  • Each team maintains their module's test coverage (>80% unit, >critical UI paths instrumented)
🏆
7. Interview Framework
Version Regression Framework (2 min answer)
1) Reproduce on target API level emulator → 2) Check Logcat for SecurityException/permission denial → 3) Check Android behavior changes page for that version → 4) Common suspects: PendingIntent mutability, exact alarms, exported components, notification permission → 5) Fix + add CI test on that API level to prevent regression
Millions of Users Framework (10 min answer)
1) Modularization (feature isolation, fast builds) → 2) Offline-first (Room single source of truth) → 3) Feature flags (kill switch, A/B testing) → 4) Performance SLAs (<2s startup, >99.5% crash-free) → 5) CI/CD (parallel tests, automated release) → 6) Monitoring + progressive delivery → 7) Team ownership model

Common Mistakes

  • For version regressions: guessing random causes without a systematic approach
  • For scale architecture: focusing only on code patterns, ignoring team structure and delivery processes
  • Not mentioning monitoring and alerting — production reliability is as important as architecture

9. Practice Questions
Your app shows a SecurityException crash on Android 14 but not Android 12. How do you diagnose it?
Hard▼
Step 1: Read the SecurityException message in Logcat — it usually names the missing permission or the component that rejected the call. Step 2: Check Android 14 behavior changes page for breaking security changes. Step 3: Common Android 14 causes: missing foregroundServiceType in manifest (AFGT requirement), background activity launch restrictions, intent redirect restrictions. Step 4: Fix and add an API 34 emulator test to CI to prevent regression.
Why must all PendingIntent calls on Android 12+ specify FLAG_IMMUTABLE or FLAG_MUTABLE?
Medium▼
Android 12 tightened PendingIntent security to prevent PendingIntent hijacking attacks. An app could potentially intercept a PendingIntent with extras and modify it before it was used. FLAG_IMMUTABLE prevents the receiving app from modifying the intent's extras (safer for most cases). FLAG_MUTABLE must be used explicitly when you intentionally want the system or another app to modify the intent (e.g., notification direct reply). Not specifying either throws an IllegalArgumentException.
How do you handle the case where a user denies the POST_NOTIFICATIONS permission?
Medium▼
On first denial: explain value of notifications with a rationale dialog (shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale() returns true), then request again. On second denial (shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale() returns false after denial): don't request again — direct to Settings: Intent(Settings.ACTION_APP_NOTIFICATION_SETTINGS). Design the app to work without notifications — they're an enhancement, not required functionality. Track notification permission state in DataStore and conditionally show notification opt-in prompts in-app.
How would you architect offline-first data for a banking app with real-time balance updates?
Hard▼
Room as single source of truth. Balance data: cache in Room with a timestamp; show stale data with "last updated X minutes ago" banner. Real-time updates: WebSocket connection when app is foreground; on balance change event, update Room → Flow auto-emits to UI. Background sync: WorkManager polls balance every 15 min (minimum WorkManager interval). On network restore: ConstrainedWork triggers immediate refresh. Sensitive operations (transfers): require network, don't allow offline. Show clear offline indicator in app bar.
What is the foregroundServiceType requirement in Android 14?
Medium▼
Android 14 requires foreground services to declare a specific type in the manifest: android:foregroundServiceType="location|camera|microphone|mediaPlayback|dataSync|phoneCall|mediaProjection|health|remoteMessaging|shortService|specialUse|systemExempted". If you start a foreground service without the correct type declared (or start a type that requires a permission you don't have), it throws a MissingForegroundServiceTypeException. This forces apps to be explicit about what the foreground service is doing.
How do feature flags improve production reliability beyond just enabling/disabling features?
Hard▼
Kill switch: instantly disable a broken feature without releasing a new app version (update propagates within minutes). Gradual rollout: enable for 1% of users first, monitor metrics, expand — same as staged rollout but within a single app version. Canary testing: enable for internal users or beta testers only. Configuration flags: change API timeouts, retry counts, page sizes without a release. Seasonal toggles: enable holiday features on a schedule. Emergency response: during an incident, flip a flag to use a backup API endpoint.
How do you test your app across multiple Android API levels in CI?
Medium▼
Firebase Test Lab: upload your APK/AAB and run instrumented tests on a matrix of real devices (API 21, 26, 28, 31, 33, 34+). Emulator matrix in CI: use GitHub Actions with multiple emulator runners (each API level in parallel). Minimum coverage: test on minimum supported API (e.g., API 26), the most popular version in your user base, and the latest stable API. Add specific regression tests when you fix a version-specific bug. This catches version regressions before production.
What is predictive back gesture and what does it require from app code?
Medium▼
Predictive back gesture (Android 13+) shows a preview of the previous screen as the user swipes back, before completing the gesture. To opt in: set android:enableOnBackInvokedCallback="true" in the manifest. Migrate custom back handling from onBackPressed() (deprecated) to OnBackPressedCallback registered with the Activity's onBackPressedDispatcher. Navigation Component handles this automatically for fragment back stack. Custom back animations must use the new Android 14 predictive back APIs (BackEventCompat).
How would you monitor and alert on ANR (Application Not Responding) events?
Medium▼
Firebase Crashlytics automatically captures ANR reports (since Crashlytics SDK 17.3+). These appear separately from crashes in the Crashlytics dashboard with a main thread stack trace. Play Console also provides ANR rate metrics. Set up alerts: in Crashlytics, configure alert thresholds; below 0.1% ANR rate is the Play Store target for "good" apps. For prevention: strict mode in debug builds (StrictMode.setThreadPolicy with penaltyDeath) catches blocking main thread operations during development.
What is the Play In-App Update API and when would you force an update?
Easy▼
Play In-App Update API has two modes: Flexible update — shows an unobtrusive download prompt, user can continue using the app, update installs in background, prompts for restart. Immediate update — full-screen blocking UI, user must update to continue. Use Immediate for: critical security patches, API contract changes where old app will break with new backend, compliance requirements. Use Flexible for: feature updates, non-critical improvements. Check for updates at app startup using AppUpdateManager.getAppUpdateInfo().

34A — Strings Coding (Kotlin)

Six string coding problems with brute-force and optimal Kotlin solutions, time/space complexity, edge cases, and interview approach.

ID: 34A Coding
🔍
1. Overview

String Problems in Android Interviews

String problems test your grasp of Kotlin's standard library, HashMap frequency counting, two-pointer technique, and the difference between StringBuilder and String concatenation. These appear in phone screens and early coding rounds.

ProblemKey TechniqueOptimal Complexity
Reverse stringStringBuilder / reversed()O(n) time, O(n) space
PalindromeTwo-pointerO(n) time, O(1) space
AnagramFrequency HashMapO(n) time, O(1) space (26 letters)
Duplicate charsFrequency map + filterO(n) time, O(k) space
First non-repeatingLinkedHashMap (preserves order)O(n) time, O(k) space
Coding Interview Mental Model
Always say: (1) "Here's the brute force approach — O(n²)" (2) "Let me optimize using a HashMap to get O(n)" (3) Write clean Kotlin. Mention edge cases: empty string, single char, all same chars, null.
🔁
2. Reverse a String
1
"hello" → "olleh"
O(n) time · O(n) space
Approach 1: Kotlin stdlib (preferred in production)
fun reverseString(s: String): String = s.reversed()

// reversed() internally uses StringBuilder — O(n) time, O(n) space
println(reverseString("hello"))   // "olleh"
println(reverseString(""))        // ""    (edge case: empty string)
println(reverseString("a"))       // "a"   (edge case: single char)
Approach 2: Manual with StringBuilder (show you understand it)
fun reverseStringManual(s: String): String {
    val sb = StringBuilder()
    for (i in s.indices.reversed()) {
        sb.append(s[i])
    }
    return sb.toString()
}

// Why StringBuilder not String?
// String is immutable — "str" + char creates a new String each time → O(n²)
// StringBuilder is mutable — append is amortized O(1) → O(n) total
Approach 3: Two-pointer in-place (show algorithmic thinking)
fun reverseCharArray(chars: CharArray) {
    var left = 0; var right = chars.size - 1
    while (left < right) {
        val temp = chars[left]
        chars[left] = chars[right]
        chars[right] = temp
        left++; right--
    }
}
// O(n) time, O(1) space — modifies array in place
🔁
3. Palindrome Check
2
"racecar" → true, "hello" → false
O(n) time · O(1) space
Brute Force O(n) time, O(n) space
fun isPalindromeNaive(s: String): Boolean = s == s.reversed()
// Creates a new reversed string — O(n) extra space
Optimal: Two-pointer O(n) time, O(1) space
fun isPalindrome(s: String): Boolean {
    var left = 0; var right = s.length - 1
    while (left < right) {
        if (s[left] != s[right]) return false
        left++; right--
    }
    return true
}

println(isPalindrome("racecar"))  // true
println(isPalindrome("hello"))    // false
println(isPalindrome(""))         // true  (empty string is palindrome)
println(isPalindrome("a"))        // true  (single char)
Variation: Ignore case and non-alphanumeric
// "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama" → true
fun isPalindromeClean(s: String): Boolean {
    val cleaned = s.filter { it.isLetterOrDigit() }.lowercase()
    return isPalindrome(cleaned)
}
🔁
4. Anagram Check
3
"listen", "silent" → true
O(n) time · O(1) space (26 letters)
Brute Force O(n log n)
fun isAnagramNaive(s: String, t: String): Boolean =
    s.toSortedSet() == t.toSortedSet()
// Sorting: O(n log n) — works but not optimal
Optimal: HashMap frequency count O(n)
fun isAnagram(s: String, t: String): Boolean {
    if (s.length != t.length) return false  // fast early exit

    val freq = HashMap<Char, Int>()

    // Count chars in s (increment) and t (decrement)
    for (ch in s) freq[ch] = (freq[ch] ?: 0) + 1
    for (ch in t) freq[ch] = (freq[ch] ?: 0) - 1

    // All counts must be 0 for anagram
    return freq.values.all { it == 0 }
}

println(isAnagram("listen", "silent"))  // true
println(isAnagram("hello", "world"))    // false
println(isAnagram("ab", "a"))          // false (length differs)

// Kotlin idiomatic — sort chars and compare
fun isAnagramKotlin(s: String, t: String): Boolean =
    s.toCharArray().sorted() == t.toCharArray().sorted()
🔁
5. Find Duplicate Characters
4
"programming" → [g, r, m] (appear more than once)
O(n) time · O(k) space
fun findDuplicates(s: String): List<Char> {
    // Step 1: Count frequency of each char
    val freq = HashMap<Char, Int>()
    for (ch in s) freq[ch] = (freq[ch] ?: 0) + 1

    // Step 2: Filter chars that appear more than once
    return freq.filter { it.value > 1 }.keys.toList()
}

// Kotlin idiomatic one-liner:
fun findDuplicatesKt(s: String): List<Char> =
    s.groupingBy { it }.eachCount()
     .filter { it.value > 1 }
     .keys.toList()

println(findDuplicates("programming"))  // [r, g, m] (order may vary)
println(findDuplicates("abcde"))       // [] (no duplicates)
println(findDuplicates(""))           // []

// Character frequency map (useful helper function)
fun String.charFrequency(): Map<Char, Int> =
    groupingBy { it }.eachCount()
🔁
6. First Non-repeating Character
5
"leetcode" → 'l' (first char that appears exactly once)
O(n) time · O(k) space
Key insight: LinkedHashMap preserves insertion order
fun firstNonRepeating(s: String): Char? {
    // LinkedHashMap maintains insertion order — crucial for "first"
    val freq = LinkedHashMap<Char, Int>()
    for (ch in s) freq[ch] = (freq[ch] ?: 0) + 1

    // First entry with count == 1 (LinkedHashMap preserves insertion order)
    return freq.entries.firstOrNull { it.value == 1 }?.key
}

println(firstNonRepeating("leetcode"))  // 'l'
println(firstNonRepeating("aabb"))      // null (all repeat)
println(firstNonRepeating("a"))         // 'a'

// Alternative: two-pass approach (HashMap then scan original string)
fun firstNonRepeatingAlt(s: String): Char? {
    val freq = s.groupingBy { it }.eachCount()
    return s.firstOrNull { freq[it] == 1 }  // scan original order
}
// O(n) time, O(k) space where k = unique chars (max 26 for lowercase)
Why LinkedHashMap?
HashMap doesn't guarantee order. If you iterated HashMap.entries to find the first unique char, you'd get a random char, not the "first" one. LinkedHashMap maintains insertion order (the order chars first appeared in the string), so iterating entries gives you chars in their original appearance order.
🏆
7. Interview Framework
Coding Interview Structure (5 Steps)
1) Understand: Repeat the problem, ask about edge cases (empty? null? case-sensitive?) → 2) Brute force: State O(n²) approach in words, don't code yet → 3) Optimize: "I can use a HashMap to reduce to O(n)" → 4) Code: Write clean Kotlin → 5) Test: Trace through your examples + edge cases

Common String Interview Patterns

PatternUse whenData structure
Frequency countAnagram, duplicates, first uniqueHashMap<Char, Int>
Two pointerPalindrome, reverse, pair sumTwo index variables
Sliding windowSubstring problems (longest unique substring)HashMap + window indices
StringBuilderBuilding result string efficientlyStringBuilder (not String)

Edge Cases to Always Mention

  • Empty string "" — usually the simplest valid case
  • Single character "a" — palindrome is true, no duplicates, etc.
  • All same characters "aaa" — all duplicates, no unique char
  • Case sensitivity — "A" == "a"? ask the interviewer
  • Unicode / multibyte characters — usually out of scope unless asked
⚡
8. Quick Revision Sheet
ProblemKotlin one-linerTimeSpace
Reverses.reversed()O(n)O(n)
Reverse in-placeTwo-pointer swap on CharArrayO(n)O(1)
PalindromeTwo-pointer: s[left] != s[right] → falseO(n)O(1)
AnagramHashMap freq count: increment s, decrement t, all 0 = anagramO(n)O(1)
DuplicatesgroupingBy { it }.eachCount().filter { it.value > 1 }O(n)O(k)
First uniqueLinkedHashMap freq → entries.firstOrNull { count == 1 }O(n)O(k)

Key insight: HashMap frequency counting is the universal string optimization. O(n²) brute force becomes O(n) with a HashMap.

❓
9. Practice Questions
Why use StringBuilder instead of String concatenation when building a reversed string?
Easy▼
String is immutable — each concatenation ("str" + char) creates a new String object. Building a reversed string with + in a loop is O(n²) time and generates n temporary String objects. StringBuilder is mutable — append() adds to an internal buffer in amortized O(1) time. Total: O(n) time, O(n) space for the result. The Kotlin + operator on Strings compiles to StringBuilder internally for small operations, but explicit StringBuilder is clearer and guaranteed efficient.
Write a function to find the longest palindromic substring in a string.
Hard▼
Expand around center approach: for each character (and each gap between characters), expand outward while characters match. Track the longest found. O(n²) time, O(1) space. fun longestPalindrome(s: String): String { var start = 0; var end = 0; for (i in s.indices) { val len = maxOf(expand(s, i, i), expand(s, i, i+1)); if (len > end - start) { start = i - (len-1)/2; end = i + len/2 } }; return s.substring(start, end+1) }. Helper: fun expand(s, l, r): Int { var left=l; var right=r; while(left>=0 && right
How do you count the frequency of each character in a string in Kotlin idiomatically?
Easy▼
val freq: Map<Char, Int> = s.groupingBy { it }.eachCount(). This uses groupingBy to group characters by themselves (identity function), then eachCount() counts occurrences. Result: {"l":1, "e":3, "t":1, "c":1, "o":1, "d":1} for "leetcode". Manual alternative: s.forEach { freq[it] = (freq[it] ?: 0) + 1 } using getOrDefault(it, 0) + 1.
What is the difference between HashMap and LinkedHashMap for first-unique-character?
Medium▼
HashMap doesn't guarantee iteration order — iterating entries might return characters in any order. LinkedHashMap preserves insertion order — when you iterate entries, characters appear in the order they first appeared in the string. For first-non-repeating, if you iterate a HashMap and find a char with count 1, it might not be the FIRST such char in the original string. LinkedHashMap guarantees the first entry with count 1 is indeed the first non-repeating character.
How would you check if two strings are anagrams in O(n) time and O(1) space?
Medium▼
Use a fixed-size array of 26 for lowercase letters instead of a HashMap. val count = IntArray(26). For each char in s: count[ch - 'a']++. For each char in t: count[ch - 'a']--. Return count.all { it == 0 }. The array has size 26 (constant) regardless of input size → O(1) space. HashMap would also be O(k) where k ≤ 26 for lowercase letters, technically O(1), but the array version is more memory-efficient.
Write a function to reverse only the words in a sentence (words in reverse order).
Medium▼
fun reverseWords(s: String): String = s.trim().split("\\s+".toRegex()).reversed().joinToString(" "). Steps: trim() removes leading/trailing spaces, split on whitespace regex handles multiple spaces, reversed() reverses the list of words, joinToString(" ") joins with single space. " hello world " → "world hello". Alternative: s.split(" ").filter { it.isNotEmpty() }.reversed().joinToString(" ").
What is the time complexity of the two-pointer palindrome check vs reversed() comparison?
Easy▼
Both are O(n) time. The difference is space: reversed() creates a new String of length n → O(n) extra space. Two-pointer uses only two index variables → O(1) extra space. For an interview, mention both, show the two-pointer solution as the space-optimized answer. In production Kotlin, s == s.reversed() is perfectly fine and more readable.
How would you find if a string contains all unique characters without using extra data structures?
Hard▼
For lowercase ASCII only: use a bitmask (Long). For each char: val bit = 1L shl (ch - 'a'). If (mask and bit) != 0L, char seen before → not unique. Else: mask = mask or bit. O(n) time, O(1) space. No HashMap needed. For full Unicode: you can't avoid O(k) space; use HashSet. Brute force without extra space: compare every pair O(n²), or sort first O(n log n) then check adjacent chars O(n).
Write a Kotlin extension function that counts vowels in a string.
Easy▼
fun String.vowelCount(): Int = count { it.lowercaseChar() in "aeiou" }. Or: fun String.vowelCount() = filter { "aeiouAEIOU".contains(it) }.length. Using a Set for O(1) lookup: val vowels = setOf('a','e','i','o','u'); fun String.vowelCount() = count { it.lowercaseChar() in vowels }. Using contains on a String is O(k) where k=10 vowels, which is effectively O(1).
How do you find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters?
Hard▼
Sliding window with HashMap: track the last seen index of each character. fun lengthOfLongestSubstring(s: String): Int { val lastIndex = HashMap<Char, Int>(); var start = 0; var maxLen = 0; for ((i, ch) in s.withIndex()) { if (ch in lastIndex && lastIndex[ch]!! >= start) { start = lastIndex[ch]!! + 1 }; lastIndex[ch] = i; maxLen = maxOf(maxLen, i - start + 1) }; return maxLen }. "abcabcbb" → 3 ("abc"). O(n) time, O(k) space.

34B — Arrays & Collections Coding (Kotlin)

Two Sum, remove duplicates, sort by criteria, groupBy, Kadane's max subarray, word frequency, and most common element — with complete Kotlin solutions.

ID: 34B Coding
🔍
1. Overview

Array & Collection Problems

Arrays and collections are the foundation of most coding interviews. Master the HashMap trick (O(n²) → O(n)), Kotlin's collection APIs, and the key algorithms like Kadane's.

ProblemKey TechniqueComplexity
Two SumHashMap: value → indexO(n) time, O(n) space
Remove duplicates (sorted)Two-pointer in-placeO(n) time, O(1) space
Sort by criteriasortedWith(compareBy)O(n log n)
Group elementsgroupBy{} / groupingBy{}.eachCount()O(n)
Max subarrayKadane's algorithmO(n) time, O(1) space
Most common elementHashMap + maxByOrNullO(n)
⚡
2. Two Sum
1
Find indices of two numbers that add to target. [2,7,11,15], target=9 → [0,1]
O(n) time · O(n) space
Brute Force O(n²)
fun twoSumBrute(nums: IntArray, target: Int): IntArray {
    for (i in nums.indices) {
        for (j in i + 1 until nums.size) {
            if (nums[i] + nums[j] == target) return intArrayOf(i, j)
        }
    }
    return intArrayOf()  // no solution found
}
Optimal: HashMap O(n)
fun twoSum(nums: IntArray, target: Int): IntArray {
    val seen = HashMap<Int, Int>()   // value → index

    for ((index, num) in nums.withIndex()) {
        val complement = target - num    // what we need to find
        if (complement in seen) {
            return intArrayOf(seen[complement]!!, index)
        }
        seen[num] = index
    }
    return intArrayOf()
}

// Trace: nums=[2,7,11,15], target=9
// i=0: complement=7, not in seen. seen={2:0}
// i=1: complement=2, in seen at index 0! → return [0,1]

println(twoSum(intArrayOf(2,7,11,15), 9).contentToString())  // [0, 1]
🔁
3. Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array
2
[1,1,2,3,3,4] → [1,2,3,4], return length 4 (in-place)
O(n) time · O(1) space
Two-pointer in-place approach
fun removeDuplicates(nums: IntArray): Int {
    if (nums.isEmpty()) return 0

    var slow = 0   // pointer to last unique position
    for (fast in 1 until nums.size) {
        if (nums[fast] != nums[slow]) {
            slow++
            nums[slow] = nums[fast]  // place next unique element
        }
    }
    return slow + 1  // length of unique elements
}

// Trace: [1,1,2,3,3,4]
// slow=0, fast=1: 1==1, skip
// slow=0, fast=2: 1!=2, slow=1, nums[1]=2 → [1,2,2,3,3,4]
// slow=1, fast=3: 2!=3, slow=2, nums[2]=3 → [1,2,3,3,3,4]
// slow=2, fast=4: 3==3, skip
// slow=2, fast=5: 3!=4, slow=3, nums[3]=4 → [1,2,3,4,3,4]
// return 4

// Kotlin idiomatic (not in-place but clean):
fun removeDuplicatesKt(nums: IntArray): IntArray = nums.toSortedSet().toIntArray()
📊
4. Sort & Group Collections
3
Sort and group elements by multiple criteria
O(n log n) · O(n) space
Sort by multiple criteria
data class Product(val name: String, val price: Double, val category: String)

val products = listOf(
    Product("Apple", 1.5, "Fruit"),
    Product("Banana", 0.8, "Fruit"),
    Product("Broccoli", 2.0, "Veg")
)

// Sort by category ascending, then by price ascending
val sorted = products.sortedWith(compareBy({ it.category }, { it.price }))

// Sort by price descending
val byPriceDesc = products.sortedByDescending { it.price }

// Sort with natural order then custom comparator
val custom = products.sortedWith(compareBy<Product> { it.category }.thenByDescending { it.price })
Group elements
// groupBy: group into Map<Key, List<T>>
val byCategory: Map<String, List<Product>> = products.groupBy { it.category }
// {"Fruit": [Apple, Banana], "Veg": [Broccoli]}

// groupingBy + eachCount: count occurrences
val words = listOf("apple", "banana", "apple", "cherry", "banana", "banana")
val wordCount: Map<String, Int> = words.groupingBy { it }.eachCount()
// {"apple":2, "banana":3, "cherry":1}

// Count and find most common word
val mostCommon = wordCount.maxByOrNull { it.value }?.key
// "banana"

// partition: split into two lists based on predicate
val (expensive, cheap) = products.partition { it.price > 1.0 }
📈
5. Kadane's Algorithm — Maximum Subarray
4
[-2,1,-3,4,-1,2,1,-5,4] → 6 (subarray [4,-1,2,1])
O(n) time · O(1) space
Brute Force O(n²)
fun maxSubarrayBrute(nums: IntArray): Int {
    var max = Int.MIN_VALUE
    for (i in nums.indices) {
        var sum = 0
        for (j in i until nums.size) {
            sum += nums[j]
            max = maxOf(max, sum)
        }
    }
    return max
}
Kadane's Algorithm O(n)
fun maxSubarray(nums: IntArray): Int {
    var currentSum = nums[0]
    var maxSum = nums[0]

    for (i in 1 until nums.size) {
        // Either extend the previous subarray, or start fresh from nums[i]
        currentSum = maxOf(nums[i], currentSum + nums[i])
        maxSum = maxOf(maxSum, currentSum)
    }
    return maxSum
}

// Trace: [-2,1,-3,4,-1,2,1,-5,4]
// i=1: current = max(1, -2+1=-1) = 1, max = 1
// i=2: current = max(-3, 1-3=-2) = -2, max = 1
// i=3: current = max(4, -2+4=2) = 4, max = 4
// i=4: current = max(-1, 4-1=3) = 3, max = 4
// i=5: current = max(2, 3+2=5) = 5, max = 5
// i=6: current = max(1, 5+1=6) = 6, max = 6
// i=7: current = max(-5, 6-5=1) = 1, max = 6
// i=8: current = max(4, 1+4=5) = 5, max = 6 → return 6

println(maxSubarray(intArrayOf(-2,1,-3,4,-1,2,1,-5,4)))  // 6
Kadane's Insight
The key decision at each element: "Is it better to extend the current subarray (currentSum + nums[i]) or start fresh (nums[i])?" Start fresh when the current sum has become negative — a negative sum is worse than starting over.

Rotate Array

// Rotate array k positions to the right: [1,2,3,4,5], k=2 → [4,5,1,2,3]
fun rotate(nums: IntArray, k: Int) {
    val n = nums.size
    val shift = k % n   // handle k > n
    val rotated = nums.takeLast(shift) + nums.take(n - shift)
    rotated.forEachIndexed { i, v -> nums[i] = v }
}

// Or in-place with three reverses:
fun rotateInPlace(nums: IntArray, k: Int) {
    val n = nums.size; val shift = k % n
    fun reverse(a: Int, b: Int) { var l=a; var r=b; while(l<r){val t=nums[l];nums[l]=nums[r];nums[r]=t;l++;r--} }
    reverse(0, n-1); reverse(0, shift-1); reverse(shift, n-1)
}
📊
6. HashMap Problems
5
Word frequency count and most common element
O(n) time · O(n) space
Word frequency from text
fun wordFrequency(text: String): Map<String, Int> =
    text.lowercase()
        .split("\\s+".toRegex())
        .filter { it.isNotEmpty() }
        .groupingBy { it }
        .eachCount()

val text = "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog the"
val freq = wordFrequency(text)
println(freq["the"])  // 3

// Top 3 most frequent words
val top3 = freq.entries.sortedByDescending { it.value }.take(3)
    .map { it.key }
Most common element in array
fun mostCommon(nums: IntArray): Int? {
    val freq = HashMap<Int, Int>()
    for (n in nums) freq[n] = (freq[n] ?: 0) + 1
    return freq.maxByOrNull { it.value }?.key
}

// Kotlin idiomatic
fun mostCommonKt(nums: IntArray): Int? =
    nums.toList().groupingBy { it }.eachCount().maxByOrNull { it.value }?.key

println(mostCommon(intArrayOf(1,3,2,3,1,3)))  // 3

// Two Sum variation: count pairs with difference k
fun countPairsWithDiff(nums: IntArray, k: Int): Int {
    val set = nums.toHashSet()
    return nums.count { (it + k) in set }
}

9. Practice Questions
Explain the HashMap trick that reduces Two Sum from O(n²) to O(n).
Easy▼
Brute force checks every pair (i, j) — O(n²). The insight: for each element x, we need to find (target - x) somewhere in the array. Instead of searching through the array again (O(n) per element), store each element in a HashMap as we go. When we encounter x, look up (target - x) in the HashMap in O(1). Total: one pass = O(n) time. We're trading space O(n) for time.
What is Kadane's algorithm and why does it work?
Medium▼
Kadane's algorithm finds the maximum sum contiguous subarray in O(n) time. At each element, it makes a greedy choice: should I extend the current subarray (currentSum + nums[i]) or start a new one (nums[i])? If currentSum is negative, starting fresh is always better — a negative prefix only drags down the sum. currentSum = max(nums[i], currentSum + nums[i]). Track maxSum = max(maxSum, currentSum) throughout. This works because the optimal subarray ends at some index and starts at the best starting point.
Write code to find all pairs in an array that sum to a target value.
Medium▼
fun findPairs(nums: IntArray, target: Int): List<Pair<Int,Int>> { val seen = HashSet<Int>(); val result = mutableListOf<Pair<Int,Int>>(); val added = HashSet<Int>(); for (n in nums) { val complement = target - n; if (complement in seen && n !in added) { result.add(n to complement); added.add(n); added.add(complement) }; seen.add(n) }; return result }. The added set prevents duplicate pairs.
How do you sort a list of data class instances by multiple fields in Kotlin?
Easy▼
list.sortedWith(compareBy({ it.field1 }, { it.field2 })) — sorts by field1 first, then by field2 for ties. For descending on one field: compareBy<T> { it.field1 }.thenByDescending { it.field2 }. Alternatively: list.sortedWith(compareByDescending { it.price }) for single descending. The lambda parameters are evaluated in order — first lambda is primary sort key, second is tiebreaker.
What is the difference between groupBy and groupingBy in Kotlin?
Medium▼
groupBy { key } immediately creates a Map<K, List<V>> — all elements grouped into lists. It's eager and materializes the entire result. groupingBy { key } creates a lazy Grouping object — you then chain operations: eachCount() (count per group), fold() (custom reduction), aggregate() (custom). groupingBy is more memory-efficient for operations that don't need the full lists, like counting. eachCount() is groupingBy's most common use.
Write code to find the intersection of two arrays (common elements).
Easy▼
fun intersection(a: IntArray, b: IntArray): IntArray { val setA = a.toHashSet(); return b.filter { it in setA }.toIntArray() }. O(n + m) time. For distinct results: b.distinct().filter { it in setA }. Kotlin idiomatic: (a.toSet() intersect b.toSet()).toIntArray(). The intersect extension function on sets directly computes set intersection.
How does the two-pointer approach remove duplicates from a sorted array in O(1) space?
Medium▼
Use two pointers: slow (last unique position) and fast (scanner). Fast advances every step. When nums[fast] != nums[slow], we found a new unique element: slow++, copy nums[fast] to nums[slow]. Since the array is sorted, duplicates are adjacent — when fast encounters a new value, it's guaranteed to be unique. This overwrites duplicates with later unique values. No extra array needed → O(1) space.
Write a function to find the majority element (appears more than n/2 times).
Hard▼
Boyer-Moore Voting Algorithm — O(n) time, O(1) space: fun majorityElement(nums: IntArray): Int { var candidate = nums[0]; var count = 1; for (i in 1 until nums.size) { if (count == 0) { candidate = nums[i]; count = 1 } else if (nums[i] == candidate) count++ else count-- }; return candidate }. Intuition: majority element "survives" against all others in a vote — its count never reaches 0 if it truly appears more than n/2 times.
How would you merge two sorted arrays into one sorted array?
Easy▼
Two-pointer approach: var i=0, j=0; result = IntArray(a.size + b.size); for each position: if a[i] ≤ b[j], take a[i], else take b[j]; after one array exhausted, copy remaining. O(n+m) time, O(n+m) space. Kotlin one-liner: (a.toList() + b.toList()).sorted().toIntArray() — O((n+m) log(n+m)) but simpler. The two-pointer approach is O(n+m) and is the optimal solution to know for interviews.
What does the partition function do in Kotlin collections?
Easy▼
partition { predicate } splits a collection into two lists: (matching, notMatching). Returns a Pair<List<T>, List<T>>. Example: val (evens, odds) = listOf(1,2,3,4,5).partition { it % 2 == 0 }. Destructuring the Pair into named variables makes it very readable. Under the hood, it's O(n) — iterates once and puts each element in one of two lists. Useful for splitting positive/negative, active/inactive, etc.
