41A — Advanced Android Debugging

Production-level debugging using Perfetto, Systrace, Android Studio Profiler, Layout Inspector, LeakCanary, Flipper, and systematic debug methodology.

ID: 41A ★ Tier 2 — Senior Differentiator
🔍
1. Overview

Why This Matters

Senior engineers debug what junior engineers can't find. The difference is knowing which tool to pick for which symptom and having a systematic methodology — not just adding print statements and hoping.

The Debugging Toolkit

ToolCategoryWhat It Finds
Android Studio ProfilerCPU / Memory / Network / EnergyMethod traces, heap dumps, request timing, wake locks
PerfettoSystem-wide traceJank, startup bottlenecks, binder calls, scheduler
Layout InspectorUI / ComposeComposable tree, recomposition counts, live state
Database InspectorRoom / SQLiteLive table data, query execution
Network InspectorOkHttp / NetworkHTTP requests, response timing, headers
LeakCanaryMemoryActivity/Fragment/ViewModel/coroutine leaks
StrictModeMain-thread violationsDisk I/O, network on main thread, leaked objects
FlipperMulti-categoryNetwork, Layout, Databases, Logs, Preferences — all in one desktop UI

Debug Categories

  • Performance debugging: jank, slow startup, ANR, frame drops — use Perfetto, CPU Profiler
  • Memory debugging: leaks, OOM, excessive allocation — use Memory Profiler, LeakCanary
  • Network debugging: API failures, slow requests, wrong payloads — use Network Inspector, Flipper
  • UI debugging: layout issues, recomposition storms — use Layout Inspector
  • Crash debugging: ANRs, exceptions, native crashes — use Crashlytics, adb logcat, Android Vitals
Senior Mental Model
Debugging has three phases: Instrument (add visibility before the problem occurs), Reproduce (create conditions to trigger the issue reliably), Isolate (narrow down to the exact line/component). Most engineers skip Instrument and wonder why they can't reproduce production issues.
⚙
2. How It Works — Tool by Tool

Android Studio Profiler

CPU Profiler

Four views for different analysis needs:

  • Call Chart: Horizontal timeline showing which methods called which, in order. Good for understanding execution flow.
  • Flame Chart: Aggregated view — width represents cumulative time. Identifies hot paths at a glance. Widest bars are the performance bottlenecks.
  • Top Down: Tree showing total time spent in each method and all descendants. Good for finding slow subtrees.
  • Bottom Up: Shows which callers spent time in a given method. Good for finding where expensive functions are invoked from.

System Trace uses Perfetto integration directly in Android Studio. Records CPU scheduling, thread states, and custom trace markers. Start it from Profiler > CPU > System Trace.

Memory Profiler

  • Heap Dump: Snapshot of all live objects. Look for Activity/Fragment instances that should have been GC'd.
  • Allocation Tracking: Records every allocation during a window — expensive, use for targeted sessions.
  • GC Events: Frequent GC means excessive short-lived allocations — profile allocations to find the source.

Network Profiler

Intercepts OkHttp traffic automatically (requires OkHttp 3.3+). Shows request timeline, headers, response body, and timing waterfall. Useful for debugging unexpected API calls or slow responses.

Energy Profiler

Shows wake lock acquisitions, jobs, and network events that drain battery. Look for wake locks held across the screen-off boundary.

Perfetto

System-wide trace tool that records CPU scheduling, Binder transactions, SurfaceFlinger, and all app threads simultaneously. The successor to Systrace.

Recording via adb

# Record a 10-second trace with CPU scheduling and frequency data
adb shell perfetto \
  -o /data/misc/perfetto-traces/trace.pftrace \
  -t 10s \
  sched freq gfx view

# Pull the trace to desktop
adb pull /data/misc/perfetto-traces/trace.pftrace ~/Desktop/

# Open in web UI
# Navigate to: https://ui.perfetto.dev — drag and drop the file

Key Tracks to Inspect

  • Main thread (UI thread): Should never block for >16ms between frames. Look for long slices.
  • RenderThread: Runs parallel to main thread — does actual GPU draw calls. Slow here means complex layouts or expensive shaders.
  • Choreographer: Frame timing. Missing a vsync = dropped frame = jank.
  • Binder: IPC calls. Excessive Binder on main thread delays frame rendering.

Custom Trace Sections

// Add custom trace markers visible in Perfetto / System Trace
import android.os.Trace

fun loadProductList() {
    Trace.beginSection("ProductRepo.loadProducts")
    try {
        // your code
        val products = repository.fetchProducts()
        processProducts(products)
    } finally {
        Trace.endSection()  // always end in finally
    }
}

// Compose: add androidx.compose.runtime:runtime-tracing dependency
// Composable recompositions appear automatically in traces

Systrace (Legacy)

Superseded by Perfetto for Android 9+. Still referenced in older documentation. Perfetto produces better traces with richer data. Use Perfetto for all new work.

LeakCanary

// build.gradle.kts — debug builds only, NEVER release
dependencies {
    debugImplementation("com.squareup.leakcanary:leakcanary-android:2.14")
}

// No initialization code needed
// LeakCanary auto-installs via a ContentProvider (AppInitializer pattern)

// What it detects automatically:
// - Activity leaks (retained after finish())
// - Fragment leaks (retained after detach)
// - ViewModel leaks (retained after cleared)
// - Coroutine scope leaks
// - Service leaks

// Watch custom objects manually:
class MyCustomManager {
    fun release() {
        AppWatcher.objectWatcher.expectWeaklyReachable(
            this, "MyCustomManager should be released"
        )
    }
}

StrictMode

// Application.onCreate() — debug builds ONLY
override fun onCreate() {
    super.onCreate()
    if (BuildConfig.DEBUG) {
        StrictMode.setThreadPolicy(
            StrictMode.ThreadPolicy.Builder()
                .detectDiskReads()
                .detectDiskWrites()
                .detectNetwork()         // network on main thread
                .detectCustomSlowCalls()
                .penaltyLog()             // log to logcat
                .penaltyDeath()           // crash — ensures issues are fixed
                .build()
        )
        StrictMode.setVmPolicy(
            StrictMode.VmPolicy.Builder()
                .detectLeakedSqlLiteObjects()
                .detectLeakedClosableObjects()   // unclosed streams, cursors
                .detectActivityLeaks()
                .detectLeakedRegistrationObjects()
                .penaltyLog()
                .build()
        )
    }
}

Layout Inspector

Connects to a running app and shows the live composable tree (for Compose) or view hierarchy. Key features:

  • Recomposition counts: Shows how many times each composable has recomposed. High counts = unnecessary recompositions = performance issue.
  • Skip counts: How many recompositions were skipped (composable was stable and inputs didn't change). High skips = good.
  • Live state inspection — see current values of state variables in composables.

Database Inspector

Connects to a running app's Room/SQLite database in real-time. Allows live SQL queries, table inspection, and seeing data as it changes. No adb pull needed.

Network Inspector

Intercepts all OkHttp traffic automatically when using Android Studio Profiler. No code changes required. Shows request/response headers, body, timing, and connection details. Works for all OkHttp-based libraries (Retrofit, etc.).

🎯
3. When to Use Each Tool

Symptom-to-Tool Map

SymptomPrimary ToolSecondary Tool
App jank / dropped framesPerfetto (System Trace)CPU Profiler — Flame Chart
Slow cold/warm startupPerfetto — App Startup trackCPU Profiler — Method Trace
ANR (Application Not Responding)CPU Profiler — System Traceadb bugreport + ANR traces
Memory leakLeakCanary (auto-detect)Memory Profiler — Heap Dump
OutOfMemoryErrorMemory Profiler — Heap DumpPerfetto — memory track
Excessive GC pausesMemory Profiler — Allocation TrackingPerfetto — GC events
Network request slow/failingNetwork InspectorFlipper Network Plugin
Disk/network on main threadStrictMode — penaltyLog/DeathCPU Profiler
Compose recompositionsLayout Inspector — recomposition countPerfetto — Compose tracing
Database query slowDatabase Inspector — query timingRoom query explain plan
Battery drainEnergy ProfilerPerfetto — wakelock track

When to Use Perfetto vs CPU Profiler

Decision Guide
  • Perfetto: System-level issues — jank, startup, Binder contention, SurfaceFlinger, scheduler. Cross-process issues. When you need to see what Android itself is doing, not just your app.
  • CPU Profiler: In-app method-level analysis — which function is slow, where time is spent in your code specifically. Faster to start, narrower scope.
  • Both together: Use Perfetto to identify when the problem occurs, then CPU Profiler method trace to find which method.

When to Use LeakCanary vs Memory Profiler

  • LeakCanary: Automatic continuous monitoring in debug builds. Zero config. Catches Activity/Fragment/ViewModel leaks with full stack trace and leak path. Should always be in every project.
  • Memory Profiler: When you need to understand heap composition — what objects exist, which are unexpectedly retained, how much memory each class consumes. Use when OOM or when you suspect leaks LeakCanary doesn't detect.

StrictMode in CI

StrictMode with penaltyDeath() should run in debug builds during CI tests. This makes disk/network-on-main-thread violations fail the build automatically — far better than waiting for performance complaints from users.

🏭
4. Production Example — 5-Second Startup Investigation
Scenario
Automotive navigation app reporting 5-second cold start time. Users complain the app is "slow to open." Using Perfetto to systematically investigate and fix.

Step 1 — Record Perfetto Trace During Cold Start

# Force-stop app to ensure cold start
adb shell am force-stop com.example.autoapp

# Start Perfetto recording
adb shell perfetto \
  -o /data/misc/perfetto-traces/startup.pftrace \
  -t 15s \
  sched freq gfx view \
  app \
  -a com.example.autoapp &

# Launch the app
adb shell am start-activity com.example.autoapp/.MainActivity

# Pull the trace
adb pull /data/misc/perfetto-traces/startup.pftrace ~/Desktop/

Step 2 — Identify Application.onCreate() Blocking Work

In the Perfetto trace (ui.perfetto.dev), search for the app's main thread. The startup track shows:

Cold Start Timeline (Main Thread) |-- Application.onCreate() .............. 2800ms ← PROBLEM | |-- AnalyticsSDK.init() ............. 1200ms | |-- MapSDK.init() ................... 900ms | |-- FirebaseApp.initializeApp() ..... 400ms | |-- SharedPrefs read (disk I/O) ..... 300ms ← StrictMode violation |-- Activity.onCreate() ................. 1100ms | |-- setContent() / inflate .......... 600ms | |-- ViewModel.init() ................ 500ms |-- First frame rendered ................ 5100ms total

Step 3 — Identify ContentProvider Init Chain

Many SDKs use ContentProviders for auto-initialization (Firebase, LeakCanary, WorkManager). These run before Application.onCreate(). In Perfetto, look for ActivityThread#installContentProviders:

// Check merged manifest for all ContentProviders
// ./gradlew :app:processDebugManifest
// Then open: app/build/intermediates/merged_manifests/debug/AndroidManifest.xml
// Count <provider> entries — often 10-20 SDKs add their own

Step 4 — StrictMode Catches Disk I/O on Main Thread

StrictMode logs in logcat during development confirmed SharedPreferences read on main thread during startup. The fix is DataStore (which is async) or moving prefs read to a background coroutine.

Step 5 — Fix: App Startup Library + Coroutines

// build.gradle.kts
implementation("androidx.startup:startup-runtime:1.1.1")

// Create lazy initializers for SDKs that don't need to be ready immediately
class AnalyticsInitializer : Initializer<Analytics> {
    override fun create(context: Context): Analytics {
        return Analytics.getInstance(context)
    }
    override fun dependencies(): List<Class<out Initializer<*>>> = emptyList()
}

// AndroidManifest.xml — register under InitializationProvider
<provider
    android:name="androidx.startup.InitializationProvider"
    android:authorities="${applicationId}.androidx-startup"
    android:exported="false">
    <meta-data
        android:name="com.example.AnalyticsInitializer"
        android:value="androidx.startup.Initializer"/>
</provider>
// Application.onCreate() — move heavy init off main thread
override fun onCreate() {
    super.onCreate()
    // Only truly critical init here

    // Move SDKs to background via coroutine
    ProcessLifecycleOwner.get().lifecycleScope.launch(Dispatchers.IO) {
        initMapSDK()
        initAnalyticsSDK()
    }
}

Step 6 — Add Baseline Profiles

// Reduce JIT compilation at startup — pre-compile hot paths
// Add to build.gradle.kts
implementation("androidx.profileinstaller:profileinstaller:1.3.1")

// Add macrobenchmark module for generating baseline profiles:
// benchmarks/src/test/.../BaselineProfileGenerator.kt
@RunWith(AndroidJUnit4::class)
class BaselineProfileGenerator {
    @get:Rule val rule = BaselineProfileRule()

    @Test fun generate() = rule.collect(
        packageName = "com.example.autoapp"
    ) {
        pressHome()
        startActivityAndWait()
        // navigate critical user journeys
    }
}
// Generates app/src/main/baseline-prof.txt — commit this file

PhaseBeforeAfterFix

5. Alternatives & Trade-offs
ToolBest ForLimitationsVerdict
Perfetto System-wide traces, jank, startup, cross-process Large trace files (100MB+); steep learning curve for trace analysis; desktop-only UI Gold standard for performance
Systrace (legacy) Older codebases referencing it Superseded by Perfetto; deprecated; less data than Perfetto Use Perfetto instead
CPU Profiler (Android Studio) In-app method traces, quick profiling sessions Profiler overhead affects results; can't see system threads; no cross-process Good for method-level analysis
Firebase Performance Production metrics, HTTP latency, custom traces in real builds Post-hoc only — not interactive; limited CPU trace depth; requires Firebase Complement to local tools
StrictMode Catching violations during development and CI Debug-only; no production data; can generate false positives from libraries Must-have in debug builds + CI
Manual logging (Timber) Business logic tracing, flow debugging No timing, no system context, can't see thread states or allocations Complement — not a replacement

LeakCanary vs Memory Profiler

Key Distinction
  • LeakCanary: Automatic, zero-config, catches leaks you didn't know about. Shows exact leak path with annotated stack trace. Best for "is there a leak?" detection.
  • Memory Profiler: Manual, interactive. Shows heap composition, class-level object counts, retained sizes. Best for "why is my app using 400MB?" analysis.
  • Use both — they answer different questions.

Flipper vs Android Studio Tools

When to use Flipper
Flipper is Meta's open-source desktop debugging platform. It bundles network inspection, layout inspection, database browser, shared preferences viewer, and log viewer in one UI — with a plugin ecosystem. Useful for teams where developers may not have Android Studio (e.g., React Native teams). For pure Android + Kotlin/Compose, Android Studio's built-in tools are equally capable and require no extra setup.
⚠
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

Pitfall 1 — Trace.beginSection() Without endSection() in finally

// ❌ BAD — if exception thrown, trace section never ends
fun processData(data: List<Item>) {
    Trace.beginSection("processData")
    doHeavyProcessing(data)  // throws if data is empty
    Trace.endSection()      // never reached on exception
}

// ✅ GOOD — always end in finally
fun processData(data: List<Item>) {
    Trace.beginSection("processData")
    try {
        doHeavyProcessing(data)
    } finally {
        Trace.endSection()
    }
}

Pitfall 2 — Memory Profiler Heap Dump Triggers GC

Requesting a heap dump pauses the app briefly and triggers garbage collection. This means the dump shows the state after GC, not a live snapshot. Objects that would have been collected appear cleaned up. For true live analysis, use allocation tracking instead, or take multiple dumps.

Pitfall 3 — LeakCanary in Release Builds

// ❌ NEVER add LeakCanary to release
implementation("com.squareup.leakcanary:leakcanary-android:2.14")

// ✅ ALWAYS debug-only
debugImplementation("com.squareup.leakcanary:leakcanary-android:2.14")

// LeakCanary adds overhead: object watcher, background analysis,
// heap dumps — unacceptable in production

Pitfall 4 — StrictMode penaltyDeath() in Release

// ❌ BAD — crashes production users
StrictMode.setThreadPolicy(StrictMode.ThreadPolicy.Builder()
    .penaltyDeath()  // crashes on violation — debug only!
    .build())

// ✅ GOOD — gate on BuildConfig.DEBUG
if (BuildConfig.DEBUG) {
    StrictMode.setThreadPolicy(
        StrictMode.ThreadPolicy.Builder()
            .detectAll()
            .penaltyDeath()
            .build()
    )
}

Pitfall 5 — Layout Inspector Slows Down Device

Layout Inspector uses live reflection to inspect the composable tree — this can significantly slow down the device during inspection, especially on older hardware. Do not use Layout Inspector while measuring performance. Use it only for debugging layout/recomposition issues, not as a general development aid while timing.

Pitfall 6 — Perfetto Trace Files Are Very Large

A 10-second Perfetto trace can be 50–200MB depending on trace categories. Analyze on desktop at ui.perfetto.dev — do not try to process them programmatically on device. Use targeted categories (sched gfx view) rather than -a all to keep file sizes manageable.

Pitfall 7 — Profiling in Debug Builds

Critical
Debug builds are 2-3x slower than release builds due to disabled optimizations, debug symbols, and ART interpreter mode. Always profile the release build variant (or a profileable build) for accurate numbers. A 500ms operation in debug might be 150ms in release — drawing the wrong conclusions from debug profiling is common.

Best Practices

  1. Add Trace.beginSection() markers around every business-critical path in debug builds.
  2. Enable StrictMode with penaltyDeath() in debug + CI from day one.
  3. Always include leakcanary-android in debugImplementation — never let it reach release.
  4. Profile release builds, not debug builds, for meaningful numbers.
  5. Record Perfetto traces early — before optimizing, to have a baseline comparison.
  6. Check recomposition counts in Layout Inspector for every new Compose screen before shipping.
🎤
7. Interview Answer Framework

30-Second Answer

"I approach production performance issues systematically: StrictMode catches main-thread violations in CI, Perfetto reveals jank and startup bottlenecks at the system level, Memory Profiler combined with LeakCanary handles memory issues, and custom Trace.beginSection() markers instrument business-critical paths so I can see them in every trace."

2-Minute Structured Answer

"My debugging approach starts at the symptom level — I pick the right tool for the symptom rather than reaching for the first one that comes to mind.

For performance issues like jank or slow startup, I start with Perfetto. It gives a system-wide view: CPU scheduling, Binder calls, SurfaceFlinger, all app threads simultaneously. I open the trace at ui.perfetto.dev, look for the main thread slices longer than 16ms between frames for jank, or for long Application.onCreate() work during startup. I add custom Trace.beginSection() markers around our business logic so they appear as named slices in the trace.

For memory leaks, LeakCanary runs automatically in debug builds — it catches Activity, Fragment, and ViewModel leaks with a full annotated path. When I need to understand heap composition, I use the Memory Profiler heap dump, but I'm aware the dump triggers GC, so it's not a live snapshot.

StrictMode with penaltyDeath() runs in every debug build and CI test — it catches disk reads and network calls on the main thread before they ever reach code review. For Compose performance, Layout Inspector shows recomposition counts per composable, which is the first thing I check when a screen feels slow.

For startup specifically, the App Startup library + Baseline Profiles are the production-grade solutions once you've identified the bottlenecks via Perfetto."

Must-Mention Points (7)

1
Perfetto for traces — system-wide, cross-process, ui.perfetto.dev for analysis; successor to Systrace
2
Memory Profiler + heap dump — heap dump triggers GC; not a live snapshot; use for heap composition analysis
3
LeakCanary auto-detection — debugImplementation only; zero config; catches Activity/Fragment/ViewModel/coroutine leaks
4
StrictMode in debug + CI — penaltyDeath() in debug catches main-thread violations before they ship
5
Custom Trace.beginSection() — instrument business paths; always wrap in try/finally; visible in Perfetto and System Trace
6
Baseline Profiles — pre-compile hot bytecode paths; generated by Macrobenchmark; committed as baseline-prof.txt
7
Layout Inspector recomposition count — high counts = unstable composable parameters; first Compose performance signal

Senior-Level Insight (Stand Out)

Say This
"I add Trace.beginSection() markers around key business flows in debug builds and run Perfetto traces as part of our Macrobenchmark CI suite — any regression in startup or scroll performance automatically fails the build. We track p95 startup time as a KPI. For Compose recompositions, I review Layout Inspector recomposition counts on every new screen before merging — a screen with 500+ recompositions on a simple scroll is a red flag we catch in code review, not in production."

Likely Follow-up Questions

QuestionShort Answer
What is a Baseline Profile? A text file listing hot code paths that the Android runtime pre-compiles (AOT) on app install, reducing JIT compilation overhead at startup. Generated by Macrobenchmark and committed to source control as baseline-prof.txt.
What is Choreographer in Perfetto? The Android component that drives the frame rendering pipeline, synchronized to the display vsync signal. In Perfetto, the Choreographer track shows if frames are delivered on time. A missed vsync = dropped frame = jank.
How does LeakCanary detect leaks? It uses a WeakReference to track objects that should be GC'd (Activities after finish, Fragments after detach). If the WeakReference is not cleared after a GC, LeakCanary takes a heap dump and uses heuristic analysis (shark library) to find the reference path keeping the object alive.
What causes a Compose recomposition storm? Passing unstable (non-stable) types as composable parameters, or reading a State object too high up the tree. When state changes, all composables reading that state recompose. Fix: make parameters stable (data classes, @Stable), hoist state down, use derivedStateOf to limit recompositions.
⚡

9. Interview Questions (Self-Check)
How to use
Try to answer each question before revealing the answer. Click the arrow to reveal.

Basic

B1 — What is the difference between Perfetto and the CPU Profiler in Android Studio?
Easy▼
Perfetto is a system-wide tracing tool that records CPU scheduling, Binder IPC, SurfaceFlinger, all app threads, and kernel events simultaneously. It captures what Android as a whole is doing. Traces are viewed in the web UI at ui.perfetto.dev. Ideal for jank, startup, and cross-process issues.

CPU Profiler (Android Studio) is focused on in-app method-level analysis. It shows call charts, flame charts, and method traces within your app's code specifically. Easier to start but narrower — it can't see system threads or other processes.

They complement each other: use Perfetto to identify when and at the system level, then CPU Profiler to identify which method in your code.
B2 — What does StrictMode detect and when should you use it?
Easy▼
StrictMode detects two categories of violations:

ThreadPolicy: Operations that shouldn't happen on the main thread — disk reads, disk writes, network operations, custom slow calls. These cause jank or ANRs if they block the main thread.

VmPolicy: Memory and resource violations — leaked SQLite objects, unclosed Closeable objects, Activity leaks, leaked registration objects.

Use StrictMode in debug builds only (gate on BuildConfig.DEBUG). Use penaltyLog() to see violations in logcat, or penaltyDeath() to crash immediately — crash mode is preferred in CI because it forces fixes rather than allowing them to accumulate.
B3 — How does LeakCanary detect memory leaks without any manual initialization code?
Easy▼
LeakCanary uses the Android ContentProvider auto-initialization pattern. The library registers a ContentProvider in its manifest that Android automatically instantiates before Application.onCreate(). Inside that ContentProvider's onCreate(), LeakCanary registers lifecycle callbacks on the Application to watch Activities, Fragments, ViewModels, and Services.

When a watched object should be garbage collected (e.g., Activity after finish()), LeakCanary creates a WeakReference to it and schedules a check. If the WeakReference is not cleared after triggering GC, LeakCanary takes a heap dump and uses its shark library to walk the reference graph and find the shortest path preventing GC. This produces a human-readable leak trace.

Intermediate

I1 — Coding Add Trace markers to this Repository method so it appears in Perfetto traces with correct begin/end even on exceptions:
Medium▼
Before: 
suspend fun syncOrders(userId: String): List<Order> {
    val remote = api.getOrders(userId)
    val local = dao.insertAll(remote)
    return local
}
After: 
suspend fun syncOrders(userId: String): List<Order> {
    Trace.beginSection("OrderRepo.syncOrders")
    return try {
        Trace.beginSection("OrderRepo.fetchRemote")
        val remote = try {
            api.getOrders(userId)
        } finally {
            Trace.endSection()  // fetchRemote
        }

        Trace.beginSection("OrderRepo.insertLocal")
        try {
            dao.insertAll(remote)
        } finally {
            Trace.endSection()  // insertLocal
        }
    } finally {
        Trace.endSection()  // syncOrders
    }
}
Key: every beginSection must have a matching endSection in a finally block to prevent orphaned sections in the trace.
I2 — What does a high recomposition count in Layout Inspector indicate and how do you fix it?
Medium▼
A high recomposition count means the composable is being re-executed far more often than needed. Common causes:

1. Unstable parameter types: Non-data-class types, interfaces, or types the Compose compiler can't confirm are stable. Every time the parent recomposes, these composables recompose too.
2. Reading state too high: A composable reads a State object that changes frequently — the entire subtree recomposes on every change.
3. Lambda references changing: Lambdas without remember { } are recreated each recomposition, causing child composables to recompose.

Fixes:
• Use data class for all parameter types (stable by Compose rules)
• Annotate with @Stable or @Immutable when appropriate
• Use derivedStateOf { } to compute derived state with built-in equality check
• Wrap lambdas in rememberUpdatedState or pass stable lambda references
• Hoist heavy state closer to where it's read
I3 — Why should you never profile a debug build for performance measurements?
Medium▼
Debug builds have several characteristics that make them 2-5x slower than release builds:

1. ART interpreter mode: Debug builds often run in interpreter mode rather than AOT-compiled mode — method calls are far slower
2. No R8/ProGuard: Code is not shrunk, inlined, or optimized
3. Debug symbols: Extra metadata is retained in memory
4. AssertionError checks: Assertions are active
5. Profiler overhead: Android Studio's profiler itself adds overhead when attached

Use a profileable or release build variant for performance measurement. You can enable profiling on a release build by adding <profileable android:shell="true"/> to the manifest in a signed release build — this allows profiling without debug overhead. Baseline Profile measurements must always be on release builds to be meaningful.
I4 — What is the difference between shallow size and retained size in a heap dump?
Medium▼
Shallow size: The memory consumed by the object itself — just its fields, not the objects it references. For example, a list object's shallow size is just the size of the list header and array reference, not the items inside.

Retained size: The total memory that would be freed if this object were garbage collected — the object itself plus all objects that are only reachable through it (i.e., would also be GC'd).

Why it matters: When looking for memory hogs in a heap dump, sort by retained size. A single ViewModel with small shallow size might have a large retained size if it holds a reference to a large list, a bitmap, or a Context. Retained size tells you the true memory cost of an object, not just its own footprint.

Senior / Scenario

S1 — Scenario An ANR is reported in Play Console on a specific device (Xiaomi Redmi Note 11) but you can't reproduce it locally. Walk through your systematic debug approach.
Hard▼
Systematic Approach:

1. Analyze Play Console ANR data:
• Download the ANR stack trace from Android Vitals. It shows the main thread state at the time of ANR (usually waiting on a lock, doing I/O, or spinning).
• Check if it's consistently on the same class/method — this suggests a race condition specific to that device's hardware or MIUI customization.

2. Check the main thread stack trace:
• Common patterns: Binder transaction waiting (ContentProvider call on main thread), synchronized block held by background thread, SharedPreferences commit() on main thread.
• MIUI-specific: Some Xiaomi devices have custom system services that add latency to Binder IPC calls — operations that take 5ms on stock Android take 500ms on MIUI.

3. Add StrictMode + custom Trace markers:
• If reproducible in a new release: add Trace.beginSection around every main-thread operation in the suspect area. Record Perfetto trace on the actual device or a MIUI emulator image.

4. Test on a MIUI emulator / remote device farm:
• Use Firebase Test Lab or BrowserStack with a Xiaomi device. Sometimes OEM customizations cause different Binder scheduling behavior.

5. Code fix patterns:
• If ContentProvider calls: move off main thread
• If SharedPreferences: migrate to DataStore
• If lock contention: reduce synchronization scope
• If database access: enforce Room's main-thread detection

Key insight: ANRs on specific OEM devices are often caused by slower Binder IPC on that OEM's system services. Operations that don't ANR on stock Android 5ms can take 500ms+ on MIUI, pushing your app over the 5-second ANR threshold.
S2 — After enabling LeakCanary, it reports an Activity leak. The leak path shows: MainActivity → MyViewModel → Repository → callback → MainActivity. How do you fix it?
Hard▼
Problem: The Repository holds a callback that captures a reference to MainActivity. Since Repository is scoped to ViewModel (which outlives Activities), this creates a leak: even after MainActivity is destroyed and recreated (e.g., on rotation), the old MainActivity instance is retained in memory via the callback reference in Repository.

Fix Strategy — never pass Activity/View references into ViewModel or Repository:
// ❌ BAD — Repository holds reference to Activity
class OrderRepository(
    private val onComplete: () -> Unit  // lambda capturing Activity
)
// ✅ GOOD — Repository emits via Flow, ViewModel collects
class OrderRepository {
    private val _events = MutableSharedFlow<OrderEvent>()
    val events: SharedFlow<OrderEvent> = _events.asSharedFlow()
}

// ViewModel collects Flow — survives rotation, no Activity reference
class OrderViewModel : ViewModel() {
    init {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            repository.events.collect { event -> _uiState.value = event.toUiState() }
        }
    }
}

// Activity just observes ViewModel — no callback reference needed
The root rule: only Activities/Fragments should hold references to Activities/Fragments. ViewModels and Repositories should communicate via Flow/StateFlow, not callbacks that capture view references.

42A — Compose Design System & Multi-Brand Theming

CompositionLocal, design tokens, MaterialTheme customisation, and how to support multiple brands from a single Compose codebase — the architecture behind scalable UI systems.

ID: 42A ⭐ Tier 1 🔥 Hot
🔍
1. Overview

What Is a Design System?

A design system is a shared language between designers and engineers consisting of three interlocking layers:

  • Design Tokens — the raw primitives: colors, typography scales, spacing values, corner radii. These are pure data, not UI code.
  • Component Library — reusable Composables that consume tokens. A PrimaryButton reads buttonBackground from the token set; it never hardcodes Color(0xFF6200EE).
  • Screen Compositions — product screens assembled from components. They contain layout and business logic, not visual decisions.

Why Multi-Brand Matters

Enterprise products increasingly deliver one codebase, multiple visual identities. Examples from production:

  • Acme Corp — two product lines have different brand colours, logo assets, and typographic tone but share all checkout, account, and loyalty screens.
  • Automotive super-app — 14 vehicle brands (each with distinct primary colour, logo, typography, and tone) running from a single Compose codebase. Each brand supplies its own token set as a data object injected at startup — zero UI code duplication.
  • Banking super-apps — white-label banking apps where each bank provides its colour palette and font; the underlying transaction, card, and KYC flows are identical.

The Three-Layer Architecture

LayerContentsBrand-specific?
Design TokensColorTokens, TypographyTokens, SpacingTokens data classes✅ Yes — each brand has its own instance
Component LibraryPrimaryButton, Card, AppBar, TextField composables❌ No — reads tokens via CompositionLocal
Screen CompositionsHomeScreen, CheckoutScreen, ProfileScreen❌ No — assembles components
Senior Mental Model
The key insight is that brand identity is data, not code. Your composables never know which brand they're rendering for — they just consume tokens from CompositionLocal. Swapping brands is swapping the data, not rewriting components. A component that reads LocalBrandColors.current.primary works for all 14 brands without a single if (brand == BRAND_X) branch.

Real-World Scale

In a real-world multi-brand automotive app, a single :design-system module maintains ~80 composable components. Each of the 14 brand modules contributes a 400-line Kotlin file that is entirely data: colours, fonts, spacing, icon drawables. No UI code is duplicated across brands. A new brand launch is a new data file + Gradle flavour — the entire app is production-ready in days, not months.

👥
2. CompositionLocal API

What Is CompositionLocal?

CompositionLocal is Compose's mechanism for implicit parameter passing. Instead of threading a value through every function signature, you provide it once at a high level and any descendant composable can read it. Think of it as a typed, scoped global that is safe to use in the composition tree.

Compose's own MaterialTheme, LocalContext, LocalDensity, and LocalFocusManager are all built on this exact mechanism.

Two Factory Functions

FactoryRecomposition ScopeWhen to Use
compositionLocalOf { }Only composables that read the value recompose on changeValues that change during a session (e.g. dark/light mode toggle, locale)
staticCompositionLocalOf { }Entire subtree below the provider recomposes on changeStable values set once at startup (e.g. entire brand config object)
Performance Note
staticCompositionLocalOf causes the entire subtree to recompose when the value changes. For brand config (set once at startup and never changed), this is perfectly fine — the cost is paid once. For frequently changing values (e.g. scroll offset), always use compositionLocalOf instead.

Reading and Providing Values

  • Reading: LocalSomething.current — reads the nearest provided value in the composition tree.
  • Providing: CompositionLocalProvider(LocalSomething provides value) { content() } — scopes the value to all descendants in the content lambda.

Full Example: Brand Color CompositionLocal

// 1. Define the token data class
data class BrandColors(
    val primary: Color,
    val secondary: Color,
    val surface: Color,
    val onPrimary: Color,
    val onSurface: Color,
    val error: Color,
    val logo: Int // drawable resource ID
)

// 2. Create the CompositionLocal with a sensible default (fallback / preview)
val LocalBrandColors = staticCompositionLocalOf {
    BrandColors(
        primary    = Color(0xFF1C1C1E),
        secondary  = Color(0xFF56CFB2),
        surface    = Color(0xFF0F1117),
        onPrimary  = Color.White,
        onSurface  = Color(0xFFE2E4F0),
        error      = Color(0xFFFF6B6B),
        logo       = R.drawable.logo_default
    )
}

// 3. Read the token anywhere in the composition tree
@Composable
fun PrimaryButton(text: String, onClick: () -> Unit) {
    val colors = LocalBrandColors.current  // no parameter needed
    Button(
        onClick = onClick,
        colors = ButtonDefaults.buttonColors(
            containerColor = colors.primary,
            contentColor   = colors.onPrimary
        )
    ) { Text(text) }
}

// 4. Provide a brand-specific value at the root
@Composable
fun BrandARoot(content: @Composable () -> Unit) {
    val brandAColors = BrandColors(
        primary   = Color(0xFFE63946), // Brand A primary
        secondary = Color(0xFF457B9D), // Brand A secondary
        surface   = Color(0xFFFFFFFF),
        onPrimary = Color.White,
        onSurface = Color(0xFF1C1C1E),
        error     = Color(0xFFD32F2F),
        logo      = R.drawable.logo_brand_a
    )
    CompositionLocalProvider(LocalBrandColors provides brandAColors) {
        content()
    }
}

Overriding in Subtrees (Nested Providers)

CompositionLocal scoping is hierarchical. You can narrow a scope within a larger tree — for example, a dark-mode preview card inside a light-mode screen can wrap its content in a new provider:

@Composable
fun DarkPreviewCard(content: @Composable () -> Unit) {
    val current = LocalBrandColors.current
    // Override only surface/onSurface for the dark preview
    CompositionLocalProvider(
        LocalBrandColors provides current.copy(
            surface   = Color(0xFF1C1C1E),
            onSurface = Color.White
        )
    ) { content() }
}
Interview Tip
Interviewers love to ask: "How does a deeply nested composable get a value without prop-drilling?" The answer is CompositionLocal. Know the API, know when to use static vs dynamic, and give a concrete example like brand theming.
🎨
3. Brand Token Architecture

Three-Level Token Hierarchy

The industry-standard approach (from the W3C Design Token Community Group, adopted by Figma, Salesforce Lightning, and Material Design 3) uses three levels:

LevelDescriptionExample
Global tokensRaw palette values — all possible colors in the systemColor(0xFFC8102E), Color(0xFFFFFFFF)
Alias tokensSemantic meaning mapped to globalsprimary = brandRed, surface = white
Component tokensComponent-specific slots mapped to alias tokensbuttonBackground = primary, cardBorderColor = border
Why This Hierarchy Matters
When the design team changes "primary = #C8102E" to "#B50024" in one place, every button, header, and active state that uses the primary alias automatically updates across all 80 components — no search-and-replace, no missed spots.

Complete BrandTheme Data Structure

// ── Token data classes ── (pure Kotlin, no Android deps)

data class ColorTokens(
    val primary:         Color,
    val primaryVariant:  Color,
    val secondary:       Color,
    val background:      Color,
    val surface:         Color,
    val surfaceVariant:  Color,
    val onPrimary:       Color,
    val onSecondary:     Color,
    val onBackground:    Color,
    val onSurface:       Color,
    val error:           Color,
    val onError:         Color,
    val outline:         Color,
    val logo:            Int   // @DrawableRes
)

data class TypographyTokens(
    val displayLarge:   TextStyle,
    val headlineMedium: TextStyle,
    val titleLarge:     TextStyle,
    val bodyMedium:     TextStyle,
    val labelSmall:     TextStyle
)

data class SpacingTokens(
    val xs:  Dp = 4.dp,
    val sm:  Dp = 8.dp,
    val md:  Dp = 16.dp,
    val lg:  Dp = 24.dp,
    val xl:  Dp = 32.dp,
    val xxl: Dp = 48.dp
)

data class ShapeTokens(
    val small:  Shape = RoundedCornerShape(4.dp),
    val medium: Shape = RoundedCornerShape(8.dp),
    val large:  Shape = RoundedCornerShape(16.dp),
    val full:   Shape = CircleShape
)

// ── Top-level BrandTheme ──
data class BrandTheme(
    val colors:     ColorTokens,
    val typography: TypographyTokens,
    val spacing:    SpacingTokens   = SpacingTokens(),
    val shapes:     ShapeTokens     = ShapeTokens()
)

Brand Registry

enum class Brand {
    BRAND_A, BRAND_B,
    BRAND_C, BRAND_D, BRAND_E, BRAND_F, BRAND_G, BRAND_H
}

object BrandRegistry {
    private val registry: Map<Brand, BrandTheme> = mapOf(
        Brand.BRAND_A to brandATheme(),
        Brand.BRAND_B    to brandBTheme(),
        Brand.BRAND_C             to brandBTheme(),
        Brand.BRAND_D              to brandDTheme()
        // ... more brands
    )

    fun get(brand: Brand): BrandTheme =
        registry[brand] ?: throw IllegalArgumentException("Unknown brand: $brand")
}

// Each brand is a pure data factory function — no UI, no Android deps
fun brandATheme() = BrandTheme(
    colors = ColorTokens(
        primary        = Color(0xFFE63946), // Brand A primary
        primaryVariant = Color(0xFFB50024),
        secondary      = Color(0xFF457B9D), // Brand A secondary
        background     = Color(0xFFFFFFFF),
        surface        = Color(0xFFF5F5F5),
        surfaceVariant = Color(0xFFEEEEEE),
        onPrimary      = Color.White,
        onSecondary    = Color.Black,
        onBackground   = Color(0xFF1C1C1E),
        onSurface      = Color(0xFF1C1C1E),
        error          = Color(0xFFD32F2F),
        onError        = Color.White,
        outline        = Color(0xFFCCCCCC),
        logo           = R.drawable.logo_brand_a
    ),
    typography = TypographyTokens(
        displayLarge   = TextStyle(fontFamily = BrandFontFamily, fontSize = 57.sp, fontWeight = FontWeight.Light),
        headlineMedium = TextStyle(fontFamily = BrandFontFamily, fontSize = 28.sp),
        titleLarge     = TextStyle(fontFamily = BrandFontFamily, fontSize = 22.sp, fontWeight = FontWeight.Medium),
        bodyMedium     = TextStyle(fontFamily = BrandFontFamily, fontSize = 14.sp),
        labelSmall     = TextStyle(fontFamily = BrandFontFamily, fontSize = 11.sp, letterSpacing = 0.5.sp)
    )
)

fun brandBTheme() = BrandTheme(
    colors = ColorTokens(
        primary        = Color(0xFF002855), // Brand B deep navy
        primaryVariant = Color(0xFF001A3A),
        secondary      = Color(0xFFB2A96A), // Brand B gold
        background     = Color(0xFF0F0F0F),
        surface        = Color(0xFF1A1A1A),
        surfaceVariant = Color(0xFF252525),
        onPrimary      = Color.White,
        onSecondary    = Color.Black,
        onBackground   = Color.White,
        onSurface      = Color.White,
        error          = Color(0xFFCF6679),
        onError        = Color.Black,
        outline        = Color(0xFF3A3A3A),
        logo           = R.drawable.logo_brand_b
    ),
    typography = TypographyTokens( /* BrandBFontFamily ... */ )
)
🌀
4. MaterialTheme Deep Dive

MaterialTheme Is Just CompositionLocal

Internally, MaterialTheme is nothing magical — it's a composable that provides several CompositionLocals:

// Simplified internals of MaterialTheme (actual Compose source)
@Composable
fun MaterialTheme(
    colorScheme: ColorScheme = MaterialTheme.colorScheme,
    typography:  Typography  = MaterialTheme.typography,
    shapes:      Shapes      = MaterialTheme.shapes,
    content:     @Composable () -> Unit
) {
    CompositionLocalProvider(
        LocalColorScheme  provides colorScheme, // → MaterialTheme.colorScheme
        LocalTypography   provides typography,  // → MaterialTheme.typography
        LocalShapes       provides shapes,       // → MaterialTheme.shapes
        content = content
    )
}

This means you can feed your BrandTheme tokens directly into MaterialTheme and every Material component (Button, Card, TextField, TopAppBar) automatically respects your brand colours.

Mapping BrandTheme → Material ColorScheme

fun BrandTheme.toColorScheme(): ColorScheme = darkColorScheme(
    primary          = colors.primary,
    onPrimary        = colors.onPrimary,
    primaryContainer = colors.primaryVariant,
    secondary        = colors.secondary,
    onSecondary      = colors.onSecondary,
    background       = colors.background,
    onBackground     = colors.onBackground,
    surface          = colors.surface,
    onSurface        = colors.onSurface,
    surfaceVariant   = colors.surfaceVariant,
    error            = colors.error,
    onError          = colors.onError,
    outline          = colors.outline
)

fun BrandTheme.toMaterialTypography(): Typography = Typography(
    displayLarge   = typography.displayLarge,
    headlineMedium = typography.headlineMedium,
    titleLarge     = typography.titleLarge,
    bodyMedium     = typography.bodyMedium,
    labelSmall     = typography.labelSmall
)

fun BrandTheme.toMaterialShapes(): Shapes = Shapes(
    small  = shapes.small,
    medium = shapes.medium,
    large  = shapes.large
)

The Full Root Composable

@Composable
fun MultiApp(brand: Brand = Brand.BRAND_A) {
    val brandTheme = remember(brand) { BrandRegistry.get(brand) }

    CompositionLocalProvider(
        LocalBrandColors     provides brandTheme.colors,
        LocalBrandTypography provides brandTheme.typography,
        LocalBrandSpacing    provides brandTheme.spacing
    ) {
        MaterialTheme(
            colorScheme = brandTheme.toColorScheme(),
            typography  = brandTheme.toMaterialTypography(),
            shapes      = brandTheme.toMaterialShapes()
        ) {
            AppNavHost()
        }
    }
}

Dynamic Color (Android 12+ Monet) vs Fixed Brand Tokens

ApproachUse CaseTrade-off
Monet dynamic color (dynamicDarkColorScheme)Consumer apps that should feel personal and native (Google apps, system apps)Loses brand identity. primary changes per user wallpaper.
Fixed brand tokensEnterprise, luxury, automotive, banking — brand recognition is paramountConsistent, predictable. Cannot adapt to user's wallpaper.
HybridConsumer apps with optional brand overrideComplex: check Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 31 and user preference flag
Interview Point
If the interviewer asks about dynamic color: "We explicitly opted out of Monet for brand-critical surfaces. Dynamic color makes sense for a personal productivity app, but for a brand app the primary colour must always match brand guidelines — those are contractual."

Custom Token Access Pattern

Always provide a type-safe accessor object so callsites are ergonomic:

// Accessor object — mirrors MaterialTheme's API style
object BrandTheme {
    val colors: ColorTokens
        @Composable
        @ReadOnlyComposable
        get() = LocalBrandColors.current

    val typography: TypographyTokens
        @Composable
        @ReadOnlyComposable
        get() = LocalBrandTypography.current

    val spacing: SpacingTokens
        @Composable
        @ReadOnlyComposable
        get() = LocalBrandSpacing.current
}

// Usage inside any composable — clean and discoverable:
@Composable
fun ProductCard(name: String, price: String) {
    Card(
        colors = CardDefaults.cardColors(containerColor = BrandTheme.colors.surface),
        modifier = Modifier.padding(BrandTheme.spacing.md)
    ) {
        Text(name,  style = BrandTheme.typography.titleLarge)
        Text(price, style = BrandTheme.typography.bodyMedium)
    }
}
🆕
5. Multi-Brand in Practice

Runtime Brand Switching

Some apps allow the user to switch brand context mid-session (e.g., a dealer app that shows inventory for multiple vehicle brands). The pattern is:

  1. Hold the active Brand in a StateFlow inside a ViewModel
  2. Collect it in the root composable with collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
  3. Pass it to the root theme wrapper — Compose re-runs the provider with the new token set
// BrandViewModel.kt
@HiltViewModel
class BrandViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val brandPrefs: BrandPreferences
) : ViewModel() {

    private val _activeBrand = MutableStateFlow(brandPrefs.getSavedBrand())
    val activeBrand: StateFlow<Brand> = _activeBrand.asStateFlow()

    fun switchBrand(brand: Brand) {
        _activeBrand.value = brand
        brandPrefs.saveBrand(brand)
    }
}

// MainActivity.kt
class MainActivity : ComponentActivity() {
    private val brandVm: BrandViewModel by viewModels()

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        setContent {
            val brand by brandVm.activeBrand.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
            MultiApp(brand = brand)
        }
    }
}

Build Flavour Approach (Static Brand Selection)

When each AAB is always for a single brand (e.g. "BrandA App" on Play Store vs "BrandB App"), use product flavours:

// build.gradle.kts (app module)
android {
    flavorDimensions("brand")
    productFlavors {
        create("brand-b") {
            dimension("brand")
            applicationId = "com.example.branda"
            buildConfigField("String", "BRAND_ID", "\"BRAND_C\"")
        }
        create("brand-d") {
            dimension("brand")
            applicationId = "com.example.brandb"
            buildConfigField("String", "BRAND_ID", "\"BRAND_D\"")
        }
    }
}

// In MainActivity — brand is statically determined at build time
val brand = Brand.valueOf(BuildConfig.BRAND_ID)
setContent { BrandApp(brand = brand) }

Hilt Dependency Injection Approach

For maximum flexibility, inject the BrandTheme directly via Hilt. The brand module provides its own Hilt module:

// In :brand-b module
@Module
@InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
object BrandBThemeModule {
    @Provides
    @Singleton
    fun provideBrandTheme(): BrandTheme = brandBTheme()
}

// Root composable reads the injected theme
@HiltViewModel
class ThemeViewModel @Inject constructor(
    val brandTheme: BrandTheme
) : ViewModel()

@Composable
fun AppRoot(themeVm: ThemeViewModel = hiltViewModel()) {
    val theme = themeVm.brandTheme
    CompositionLocalProvider(
        LocalBrandColors     provides theme.colors,
        LocalBrandTypography provides theme.typography,
        LocalBrandSpacing    provides theme.spacing
    ) {
        MaterialTheme(
            colorScheme = theme.toColorScheme(),
            typography  = theme.toMaterialTypography()
        ) { AppNavHost() }
    }
}
Real-World Answer
"In a multi-brand app I worked on, the base app module had no brand knowledge whatsoever. Each brand module (e.g. :brand-premium, :brand-economy) injected its token set via Hilt at app startup. The NavHost wrapped everything in CompositionLocalProvider with that brand's tokens. We could build brand-specific AABs from the same source tree with just a Gradle flavour switch. CI produced all brand APKs from one pipeline run."
📂
6. Design System Modules

Recommended Module Graph

// Dependency direction: → means "depends on"
:design-system-tokens        // Pure Kotlin — ColorTokens, TypographyTokens, SpacingTokens
        ↑
:design-system-components    // Compose composables — PrimaryButton, AppCard, BrandLogo
        ↑
:brand-a-theme    // brandATheme() data function
:brand-b-theme      // brandBTheme() data function
:brand-b               // brandBTheme() + Hilt module
        ↑
:feature-home                // HomeScreen uses BrandTheme, imports :design-system-components
:feature-checkout
:feature-account
        ↑
:app                         // Ties everything together — depends on flavour's brand module + features

Module Contents

ModuleContentsDependenciesOwner
:design-system-tokensColorTokens, TypographyTokens, SpacingTokens, ShapeTokens data classesPure Kotlin only — no android deps, no ComposeDesign System team
:design-system-components~80 composables: PrimaryButton, AppCard, BrandLogo, TokenText, BrandScaffold…:tokens, Compose, Material3Design System team
:brand-XOne BrandTheme data factory + Hilt module (optional):tokens onlyEach brand team
:feature-*Screen composables using components:components, domain layerFeature teams
:catalogStandalone app rendering every component in every brandAll brand modules + componentsDesign System team

Why Separate :design-system-tokens from :design-system-components?

  • Compile isolation: Brand token modules have zero Compose transitive dependencies. Pure Kotlin JVM modules compile in milliseconds and can be unit-tested without Robolectric.
  • Designer handoff: Designers export Figma tokens as JSON, a script generates ColorTokens data classes, and the change lands in :tokens only — no component code is touched.
  • Testability: Token correctness is testable as pure Kotlin assertions: assertEquals(Color(0xFFC8102E), brandATheme().colors.primary).

The Catalog App (Storybook for Android)

A :catalog module is a standalone debug APK that renders every component in every brand theme side by side. Benefits:

  • QA and designers can review all brand permutations without running the full app
  • Catches token mismatches at design-review time, not production
  • Can be used for automated screenshot tests: render every component × every brand, compare to golden images
@Composable
fun CatalogScreen() {
    LazyColumn {
        Brand.entries.forEach { brand ->
            val theme = BrandRegistry.get(brand)
            item {
                Text(brand.name, style = MaterialTheme.typography.titleLarge,
                     modifier = Modifier.padding(16.dp))
            }
            item {
                CompositionLocalProvider(
                    LocalBrandColors     provides theme.colors,
                    LocalBrandTypography provides theme.typography,
                    LocalBrandSpacing    provides theme.spacing
                ) {
                    MaterialTheme(colorScheme = theme.toColorScheme()) {
                        ComponentShowcase() // renders buttons, cards, inputs
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

Component Contract

Every component in :design-system-components must satisfy this contract:

  • ❌ No hardcoded Color values in the component body
  • ❌ No direct reference to MaterialTheme.colorScheme.primary for brand-differentiated visuals
  • ✅ All visual values read from LocalBrandColors.current, LocalBrandTypography.current, LocalBrandSpacing.current
  • ✅ Component is @Preview-able with an explicit brand provider (no ambient magic needed for previews)
⚠️
7. Pitfalls & Best Practices

Common Mistakes

❌ Pitfall 1 — Hardcoded Colors in Components

Writing Color.Red or Color(0xFFFF0000) directly inside a component body silently breaks brand theming. The component will ignore whatever the brand token says for error.

// ❌ WRONG — hardcoded, brand-unaware
fun ErrorText(msg: String) = Text(msg, color = Color.Red)

// ✅ CORRECT — brand-aware
fun ErrorText(msg: String) = Text(msg, color = LocalBrandColors.current.error)
❌ Pitfall 2 — Reading MaterialTheme.colorScheme.primary When You Need Brand Primary

If you use MaterialTheme.colorScheme.primary in a custom component and the brand adds a custom brandPrimary that diverges from M3's primary (e.g. for a gradient button), the component silently shows the wrong colour. Always read from your own LocalBrandColors.current.primary in custom components.

❌ Pitfall 3 — staticCompositionLocalOf for Frequently Changing Values

Using staticCompositionLocalOf for a value that changes frequently (e.g. a scroll position, a counter, a dark/light toggle that users can flip 10 times per minute) will cause the entire subtree below the provider to recompose every time. For volatile values, use compositionLocalOf — only the composables that actually read the value recompose.

❌ Pitfall 4 — Forgetting to Test Each Brand Theme

Token mismatches only appear at runtime — a brand might accidentally set onPrimary = Color.Black when the button background is also dark, making text invisible. Without brand-specific screenshot tests, this ships to production. Write a parameterised screenshot test that covers all brands for every component.

Best Practices

✅ Always Read From Your CompositionLocal
Every component reads LocalBrandColors.current (or your BrandTheme.colors accessor). Never cache it outside the composable scope — let Compose handle recomposition correctly.
✅ Static for Brand Identity, Dynamic for Session Values
staticCompositionLocalOf for the full brand config object (changes once: at app startup or brand switch). compositionLocalOf for dark mode, locale, or any value that changes during a user session.
✅ Brand-Agnostic Screenshot Tests
Write one screenshot test per component that iterates over all brand themes: 
@RunWith(Parameterized::class)
class PrimaryButtonScreenshotTest(private val brand: Brand) {
    companion object {
        @JvmStatic @Parameterized.Parameters
        fun brands() = Brand.entries.toList()
    }
    @Test
    fun screenshotMatchesGolden() {
        val theme = BrandRegistry.get(brand)
        composeTestRule.setContent {
            CompositionLocalProvider(LocalBrandColors provides theme.colors) {
                PrimaryButton(text = "Order Now") {}
            }
        }
        composeTestRule.onRoot().captureRoboImage("golden/button_${brand.name}.png")
    }
}
✅ Keep Token Data Classes in Pure Kotlin Module
Token data classes must have zero Android framework dependencies. ColorTokens should use Compose's androidx.compose.ui.graphics.Color (which is multiplatform-ready), but no Context, no Resources, no @DrawableRes integers if you want maximum portability. Test them as fast JVM unit tests.

Quick Reference Decision Table

ScenarioUseReason
Entire brand config loaded at startupstaticCompositionLocalOfStable; full tree recompose on change is acceptable once
Dark/light mode togglecompositionLocalOfChanges per session; only reading composables should recompose
Current screen localecompositionLocalOfCan change mid-session in some apps
Font scale / accessibility settingsCompose's built-in LocalDensityAlready handled by the framework
Brand-specific A/B test flagcompositionLocalOfMay be updated by remote config mid-session
🎯
8. Interview Framework

30-Second Answer

"A design system in Compose is built on CompositionLocal. You define design tokens — colors, typography, spacing — as plain Kotlin data classes. Each brand provides its own token set. CompositionLocalProvider injects the correct tokens at the root of the composition tree. Every component reads LocalBrandColors.current — it has zero knowledge of which brand it's running under. Swapping brands means swapping one data object, not touching any component code."

2-Minute Answer (Expanded)

Build from the 30-second base and layer in:

  1. Token hierarchy: "We use three levels — global palette → semantic alias tokens → component tokens. This means a single change to primary propagates to every consumer automatically."
  2. staticCompositionLocalOf vs compositionLocalOf: "Brand config uses static because it's set once. Dark mode toggle uses dynamic because only the reading composables should recompose, not the whole tree."
  3. MaterialTheme integration: "We map our BrandTheme tokens into MaterialTheme's ColorScheme and Typography, so all Material components like Button and TextField automatically use brand colours without any extra wiring."
  4. Module structure: ":design-system-tokens is pure Kotlin — no Android deps. :design-system-components holds the composables. Each brand lives in its own :brand-X module that's just a data file + optional Hilt module."
  5. Build approach: "We use Gradle product flavours for static brand selection — each AAB is for one brand. For apps that support runtime switching, a ViewModel holds the active brand in a StateFlow and the root composable collects it with collectAsStateWithLifecycle."
  6. Testing: "We have a parameterised screenshot test for every component that iterates over all brand themes. Token mismatches show up as golden file diffs in CI, not in production."

Must-Mention Checklist

1
CompositionLocal / staticCompositionLocalOf for stable brand config — know why static is appropriate and when to use the dynamic variant instead.
2
Token hierarchy: global → alias → component — single source of truth; one change propagates everywhere.
3
MaterialTheme wrapping — map your brand tokens into ColorScheme so Material components remain compatible without special casing.
4
Module separation: :design-system-tokens, :design-system-components, :brand-X — compile isolation and fast iteration.
5
DI / build flavours for brand injection at app startup — no hardcoded brand checks in shared code, clean separation of concerns.
6
Catalog app for component isolation testing — every component × every brand, automated screenshot diffing in CI.

Signal Words That Impress

  • "Brand identity is data, not code" — shows architecture maturity
  • "staticCompositionLocalOf is appropriate because it's a stable value" — shows performance awareness
  • "We map our tokens into MaterialTheme.colorScheme so Material components stay compatible" — shows ecosystem knowledge
  • "Our :tokens module has zero Android dependencies" — shows modularisation expertise
  • "Parameterised screenshot tests over all brand themes in CI" — shows production quality thinking
❓
9. Interview Questions
Q1. What is CompositionLocal and why is it used for theming in Compose?
Easy⌄

What to say: CompositionLocal is Compose's mechanism for passing values implicitly down the composition tree without threading them through every function parameter. It's like a scoped, typed ambient value.

For theming, it's ideal because the theme affects hundreds of composables across many layers of the tree. Without it, you'd need to pass colors: ColorTokens as a parameter to every single composable — including ones that just pass it through without using it (prop drilling). CompositionLocalProvider injects the value once at the root; any descendant reads it with LocalSomething.current.

"CompositionLocal provides implicit parameters to the composition tree. For theming, this avoids prop-drilling brand colors through every composable. The theme is provided once at the root, and any component anywhere in the tree reads it via LocalBrandColors.current. It's how MaterialTheme itself works under the hood."
Q2. What is the difference between compositionLocalOf and staticCompositionLocalOf?
Easy⌄

Key difference: recomposition scope.

  • compositionLocalOf { } — When the value changes, only the composables that read the local recompose. More granular and efficient for values that change during a session.
  • staticCompositionLocalOf { } — When the value changes, the entire subtree below the provider recomposes. The word "static" means Compose doesn't track individual read points — it assumes the value is stable.

When to use each: Use static for brand config (set once at startup, stable for the app lifetime). Use dynamic for dark/light mode, locale, or anything a user can toggle mid-session.

"staticCompositionLocalOf recomposes the whole subtree on change — acceptable for brand config that's set once. compositionLocalOf only recomposes the composables that actually read the value, so it's better for volatile data like dark mode state."
Q3. How would you support two brands with different primary colours from a single Compose codebase?
Medium⌄

Step-by-step answer:

  1. Define a ColorTokens data class with a primary: Color field (and all other tokens).
  2. Create a staticCompositionLocalOf<ColorTokens> with a default value.
  3. Create one instance of ColorTokens per brand with brand-specific values.
  4. At the root of the composition, wrap in CompositionLocalProvider(LocalColorTokens provides brandColors).
  5. In every component, read LocalColorTokens.current.primary — never hardcode colours.

For build-time selection use Gradle flavours; for runtime switching use a ViewModel StateFlow feeding the root provider.

"Define a ColorTokens data class, create staticCompositionLocalOf for it, instantiate one per brand, and provide the correct instance at the composition root. Components read LocalColorTokens.current.primary. Swapping brands is swapping the data object, no component code changes."
Q4. Where in the composition tree would you place CompositionLocalProvider for a multi-brand app?
Medium⌄

As high as possible — ideally wrapping the NavHost or the outermost content composable inside setContent { }.

It must be above any component that reads the local. If you place it inside a feature screen, only that screen's composables get the brand colours; the rest of the app falls back to the default value. In a multi-module app, the provider sits in the :app module's root composable, above the navigation graph.

Typically: Activity.setContent → BrandTheme wrapper → MaterialTheme → NavHost → screens

"At the very root — in setContent in MainActivity, wrapping MaterialTheme and NavHost. This ensures every screen and every component in the navigation graph inherits the brand tokens without any composable needing to know where the tokens came from."
Q5. A component deep in the tree needs a brand-specific logo drawable. How does it get it without passing a parameter through 10 composables?
Hard⌄

This is exactly the problem CompositionLocal solves. Include the logo drawable resource ID inside your BrandColors (or a dedicated BrandAssets) data class:

data class BrandColors(..., val logo: Int /* @DrawableRes */)

// Deep component — no parameter needed
@Composable
fun BrandLogo() {
    val logoRes = LocalBrandColors.current.logo
    Image(painterResource(logoRes), contentDescription = null)
}

The token set provided at the root includes the drawable resource. The deep component reads it without a single caller needing to thread the parameter. For more complex asset sets, create a separate BrandAssets data class provided via its own LocalBrandAssets.

"Include the logo drawable ID in the BrandColors token set. LocalBrandColors is already provided at the root, so any composable at any depth reads LocalBrandColors.current.logo — zero prop drilling, zero parameter threading."
Q6. Your design team adds a new token (errorSecondary). What's the safest way to roll it out without breaking existing brand implementations?
Hard⌄

Add the field with a default value in the data class. Because it's a data class with a Kotlin default, existing brand instantiations that don't yet specify errorSecondary will compile without changes:

data class ColorTokens(
    val error: Color,
    // New token — defaults to a safe fallback derived from existing token
    val errorSecondary: Color = error.copy(alpha = 0.6f)
)

Rollout plan:

  1. Add errorSecondary with a default to ColorTokens in :design-system-tokens.
  2. Use it in the new component in :design-system-components. All existing brands compile — they get the default.
  3. Each brand team progressively overrides the default with their correct brand value in their own :brand-X module.
  4. When all brands have explicitly set it, the default can optionally be removed (breaking change — communicate in advance).
"Add the token with a sensible default value derived from existing tokens — e.g., error.copy(alpha=0.6f). All existing brand implementations compile immediately. Each brand team can then explicitly set the correct value in their own module at their own pace, without a big-bang migration."
Q7. How does MaterialTheme relate to your custom brand token system? Should they coexist or replace each other?
Hard⌄

They should coexist, with your brand tokens feeding into MaterialTheme.

MaterialTheme provides LocalColorScheme, LocalTypography, LocalShapes — the same CompositionLocal mechanism. Material components (Button, Card, TextField, TopAppBar) read from MaterialTheme.colorScheme. If you completely bypass MaterialTheme, every Material component needs manual colour overrides — that's hundreds of lines of boilerplate.

The correct architecture:

  • Your custom LocalBrandColors is the source of truth for brand tokens.
  • You map brand tokens → ColorScheme via an extension function and pass them to MaterialTheme.
  • Material components automatically pick up brand colours via MaterialTheme.colorScheme.
  • Custom components read from LocalBrandColors.current directly, so they can use brand-specific tokens that M3 has no equivalent for (e.g. logo, errorSecondary).
"They coexist. Our brand tokens are the source of truth — they feed into MaterialTheme via a toColorScheme() mapping. Material components use MaterialTheme automatically. Our custom components read from LocalBrandColors.current directly for brand-specific tokens that M3 doesn't have a concept for."
Q8. How would you test that each brand theme renders correctly without writing 14 copies of every UI test?
Hard⌄

Parameterised screenshot tests using Roborazzi (or Paparazzi for pure JVM):

@RunWith(ParameterizedRobolectricTestRunner::class)
class PrimaryButtonTest(private val brand: Brand) {

    @get:Rule val composeRule = createComposeRule()

    companion object {
        @JvmStatic
        @ParameterizedRobolectricTestRunner.Parameters(name = "{0}")
        fun brands() = Brand.entries.toList()
    }

    @Test
    fun primaryButton_matchesGolden() {
        val theme = BrandRegistry.get(brand)
        composeRule.setContent {
            CompositionLocalProvider(LocalBrandColors provides theme.colors) {
                MaterialTheme(colorScheme = theme.toColorScheme()) {
                    PrimaryButton("Order Now") {}
                }
            }
        }
        composeRule.onRoot().captureRoboImage("golden/PrimaryButton_${brand.name}.png")
    }
}

One test class covers all 14 brands via the @Parameters list. Golden images are stored in the repo. Any token mismatch surfaces as a visual diff in CI. New brands automatically get coverage by being added to the Brand enum — no new test code needed.

"Parameterised screenshot tests with Roborazzi. One test class iterates over all Brand enum values, wraps each component in the correct CompositionLocalProvider, and compares against golden images. New brands are covered automatically by being added to the Brand enum — zero additional test code."
